chapters.volume: Volume Two: Three Years of Bowing
chapters.content:
The seminar was in the new law building, all glass and polished floors, and Si-Yuan went to it in sunglasses and a cap pulled low, because she was playing a detective’s assistant next year and wanted to watch someone who did the real thing.

Si-Jie had found the talk. Si-Jie had also, within two minutes of sitting down, found a girl to talk to: a quiet one in the next seat with a notebook and the look of someone who’d come on purpose.

“Wonderful. I’m Si-Jie. Psychology, final year. Are you psychology?”

The girl said her name was Eliana and that she wasn’t. Si-Jie tried criminology, law and secret detective, and when Si-Yuan and Si-Wei came down the row behind her she waved a hand at them.

“These are my sisters. Si-Wei does business, and she’s going to run the world and be rude to it. Si-Yuan’s an actress. She’s playing a detective next year and wants to know how to look clever.”

“I’m here to look at how he stands,” said Si-Yuan from under the cap, and pointed at the empty lectern.

Si-Wei looked at Eliana over her coffee. “Don’t let Si-Jie talk you into anything. She’ll have you at lunch by twelve.”

Arthur Kao began at ten, without notes. He wasn’t tall. He wore a dark suit and a plain watch, and he didn’t pace or wave his hands, and when a student asked a question he waited until she’d completely finished before he answered. Si-Yuan opened her notebook. Stillness. Doesn’t waste a movement. Later: He listens with his whole face.

“People assume deception is easy to see. They look for nerves. Eyes that won’t settle. Hands. Those tell you someone’s uncomfortable. They don’t tell you why. Look for change. What a person does differently when the subject moves,” he said.

Si-Jie put her hand up halfway through the morning and gave an answer that was confident and possibly a little too confident, and Arthur listened, and said, “That’s one interpretation. What evidence would support it?”

“You’re asking me to justify my answer.”

“I’m asking you to tell what you know from what you’ve assumed.”

A few people laughed. Si-Jie’s eyes narrowed. Si-Yuan looked down at her notebook to hide her face, because she knew that expression. It was the one Si-Jie wore when she’d decided someone was going to be a problem.

They had lunch in the canteen with Eliana, who’d been at a table with them by half past twelve without quite agreeing to it, and in the afternoon Arthur put everyone in groups with invented case files. When the session broke up Si-Jie went straight to the front, and Si-Yuan, who’d meant to stay at the back, found herself pulled along by the sleeve.

“She’s been studying how you stand,” Si-Jie told him.

Si-Yuan turned on her. “Si-Jie.”

“You have.”

Arthur’s brow moved a fraction. “And what have you learned?”

Si-Yuan considered him from under the cap. “That you don’t move unless you have a reason.”

“That’s a fair observation.” It got a real smile out of him, there and gone, and then he turned to Si-Jie and asked whether she was coming to the next one.

“Is that an invitation?”

“It’s open to registered participants.”

“That’s a very academic way of saying yes.”

“Then register,” said Arthur Kao.

At five Si-Jie made Eliana swap numbers, and Si-Wei put her in a group chat called YEN GIRLS AND ONE HOSTAGE, and Si-Yuan sent a photograph into it within the minute of Si-Jie looking outraged. They were standing in the foyer laughing about it when a young man came over and asked Eliana out in front of half the building, and before she could answer someone took her hand and said, “She’s with me,” and the young man went away. Si-Jie looked at the newcomer, and at their hands, and at Eliana, with dawning joy.

“Who is this?”

“Yu Chen,” said Eliana, going red.

“Wang Yu Chen,” he said, and shook Si-Jie’s hand with his free one, and didn’t let go of Eliana’s.

On the steps outside, Si-Wei leaned in. “You’ve got a problem.”

“What problem?” said Si-Jie.

“You like the professor.”

“I do not.”

Si-Yuan walked between them with the cap pulled down again, and for a little while the three of them were only sisters going down a hill, arguing about nothing, with nobody asking anything of her.

✦ ✦ ✦

The call came the next afternoon, while she was in the make-up chair.

“Are you sitting down?” said Qiao-jie.

Si-Yuan looked at herself in the mirror. Someone was painting out the shadow under her eye. “Should I be?”

“A French production company has asked if you’ll audition for a film. It’s a co-production. The director is Étienne Moreau.”

The make-up artist’s brush stopped. Si-Yuan didn’t move at all, and the artist leaned in and said her name.

She’d been twelve, cross-legged on the living-room floor, her mother asleep on the sofa and her sisters arguing with the television, when she’d watched one of his films with subtitles. Nothing much happened in it. A woman stood in a railway station with a paper cup of coffee and watched trains come and go, and Si-Yuan had cried, and when the credits came up she’d written his name in a notebook in her uneven handwriting, and under it: I want to make something that feels like this one day. The notebook had gone with her through acting classes and auditions and her first part with lines.

“Is it real?”

“I’ve checked the company. It’s real.”

The part was a young woman living in Paris, caught between the life she’d made there and the family she’d left. It would shoot mostly in French and English, with a few scenes in the northern language. There’d be a final round in Paris. If they chose her, filming would start in January, for about three months.

She rang Pengcheng that evening from the hotel by the location. He answered on the fourth ring and said he was reviewing a document.

“Can I tell you something? I’ve been asked to audition for a film. The French director. The one I’ve told you about.”

There was a pause. “Moreau.”

“You remember!”

“You’ve mentioned him.”

“I’ve mentioned him a lot.”

“Yes. Where would it shoot?” She could hear him not quite laughing at her.

“Paris. Three months, maybe more.”

He was quiet, but she knew he was listening. “That’s encouraging.”

“That’s all?”

“I’m pleased for you, Si-Yuan.”

“You sound like someone telling me the office printer’s been fixed.”

He did laugh then. “Congratulations. Properly. Read the terms before you get excited.”

“You’re a lawyer even when I’m telling you good news.”

“It’s a hazard of the work. I hope you get it,” he said, and the second part came out softer.

She lay back on the bed with the phone against her ear, and for that moment it was enough.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Monday his mother asked them to dinner. Si-Yuan went in a navy dress with long sleeves and the diamond earrings he’d given her for her twentieth birthday, and bowed to his father, and to Madam Yang, and sat beside Pengcheng, and listened to a discussion of a recent appeal. She’d become good at listening.

After the second course his mother put her chopsticks down. “I hear you’ve had an overseas offer.”

Si-Yuan’s fingers found the edge of her napkin. “An audition, Madam. A French film.”

“In Paris. For how long?”

“If they choose me, from January, for about three months.”

“And you’d be living there.”

“Yes. The production would arrange somewhere.”

“Alone?”

“My agency would—”

His mother lifted her cup. “That isn’t what I asked. You’d be living there without your husband.”

The word sat on the table between them. They were engaged, and the engagement had never been announced. Pengcheng answered before she could. “We’re not married yet, Mother.”

Madam Yang turned back to Si-Yuan. “I’m aware of that. Then this is the time to think about what sort of life you’re building. I don’t think it’s suitable. Your work already means travel and long hours with strangers and a public life. Months abroad would make everything more complicated.”

“It’s a fixed schedule. It’s a director I’ve wanted to work with for years.”

“That may matter to you.”

“It does.”

His mother set the cup down. “But personal ambition can’t always come first. No actress of mine will be living abroad.”

Si-Yuan looked at her. It was a strange sentence. Not I’d rather you didn’t, not even I have concerns. No actress of mine. As though she’d already been filed under a heading, and the heading came with rules.

Pengcheng put his chopsticks down. “She’s been offered a professional opportunity. There’s no decision to discuss.”

“I’m discussing what’s appropriate.”

“She can decide what’s appropriate for her career.”

His mother’s mouth moved. “Can she?”

Si-Yuan’s shoulders went tight. She knew what she was supposed to do. She’d spent nearly two years learning it. But something in her was tired tonight. “I wouldn’t decide anything without talking to Pengcheng,” she said carefully.

“Good,” said his mother, and that was the end of it. Not because anything had been settled, but because there was nothing more Si-Yuan could say that wouldn’t be taken as an argument.

In the car he drove a while in silence. “Don’t take what she said too seriously.”

“Which part?”

“All of it.”

“That’s a lot to ignore.”

He took her hand across the console. “Read the contract. Talk to your agency. If the terms are good, we’ll talk properly.”

“Would you be all right with it? Me going?”

He didn’t answer straight away. “Three months isn’t long.”

“That isn’t what I asked.”

His thumb moved once over her knuckles. “I don’t see why it would be a problem.”

It came so easily that she almost believed the dinner had been a passing unpleasantness. She let it rest.

✦ ✦ ✦

The audition was on Wednesday, on a video call from a conference room at the agency, in a plain white blouse against a plain wall. They asked her to play the scene twice, the second time with a different note, and the second time she didn’t cry. She sat still. Qiao-jie squeezed her shoulder afterwards and said, “That was good,” and wouldn’t take it back when Si-Yuan asked if she was sure.

On Friday the production wrote. They didn’t want her for a supporting part. They wanted her as the lead.

She read it slowly and covered her mouth with her hand. She rang Qiao-jie, who’d already seen it, and laughed and pressed the heel of her hand into one eye, and then she rang Pengcheng, who was in a meeting, and sent a message instead.

Si-Yuan: I got it. The lead.

Pengcheng (Boyfriend, Apparently): Congratulations. That’s wonderful news.

Si-Yuan: I’m going to Paris.

The dots appeared, and stopped, and came back.

Pengcheng (Boyfriend, Apparently): Let’s talk about it when I’m home.

It wasn’t a no. It wasn’t anything else, either.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Sunday morning she was on the floor of his flat with the script spread round her when his mother rang. He took it in the study with the door not quite shut, and his mother’s voice carried.

“She should decline it.”

“It’s an important film, Mother. She’s the lead.”

“She’s an actress. There’ll be other films. She can’t live abroad for months. People will talk.”

“People talk regardless.”

“That isn’t a reason to give them more. I’ve told you my position.”

There was a long silence on his side, and then he said, “I’ll speak to her,” and came out and sat on the sofa, and told her his mother didn’t think the arrangement was suitable.

“I see.”

“Have you thought about the practical side? Send me the full contract when it comes. I’ll look at the terms.”

She nodded and wrote something in the margin.

“Are you still considering it?” he asked.

It was an ordinary question in an ordinary voice, and it made her feel strangely alone. “Would you like me to?”

He frowned. “I want you to make the right decision.”

She looked down at the script for a long time. Then she smiled, the small polite smile she’d learned at his mother’s table. “I’ll think about it.”

“Good,” he said, and reached out and tucked her hair behind her ear, and she leaned into his hand, because she still loved him. That was the difficult part.

On Monday evening she took him the revised offer. It was good. The production had agreed to most of what Qiao-jie had asked for.

“Any concerns?” he said.

“Not about the contract. Your mother doesn’t want me to go.”

“She doesn’t. I’ve told you I don’t think three months is a problem.”

“Then why haven’t we decided?”

“Because I don’t want you to rush into something without thinking it through.”

“I’ve thought it through. The work, the schedule, the travel, the language. I’ve wanted to work with him since I was twelve. I don’t think you understand how much this means.”

“Then explain it to me.”

She almost laughed. She’d told him the name, the films, the notebook. She’d rung him when the call came and again when the offer came. She’d been excited in front of him, and careful in front of him, and she’d waited the whole week for him to say he wanted her to go, and he still wanted her to explain why it mattered.

“Never mind.”

“Don’t do that. Don’t say something’s wrong and then refuse to talk about it.”

She looked at the folder in her hands. “I’ve been talking about it for a week. I’ll turn it down.”

His brows drew together. “Because of my mother?”

For once it was the right question. She could have said yes. She could have said she was doing it because she couldn’t face one more dinner where her future was a family inconvenience, because she was tired of standing between his mother’s rules and his silence. “I don’t want to create difficulties.”

“You wouldn’t be.”

“It’s fine.”

She wanted him to say it first. Go. I’ll deal with my mother. You don’t have to give this up for me. The words stayed behind her teeth. He took her hand and kissed her knuckles, and asked if she was disappointed, and she said a little, and he said they’d find another opportunity. He believed that. He believed time was generous. She knew some things don’t come twice.

The next morning Qiao-jie rang the production with Si-Yuan beside her, and explained that she couldn’t accept for personal reasons, and the casting director was gracious about it. Afterwards Qiao-jie asked if she wanted them told she might reconsider if the dates moved.

“No.”

At the door Si-Yuan stopped. “Please don’t tell anyone I turned it down because of family. I don’t want people to think I couldn’t manage it.”

She wanted the loss to stay hers.

That night the production sent her a few stills anyway, with a note thanking her for considering it. The first one was a woman on a railway platform with a paper cup of coffee and a train blurred behind her. She knew it at once. She saved it, and opened the old notebook to the first page, to the name she’d written at twelve, and wrote the date under it.

October 2024. I was offered the film.

The next sentence wouldn’t come for a long time. Then she wrote I turned it down, and closed the book, and got into bed beside him. He reached for her without waking and put his hand at her waist.

She knew that if she told him the truth, that she’d never wanted another opportunity and had only wanted this one, he’d listen. He’d probably understand. But understanding after the decision was made was becoming a familiar kind of comfort. He never asked her why.

chapters.title: Her Sisters Notice
chapters.desc: Si-Jie notices she’s stopped talking. Si-Wei notices she’s stopped eating. Triplets on the floor of her flat. He brings soup and doesn’t stay.
chapters.volume: Volume Two: Three Years of Bowing
chapters.content:
Si-Jie noticed first, and what she noticed was what Si-Yuan had stopped saying.

Si-Yuan was the one who filled a silence without noticing she’d done it. She talked about scripts while she brushed her teeth and complained about directors while she looked for her keys, and she sent her sisters photographs at unreasonable hours of things that reminded her of them: a crooked cloud, a dog in a raincoat, a dessert she swore looked exactly like Si-Wei’s personality. Lately her messages had shrunk. Finished filming. Going home. I’m fine. Si-Jie had never trusted anyone who said they were fine without being asked.

So on a Saturday afternoon in November she turned up at Si-Yuan’s flat with a paper bag of pastries and no warning at all.

Si-Yuan opened the door in an oversized T-shirt and loose trousers, with her hair tied up anyhow and a crease on her cheek from the pillow. “You’re here.”

“That’s a very warm welcome. Clearly you weren’t expecting me, or you’d have put trousers on.”

“I’m wearing trousers.”

“Those are pyjamas. Move. I’m starving,” said Si-Jie, and walked past her into the kitchen.

“You sent me a photograph of your lunch.”

“That was five hours ago. I’ve changed.”

Si-Yuan smiled. It was the oldest conversation they had, older than the bedroom the three of them had shared as girls and fought in over hair clips. But the smile went away too quickly, and Si-Jie saw it go. She put the pastries on the counter and looked at the container on the side.

“Is that from yesterday?”

“Maybe.”

“Si-Yuan.”

“I’ll eat it later.”

Si-Jie had known her for twenty years, which was all of them, and she knew the difference between someone who wasn’t hungry and someone who’d stopped trying to be. If Si-Yuan were only busy she’d complain about it. If she were tired she’d ask for a nap. If a director had annoyed her she’d do his face until both her sisters were crying with laughter. This quiet had no shape. It was as though she’d taken something out of herself and put it somewhere nobody could reach.

“Where’s Si-Wei?” Si-Yuan asked.

“On her way. I told her. You’re welcome.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Si-Wei came forty minutes later, without food. She brought a book Si-Yuan had left at her flat and a packet of throat lozenges.

“Why have you got those?”

“You sounded hoarse yesterday.”

“I was filming.”

“I know. Are you drinking enough water?”

Si-Yuan looked from one to the other. “Are you both here to inspect me?”

“Yes,” said Si-Jie from the floor.

They didn’t sit on the sofa. They never did, the three of them. Si-Jie pulled a cushion down, Si-Wei sat against the coffee table, Si-Yuan fetched a blanket, and inside ten minutes the living room was bare feet and phones and snacks and half-drunk cups. Si-Jie produced the egg tarts with a flourish.

“These aren’t from the bakery by your university,” said Si-Yuan.

“How would you know?”

“Their pastry’s thinner.”

Si-Wei took one. “She’s right.”

“Why do I buy either of you anything?”

“Because you love us,” said Si-Wei.

“It’s a weakness,” said Si-Jie, and Si-Yuan laughed properly, and Si-Jie looked at her and thought: still in there.

For a while they talked about nothing. Si-Jie complained about her coursework and a presentation she was dreading, and mentioned Arthur, in a voice that was trying hard to be casual.

“He’s very particular,” she said, breaking a tart in half.

Si-Wei looked up. “Who?”

“Don’t.”

“Arthur? What’s he particular about?” said Si-Yuan.

“Everything.”

“That doesn’t sound like a complaint,” said Si-Wei.

“It is when he does it.”

“Does he correct you?”

“Only when I’m wrong.”

“Which is often,” said Si-Wei, and got a tissue thrown at her.

Si-Yuan pulled her knees up. “Have you been seeing him?”

Si-Jie studied the pastry in her hand. “About five weeks.”

“Five weeks? And you’re telling us now?”

“I didn’t say we were dating.”

Si-Wei raised an eyebrow. “Fine. We’re seeing each other,” said Si-Jie.

“You’re blushing.”

“It’s warm in here.”

Si-Wei glanced at the thermostat. “It’s twenty-one degrees.”

Si-Yuan reached across the blanket and squeezed Si-Jie’s knee. “Are you happy?”

It caught her off guard. Her face went soft before she could stop it. “Yes. He makes me think before I speak.”

“That’s a miracle,” said Si-Wei.

Si-Jie ignored her. “And he listens. Properly. Even when I say something stupid. He knows everything.”

She said it lightly. Si-Yuan looked at her a moment longer than she needed to, and wondered what it would feel like to be loved by someone who knew everything about you and still chose to stand next to you. Then she reached for another tart and said, “Tell us more,” and Si-Jie did, for twenty minutes.

✦ ✦ ✦

Si-Wei was harder. She always had been. Where Si-Jie talked before she thought, Si-Wei thought so much that people took her silence for not caring. She did care. She only liked to keep a thing to herself until she understood it.

Her phone buzzed twice that evening, and she turned it over before either of them could see. It buzzed again a few minutes later, and she sighed at it.

“Someone’s persistent,” said Si-Jie.

“Someone’s got work.”

“At this hour?”

“Some people have proper jobs.” Si-Wei looked pointedly at Si-Yuan, who threw a cushion, which Si-Wei caught. The phone lit up again on the floor beside her, face up this time, for one second too long.

Geum Sung Jae (Ignore).

Si-Wei snatched it up. Si-Jie had already read it.

“Who’s Geum Sung Jae, and why are you ignoring him?”

“No one.”

“No one?” said Si-Yuan.

“Someone. A friend.”

“A friend who texts you at nine at night. Is he handsome?”

“That’s irrelevant.”

“That’s a yes. Should we know him?” said Si-Jie, delighted.

“No.”

Si-Yuan was smiling, but she didn’t push, and after a moment Si-Jie didn’t either. Si-Wei would tell them when she was ready. Until then Sung Jae, whoever he was, belonged to her.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was close to midnight when it turned. Si-Jie was on her front with her chin on a cushion, Si-Wei was scrolling, and Si-Yuan was cross-legged by the coffee table shredding the corner of a paper napkin. She’d hardly eaten. Si-Jie watched her for a while.

“What’s going on?”

“Nothing.”

“Don’t.”

Si-Wei put her phone down. The room went still.

“You’ve been quiet for weeks,” said Si-Jie.

“I’m tired.”

“You’ve stopped eating properly,” said Si-Wei.

“How would you know?”

“Because I know you.”

Si-Yuan rubbed her thumb along the side of her first finger. Their mother used to call it her thinking habit: whenever she was deciding whether to tell the truth she’d rub her fingers together, smoothing out something nobody else could see.

“Did something happen at work? Did someone say something? Is it the film?” said Si-Jie, gently. Si-Yuan’s hand stopped.

Si-Wei’s eyes sharpened. “What film?”

“The Paris one. Did they offer it to you?” said Si-Jie.

A nod.

Si-Yuan nodded at every question. “The director you like? And you got the part?”

“The lead.”

Si-Jie sat up, and her voice was full of something between joy and disbelief. “Si-Yuan. Why didn’t you tell us?”

“I was going to.”

Si-Wei hadn’t moved. “Did you accept?”

The smile went. “No. I turned it down.”

“Why?”

She looked at the floor. “Pengcheng’s mother doesn’t want me to go. She doesn’t think it’s suitable.”

Si-Jie’s face changed first, into something closer and more personal than anger. “Suitable.”

“Did Pengcheng say he didn’t want you to go?” asked Si-Wei.

“No.”

“Then why did you turn it down?”

She said it gently, which made it harder. “I didn’t want to make things difficult.”

Si-Jie moved over and took her hand. “Did you want to go?”

Si-Yuan’s eyes filled, and she pressed her lips together to keep them still. “Very much. I was tired. I’ve spent so long trying to make things easier. I thought if I was patient, if I was polite, if I understood how their family worked, one day it would be enough. I know it’s not a big thing. It’s only a film. There’ll be other directors.” Her voice broke halfway, and she looked away to finish it.

“Stop. Don’t make it smaller because you lost it,” said Si-Jie, firmly, holding her hand in both of hers.

That landed harder than Si-Yuan had expected. Her face crumpled, and she bent her head too late to hide it, and Si-Wei moved over without a word and put a hand on the back of her head, and for a while the three of them sat tangled up on the floor. Nobody asked her to explain herself more carefully. Nobody reminded her that families meant compromise, or told her there’d be another chance. They let her cry.

“I really wanted to go. I’ve wanted something like that since I was twelve,” she said at last, small.

“I know,” said Si-Jie, with her cheek against her hair.

Si-Wei’s fingers moved through her hair. “You don’t have to defend why it mattered.”

That was when she cried properly, the way you cry after holding something in too long.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was past one when she leaned back against the sofa. Si-Jie had gone to make tea. Si-Wei stayed beside her.

“Does he know?”

Si-Yuan looked at the ceiling. “He knows everything. About the offer, the director, the dates, the contract. He knows I turned it down.”

“Does he know you didn’t want to?”

No answer.

“Did you tell him how much you wanted it?”

“Yes.”

Si-Wei’s voice was gentle. “Then why are you saying he knows everything as if that settles it? Knowing something happened isn’t the same as understanding what it cost you.”

“He said we’d find another opportunity.”

“And what did you say?”

“Nothing. I didn’t want to argue.”

Si-Wei nodded slowly. She understood that answer better than she wanted to. “You’re allowed to argue for yourself. Does he know you’re unhappy?”

Si-Yuan looked at her hands. “I don’t know.”

Something went across Si-Wei’s face that was more sadness than anger at him. She knew her sister had been waiting for him to notice, and she knew how long a person can wait when they love the one they’re waiting for.

Si-Jie came back with three cups and sat down between them and took a long breath. “Right. We’re not solving this tonight. We’re also not letting you skip meals.”

“You sound like Mum.”

“Good. Mum’s always right about food.”

Si-Wei put a cup in Si-Yuan’s hands. “Drink.”

“You don’t have to do all this.”

Si-Jie stared at her. “You’re our sister.”

“Unfortunately we’re attached,” said Si-Wei, and sipped her tea, and Si-Yuan laughed, wet and quiet and real.

They stayed on the floor until nearly three. Si-Jie told them about a dinner the week before, when Arthur had listened to her argue about a research paper and then calmly pointed out that she’d misread the central idea.

“Did you get angry?”

Si-Jie looked into her cup. “Obviously. He bought me a coffee. It didn’t work. I told him he was annoying, and he said he knew. He makes me feel like I can say things.”

She didn’t notice what she’d said; she was already reaching for the last tart. But Si-Yuan kept the sentence, and lay awake later wondering when she’d stopped feeling like that.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Monday Pengcheng came to her flat at a quarter to nine at night with a thermal box in one hand and a paper bag in the other.

“Have you eaten?”

“Not yet.”

He went into her kitchen and set things out on the counter. “I thought not. Soup, rice, some greens.”

“You cooked?”

“Our housekeeper did. I asked her this afternoon.”

She leaned on the counter and watched him check the soup with the back of his hand. “How did you know?”

“You’ve been leaving dinner. You told me last week you weren’t hungry.”

He’d noticed. Something in her answered that before she could stop it. He put a bowl in front of her, and she took the first spoonful: ginger, chicken, a little pepper, the soup his family made when someone was worn out. He stood across the counter and watched her eat, and asked if it was all right, and she said it was.

Then he looked at his phone. “I have to go. I’ve a client call shortly. I need to be back at chambers.”

Her spoon stopped halfway. “Now?”

He came round and brushed his thumb across her cheek. “Keep the rest for tomorrow. Don’t skip breakfast. You’re tired.”

“Filming.”

He kissed her temple and picked up his coat, and at the door she said his name, and he turned.

She wanted to ask him to stay. She didn’t need him to make her dinner. She wanted him to take his coat off and loosen his tie and complain about his client, and let her tell him about the scene she couldn’t crack. She wanted to ask whether he remembered the film. Whether he remembered the director’s name. Whether he knew she still had the email. Whether he understood that a bowl of soup wasn’t what she’d been waiting for. But she could see in his face that he was already in the call, so she told him to drive carefully.

“I’ll ring you later,” he said, and went, and the door closed. The soup was still warm. She finished the bowl.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Thursday Si-Jie rang at lunchtime and said they were coming over again.

“Don’t you two have lives?”

“Several. You’re one of them. Arthur might ring later.”

“Then go and see him.”

“I didn’t say I was going.”

“Si-Jie? I’m happy for you.”

There was a silence on the line, and then Si-Jie’s voice went soft. “Thank you.”

That evening they were on the floor again, with noodles from Si-Jie and fruit and pastries from Si-Wei and the drinks Si-Yuan had bought on the way home. Si-Jie’s phone lit up and she tried to look unbothered, and Si-Wei told her to answer it, and she did, and her voice changed the moment she said hello. It went soft and attentive. Si-Yuan and Si-Wei looked at each other.

Si-Jie told him she was with her sisters, both of them, and then held out the phone. “He wants to say hello.”

Si-Yuan took it. “Hello?”

Arthur’s voice was calm and clear. “Si-Yuan. How’s the detective?”

“Finished, actually. The seminar helped.”

“Good. Look after your sister.”

She looked at Si-Jie, who was pretending not to listen. “I think she looks after herself.”

“She does,” said Arthur, and the way he said it made her smile.

“Goodnight, Professor.”

She handed the phone back, and Si-Jie put it to her ear and demanded to know why he’d talked to her sister for so long, and Si-Wei said she was jealous, and Si-Jie said she wasn’t, and they were all three laughing by the time she hung up.

Later, with Si-Jie in the bathroom and Si-Wei putting leftovers away, Si-Yuan looked at the two of them and thought they were happy. Imperfectly, both of them. Si-Jie was learning to let someone close. Si-Wei had a name on her phone she pretended not to care about. And Si-Yuan was learning that you could be surrounded by people who loved you and still be lonely in the one place you’d expected to be understood.

She looked at the empty bowls on the coffee table. For the first time in weeks she’d finished her dinner without anyone reminding her. Si-Wei noticed, and didn’t say so, and carried the bowls into the kitchen. When Si-Jie came back she lay down with her head on Si-Yuan’s shoulder.

“Stay like this a bit.”

“You’re heavy.”

“You’re comfortable,” said Si-Jie, and Si-Wei sat down on the other side, and the three of them stayed close enough on the floor that none of them had to ask whether the others were still there.

chapters.title: The Banquet
chapters.desc: His mother’s sixtieth birthday banquet, three hundred guests. At the head table his mother says, loud enough, “Some girls marry up by the hour.” He looks at his plate. She stands, bows, and leaves. The cruellest scene in the book: written slow.
chapters.epigraph: “Some girls marry up by the hour.”
chapters.volume: Volume Two: Three Years of Bowing
chapters.content:
The invitation was ivory card with the family crest pressed in gold. The Sixtieth Birthday of Madam Yang. Three hundred guests in the private ballroom of the best hotel in the city, a string quartet, flowers flown in from abroad, three generations of the legal profession and anyone who remembered when Pengcheng’s grandfather had still sat on the bench. It was less a birthday than a reminder of who mattered to the Yangs, and that the Yangs still mattered.

He’d put it on her dining table beside her script three weeks before. “My mother’s birthday is on the seventh.”

“Do you want me to come?”

He’d looked surprised that she’d asked. “Of course.”

So she’d asked Si-Jie to help her choose a dress, and Si-Jie had sent photographs of three, and then a series of increasingly short messages.

Si-Jie (Questions): The navy one.

Si-Yuan: The champagne one’s prettier.

Si-Jie (Questions): The navy one. You look like yourself in it. Don’t spend another two years dressing for a woman who’s never going to approve of you.

Si-Yuan had sent back a photograph of the navy dress, and Si-Jie had answered You’re welcome before she’d said thank you. She didn’t tell Si-Jie she’d thought about leaving off the earrings he’d given her. In the end she wore them. They were beautiful, and she still loved him.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came for her on Saturday the seventh of December in black, his hair combed back and his face set in the composure he took into important meetings. She was at the mirror when he came in, and he stopped in the doorway.

The navy fell straight from her shoulders, with fitted sleeves and a plain neck, and her hair was swept into a low knot with a few strands left loose, and the diamonds caught the light when she turned her head. She didn’t look older than she was, or like someone pretending to more polish than she felt. She looked like herself.

He tucked one of the loose strands behind her ear and touched the earring with one finger. “Beautiful. You’re wearing them.”

“Do you not like them?”

“I like seeing you in them,” he said, and put his hand at her waist, and they went.

✦ ✦ ✦

The ballroom was already full. Round tables stood under chandeliers, waiters moved between them with trays, and the stage at the far end held an enormous photograph of his mother among pale flowers and gold lettering. The head table stood directly in front of it.

People reached for him the moment they were through the door. Young Master Yang. Counsel Yang, congratulations on the appointment. He answered each of them with exactly the right amount of courtesy, and Si-Yuan smiled and bowed whenever someone was introduced. A few looked at her a second longer than they needed to and then turned back to him. She was used to that.

His mother was already seated, in deep burgundy with a diamond necklace that had been her own mother’s. She smiled when she saw her son.

“Happy birthday, Mother,” he said, and bent to kiss her cheek.

Si-Yuan bowed and held out her gift. “Happy birthday, Madam Yang.”

His mother glanced at the box and said thank you, and her eyes went down the navy dress and came back up. “Navy. Quite understated.”

“Thank you, Madam.”

Pengcheng drew out the chair beside his mother for her and took the one on her other side.

The first hour went by without anything happening. There were speeches, and a short film of his mother’s life, and toasts. His father called her intelligent, disciplined and formidable, and the room laughed, and Si-Yuan applauded with everyone else. She watched the woman beside her take in the admiration of three hundred people and wondered, not for the first time, what it would be like to be seen by her without having to earn it.

✦ ✦ ✦

By the third course the room had relaxed into the roar of three hundred people talking over one another. A senior barrister raised his glass: sixty years old and still the most formidable woman in any courtroom. Everyone laughed. Pengcheng lifted his glass, and Si-Yuan lifted hers.

A woman across the table leaned towards her. “I’ve seen your dramas, Miss Yen. Are you working on anything new?”

“A new series. We’re filming now.”

“Her schedule is always very full,” said his mother.

Si-Yuan’s fingers tightened on her chopsticks. She knew that tone, the small lift at the end of a sentence, the words chosen to sound harmless until you thought about what they were for. She’d heard it at the New Year table and at every gathering where his mother talked about women who knew their place. She’d learned to recognise it, and she’d learned not to answer.

“The production’s going well, Mother,” Pengcheng said mildly.

“I was only saying that she’s busy.”

“She’s working.”

His mother laid her chopsticks on the rest beside her bowl and smiled, and said it in the light, carrying voice of a woman making an amusing observation over dinner. “Yes. Working. Some girls marry up by the hour.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t raise her voice. She didn’t need to. The people nearest the head table heard it. The woman across from them stopped smiling. The barrister lowered his glass. At the next table someone turned round. Si-Yuan went completely still.

The sentence was perfectly clear, and for a moment that was the trouble. Some girls. Marry up. By the hour. The words came apart in her head and settled, each of them, somewhere she’d never be able to reach in and take it out.

His mother was smiling. Only just. Enough to make it plain that the remark had been meant, and that she expected the people round her to understand it. Si-Yuan turned her head and looked at Pengcheng.

He’d heard. She knew he’d heard because his hand had stopped. His chopsticks were still in it. His eyes were on his plate.

He could have put the chopsticks down. He could have said his mother’s name, or told her that the woman beside him was his fiancée, who’d spent the best part of two years trying to earn a chair at this table, and that he wouldn’t have her spoken about as though she were something bought. He could have done anything.

He looked at his plate. There was a smear of sauce near the rim, and he noticed it, and the folded napkin, and the chandelier upside down in his water glass. His jaw tightened. He was weighing it: his mother’s birthday, three hundred guests, half the bar, his father’s clients, what it would cost to turn the head table into a scene. He was calculating, and while he calculated the woman beside him sat perfectly still and waited.

One second. Two. Three.

She looked at the line of his jaw, the crease that came between his brows when he concentrated. The man who’d sat up with her until three in the morning before an audition. The man who’d written thirteen pages to save her contract. The man who’d told her sisters, years ago, that he’d never ask her to stop acting, even if his family disagreed. He was sitting so close that their sleeves touched, and he was looking at his plate.

Something moved inside her, slowly and without a sound, like a thread being drawn through cloth until the last stitch came free.

She’d spent nearly two years learning to bear his mother’s disapproval. The cold greetings, the congratulations that never came, being talked about in front of her like furniture. She’d borne the film. She’d even borne the thought that if she tried hard enough there’d be a day she could sit at this table without having to justify being alive. Disapproval she could bear. This was humiliation, in front of three hundred people, on the birthday of the woman she’d spent two years trying to respect.

She laid her chopsticks down, carefully. The sound was almost nothing. Pengcheng heard it and turned his head a fraction.

“Si-Yuan?”

She put her napkin beside her plate and stood, and her chair went back with a clear sound on the polished floor, and people looked up all round them, and he turned properly in his seat.

For a second he saw her face. Later, remembering it, that was what frightened him. She wasn’t glaring at him, and she wasn’t crying. Her eyes were bright and dry and her face was composed in a way he’d never seen, and she looked at him like someone who’d finally understood something. Then she turned to his mother, and bowed.

Exactly once. It was a proper bow. It had nothing in it of the girl who’d first come to this family’s house with a gift box and her greeting rehearsed in the car, or of the woman who’d bowed to her more than a hundred times since in the hope of being let in. Her back went to exactly the right angle, her hands rested together in front of her, her head came down, and when she straightened she didn’t smile.

“Madam Yang. Thank you for inviting me.”

For the first time that evening his mother’s expression changed. “Si-Yuan.”

Perhaps it was a warning. Perhaps she was meant to sit down and apologise for drawing attention to the table. Si-Yuan looked at Pengcheng, who’d half risen from his chair.

“Where are you going?”

“I’m leaving.”

“Wait.”

It was the first word, and it had come too late. “Enjoy the banquet,” she said, and walked away from the head table with her shoulders straight and her chin level.

She could feel every eye in the ballroom, some openly and some sideways. A waiter stepped out of her way. The quartet went on playing; nobody had told them to stop. At the door she gave her card to the attendant, who looked bewildered, and she thanked him, and went out, and the doors closed behind her.

✦ ✦ ✦

Inside, Pengcheng was still standing. The barrister cleared his throat and suggested the next course.

“Mother.”

She lifted her glass. “Sit down. You’re drawing attention.”

“You shouldn’t have said that.”

“I was making an observation.”

“About my fiancée.”

“Then perhaps your fiancée should think about how she presents herself.”

“Not here,” said his father.

The quiet round the table expected him to restore order and give the evening back to the rhythm his mother had arranged. For years he’d have done exactly that. A disagreement was for private. An insult was to be read generously. But she was gone, and he hadn’t stopped her, and her glass was untouched beside her folded napkin.

“Don’t make a scene,” said his mother.

He looked at her, and almost said something, and lowered his eyes and picked up his phone instead. That was a choice too.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t cry in the lift, or in the lobby, or under the awning outside in the cold. There were three missed calls already. Then a message.

Pengcheng (Boyfriend, Apparently): Where are you?

He hadn’t asked if she was all right. He wanted to know where she was.

Si-Yuan: I’ve left.

In the taxi she watched the hotel go small in the back window, the ballroom glowing above the entrance. Three hundred people would go home with a story. Some would call her sensitive. Some would say she’d embarrassed the family. All of them would remember. She turned to the window, and then, at last, she cried.

✦ ✦ ✦

He rang again once she was home. She was on her bedroom floor with her shoes by the wardrobe and her earrings on the dressing table and the navy dress still on, and this time she answered.

“Are you all right?”

“No.”

“I’m sorry. I should have said something.”

“Yes.”

“I was going to speak to her.”

“You were sitting next to me. You heard her. You looked at your plate.”

He didn’t answer.

Her voice shook, and she let it. “Do you know what I wanted? I didn’t want you to shout at her, or ruin her birthday. I wanted you to look at me. I wanted you to put your chopsticks down and tell her not to talk about me like that. I wanted to know that after all this time I wasn’t going to sit beside you while someone humiliated me and you pretended you hadn’t heard. Why didn’t you?”

There was a long silence on the line. “I didn’t want to make a scene at her birthday.”

What went through her was colder than surprise. “You didn’t want to make a scene.”

“That isn’t what I meant.”

She looked at the ring on her finger, catching the lamp. “It’s what you did. Goodnight, Pengcheng.”

He came anyway. At twenty-six minutes past ten the doorbell went, and then a message saying he was outside. She opened the door in the end, in an old T-shirt with her face washed, because she didn’t want him standing outside her flat like a stranger. His tie was pulled loose.

He sat on her sofa with a space between them and said all of it, and every word was right. He’d let his mother humiliate her. It had been unacceptable. He’d speak to his mother and make it clear she couldn’t treat her like that. And Si-Yuan felt no relief at all, because she’d needed it in the ballroom, while his mother was still speaking, while there was still a chance she wouldn’t have to stand up and bow her way out of the room.

He loved her. She could see that, and perhaps that was why it was so hard to explain. If he’d agreed with his mother she could have hated him. But he loved her in the quiet private ways that had once made her feel safe. He kept her medicine at his flat. He knew which side of the bed she liked. And when she’d needed him to stand beside her in front of everyone, he’d looked down.

She took her hand out of his. “Can you go home tonight?”

He looked at her a long time, and nodded, and at the door he started to ask if he could hold her and didn’t finish.

“Not tonight.”

“I love you,” he said.

For a second she nearly said it back. She didn’t. The door closed.

✦ ✦ ✦

She rang Si-Jie, who heard her not speak and said she was coming. Si-Wei only asked where she was. They were there inside twenty-five minutes, Si-Jie in a coat thrown over whatever she’d been wearing, Si-Wei with a bag from the convenience store downstairs, and they found her on the floor by the sofa.

When she could, she told them. “His mother said some girls marry up by the hour. In front of three hundred people.”

Si-Jie’s arms tightened round her. Si-Wei went still. “Where was Pengcheng?”

Si-Yuan’s face crumpled. “Beside me. He looked at his plate. I stood up and bowed once and left. I didn’t know what else to do.”

Si-Jie took her face in both hands. “Listen to me. You didn’t embarrass anyone. You didn’t ruin her birthday. Don’t carry that.”

“Did he come here?” said Si-Wei.

“He said he’s sorry.”

“Did he defend you?”

“After.”

Si-Wei closed her eyes. “Of course.”

They stayed on the floor with the congee Si-Wei had brought and a packet of tissues, and this time Si-Yuan didn’t tease anyone or ask about Sung Jae. She leaned on them, and they held her.

When she went to bed she put the earrings in their box in the drawer, and then she took off the ring, not angrily, and set it beside them. She remembered his kitchen and the eleven days and how happy she’d been. Then she remembered the plate. She closed the drawer.

Before she put the phone down she opened his contact and looked at it, and took out (Boyfriend, Apparently), and left only his name.

Si-Jie lay down beside her. Si-Wei turned off the lamp and stopped in the doorway. “Yuan? You’re allowed to stop trying.”

Si-Yuan didn’t answer, and Si-Wei left the door open a crack.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Sunday morning he rang his mother at breakfast.

“You humiliated her. Everyone understood what you meant. Don’t do it again.”

“You let your fiancée walk out of my birthday in front of three hundred people, and now you ring me to lecture me?”

“Because you insulted her in front of three hundred people.”

“Then perhaps you should decide which matters more to you, this family or that girl,” his mother said coolly.

He looked at the phone for a while after she’d hung up. Then he wrote to Si-Yuan.

Pengcheng: I spoke to my mother. I told her what she said was wrong. You shouldn’t have been treated that way.

Si-Yuan read it at her kitchen counter over a bowl of congee, with Si-Jie’s note beside it: Eat something. Don’t argue. Love you. He’d finally said the words she’d waited for. He’d said them to his mother, the morning after, when she’d already gone. Some apologies don’t arrive in time to save anything.

She finished the congee and washed the bowl and went back to bed without replying.

chapters.title: Silence
chapters.desc: Her twenty-first birthday comes and goes. She waits for him to call. He doesn’t know what he would say. He sits outside her building all night. She doesn’t come down.
chapters.volume: Volume Two: Three Years of Bowing
chapters.content:
On Friday morning the first thing Pengcheng did was look at his phone, and there was nothing from her.

He hadn’t expected anything. He’d told himself not to. All the same his thumb went to her name before he’d properly opened his eyes, and the last message in the conversation was still his, sent five days before: I spoke to my mother. I told her what she said was wrong. You shouldn’t have been treated that way. Delivered. Read. Unanswered.

It was the thirteenth of December. She was twenty-one today, and so were her sisters.

He’d had two of her birthdays. On the first she’d rung him a minute after midnight and demanded to know whether he was going to wish her happy birthday or not, and he’d said he’d been waiting for the minute to finish. On the second he’d taken her to a small restaurant she liked, and the owner had brought out a cake because he’d mentioned the date when he booked, and she’d blown out the candles and refused to tell him what she’d wished for. He’d meant to ask her again this year. He’d thought there’d be a great many years to ask.

He opened the conversation and typed Happy birthday, Si-Yuan. It looked small. He added I hope you have a good day, and took it out again. He wrote I know things are difficult between us, but I still want to, and stopped there, because the message had already become about him: about what he wanted, about reaching her without having to find out whether she wanted to be reached.

He deleted all of it.

✦ ✦ ✦

Across the city Si-Yuan woke with one hand under her cheek and the other on the empty side of the bed, and for a few seconds she forgot. Then her phone lit with a birthday notice from an app she never used, and she sat up. The group chat was already loud.

Si-Jie (Questions): HAPPY BIRTHDAY TO US. I LOVE YOU BOTH. I AM COMING OVER WITH A CAKE.

Si-Wei (Watching): Happy birthday. Both of you. Eat properly today. Coffee isn’t breakfast.

Si-Jie (Questions): DON’T OPEN THE DOOR UNTIL I’M THERE.

Si-Wei (Watching): She means don’t open the door until she’s found somewhere to park.

Si-Yuan sent a row of hearts and scrolled past messages from Qiao-jie, from the crew, from old classmates and from fans who’d followed her since her first drama. His name wasn’t there.

It was all right, she told herself. She’d known this birthday would be different. If he’d forgotten she could have been angry, and anger was easy to explain. But Pengcheng didn’t forget dates. He remembered court deadlines and contract dates and the name of the restaurant where she’d once said she liked the dumplings. If he didn’t ring, it would be because he didn’t know what to say.

And for the first time she didn’t want to make it easier for him.

✦ ✦ ✦

Si-Jie arrived late in the morning with two shopping bags and a cake box and enough energy for all three of them, and hugged her in the doorway.

“Happy birthday.”

“Happy birthday to you too.”

Si-Jie held her at arm’s length. “Twenty-one. You look exactly the same.”

“We all look exactly the same. That’s the point of us.”

“I look slightly better,” said Si-Jie, and Si-Wei came in behind her with a paper bag of food and said nothing at all to that, which was worse than an answer.

Si-Yuan laughed. It was a small sound, but both of them heard it, and Si-Jie looked relieved, and Si-Wei put the food down on the counter as though she hadn’t noticed anything.

They spent the afternoon on the floor. Si-Jie decorated the table anyway, for photographs. Si-Wei said the cake was too sweet and had two pieces. They argued about which pictures could be posted, and made the cake hold three candles, and sang to each other badly in three keys. For a while the flat felt the way their bedroom had at home, three girls and too many clothes and someone always shouting about a hair clip.

Later Si-Jie showed her a photograph from the year before. The three of them on a sofa at a family gathering, Si-Yuan in the middle laughing at something out of frame, Si-Wei wearing her usual look of mild disapproval. In the background Pengcheng stood near the doorway. He wasn’t looking at the camera. He was looking at her.

“Do you want me to delete it?”

“No. Keep it.”

Si-Jie didn’t argue. While Si-Wei was cutting fruit she sat beside her on the sofa. “Has he rung?”

“No.”

“Do you want him to?”

She could have said no. It would have been more dignified. But she was tired of pretending that because something was missing she’d stopped wanting it. “Yes. I want him to ring and remember it’s my birthday. I want him to say something that isn’t an apology, and ask how I am, and sound like he’d rather be here.”

Si-Jie took her hand. “That’s not too much to want.”

“I don’t know what I’d do if he did.”

“Then you don’t have to decide until he does.”

The phone lay face up beside her on the sofa, and stayed dark.

Towards evening Si-Jie’s own phone went, and she took it into the corridor, and came back pink.

She was already looking for her coat. “Arthur’s taking me away tomorrow. For my birthday. He won’t say where. I haven’t packed. I don’t know what to pack for somewhere he won’t tell me about.”

“Pack for rain,” said Si-Wei.

“How do you know it’ll rain?”

“Because he’s planned it, and he’ll have planned for rain.”

Si-Jie hugged them both twice and made Si-Yuan promise to eat the rest of the cake, and left in a rush of scarf and bags. The flat was quieter after.

✦ ✦ ✦

Pengcheng was still in his chambers that evening. He’d finished everything that needed him. He’d taken a call from his father, reviewed two matters and asked Ms. Lui to move Monday’s meeting. He’d done everything that could be done except ring her.

Then a photograph appeared. Three sisters on a living-room floor with a cake between them, Si-Yuan in the middle in a cream jumper, Si-Jie leaning on her cheek and Si-Wei holding two fingers up behind both their heads. Twenty-one, three times over.

He made it bigger. She was smiling, with her eyes narrowed and her cheeks lifted. It was the smile she’d had before she learned to check whether a room was pleased with her. He should have been relieved. What he felt instead was an ache under his ribs he couldn’t name. He’d wanted to be there. He’d wanted to watch her make a wish and complain when she wouldn’t tell him what it was.

In the cabinet beside his desk was a small paper bag he’d bought two weeks before, before the banquet: a fine gold bracelet with one small red stone, because she’d once said she liked jewellery that looked simple until someone came close enough to see. He’d imagined fastening it round her wrist. He’d imagined her turning her hand under the light.

He picked up the phone. He could still ring. He could say happy birthday and that he missed her and that he was sorry. But he’d said sorry already, and he was beginning to understand that another apology with nothing behind it would only ask her to comfort him for feeling guilty. He put the phone down.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her phone lit while she and Si-Wei were clearing up. Her heart moved before her head could stop it. It was a girl from wardrobe. Happy birthday! Let’s celebrate when you’re back on set.

She answered and put the phone face down. Si-Wei was watching.

“Do you want me to take that away from you?”

“Why?”

“Because you keep looking at it.”

Si-Yuan didn’t argue. Si-Wei dried her hands and came and stood beside her, and Si-Yuan leaned on her shoulder.

“You don’t have to wait for him to make your birthday feel like yours,” said Si-Wei.

“I know.”

She did know. She’d had cake and her sisters, and people had been glad she existed. She wasn’t alone. But there was a particular sort of absence that other people couldn’t fill, however many of them there were and however much they loved you. She hadn’t wanted a grand gesture. She’d wanted him, and she hated that she still did.

✦ ✦ ✦

Saturday went by. On Sunday he worked, because working was the thing he knew how to do. He spoke at a meeting with his usual precision, and nobody noticed anything. When Ms. Lui brought in lunch, he found he’d ordered for two from the noodle place Si-Yuan liked, the one that packed the chilli separately because she didn’t like it touching the noodles. He opened the box and closed it again.

In the evening he drove to her building. He hadn’t meant to. He’d told himself she needed space, and that turning up at her door when she’d asked him to go home would only make it worse. He parked across the road where he’d always waited to collect her after late shoots, and he could see the lobby and the security desk, and he didn’t go in.

He watched people come and go. A rider with a delivery. A woman in a dark coat with a shopping bag. The guard changing shifts. He told himself he only wanted to know she was home and safe.

Later her light came on. He knew the window. He knew where she kept her reading lamp and that the curtains never quite met in the middle, and how the warm light fell across her living-room wall. A shadow moved behind the curtain, and for a moment he let himself think she might have seen the car.

He could tell her he was downstairs. He could ask whether she’d come down for five minutes, and promise not to come up unless she wanted him to. His thumb hovered over her name. Then he remembered her asking him to go home, in the middle of her living room, and how he’d gone, and how he’d thought that giving her space was right.

He was beginning to understand that he often used the right thing as a way round the difficult one. Still, he didn’t send it.

✦ ✦ ✦

The building went dark window by window. Hers stayed lit a long time. He wondered whether she was reading. She read scripts late, cross-legged on the sofa with her hair over one shoulder, and when the words stopped making sense she rubbed the bridge of her nose and complained, and he’d take the script away, and she’d tell him he was boring, and he’d tell her he’d heard that before, and she’d put her head on his shoulder.

It was the ordinary things he missed. The hair clips she left on his desk. The way she drank from his glass without asking. The way she called his name from another room, not because she needed anything but because she wanted him to hear her. He’d been the person she turned to without thinking. He had nobody to blame for losing that but himself.

Some time after two he let himself look at the banquet properly. The three hundred people. His mother’s voice. Her chopsticks laid down on the cloth. The exact moment she’d looked at him. She hadn’t looked angry. She’d looked at him like someone giving a man one last chance to be who she’d believed he was. And he’d looked down.

He’d told himself for years that he was protecting the people he loved from the cost of conflict, choosing the right moment, the measured answer, the least damage. He’d never once asked her what she needed. He’d never understood that when someone insulted her in front of him, saying nothing was a decision. He’d made it. She’d paid for it.

The bracelet was in its bag on the passenger seat. He hadn’t decided to bring it. He opened the box and looked at the small red stone, and imagined her holding out her wrist, and asking why he’d bought it, and then saying, gently, that she didn’t want it. He closed the box.

✦ ✦ ✦

At twenty to eight on Monday morning Si-Yuan went to the kitchen for water, and from the window she saw the car.

She didn’t know it at first. Then she did, and her hand stopped halfway to her mouth. It was parked in the place he’d always used when he collected her after late shoots. She remembered dropping her bag between her feet in the passenger seat and asking why he always came early, and his saying it was because she was always late, and her saying yesterday didn’t count because she’d been hungry, and his laughing, and her being so pleased with herself that she’d leaned over and kissed his cheek.

He was sitting in that same car. Alone. She thought he’d been there all night.

For one second she wanted to put on a coat and go down and knock on his window. She wanted to see his face when he looked up. She wanted him to get out of the car and hold her. Then the banquet came back: his still hands, his eyes on his plate, the long quiet after her name had been made into something shameful.

He was here now, after her birthday had gone, after she’d waited and he’d chosen not to ring. She couldn’t tell whether he was finally trying to reach her or only finding a way to be near her without having to ask again. She was too tired to find out.

She typed I saw you, and looked at it, and deleted it, and went back to bed.

✦ ✦ ✦

Down in the car Pengcheng saw a curtain move, and straightened, and waited. The curtain fell back. Nothing else happened.

His father rang an hour later. “Where are you?”

“Outside Si-Yuan’s.”

There was a pause. “Have you spoken to her?”

“No.”

“Then what are you doing there?”

Pengcheng didn’t answer.

His father sighed. “Sitting outside someone’s home isn’t an apology, son.”

He knew what his father meant. He’d been waiting for her to come down. He’d been waiting for her to take the first step and make the hard part easier for him, the way she’d done so many times before. Even now, he was waiting.

“I’ll come back,” he said, and started the engine, and drove away without seeing her.

✦ ✦ ✦

She heard it go. She went back to the window anyway and looked at the empty space until she was certain. A few minutes later her phone buzzed.

Pengcheng: I was downstairs.

Pengcheng: I didn’t want to disturb you.

There was something almost unbearable in that. He hadn’t wanted to disturb her. He hadn’t rung on her birthday because he didn’t know what to say. He hadn’t come up because she’d asked him to go. He hadn’t wanted to make a scene at his mother’s banquet. He’d spent years finding reasons not to disturb the peace, and every time she’d been the one left living with the disturbance.

Pengcheng: I wanted to wish you a happy birthday.

She closed her eyes. She’d wanted that too, more than she’d admit. She could tell him she’d seen him and had nearly gone down. She could tell him she’d spent her birthday checking her phone after promising herself she wouldn’t. She could tell him she missed him. But she couldn’t bear to be the one explaining the distance between them again, not now he’d begun to see it.

She put the phone on the bed beside her, and didn’t reply.

✦ ✦ ✦

That night he put the bracelet in the drawer of his desk at home, where she’d once left a hair clip that was still there. He opened their conversation and didn’t send anything.

For the first time he understood that silence could be more than an absence of words. It could be a distance someone put between themselves and the person who’d hurt them. He’d always believed that if he waited, if he stayed patient and reasonable, the people he loved would come to understand him. He’d mistaken their patience for forgiveness. And she’d stopped being patient.

Across the city Si-Yuan lay in the dark. Her birthday had been over for three days. She’d laughed with her sisters, eaten well and been loved, and still, when she closed her eyes, she saw the car outside her building and remembered how fast her heart had gone. She couldn’t forgive herself for that part. She knew she still loved him. What she couldn’t forgive was that some part of her was still waiting for him to become the man she’d spent two years believing he was.

He’d sat outside her building all night, close enough to see her window, close enough to hope she might come down. He’d wanted her to know he was there.

He’d never once given her a reason to open the door.

chapters.title: She Leaves
chapters.desc: She takes the film in Paris. The ring left on his desk with a note: “You never once said no to her.” He keeps the note in his jacket.
chapters.epigraph: “You never once said no to her.”
chapters.volume: Volume Two: Three Years of Bowing
chapters.content:
Qiao-jie forwarded the email on a Friday morning in January with a note on top. They’re asking whether you’d reconsider. The schedule’s moved. The role’s still yours, and Moreau wants to talk to you himself.

Si-Yuan read it once, and again, and then put the phone down and went to the kitchen and poured herself a glass of water and came back and read it a third time.

Below the note was the director’s message. He remembered her audition. He remembered their conversation about Ning Yue. He’d been disappointed when she withdrew, and he understood that circumstances changed. If she was still interested, he’d be glad to talk again.

She sat still at the table. She was twelve again, watching one of his films twice in a weekend and then spending a month telling her sisters about the way he filmed silence. She was twenty, in a small room with a script in her hands, trying not to show how much she wanted it. Then she was at his mother’s dining table hearing No actress of mine will be living abroad, and in his car hearing him say that three months wasn’t long, and asking him whether he wanted her to go, and his telling her he wanted her to make the right decision.

She’d turned it down because she’d wanted to be easy to love. Her phone rang.

“Did you read it?” said Qiao-jie.

“Is the part really still free?”

“They wouldn’t be asking if it weren’t. He’s seen your withdrawal. He still wants you.”

Si-Yuan looked towards the bedroom, where the ring had been in the dressing-table drawer since the night of the banquet. “Can you set up a call?”

There was a short pause. “Are you sure?”

“I am.”

Qiao-jie’s voice went soft, which it almost never did. “I’ll arrange it.”

After she rang off Si-Yuan opened the email again. This time she didn’t read it as something she might lose. She read it as something she was allowed to want.

✦ ✦ ✦

The call was that afternoon. Moreau talked about the new schedule, about Ning Yue, about the changes to the script, and Si-Yuan asked her questions in careful English and wrote the answers down. On the first page of her notebook was the character’s name, and under it, smaller, a line from the original audition notes: She has spent so long waiting for permission that she has forgotten she can choose.

When he asked whether she was still interested, she touched the edge of the page.

“Yes. I’d like to do it.”

He laughed, warmly. “Good. I was hoping you’d say that.”

“Thank you for asking me twice.”

“Let’s make it worth the wait.”

She sent Qiao-jie a message afterwards. Please tell them I accept. She looked at the words for a while. What she felt wasn’t quite excitement and wasn’t quite relief. It was steadier than either. For the first time in a long while she’d made a decision without first imagining how someone else would take it.

✦ ✦ ✦

Pengcheng was reading a draft opinion when Ms. Lui put her head round the door and said that Miss Yen was in reception.

He stood up at once. “Did she say what it’s about?”

“She said she’d wait.”

He straightened his cuffs, and stopped himself. For a foolish moment he let himself wonder whether she’d come because she was ready to talk. Perhaps the weeks had given her time to miss him as much as he’d missed her. He knew better than to expect it. But hoping had always come easier to him than acting.

She was standing at the reception window in a pale grey coat over a black dress, with her hair loose. She looked thinner than in December, or perhaps he only hadn’t seen her properly for too long. She had a small envelope in her hand.

“Pengcheng.”

“Si-Yuan. Have you been well?”

“Yes. Thank you.”

The politeness hurt more than he’d expected. “Will you come through?”

He walked ahead of her and slowed when he realised she was keeping her distance. She used to catch up. She used to put her hand in his in the corridor and complain that his office was too cold, and once she’d taken his coffee without asking and told him he drank it like a man being punished.

His office was as she remembered it: the bookshelves, the dark desk, the framed photograph of his family by the window. Her eyes went to the photograph and away.

“Would you like some tea?”

“No, thank you. I won’t be long.”

Something in the way she said it made him stop. He went behind his desk. She put the envelope on it, and through the open flap he saw the small velvet box. He didn’t touch it. The room went quiet.

“I’ve accepted the film in Paris. The one I told you about in October. The director asked again, and the schedule’s changed, and I said yes this afternoon.”

The words took a moment to arrive. “When do you leave?”

“Next week. It’ll be months.”

He wanted to ask whether she was going alone, and where she’d stay, and whether Qiao-jie had found her somewhere safe, and whether she’d read the revised contract and wanted him to look at it. He knew how to take care of those things. He always had. They weren’t the questions that mattered.

“Is it what you wanted?”

A faint, almost disbelieving look crossed her face. “Yes.”

He swallowed. “Then I’m glad you said yes. About the ring—”

“I don’t think I should keep it. I can’t go on wearing it as though we’re still walking towards the same thing.”

“Do you still want to marry me?”

It came out too fast. Once she’d have answered before he finished. She’d have shown him her hand. She’d have admitted she’d already imagined the wedding while pretending she hadn’t. Now the question seemed to reach her from some other year.

“I wanted to,” she said.

His jaw tightened. “Wanted.”

“I wanted to marry you, Pengcheng.”

He could have asked her to stay. He could have promised that it would be different with his mother, that she’d never stand alone again, that nobody would speak about her like that in front of him. He’d said some of it already. But the words that mattered weren’t promises about later. They were the ones he hadn’t said when she’d needed them.

“Can we talk about this properly? Not with you standing there and a ring between us.”

“I think the ring belongs here.”

“It belongs to you.”

“Not any more.”

He flinched, and she saw it. For a second her face softened by instinct and her fingers moved, as though she’d reach across the desk. Then she stopped. She’d spent so long reaching first.

“I need you to understand something. I didn’t leave because your mother was difficult. I knew she didn’t like me. I knew she thought I wasn’t suitable. I tried, didn’t I? I learned how to greet everyone. I learned what to wear and when to speak and which relatives mattered. I tried so hard not to embarrass you. I thought if I kept trying she’d see that I loved you and wasn’t trying to take anything. That I wanted to belong.”

Her voice didn’t break. That made it worse.

She looked straight at him. “What I could never understand was why you let me do it alone. At the banquet I wasn’t waiting for you to fight her. I didn’t want you to shout or humiliate her back. I wanted you to say no. Once. You never once said no to her.”

He went completely still. She didn’t say it angrily. There was no accusation left in her voice, and she wasn’t trying to make him feel the full weight of it. It was the truth she’d stopped trying to soften.

“You’d say you’d speak to her afterwards. You’d say you’d explain, you’d deal with it. Every time she made something hard for me, you waited till we were alone to say you were sorry. And then I had to go back and do it again.”

He looked down, and the banquet came back so exactly that he could almost hear her chopsticks touch the cloth. “I should have stood up for you. I was wrong.”

“I know.”

She wasn’t waiting for him to say it. That was what frightened him. For years he’d believed that if she understood his reasons she’d forgive him: the family, the timing, his mother’s position, the cost of a public quarrel. He’d never once considered that she understood every one of them, and only didn’t believe any of it was worth what he’d asked her to give up.

“Is there nothing I can do?”

“That’s what I’ve been asking you to do,” she said, and picked up her bag.

He came round the desk. “Will you ring me when you land?”

It was such a familiar thing to ask. He used to ask her to ring when she reached the studio, when she got home from a late shoot, when her flight came in. He’d never had to ask twice. Now even that felt like something he’d no right to expect.

“I don’t know,” she said.

He wanted to tell her he loved her. He wanted to tell her about the bracelet in his drawer, and the night outside her building. He wanted to tell her he’d mistaken her patience for an endless supply of chances. He couldn’t find a way to say any of it without making her responsible for what came next.

“I’m glad you’re going,” he said.

Something moved across her face. “Thank you.”

The door closed behind her.

✦ ✦ ✦

He stood where he was. Outside, a phone rang, someone laughed in reception, the printer started up. The world went on.

He opened the envelope. The ring was the one he’d chosen in April, after standing at a counter for an hour because he’d wanted something that would suit her when she was old and that she could wear every day without thinking about it. He’d imagined it on her hand for the rest of their lives.

Under the box was a folded sheet of paper he hadn’t noticed. The handwriting was hers: the small upward tilt of the letters, the long last stroke she gave the word you. There was one sentence.

You never once said no to her.

He sat down slowly. He’d heard her say it. Seeing it in her hand made it different. She hadn’t written it in anger. She’d taken the time to write it down, so that he’d have it after she’d gone.

His first instinct was to put it in the desk drawer, somewhere safe. Instead he folded it along its crease and slipped it into the inside pocket of his jacket, carefully, so the paper wouldn’t tear.

Ms. Lui knocked later to say his next meeting had arrived. He asked for five minutes. She hesitated in the doorway. In six years she’d never seen him keep anyone waiting, and she’d never seen him look at one sheet of paper for most of an afternoon. She said nothing and closed the door.

He took the note out again. He thought of all the times Si-Yuan had asked him whether his mother liked her. All the times she’d asked whether she’d done something wrong. All the times she’d looked at him across a dining table, waiting for him to notice. He’d told her she was doing well. He’d told her not to worry, that his mother was difficult with everyone.

He’d never told his mother to stop.

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening her suitcase lay open on the bed with little in it: jumpers, a wash bag, her passport, and the script on top. She opened the dressing-table drawer. The space where the ring had been was empty. Beside it were a hair clip, a spare charger, an old photograph of the three of them, and the box with the diamond earrings she’d worn to the banquet. He’d given them to her on her twentieth birthday and fastened one himself, and told her they suited her.

She took them out and looked at them, and put them back, and closed the drawer.

Si-Jie rang. “Did you do it?”

“I gave him the ring.”

“Did he ask you to stay?”

“Yes.”

“And?”

“I left.”

Si-Jie was quiet. “Are you all right?”

Si-Yuan thought about it. She didn’t feel all right. She didn’t feel free yet, either. There was sadness and fear, and under them a strange lightness that made her feel almost guilty. “I think I will be.”

“That’s enough for today. We’re bringing dinner.”

“You don’t have to.”

“We know,” said Si-Jie, and rang off.

Si-Yuan looked round the room. There were traces of him everywhere, none of them obvious. A book he’d recommended. A mug he’d bought her. The spare charger he always kept on her side of the bed. The blanket he’d once complained was too thin. She’d have to decide what to do with all of it, but not tonight. Tonight she’d pack.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was still awake near midnight with his jacket over the back of the chair. He’d read the note so many times he knew the slope of every letter. He could have thrown it away, or put it in a drawer and called it something she’d left behind. He kept it close. He didn’t want to remember the pain. He wanted never to forget what he’d done.

He opened her conversation and typed.

Pengcheng: I won’t ask you to come back. But I want you to know I love you. I should have said no. I should have chosen you when it mattered, not afterwards.

It was true. It was also too late to change anything. He sent it anyway, and watched it show as delivered, and waited, and set the phone down.

Across the city Si-Yuan was on the floor between her sisters eating from a takeaway carton when her phone buzzed beside her. She read it, and locked the screen, and went back to the argument Si-Jie was having with Si-Wei about whose turn it was to visit their mother.

She didn’t delete it. She didn’t answer it either.

On his desk the ring stayed in its velvet box. In his jacket the folded note lay against his chest. And on the other side of the city she was packing for a life she’d once been asked to refuse. She hadn’t stopped loving him, and she’d have to learn to live with that. But she was going to Paris, and this time she wasn’t waiting for anyone’s permission.

chapters.title: An Ocean
chapters.desc: Paris: night shoots on the river, a new language, nobody who knows how to bow. She wears red again. She still checks her phone.
chapters.epigraph: “She’s trying very hard not to need anyone.”
chapters.content:
The first thing Si-Yuan learned about Paris was that the cold was different by the river. It wasn’t colder than the winters she knew at home. The wind only had more room, and crossed the water before it found its way under her coat, and lifted the ends of her scarf, and made her fingers ache whenever she took them out of her pockets.

The second thing she learned was that nobody here knew how to bow.

Not the director, or the assistant director who shouted across the set, or the old woman who sold coffee from a hatch near their location, or the driver who’d brought her in from the airport. People nodded. They shook hands. When they knew one another well enough they kissed each other’s cheeks. But nobody lowered their head and measured the angle, and nobody watched to see whether she’d bowed deeply enough or laughed too loudly.

It should have felt like freedom, and sometimes it did. At other times she’d find herself in a room full of strangers checking, out of pure habit, whether she was doing something wrong. On her fourth morning she apologised to a woman who’d bumped into her, and the woman looked surprised and then smiled and told her not to worry, and walked on. Two words, with no lecture in them and no reminder of whose space she’d come into. Si-Yuan stood on the pavement a second longer than she needed to, and laughed at herself.

✦ ✦ ✦

The production had rented her a flat in the eleventh, on a quiet street with a bakery underneath and a grocer’s round the corner. It had tall windows and pale floorboards and a narrow balcony too cold to use in February. The heating had opinions. The shower took its time.

She hadn’t meant to compare it with his flat. It happened when she opened the cupboard and found that the last tenant had left one coffee cup behind. Pengcheng always had two. Even living alone he’d kept two, and when she’d asked him why he’d said in case someone came over, and when she’d asked who, he’d said, You, apparently. She’d taken the better cup. Now she stood in a strange kitchen holding the only one, and felt foolish, and put it back.

She unpacked. Clothes in the wardrobe, scripts on the desk, passport in the drawer. At the bottom of the case was a dark red dress with a plain neckline and sleeves that stopped just above the wrist, bought between two shoots because the colour had made her feel brave. She’d worn it to his mother’s in the May before last, and his mother had looked at it before she looked at anything else and asked whether there was an occasion. Pengcheng had told her she was beautiful in red. By August she’d stopped wearing it to the Yangs’, and then she’d stopped wearing it at all. She’d bought navy instead, and grey, and beige: colours that didn’t announce themselves when she came into a room.

She shook it out. It had creased on the flight. She held it against herself in the mirror, and for a moment she saw the girl who’d bought it without thinking twice. Then she hung it in the wardrobe, where she’d see it every time she opened the door.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first week was hard, though nobody was unkind. If anything they were patient. The production had found her a language coach for the French lines, Moreau spoke English easily, and people translated for her when the talk ran fast.
