Still, there were moments when a joke went round the set and everyone smiled before she’d caught it, or someone asked her something and she stood there hunting for the word.

At home she could read any room. She knew when to speak and when to step aside, and she could catch the smallest change in someone’s face and adjust before anything went wrong. Here she couldn’t. She had to ask people to say things again. She had to admit when she didn’t understand. At first it made her feel clumsy, and then, slowly, she found she liked it. There was something honest in not knowing. You could ask. Nobody seemed to think less of her for it.

In a rehearsal one afternoon she misread a direction and came into the scene too early. The actor opposite her stopped. Moreau looked at her and smiled.

“Again. You’re impatient.”

“Sorry.”

He pointed at her mark on the floor. “Don’t be sorry. Use it. She’s waited for someone a very long time. She doesn’t want to wait any more. That’s why she comes in early.”

She came in early again, on purpose, and the scene worked, and he nodded, and she looked down to hide her face. It was the first time in months a mistake of hers had turned into something useful instead of something to correct.

✦ ✦ ✦

The night shoots began in the second week, on a stretch of the Seine where the lights from the bridges broke up on the water. In the scene Ning Yue walked along the river after an argument, without an umbrella, in a coat too thin for the weather, with her hair damp from the mist. On paper it was simple. Walk. Stop. Look at the water. Take out the phone. Decide not to ring.

In rehearsal Moreau came and stood beside her. “Don’t play sadness. She isn’t crying. She’s trying very hard not to need anyone.”

On the third take the wind got up and the crew stopped to secure the lights, and someone came at her with a blanket, and she shook her head. Moreau walked over.

“Cold?”

“A little. I’m ready.”

He looked at her. “You don’t have to be brave for the camera.”

“I’m not,” she said, and he seemed satisfied, and they went again.

She walked. Ning Yue had left a man who loved her and couldn’t give her what she needed, and she’d told herself she was finished. The river went by beside her, dark and restless. She stopped, and took out the phone, and the screen lit her face, and she looked at a name, and locked it.

For a few seconds after cut nobody said anything. Then Moreau said it was good, and the assistant director asked for one more for safety.

During the reset she looked at her real phone. There were two messages.

Si-Jie (Questions): How’s Paris? What did you have for dinner?

Si-Wei (Watching): She means did you have anything that wasn’t bread.

She sent them a photograph of the river and told them to stop worrying. Si-Jie said she’d worry as much as she liked. Then, without quite meaning to, Si-Yuan scrolled to his name. His picture was the same one it had always been, from some legal dinner years ago, dark suit and white shirt and a face composed almost to severity. The last message was from January, the one about loving her, and under it was her silence.

“Ready?” someone called.

“Yes,” she said, and put the phone away, and went back to her mark.

✦ ✦ ✦

By the end of the month she could order coffee without looking at her phone. She knew the way to the production office and which streets filled up in the afternoon and which bakery made the small almond pastries she liked. She knew the woman at the grocer’s spoke some English and the man who brought back her laundry said the same cheerful thing every time. She’d learned to walk down a street without checking whether she was taking up too much of it.

And she’d learned that being alone in another country wasn’t the same as being lonely. Some days she was perfectly content. She liked walking home with her hands in her pockets. She liked going into bookshops with no intention of buying anything, and sitting at café windows listening to conversations she couldn’t follow. She liked that nobody here knew her as someone’s fiancée. Nobody had heard of the Yangs. Nobody knew she’d once counted her bows. When Moreau introduced her to new crew he said, “This is Si-Yuan. She’s Ning Yue,” and that was all, and every time she heard it she felt a small, private happiness.

✦ ✦ ✦

Late one Thursday she sat on the floor by her suitcase to finish unpacking, and found a pouch of photographs. Si-Jie asleep on her shoulder on a flight. Si-Wei holding up a book with an unimpressed face. And one of her and Pengcheng outside a restaurant, taken by Si-Jie when they weren’t looking. His hand was at the small of her back. She was looking up at him, laughing, and he was looking down at her. The light was poor and half her face was blurred because she’d moved. She remembered the evening anyway. She’d come off a shoot starving and he’d refused to let her eat instant noodles in his car and taken her somewhere proper, and she’d complained about the prices, and he’d told her not to read them, and she’d read them anyway, and he’d laughed.

On the back, in Si-Jie’s writing: You two are disgustingly obvious.

She smiled, and then didn’t. She didn’t throw it away and she didn’t put it up. She put it in the bottom of the drawer.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her sisters rang on Sunday. Si-Jie’s face filled the screen.

“Show me the flat.”

“You’ve seen the flat.”

“That was three weeks ago. Things change.”

Si-Wei’s voice came from somewhere behind her. “Nothing’s changed in three weeks.”

Si-Yuan laughed and turned the phone round and showed them the kitchen and the living room and the balcony, and Si-Jie gasped at the street, and Si-Yuan said it was only a street, and Si-Jie said it was a street in Paris, and that was different.

Si-Wei leaned into the frame. “Are you sleeping?”

“Yes.”

“Your eyes say you aren’t.”

“My eyes are working nights.”

They talked for an hour. Si-Jie told a long story about Arthur, who’d apparently formed an opinion on every restaurant in the city, and Si-Wei said she was telling it wrong and refused to tell it properly. Si-Yuan lay on the sofa and listened to the rhythm of them, which hadn’t changed since they were six.

Near the end Si-Jie asked, gently, whether she missed anyone else.

Si-Yuan looked into her cup. “Sometimes.”

Neither of them asked who. Afterwards she opened her messages. Above the January one was a photograph he’d sent her once, long ago, of his desk with her hair clip on it. You left this here. She’d written back Keep it, and he’d written I was planning to. She remembered laughing. She remembered how easy it had been to be loved by him when there was nothing hard to ask.

She could ask how he was. She could send him the river and say the night shoots were beautiful. He’d answer. He’d ask whether she was warm enough and whether the production was looking after her. He’d remember all the small things. He’d be kind, and she’d be tempted to mistake kindness for change. She put the phone away.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the last Friday of February the production had a dinner, nothing formal, in a small restaurant near the office. She stood at the wardrobe and her hand went past the black dress and the navy and the beige jumper, and stopped.

She changed, and brushed her hair, and put on a little lipstick, and looked in the mirror. The red fitted exactly as she remembered. It didn’t look loud, or wrong, or like someone trying too hard. It looked like her. His mother’s voice came back without being asked for, Is there an occasion?, and Si-Yuan looked at her reflection and lifted her chin. She wasn’t in that house. There was no reason to change.

Moreau arrived late and apologised in French. Two of the producers argued fondly about bread. Someone told her the colour suited her, and she said thank you, and that was the end of it. Nobody asked whether it was too bright. Nobody looked at her clothes as a statement about the family she might one day marry into. They thought she looked nice.

When Moreau raised his glass he thanked the crew for the night shoots and the actors for their patience, and then he looked at her. “To Ning Yue. She’s given this film its heart.”

She looked down, embarrassed, and he told her not to thank him, she’d done the work.

She walked part of the way home. People sat outside under heaters. A couple went past sharing one scarf. Her phone buzzed in her pocket and she had it out before she’d thought about it.

Si-Jie (Questions): Did you eat enough? Send me your outfit.

She took a picture under a streetlamp and sent it.

Si-Jie (Questions): RED!!!!!

Si-Jie (Questions): FINALLY. You look beautiful. I missed seeing you in red.

Si-Yuan stopped walking.

Si-Yuan: I missed it too.

She didn’t explain. She didn’t need to.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her alarm went at a quarter past five the next morning for an early call, and among the notifications was his name. The message had come in the middle of her night.

Pengcheng: I saw the production’s photographs. The night scenes look beautiful. I hope you’re keeping warm.

No apology. No request. Nothing about the ring. He’d seen the studio’s pictures. He knew she was working, and filming by the river, and he’d noticed.

She typed Thank you. It’s cold here. It was harmless. She could send it without promising anything, and let him know she’d read him without opening the door. Her thumb moved towards the arrow. Then she remembered how she’d looked at him at the banquet, and the months before it, and the years before that. She deleted it and got up.

✦ ✦ ✦

Across the ocean he saw that it had been read, and nothing else. He was in the back of a car on the way to a meeting with Ms. Lui in the front seat, and he’d sent it without expecting an answer. That was what he’d told himself. He looked at the conversation once, and again.

Ms. Lui turned in her seat. “The documents are in your email, Mr. Yang. Shall I take you through the schedule before we arrive?”

“Yes,” he said, and opened it, and didn’t send anything else.

✦ ✦ ✦

That night she was by the river again in a dark coat over her costume with a red scarf tucked under the collar, while the crew moved the camera.

Moreau came over while they relit. “Tonight she’s decided she won’t ring him. She’s made the decision. She hasn’t accepted it yet.”

Ning Yue walked beside the water with her hands deep in her pockets. She stopped at the railing. She opened the phone, and the audience would never see the name. Her thumb hovered. Then she locked it, and the camera came in close, and she stood still, neither crying nor smiling, only looking at the river and how something could be so close and still impossible to reach.

Moreau called cut, and looked at the monitor, and then at her. “That was it. You understand her.”

Someone brought her a hot drink and she held it in both hands, and across the river the lights went on moving on the water.

✦ ✦ ✦

When she got home she hung the scarf over a chair and checked her phone while the kettle boiled. Nothing. She opened his conversation anyway and scrolled up to the hair clip.

She missed him. She missed the way he listened when she talked about work. She missed his dry humour and his careful hands and the extra bottle of water he always brought. She missed the man who’d waited for her at a noodle stall till four in the morning because she hadn’t eaten. She missed being loved in small ordinary ways that had once made her feel safe.

She also remembered that none of it had kept her from being humiliated, and that he’d been sitting beside her when it happened.

She closed the conversation and turned off the kitchen light.

There were ten thousand kilometres between Paris and home, an ocean and seven hours and a language she was still learning, and a life that was slowly becoming hers. Distance, she was finding, didn’t make someone easier to forget. It only made the memories quieter. She still looked at her phone when she woke. She still looked for his name when the screen lit. She hadn’t stopped loving him.

She’d stopped arranging her life round the chance that he might finally choose her.

She wore the red dress again the next week, and the week after that. Nobody told her it was too much. For the first time in years she looked in the mirror without wondering who’d approve, and liked what she saw.

chapters.title: His Office Without Her
chapters.desc: He wins every case. Nobody notices he’s stopped going home. He sleeps in his chambers and reads every interview she gives.
chapters.epigraph: “I’m more able to be alone than I used to believe.”
chapters.content:
The judgment came on a Thursday afternoon, after three weeks of hearings, hundreds of pages of evidence, two expert witnesses and a dispute involving enough money to make the most experienced silks careful.

Pengcheng had been careful. He’d also been relentless. He stood while the judge read the ruling, with his face composed and his hands resting lightly on the bench in front of him. Across the court his opponent looked down at his notes. Beside him one of the clients let out a breath he seemed to have been holding since the first morning. It went their way.

The client turned to him at once and shook his hand with both of his. “Counsel Yang. We couldn’t have done this without you.”

“Thank you. My team will send the written summary and the next steps tomorrow.”

“Tomorrow? You should be celebrating tonight.”

Pengcheng gave him a small, polite smile. “There are a few matters to close.”

“Of course there are,” said the client, laughing.

His junior came over afterwards with his files under his arm. “That was excellent, sir. Are you going home tonight?”

“Eventually. Have you checked the costs schedule?”

It wasn’t an unusual answer. That was why nobody questioned it.

✦ ✦ ✦

His chambers had become the place he slept.

It had started by accident. A late filing, an early hearing, a client ringing at midnight about a document that couldn’t wait. He’d worked till dawn, showered in the small bathroom off his room, put on a clean shirt and gone straight to court. Then it happened again, and again, until the room had acquired a spare toothbrush, a change of clothes, a charger and a blanket one of the pupils had found in a store cupboard. The sofa was long enough if he turned on his side. It wasn’t comfortable. He’d stopped minding.

That night he came back from the celebratory drinks he hadn’t drunk and loosened his tie, and the city outside the window was mostly dark. His phone buzzed.

Father (Reads Everything): Heard about the judgment. Well done.

Pengcheng: Thank you.

Father (Reads Everything): Your mother would like you at dinner on Sunday.

He looked at it, and put the phone down without answering, and opened his laptop. There were emails, a memorandum to prepare, two matters listed for the following week. He worked until the windows went grey. Then he turned off the lamp and lay on the sofa with the blanket that didn’t reach his feet, and slept for a few minutes, and woke reaching for the phone.

Nothing had rung. There was no notification. He’d simply woken with the thought that something might have come. He opened her conversation. Her last message to him was months old. He looked at it a while, and locked the screen, and put the phone by his head.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first interview turned up on a Tuesday. Ms. Lui sent him the link because the clerks had been keeping an eye on the coverage of the Paris film, and she said, neutrally, that Miss Yen had spoken to a French paper.

He waited until the door had closed before he opened it.

There was a photograph at the top. She was sitting at a tall window in a dark jacket and a plain white blouse, her hair tied loosely, smiling at someone outside the frame. She looked different. Not older. Less guarded. He made the picture bigger.

The interview was in French. He knew some: enough to recognise contract phrases and to follow a conversation if the other person was patient. Not enough for this. He opened a second window with a dictionary in it and began.

The first paragraph took him eleven minutes. He wrote the words he didn’t know in a notebook: interprétation, personnage, attachement. The journalist had asked whether it was difficult to play a woman so alone. Her answer was longer, and he took it apart word by word, checking every tense. She’d said that loneliness wasn’t always the absence of people. Sometimes it was having to explain yourself so many times that in the end you stopped trying.

He stopped typing and read the French again. He wondered whether she’d thought of him when she said it. He wondered whether the journalist had asked about her private life, and whether she’d answered.

By the end of the week he’d read three. A short piece about the production. Another about how she prepared a role. The third was a video with English subtitles, in which she answered some of the questions in French, and he watched it twice: once for her voice, once for the words. She spoke with more confidence than she used to at home. She didn’t hurry to fill a pause. When she didn’t understand a question she asked the journalist to say it again, instead of smiling and pretending.

He noticed that. He remembered her in his car after family dinners, asking whether she’d said something wrong. He’d always told her she hadn’t. He’d never once asked why she needed to check.

Near the end the journalist asked what she’d learned about herself abroad. She thought about it. “That I’m more able to be alone than I used to believe.”

He paused it on her face, looking slightly away, listening to the next question. He played the sentence again, and once more, and then closed it, and didn’t open another article for the rest of the day.

✦ ✦ ✦

At chambers nobody saw anything. He still came in first. He still knew every detail of every brief and caught the smallest inconsistency in an opponent’s skeleton argument. His colleagues still called him reliable. His mother mentioned his judgment to an acquaintance. His father was pleased.

Only the room had changed. Papers that should have been filed lay on the desk. A cup stood by the monitor. His shirts lived in the bottom drawer now, folded beside a spare pair of trousers.

He’d stopped going home because there was nothing there that needed him. His flat was exactly as he’d left it. The cushions were straight and the kitchen was clean, and the second cup was still in the cupboard, and her toothbrush still in the bathroom, and her hair clip still in the drawer of his desk. It was easier to leave it all where it was. Then nothing had to be decided.

On the second Friday of the month his junior found him asleep on the sofa when he came in early.

“Counsel Yang?”

Pengcheng opened his eyes and for a moment didn’t know where he was. Then he sat up and asked the time.

His junior looked at the blanket. “Did you stay here again?”

“I had work.”

“You’ve been staying here quite a lot, sir.”

“Is there a problem with the work?”

“No, sir. None at all.”

The young man was leaving when he saw the open laptop, and the French page, and the photograph. “That’s Miss Yen, isn’t it? I saw the production photographs. She looks happy.”

It was an innocent remark. It was enough to stop Pengcheng’s hand on the lid.

“Does she?”

“In the pictures, yes.”

“That’s good,” said Pengcheng, and closed the laptop, and when he was alone he went and washed his face and changed his shirt.

✦ ✦ ✦

The second big case came the following week: complicated, politically awkward and already drawing attention from three sets of chambers. The client wanted someone who could run the strategy without letting the dispute turn into a public show. Pengcheng was briefed to lead, and accepted at once.

He was at his sharpest. He saw what nobody else had seen. He anticipated the other side’s points and took them apart before they could be made. When a pupil made a mistake in a draft he corrected it without humiliating him. He was calm and precise and unusually patient.

One evening his father came to the door of his room and stood there watching him read.

“You’re still here.”

“Father.”

His father came in and looked at the sofa. “Your mother says you haven’t been to dinner in weeks. Are you sleeping here?”

“Sometimes. It’s convenient.”

His father sat down opposite him. “That isn’t a reason to stop living. How is Si-Yuan?”

The pen in Pengcheng’s hand stopped. “She’s in Paris.”

“I know where she is. I asked how she is.”

“I’ve read some interviews. She seems well.”

“Have you spoken to her?”

“She doesn’t want to speak to me.”

“Did she say so?”

“She hasn’t answered.”

His father was quiet. “You can’t spend your life treating silence as the answer to every question. First go home. Sleep in your own bed. Eat something that didn’t arrive in a box. Then decide what you want.”

Pengcheng almost smiled. “You make it sound simple.”

His father stood. “It isn’t. Neither was the case you won last week, and you didn’t avoid that because it was difficult.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He bought a dictionary from a bookshop near chambers, a real one with thin pages and small print, and kept it by the sofa. He could have pasted whole paragraphs into a translation program and understood them in seconds. He wanted to know what she’d actually said. He wanted her choice of words, and the small differences between what the journalist asked and what she answered.

He learned the words for river and night and memory and distance. He learned the difference between manquer and perdre: to miss someone, and to lose them. A journalist asked her whether she missed home, and she said yes, but that she was learning home wasn’t always a place you could go back to unchanged. He wrote the translation in his notebook and looked at it and turned the page and didn’t write anything else that night.

Late one Wednesday he found a longer one in an arts magazine. In the photograph she was sitting on a low wall by the river in a long dark coat and a red scarf, and the wind had her hair, and she was smiling. He looked at it before he started reading.

The journalist asked about Ning Yue and love. Si-Yuan said people sometimes confused patience with devotion.

He looked up patience, and dévouement, though he knew them both. She said patience could be beautiful when it was shared, when two people were each willing to wait for the other. But when only one of them was expected to wait, it became something else. He leaned back in his chair.

He remembered her asking him, more than once, whether his mother would ever accept her. He remembered telling her it would take time. He remembered how she’d looked at him the last time, when she said she’d already given it two years. He’d thought he was being patient. He’d thought he was letting things settle, and that his mother would grow used to her, and the family would find a way.

But she’d been the one waiting. She’d been the one adjusting. She’d been the one making herself smaller while he called it time.

There was another question. Do you think love is enough?

“No. Love matters, but it can’t be the only thing a person is given. You need respect too. You need to know the person beside you won’t leave you alone when it gets hard.”

He closed his eyes. The building was silent except for the air conditioning and a lift somewhere far off. He’d won two major cases in a month. He’d been praised by people whose approval had mattered to him since he was a boy. He’d done everything that was expected of him. And he couldn’t remember the last time he’d made her feel safe.

At the end the journalist asked whether she was happier in Paris. “I think I’ve become more honest with myself.”

He wanted her happy. He wanted her to wake without thinking of him, and love her work, and wear what she liked, and walk through Paris without carrying his family on her back. He also wanted to be the person she told about it. He couldn’t separate the two any longer.

He typed I read your interview. You said something about patience. I think I understand it now. Then he deleted it. He had no right to announce that he understood, as though understanding were something you got from a dictionary.

✦ ✦ ✦

At the end of the month his father rang and told him, without asking, that he was coming to the flat for dinner. Pengcheng nearly refused. Then he looked at the sofa and the blanket and the shirt in the drawer, and said yes.

The flat was dark when he let himself in. He turned on the lights. Everything was as he’d left it. He took the second cup out of the cupboard and put it beside his own, and stood looking at the two of them, and couldn’t remember the last time he’d used them together.

His father noticed the cups and said nothing. They talked about chambers and the two cases, and Pengcheng’s attention kept going to the phone beside his plate.

“Are you expecting someone?”

“No.”

“Then stop looking at it.”

He put it in his pocket. After a while his father asked whether he still meant to marry her.

“Yes.”

“Does she know that?”

“I told her I love her.”

“That isn’t what I asked.”

Pengcheng looked at the table. “She gave the ring back. I haven’t changed my mind.”

His father looked at the window. “Then you need to understand that she may have changed hers. Your mother has spent most of her life believing that keeping the family’s position is the same as protecting the family. I won’t pretend I haven’t done well out of that belief. But a woman who marries you isn’t marrying our name. She’s marrying you.”

“I know.”

“Then you should have behaved as though you did.”

There was no anger in it. That made it harder to put aside.

“I should have,” said Pengcheng.

At the door his father put a hand on his shoulder. “Come home next week. Not for your mother. For yourself.”

✦ ✦ ✦

When he’d gone, Pengcheng put the second cup back in the cupboard and opened the magazine interview again. There was one sentence he wanted exactly. He found it and looked up every word, though he knew most of them, and wrote it out slowly in his notebook.

On ne peut pas demander à quelqu’un de rester indéfiniment devant une porte qui ne s’ouvre jamais.

You can’t ask someone to stand for ever in front of a door that never opens.

His pen stopped. He could almost hear her say it. Not to a journalist. To him. He wondered when she’d learned to say such things without crying, and how many times she’d tried to tell him before she stopped.

He fell asleep at the table with the notebook open and the dictionary beside it. On the last page, under the translations, he’d written one line in characters, and not translated it, because it wasn’t for the article. It was for him: I finally understand, and she isn’t here.

In Paris she was asleep with a red scarf over the back of a chair and a scene to learn in the morning. She was building a life.

He’d become fluent in the language of contracts because he’d spent his life learning to protect people with words. Now he was learning another language for a woman who’d stopped asking him to speak. He read every interview. He translated every answer. He learned the words she used for patience and loneliness and love. He couldn’t translate any of them into a way back to her.

chapters.title: Her Sister’s Wedding Plan
chapters.desc: Si-Jie rings her in Paris the morning after she finds Arthur’s notebook, and talks about her wedding anyway. Calls across three time zones. Si-Yuan laughs for the first time in months.
chapters.epigraph: “There. That’s what I wanted. That’s why I rang.”
chapters.content:
The phone went at two in the morning. Si-Yuan was on the floor of her flat with one knee drawn up and a half-learned script beside her, and outside a thin rain was falling on the street. A delivery scooter went past and round the corner, and the quiet came back. Then the screen lit with Si-Jie’s face.

“Are you asleep?”

“It’s two in the morning here.”

Si-Jie pushed her face closer to the camera, and behind her a city in daylight slid past a bus window. “I know. It’s nine here. I worked it out. This is a family emergency.”

“Is someone dead?”

“No.”

“In hospital?”

“No.”

“Then it isn’t an emergency.”

“It concerns my future husband.”

Si-Yuan put the script down slowly. “Your what?”

“Do you know another profiler I’m romantically involved with?”

“Last time I asked, you were still deciding whether you liked him.”

“That was months ago.”

“It’s March.”

“Exactly. Months,” said Si-Jie, and Si-Yuan laughed.

It was a small sound, and almost unfamiliar. She hadn’t realised how long it had been since she’d laughed without first checking whether she ought to. Si-Jie heard it. Her face went gentle for half a second, and then she spoiled it on purpose.

“Good. You’re laughing. I’ve got more. Hold on, I’m adding Si-Wei.”

The screen split. Si-Wei was at a desk by a window with her hair clipped back and a cup of tea at her elbow, and the light behind her was a different light again.

“Why am I here?”

“Because we’re discussing my wedding.”

“Where are you?” said Si-Yuan.

“Seoul. A week of a course. It’s ten in the morning and I was reading.”

Si-Jie leaned in. “She went to Seoul for a course, and Sung Jae happens to be from Seoul, and none of us is allowed to mention it.”

Si-Wei looked at her without any expression at all, and then turned to Si-Yuan, which was its own answer. “Has Arthur proposed?”

“No.”

“Then there’s no wedding.”

“Not yet.”

“Then there’s no wedding.”

“Why are you both so unsupportive?” said Si-Jie.

Si-Yuan tucked her chin onto her knee. Three cities, three clocks, three faces in the same mirror. For a few minutes the talk wandered the way it always had when the three of them were together. Si-Jie complained about a lecturer. Si-Wei corrected a fact. Si-Yuan listened and felt herself pulled back into a rhythm much older than any of them being grown up.

Si-Yuan was laughing at them both when Si-Jie’s face changed, and she said it like something that had been waiting behind her teeth the whole time.

“I found something. Arthur’s notebook, in his desk, last night. I was looking for a charging cable.”

Si-Wei looked up from her tea. “You read it?”

“Every page is about me. Since the seminar. What I eat. When I cry. How long I sleep. Things I said. Things I did. Things I apparently didn’t say.”

“Did he write it for work?” said Si-Wei.

“He says it isn’t work. He says he wanted to understand me.”

Si-Yuan went still on the floorboards. She knew that voice. It was the one Si-Jie used when she’d decided not to cry in front of anyone. “What did you ask him?”

“Whether I was his partner or his experiment.”

“And?”

“He said he didn’t know. So I left.”

“Did he try to stop you?” said Si-Yuan, over the top of Si-Wei swearing under her breath.

“No.”

“Did he follow you?”

Si-Jie stared at the screen. “How do you know?”

“He did, didn’t he?”

“He followed the taxi. He stopped outside my building. He didn’t come up.”

Si-Wei sat forward. “That doesn’t make it better.”

“I know.”

“Has he rung? Sent anything?” said Si-Yuan.

“No.”

Si-Yuan nodded slowly. “Good. At least he stopped himself.”

“That’s a very generous interpretation,” said Si-Wei.

“It isn’t an excuse. It’s a distinction. Whether he keeps to it is another matter,” said Si-Yuan.

Behind Si-Jie the bus went over a bump and the city jolted past the window. “I love him. I don’t want to stop.”

“Nobody’s asking you to,” said Si-Wei, more gently.

Si-Yuan heard herself laugh before she knew she was going to. Both of them looked at her.

“Sorry. It’s just that between the three of us we’ve managed to find men who make simple things extraordinarily difficult.”

Si-Wei stared at her and laughed too. Si-Jie made a noise that was half a laugh and half something else, and wiped her eyes with her sleeve, and Si-Yuan thought that she’d never in her life wanted so badly to be on a bus.

“You can love him and still be angry. You can miss him and still not want to see him. You can understand why he did it and still decide it wasn’t acceptable. And you don’t have to make it easier for him because he’s bad at not knowing things,” she said.

“Exactly. Now eat something,” said Si-Wei.

“Why?”

“Because we know you. Did you have breakfast?”

Si-Jie didn’t answer. Both of them looked at her.

“I had coffee.”

“That isn’t breakfast,” said Si-Yuan, and for the first time Si-Jie smiled properly.

“Don’t laugh at the next part. When I’m anxious, I talk faster and get very precise about small details. When I’m upset, I stop asking questions and start making statements. When I’m uncomfortable, I touch my left earring. He wrote all that down.”

Her hand was on her left earring. Si-Yuan pressed her lips together. Si-Wei looked down at her tea.

“I’m not laughing. I’m listening,” said Si-Yuan, before Si-Jie could accuse her.

“Did he write anything nice?” said Si-Wei.

Si-Jie hesitated, and Si-Wei saw it. “Ah.”

“It isn’t important.”

“Then tell us.”

Si-Jie sighed, as if giving in were the quickest way out. “He wrote that I get quieter when I’m really happy. That I let a conversation stop without rushing in to rescue it.”

None of them said anything for a moment.

“Is it true?” said Si-Yuan.

Si-Jie’s eyes went somewhere off the edge of the screen. When they came back the fight had gone out of her. “Yes. With him.”

“Then that part’s nice,” said Si-Yuan.

Si-Jie narrowed her eyes at the screen. “It’d be nicer if he hadn’t turned me into a research project. How are you?”

“I’m fine.”

Si-Wei looked at her the way she’d looked at all of them since they were six.

“I am,” said Si-Yuan, and laughed again, more easily this time, and Si-Jie pointed at the screen in triumph.

“There. That’s what I wanted. That’s why I rang.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Si-Yuan looked at the script beside her. A few months before, she’d have spent this hour checking her phone and wondering whether he was awake. Now she was on a floor in Paris at two in the morning listening to her sisters argue about a notebook.

She hadn’t stopped missing him. Some nights she still remembered the exact weight of his hand on her back, and the way he stood in his kitchen with his sleeves rolled up reading something while the water boiled, and the particular quiet of his flat when she was in it. But she’d begun to find out that a life could have an absence in it without being made of one.

“I miss you both,” she said.

Si-Jie made a face. “That’s unfair. You can’t say things like that when I’m already emotional.”

“You’re always emotional.”

“I am not.”

Si-Wei leaned towards her camera. “Don’t hurry home for us. Come back when you’re ready.”

“I will.”

Then Si-Jie sat up. “I’ve got another question. What do you think about wedding dresses?”

“Whose wedding?”

“Mine. Hypothetically. After he’s answered the question properly. You’re an actress. You know about clothes. I want something elegant. Not too traditional and not too plain. Something that looks beautiful when I walk.”

Si-Wei opened her eyes. “You’ve already pictured yourself walking up the aisle?”

“Haven’t you?”

“No.”

“Liar.”

“I’m not the one planning a wedding without a proposal.”

Si-Yuan put her hand over her mouth. The laughter that came was louder than before. Si-Jie accused Si-Wei of ruining everything and Si-Wei calmly denied it, and then they were arguing about whether a wedding should be large or small, and whether Arthur would like something traditional, and which of them would cry at the vows.

“He’ll cry first,” Si-Jie announced.

“Arthur? He barely changes his face.”

“Exactly. He’ll be holding it in.”

“You’re already imagining his face,” said Si-Yuan.

“I know his faces.”

Si-Wei raised an eyebrow. “According to his notebook or yours?”

Si-Jie gasped, and Si-Yuan laughed so hard she had to put the phone away. When she picked it up again both of them were smiling at her, and for a second she saw them as they’d been at ten: Si-Jie in the middle of something, Si-Wei pretending not to care, and herself between them laughing because she knew neither of them would ever let her sit alone for long.

Something loosened in her chest. No wound was closing yet. Something she’d thought she’d lost was slowly coming back.

✦ ✦ ✦

The call went on for another forty minutes. Si-Jie said that if he wrote, she wasn’t going to answer yet. She wanted him to find the answer first, and she didn’t know how long that would take him.

“Tell him what you need,” said Si-Wei.

“That’s a terrible strategy.”

“It’s the only one there is,” said Si-Yuan.

“You’re both very unhelpful. Show me your flat before you go.”

Si-Yuan turned the camera and showed them the little living room, the kitchen, the books stacked by the sofa, the coat by the door. Si-Jie said it needed more colour. Si-Wei said it looked perfectly fine. Then the camera went past the open wardrobe and Si-Jie spotted the red dress.

“You’re still wearing it?”

“Sometimes.”

“Good. Buy another one.”

“Why?”

“Because you need more than one red dress.”

“That’s your contribution to her recovery?” said Si-Wei.

“It’s a very important contribution,” said Si-Jie, and blew a kiss, and her bus came to a stop, and she was gone.

✦ ✦ ✦

At home it was a bright, ordinary Thursday morning, and Si-Jie got off the bus two stops early because she couldn’t sit still. The notebook was in her bag. She’d taken it from his flat in the middle of the night, and she hadn’t decided whether she’d give it back.

She sat on a bench outside the faculty with it on her knees. The handwriting was neat, almost painfully so. There were no suspects in it and no photographs of anything terrible. It was smaller than that, and more personal, and there were no verdicts, which was almost worse. He’d simply been paying attention.

Under the date of their last dinner he’d written that she’d asked whether he ever got tired of listening to people, and that he’d said no, and that she’d seemed relieved and hadn’t asked why. She remembered the evening. She’d been talking too much, jumping from his work to his childhood to his family, and she’d stopped herself and asked, and he’d looked at her and said no, and she’d laughed and changed the subject. She hadn’t known he’d kept it.

She opened their conversation and typed that she had his notebook, and deleted it. She typed a question, why he hadn’t told her, and deleted that too. Then she put the phone away. She was going to make him answer the question properly. Not today.

She was still angry. Liking someone didn’t give you permission to turn them into a set of observations, and loving them didn’t either. But she knew something else as well. She liked being noticed. She liked that he remembered things she’d forgotten saying.

Perhaps the trouble wasn’t that he noticed. Perhaps it was only that he’d never thought to let her know.

✦ ✦ ✦

In Paris it was still the middle of the night, and Si-Yuan stood at her kitchen window with a cup of tea. The rain had stopped. Across the street a few windows were still lit, and somewhere down below someone was laughing. The group chat had gone on without her.

Si-Jie (Questions): I have decided my wedding will be beautiful.

Si-Wei (Watching): You don’t have a wedding.

Si-Jie (Questions): I have a vision.

Si-Wei (Watching): You have a notebook.

Si-Jie (Questions): It’s HIS notebook.

Si-Jie (Questions): I’m blocking you.

Si-Yuan: I want to see the dress.

Si-Jie (Questions): I knew you’d understand me.

Si-Wei (Watching): Don’t encourage her.

Si-Yuan: Too late.

She did the sum without meaning to. It was half past ten at home. He’d be in chambers at his desk, with the door shut and his jacket on the back of the chair, reading something that mattered to someone. She knew exactly how he’d look doing it. The thought came and stayed a moment, and then it went the way a cloud goes over a window, and the room was the same room afterwards.

She put the phone down. For the first time in months she didn’t feel the need to open another conversation. She didn’t look for his messages or scroll back through old photographs or wonder whether he was awake. She finished her tea.

Then she went back to the living room and picked up the script. The words were still French, and the sentences still took effort, and there were still nights when she missed a man she’d once believed would be beside her always. But she was here, and working, and her sisters were in love, or nearly, and one of them was planning a wedding nobody had proposed.

The edges of the sky were going pale. She read the first line aloud, stumbled on a word, and tried it again. This time she didn’t apologise to the empty room. She laughed at herself and went on.

chapters.title: The Letter
chapters.desc: Two weeks home between shooting blocks. He writes her a letter by hand: two pages, all apology, no change. She doesn’t answer, but she keeps it in her script. On Saturday the 26th she’s on the university hill with her sisters when Eliana Lin walks past holding a boy’s hand in public, and Si-Yuan takes her sunglasses off to see.
chapters.epigraph: “So that’s why you smile at your phone.”
chapters.content:
The airport doors opened and the warm wet air of home settled on her skin. Paris had been cold when she left, the kind of cold that got under a coat and stayed. Here the warmth came at once, with the smell of rain on hot pavement and traffic and food from somewhere beyond the arrivals hall.

Qiao-jie was waiting by the exit with a driver, and took the suitcase out of her hand before she could object. “Welcome home. You look tired.”

“I am.”

“You don’t even sound like you want to complain about the flight.”

“I’ve been complaining in French for two months. I’m worn out with it.”

Qiao-jie laughed, which she did about twice a year, and Si-Yuan followed her out to the car. She had two weeks between shooting blocks: fourteen days at home before Paris again, the interiors and the last night sequence. Her sisters had already planned most of them. She’d promised to see them. She hadn’t promised anyone else.

✦ ✦ ✦

He found out on Tuesday morning, and not from her. A short piece on an entertainment page about the Paris film, with a photograph of her outside a cinema with Moreau, said she’d be home briefly between blocks. He read it once, and again, and knew the dates before he’d got to the end of the paragraph. Fourteen days.

Ms. Lui knocked to say his client had arrived. He asked for five minutes.

He hadn’t spoken to her in months. There had been messages, a few careful sentences, most of them unanswered, and he’d stopped sending them so often because he didn’t want his regret to become one more thing she had to manage. He knew she was working. He knew she was doing well. He knew she’d gone back to wearing red. He knew all that from interviews and photographs and the odd remark at a dinner. He knew a great deal about her life. He wasn’t in it.

That afternoon he took a sheet of writing paper from his desk drawer. He’d started a letter once before, weeks ago, and stopped after a paragraph because everything he wrote sounded like a submission establishing that he understood his own failings. He’d been trained to build arguments: find the issue, marshal the facts, meet the objections, reach a conclusion that would stand. None of it was any use here. He picked up a pen anyway.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her sisters came on Wednesday evening. Si-Jie arrived talking, with two bags of food. “I brought dinner. You’re thin.”

“I’ve been home for a day.”

Si-Jie looked at her face. “I can tell. You look different. In a good way. Your skin’s better.”

“That’s because I’ve been sleeping.”

“You’ve learned how to sleep? Paris has done wonders.”

Si-Wei came twenty minutes later with a box of pastries, kissed her cheek and looked round the flat. “Have you unpacked?”

“The clothes. Not the books. I haven’t decided where they go.”

Si-Wei nodded, as though that were a perfectly reasonable position.

They ate on the floor. Si-Jie said Arthur had become impossible to book for dinner because of a case. Si-Wei talked about a project. Si-Yuan told them about the night shoots and the language and how odd it was to grow used to a city that had made her feel like a visitor.

“Do you miss it?” said Si-Wei.

“Parts. The bakery downstairs. The walk to the set. The café where the owner remembers what I have.”

Si-Jie leaned in. “Has he got a handsome son?”

“No.”

“Shame.”

“Can you let her finish one sentence?” said Si-Wei.

“I’m gathering information.”

For the whole evening nobody mentioned Pengcheng, and Si-Yuan was grateful. It wasn’t that she wanted to pretend he’d never existed. She was tired of every conversation about her life turning into a conversation about what had happened between them. She wanted to be a woman who’d gone abroad to make a film, not a woman who’d left her fiancé. That evening they let her.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Thursday he finished it at the dining table in his flat, where she used to sit with her feet tucked under her eating soup and reading her lines out loud. The flat had become orderly in a way it never was when she was in it. Nothing on the sofa. No hair clips by the basin. He’d once thought he liked an orderly home. He understood now that he’d liked having her in it more.

It was two pages, by hand. He apologised for the banquet, and for the years before it: for the small humiliations he’d watched her bear and the larger ones he’d let happen because he’d believed keeping the peace was the same as being reasonable. He apologised for the film, for letting his mother’s opinion into a decision that should have been hers alone. He apologised for the contract he’d renegotiated behind her back the first year, and for an anniversary he’d remembered at three in the morning.

He wrote that he’d loved her, and crossed it out, and wrote that he loved her, and that saying so mended nothing.

There was another sentence he wanted to write. I won’t let it happen again. He looked at it in his head a long time, and didn’t write it. He’d said things like it before. He’d promised to talk to his mother. He’d promised to do better. He’d once told her sisters he’d never ask her to stop acting. He’d made promises in private and broken them in public, and he didn’t know how to make a new one worth believing. So he finished without one.

At the bottom of the second page he wrote: You deserved someone who would stand beside you when it was hard. I’m sorry I made you feel alone while I was sitting next to you. He signed it, and put it in an envelope, and left it on his desk all the next day in case a better way to send it occurred to him. None did.

✦ ✦ ✦

It came to her through Qiao-jie on Monday, after lunch, at a fitting. Her name was on the front in the neat straight hand she’d have known anywhere. Qiao-jie asked whether she wanted it put somewhere. Si-Yuan said no, and sat alone in the dressing room with it on her lap.

She hadn’t expected him to write. Not because she thought he had nothing to say. She’d believed he’d go on keeping it to himself. She opened it carefully.

I’ve started this several times. The first time I wrote about the banquet. The second time I wrote about the film. The third time I realised I was separating things that had never been separate.

I made you feel you had to earn a place next to me. I watched you learn my family’s rules. I watched you change how you dressed and how you spoke at dinners. I knew you were trying, and I knew my mother was hard on you, and I knew you were unhappy. And I let you keep trying. I told myself I was giving her time. I told myself that arguing would make it worse, and that you knew I loved you, and knew I didn’t agree with everything she said. I was wrong to think any of that was enough.

At the banquet I heard her. I knew it was cruel and I knew it was meant for you. I remember the chopsticks in my hand. I remember thinking that I should speak. I remember not speaking. There’s no explanation that makes it acceptable. I was afraid of embarrassing her, and of the family, and of a scene in front of people whose opinions shouldn’t have mattered more than yours.

I’m sorry you had to leave the table alone. I’m sorry you had to explain to me what I should have understood. I’m sorry the person you came with was the one who made you feel most alone.

The film was yours. You’d wanted it for years, and I let you believe that taking it would make your life with me harder. You should never have had to choose between your work and being loved.

I can’t ask you to come back. I can’t ask you to forgive me because I’ve finally found words for what I did. I only want you to know that I understand more than I did when you left. I hope the film is everything you wanted. I hope Paris is kind to you. I hope you keep wearing what you like and taking the parts you want and deciding things without wondering how anyone will take it. You deserved all of that long before you went. I’m sorry I didn’t give it to you.

She read to the end and turned the page over, though there was nothing on the back. Then she read it again. The second time she noticed how many times he’d written I understand, and I should have, and how many of the sentences were about things he’d failed to do.

There wasn’t a lie in it. That was what made it difficult. She believed he was sorry. She believed he’d spent months turning the banquet over. She believed he loved her. But the letter didn’t tell her anything he’d done differently. It didn’t say what would happen the next time his mother spoke to someone he loved like that. It didn’t say he’d chosen anything. It was the letter of a man who’d finally understood the shape of what he’d done, and hadn’t yet changed how he lived.

She could reply. She could tell him she’d read it and understood and was glad he’d said it. Then he’d answer, and she’d answer, and they’d start talking carefully, a message at a time, each of them trying not to open the wound, and sooner or later she’d find herself explaining what she needed all over again. She wasn’t ready to do that.

So she put the envelope in her script folder, the Paris script she carried everywhere, its margins full of notes in three languages, between two scenes she hadn’t shot yet. She left her phone where it was.

✦ ✦ ✦

He checked his messages that night, and the next. He’d sent it without asking for an answer, and he told himself he should be able to respect that. He argued a liability clause the next morning in a voice that never changed. At noon his mother wrote.

Mother (Senior Counsel): Your father expects you at dinner on Sunday. There are chambers matters to discuss.

Pengcheng: I’ll be there.

He’d written her two pages about the man he should have been. He was still living exactly as the man he’d always been.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Saturday morning Si-Jie wanted to go up to the university, because she said she missed it, and Si-Wei said she missed Arthur, and Si-Yuan thought both things were true. They sat on the steps by the upper courtyard in the sun, Si-Wei with a coffee, Si-Yuan in a loose white shirt with her sunglasses on and her hair tied back, Si-Jie leaning on her hands in the middle telling them about Arthur’s latest case.

She stopped in the middle of a sentence with her mouth open.

Si-Yuan followed her eyes. A girl was coming up the hill from the library: loose hair, a bag on one shoulder, and her hand in the hand of a tall young man walking beside her. They weren’t keeping a careful inch apart. Their fingers were laced together, and neither of them seemed to care who saw. It was Eliana Lin, from Arthur’s seminar in October, and the young man was the one who’d taken her hand in the foyer that day and told a hopeful boy she was with him. Wang Yu Chen.

Eliana saw them, and her face went through several things at once. “Don’t.”

“I haven’t said anything,” said Si-Jie.

“You’re about to.”

“I am about to. Are you two finally—” Si-Jie put her hand on her heart.

“Yes,” said Yu Chen.

Eliana turned and stared at him.

“You were taking too long,” he said.

Si-Jie made a noise like a kettle. Si-Yuan took off her sunglasses to see better. Si-Wei looked at Eliana over her coffee with the face of someone who’d predicted this on a whiteboard. “So that’s why you smile at your phone.”

“I don’t smile at my phone.”

“You absolutely do,” said all three of them.

Si-Jie, who couldn’t help herself, said she needed to know what she was allowed to tell people. Eliana opened her mouth, and Si-Yuan saw her decide. Yu Chen was looking at her and saying nothing at all. He was waiting to see what she’d choose.

“You can tell people we’re together,” said Eliana.

Si-Jie stepped forward and hugged her. Eliana went stiff for half a second and then hugged her back, and over Si-Jie’s shoulder Si-Yuan saw Yu Chen watching her with a look of plain pride. Not because she’d held his hand. Because she’d stayed.

They went on up towards the gates, and the three of them sat down again.

“Did you see how he held her hand?” said Si-Jie.

“Yes,” said Si-Wei.

“And she didn’t let go.”

“You hardly know them.”

“I know enough. She looks happy.”

That made Si-Wei quiet.

Si-Yuan watched them go, a hand held in daylight, a girl who’d plainly spent a long time hiding something deciding in front of three near-strangers that she wouldn’t any more. Something in her chest hurt and was glad at the same time. She’d had a love she couldn’t show for a long while, and then one she showed carefully, at the right angle, in the right colours, to people who’d never approve of it. She’d never once had it held up the hill in front of everyone by someone who’d waited to see what she’d choose.

“Arthur should hold my hand more,” said Si-Jie, leaning back.

“Doesn’t he?”

“He does. He should do it more.”

“Then tell him.”

“I shouldn’t have to tell him.”

“That’s a dangerous philosophy,” said Si-Yuan, and put her sunglasses back on, and they stayed in the sun until it got too hot.

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening the envelope slid out of her script onto the table. She’d carried it all day without thinking, up the hill and back, and the paper had softened along the folds. She didn’t reread it all. She looked at the last paragraph.

There’d been a time when she’d have wanted nothing more than for him to write that. That he was proud of her. That he wanted her to go. That she didn’t have to make herself smaller to fit into his life. She’d wanted those words for so long. Now they were on paper they seemed strangely far away.

She folded it and put it back between the scenes she hadn’t filmed. She didn’t throw it away and she didn’t put it anywhere special. She kept it, because the apology mattered, and the years had mattered, and she’d loved him. Keeping a letter wasn’t the same as agreeing to go back to the man who’d written it. Her phone buzzed.

Si-Jie (Questions): I’ve decided Arthur should propose.

Si-Wei (Watching): He hasn’t asked.

Si-Jie (Questions): I’m preparing the atmosphere.

Si-Wei (Watching): Please don’t.

She sent them a photograph of the Paris script and said goodnight, and opened it, and read.

Across town he sat at his dining table looking at his phone. He didn’t know she’d carried his letter up a hill that morning, or read the last paragraph again that night, or kept it. He knew only that he’d written two pages to a woman who’d once answered every message he sent within the minute. He wanted to believe the silence meant she was thinking. Perhaps it did. But thinking wasn’t the same as coming back, and an apology, however carefully written, couldn’t turn into a different kind of love just because it had finally found the right words.

chapters.title: Silence Is a Choice
chapters.desc: Si-Jie tells him exactly what his silence was. “Saying nothing is taking her side.” He has never once heard it put that way.
chapters.content:
He was halfway through a settlement agreement when Ms. Lui put her head round the door and said that Yen Si-Jie was in reception without an appointment, and that she’d said he’d know what it was about.

He had a call in twenty minutes and two documents waiting for his signature. He looked at the clock. “Show her in.”

Si-Jie came in with a handbag on one arm and a paper cup of coffee, her hair tied back and her face composed in a way that made him wary at once.

“Am I interrupting?”

“Yes.”

“Good. Then I won’t waste your time,” she said, and closed the door behind her.

He offered her the chair. She said she’d rather stand. He put his pen down.

“You sent her a letter.”

“Yes.”

Si-Jie put her coffee on the corner of his desk. “I’ve seen it. Not because she showed me. It fell out of her script folder while she was looking for a page, and she let me read it, and then she put it back. She didn’t say anything about it.”

“I understand.”

“No. I don’t think you do.”

She’d rehearsed this on the bus. Not because she didn’t know what she meant to say, but because she knew he was good at making a conversation sound finished before it had started. He could hear an accusation, find the reasonable part of it, acknowledge that, and answer it so that the person speaking felt heard and went home. She’d watched him do it at dinners. She’d watched him do it to her sister. She wasn’t going to let him do it to her.

“Two pages. All apology. You described everything she went through. The dinners, your mother, the film, the banquet. You even remembered what she changed about herself. You remembered she stopped wearing red,” she said.

“I remember.”

There was no admiration in it. “Of course you do. Do you know what the problem is?”

“I imagine you’re going to tell me.”

“That’s exactly what I mean. You still think this is something you can manage by listening carefully and giving the right answer. You don’t have to say it. You do it with your face,” said Si-Jie, and pulled the chair out after all and sat down.

He was silent.

She leaned forward with her hands on her knees. “The letter wasn’t bad. It was honest. I think you meant every word. But you apologised as though it was a run of unfortunate incidents. As though things happened near you.”

His jaw tightened a fraction. “That isn’t how I meant it.”

She took a breath. “I know. That’s why I’m here. Your mother didn’t just insult my sister. She told three hundred people that Si-Yuan was beneath your family and had no right to that chair. And you sat beside her and heard every word, and you knew she was waiting for you, and you didn’t say anything.”

“Yes.”

“She didn’t need you to win an argument. She didn’t need you to humiliate your mother back or stand up and make a speech about love. She needed you to make it plain that what was said was unacceptable. She needed you to stop treating her dignity as something to be weighed against your family’s comfort.”

“I should have.”

“You keep saying that. Stop saying it as if it were an answer.”

The room went quiet. Through the glass, pupils moved between rooms. A phone rang down the corridor. It was an ordinary morning.

“Can I ask you something? If your mother had said that about me, at that table, what would you have done?” said Si-Jie.

He didn’t answer at once. “I’d have objected.”

“At the time?”

“Yes.”

“Even if it embarrassed her? Even if the whole room heard?”

“Yes.”

Si-Jie leaned in. “Then why was it different with Si-Yuan? Was it because she’s an actress?”

“No.”

“Because she’s not from a legal family?”

“No.”

“Because you thought she’d put up with it?”

His eyes moved, and she saw it, and sat back.

“There. You thought she’d understand. You thought she knew your mother was difficult, and knew you loved her, and knew you didn’t agree. So you let her absorb it. You let her be humiliated because you were sure she’d understand why you couldn’t defend her.”

“I wasn’t unable to defend her.”

“Then what were you?”

He didn’t answer.

“Comfortable,” said Si-Jie.

It landed harder than she’d meant it to, and she watched it land and didn’t take it back. “She learned your family’s rules. She remembered everyone’s likes and dislikes. She changed her clothes and the way she talked. She learned when to smile and when not to. She kept going to those dinners when she cried in the car afterwards. Do you know how many times she asked me whether your mother might come to like her? Neither do I. I stopped counting. She used to tell us about the dinners. Not all of it, because she didn’t want us to hate your family. She’d tell us one thing your mother said, and then straight away explain why she probably hadn’t meant it like that. She was always explaining your mother to us.”

He looked at the desk.

“When she turned the film down she didn’t tell us it was because she was frightened of upsetting you. She told us she didn’t want to make difficulties. She’d wanted it since she was twelve.”

“I know. I thought she should decide for herself.”

Si-Jie looked at him. “She did decide. She decided by what she thought you could bear. That isn’t choosing. Do you know how maddening it is to hear you say you know? You know everything now. What she wanted, what she needed, what you should have done. You can describe it beautifully. You could write another two pages. She doesn’t need another letter explaining her own life to her.”

His voice was quiet. “What does she need?”

She picked up her coffee and didn’t drink it. “I don’t know. And I’m not going to give you a list so you can tick it off and come back with proof. I know you. You’ll want to know what the correct step is. I’m not here for that. I’m here because you still don’t understand what your silence did.”

He waited.

She held his eyes. “People like to pretend that saying nothing means they haven’t taken a side. That if they don’t agree with the person being cruel, but don’t disagree out loud either, they’re somehow neutral. When someone’s being humiliated and you sit next to the person doing it, your silence doesn’t protect the one being hurt. Saying nothing is taking her side.”

There was no force in it. No raised voice. A sentence, said plainly, with nowhere in it for him to stand.

He stared at her. For a few seconds he didn’t seem to have heard. Then his eyes went, slowly, to the empty chair beside the window, where Si-Yuan used to sit with her feet up complaining that his room was too cold. He remembered her in it after the photograph, after the studio had reached for the morality clause and he’d answered them in thirteen pages, looking at him as though he’d hung the moon. He’d thought the banquet was the same. He’d thought that not agreeing with his mother was enough. He’d thought that because he loved her, she’d know whose side he was on.

She’d been sitting next to him, and he’d said nothing.

Si-Jie watched it reach him, not all at once but in pieces. The chopsticks in his hand. His mother’s voice. Three hundred people. Si-Yuan’s face turning towards him, and the second she’d waited, and the moment he’d looked down. He’d always thought of his silence as a failure to step in. He had never once considered that to her it had sounded like agreement. He’d never once heard it put that way.

“I didn’t agree with her,” he said.

“She didn’t know that.”

“I was going to speak.”

Si-Jie stood up. “But you didn’t. You thought you could wait till later. Speak to your mother in private. Apologise to Si-Yuan afterwards. You thought if you loved her enough in private she’d understand why you couldn’t stand next to her in public. And she was sitting there alone while you did the sum.”

He looked up at her. “Does she still love me?”

It came out before he could stop it, and it was the first thing he’d said all morning that didn’t sound like a lawyer establishing a fact. It sounded like a man frightened of the answer.

Si-Jie looked at him a long moment. “I think so. That isn’t the same as wanting to come back. She kept your letter. Don’t make that into more than it is. She didn’t throw it away, so it mattered to her. It doesn’t mean she’s waiting.”

At the door she turned. “My sister doesn’t need someone who understands her suffering after it’s happened. She needs someone who doesn’t let her suffer alone in the first place.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t move for several minutes. Ms. Lui came to say his next client was waiting and he asked for ten.

On the desk were his copy of the letter, the Paris contract Qiao-jie had once sent him to look over and he’d never returned, and a memorandum from his father about the running of chambers. Three pieces of paper, three separate matters. He found himself looking at them as one matter.

He’d been privately proud of the letter. Not of what was in it, but that he’d managed at last to put it into words. He’d thought it was a step. It was. But he’d mistaken naming a failure for correcting it. He’d apologised for being silent. He hadn’t touched the arrangements that had made his silence so easy.

His mother still expected him at Sunday dinner, and he still went. He still took her instructions without asking why. He still let her decide which matters were fit to be discussed and which were to be left alone. He’d never told her that what she’d done was unacceptable. He’d never said it in the way that counted, in a way that changed what he did next.

Mother (Senior Counsel): Your father says you’ve been hard to reach. Don’t forget Sunday. There’s a good deal to discuss.

He read it and noticed, for the first time, how naturally he’d already been planning to go. Not because he wanted to. Because he always had. He’d called it duty, and respect. He’d never asked whether obedience was still respect when it asked him to accept the humiliation of someone he loved.

✦ ✦ ✦

His father came by that evening, as he’d started doing, with no particular reason and a box of the almond biscuits from the shop by the courts. Pengcheng told him what Si-Jie had said. All of it, including the sentence.

His father listened without interrupting, and then leaned back in his chair. “She’s right.”

Pengcheng looked at him.

His father turned a biscuit over in his fingers. “You’ve always believed that if you don’t openly support a thing, you haven’t supported it. People don’t hear silence as a principle. Your mother made a remark. You sat beside her. Everyone saw. Do you know what I thought when you told me she’d gone? I thought you’d finally been handed a consequence you couldn’t negotiate.”

It was blunt, and he didn’t soften it.

“You’ve always had time. Time to think, time to wait until your mother was in a better mood, time to speak privately afterwards. Si-Yuan was living through those moments while you waited for them to pass. You can’t go back and stand up at that table. But you can decide what sort of man you’ll be when the next hard moment comes. Not for her, and not to win her back. For you. And stop deciding things by whether she’ll reward you for them.”

For once Pengcheng had no answer.

✦ ✦ ✦

In Paris it was the middle of a long afternoon in a rehearsal room when her phone buzzed.

Si-Jie (Questions): I saw Pengcheng today. At his chambers.

Si-Yuan: Were you nice?

Si-Jie (Questions): No. I told him the truth. About his silence.

Si-Yuan didn’t ask what exactly. She could imagine. Si-Jie had never been any good at hiding what she felt when someone she loved had been hurt.

Si-Yuan: You didn’t have to.

Si-Jie (Questions): I know. You don’t have to do anything with it. I just didn’t want him to go on thinking that being quiet meant he hadn’t chosen.

She read that twice. The light over the head table came back, and the click of chopsticks on porcelain, and the way he’d looked down. She’d never needed him to say anything extraordinary. One sentence. One refusal. One sign that she wasn’t alone.

She put the phone in her bag and picked up the script. In the scene, Ning Yue had to speak to a man she loved after finding out he’d known the truth all along. She read it through without saying it aloud, and turned the page.

She wouldn’t ask him what he was doing now. She wouldn’t ask whether he’d finally spoken to his mother. She wouldn’t make her sisters into messengers. If he changed, he’d have to do it without expecting her to watch. And if he never did, she’d still have to live.

✦ ✦ ✦

That Sunday he went to dinner, because he’d said he would, and sat through it, and noticed everything. He noticed his mother correct the housekeeper twice. He noticed his aunt agree with every opinion before it was finished. He noticed the chair at the end of the table nobody sat in now, where Si-Yuan used to sit, and that nobody mentioned it. He noticed himself agree, out of habit, to a client lunch his mother had arranged without asking him, and the moment after he’d agreed, he noticed it again.

He said nothing that night. But at home afterwards he opened his laptop and found the chambers papers he’d been putting off for years. His mother’s hand in client relationships that should have been the partners’. Decisions taken at her dining table and minuted later. The assumption, everywhere, that he’d one day take a larger part of it without questioning how it was built. He’d always known it was complicated. He’d also known it wasn’t quite right. He made notes until after midnight: no letter this time and no apology, only a list of what needed to be decided, and who by, and with which papers.

It wasn’t a transformation. He hadn’t become brave in one conversation. But for the first time he was looking at the thing he’d always used as his excuse, and beginning to understand that changing it was going to cost him.

✦ ✦ ✦

At the end of May an invitation to the next family dinner came through his mother’s secretary, with nothing in it to show that anything had been said by anyone. He had a meeting that evening that he could have used. He didn’t use it.

Pengcheng: I won’t come this time.

She rang within ten minutes. “Why not?”

“I don’t want to.”

“That’s not a reason.”

He looked out at the harbour from his window. “I know. I’ll come when there’s something the family needs me for. I won’t sit at dinners and behave as though what happened in December was acceptable.”

“You’re making this very difficult.”

“I know.”

“Your position in this family—”

“I’ve a meeting, Mother. I’ll speak to Father later.”

He rang off. His hand stayed on the phone. He didn’t feel victorious. He felt unsettled, almost sick. He’d stepped out of a room he’d always lived in, and he couldn’t see where the next door was.

But he’d said no. Not to win her back, and not because he thought she’d hear of it. He’d said it because he should have said it long before, and because at last he understood that his silence had never been the absence of a choice. It had been a choice. He’d only been comfortable with who paid for it.

chapters.title: His Mother’s House
chapters.desc: He goes to his mother’s house and doesn’t bow. He says one sentence and she laughs at him. He leaves without the second sentence.
chapters.content:
The house hadn’t changed. He noticed it on the steps. The stone was polished, the hall smelled faintly of sandalwood, the flowers on the console table had been replaced but the vase was the same one that had stood there all his life. Everything was in its place, including the silence.

His mother had asked him to come that afternoon. Not invited: asked. The message had come through the family secretary with a time and an expectation and no explanation, and he’d answered that he’d be there. He hadn’t told his father.

The housekeeper opened the door. “Young Master.”

“Good afternoon, Auntie.”

“Madam’s in the study. She asked that you wait in the reception room first.”

He went through. The reception room was where the portrait hung: his grandfather in his judicial robes, painted the year he was raised to the bench, looking down at the room with the expression of a man who’d never once been asked to explain himself. Si-Yuan had bowed to it at her first New Year, lower than she’d ever bowed to anyone, and come out to the car and asked him whether she’d done it right.

For thirty years he’d lowered his head to it every time he came into this room. It was so much a part of coming into the house that he’d never thought of it as a thing he did. He stood in front of it now with a folder under his arm and found that he was looking at it straight. He didn’t bow. He noticed that he hadn’t, and waited to see whether he’d feel he ought to, and didn’t.

He remembered her that first afternoon, the twenty-second of January, the first day of the year, in a cream coat she’d bought for the occasion, stopping for half a second under the portrait and asking whether his grandfather had been a judge. Chief justice, he’d told her, low, and she’d looked up at the old man again and gone still, and then she’d bowed, and he’d watched her do it and thought how lovely she was and said nothing else at all. It hadn’t occurred to him that she was frightened. It hadn’t occurred to him that he could have told her she didn’t need to bow so low. He’d thought the bow was the house’s business, not his.

The housekeeper came back and said Madam would see him.

✦ ✦ ✦

He knew the way without being shown, along the corridor to the room at the back where his mother kept her correspondence and the family papers and the books she still quoted on the history of chambers. He’d spent much of his childhood in that room. At fifteen he’d sat across that desk while she took his arguments apart and taught him that composure wasn’t the absence of feeling but the ability to keep feeling from interfering with judgment. He’d learned it well. Perhaps too well.

She was at her desk in a pale blouse and pearls, with her reading glasses low on her nose, and she didn’t look up.

“You’re late.”

He looked at the clock on the wall. “I’m on time.”

She turned a page. “Your father says you’ve been difficult.”

“Father and I have talked.”

“Not enough, apparently. Sit.”

He didn’t. She looked up then and took him in: the dark suit, the tie, the folder.

“What’s that?”

“Papers about chambers. A proposal to review how client responsibilities are allocated and who decides.”

She took off her glasses. “I didn’t ask you to bring papers.”

“I know. I thought we should discuss it.”

“I asked you here because there are things you’ve been avoiding. Your refusal to come to dinner. Your refusal to answer my calls. Your father’s unnecessary involvement in decisions that belong in this house.”

“Those decisions belong to the partners.”

She gave a small smile with no belief in it. “You’ve become very particular about procedure.”

“I always was.”

“Not when it suited you.”

It was quiet, and he knew what she meant. For years he’d accepted the informal arrangements when they were to his advantage: her introductions, her clients, her dinners where things were decided and minuted later. He’d hardly questioned any of it while he could do his work inside it. Now that he was questioning it she took it as an insult.

“Is this because of that girl?”

“Her name is Si-Yuan.”

“I know her name.”

“Then use it.”

She looked at him, and for a moment he thought she’d answer the correction. Instead she picked up her glasses again. “You still behave as though I’d committed some unforgivable crime.”

“You humiliated her.”

“I’ve already told you I was speaking generally.”

“You weren’t.”

“Must we go through this again?”

He put the folder on her desk. She opened it and read the first page and the second, and closed it.

“You’ve discussed this with your father. Without me.”

“It’s a matter for chambers.”

She folded her hands on the folder. “I’m aware of what it’s a matter for. You’ve been given opportunities other people spend their lives trying to get. Your grandfather’s name. Your father’s support. This family. You’ve benefited from all of it. And now you come here to tell me how to conduct myself?”

“No.”

“Then what exactly do you want?”

✦ ✦ ✦

He’d come to say two things. The first was the folder: it had documents and precedents, and it could be argued and amended and minuted. The second had none of that protection. He’d rehearsed both in the car. He’d thought through her objections to the first, and what he’d say if she accused him of resentment.

He hadn’t prepared for the feeling of being a boy again, standing in front of this desk waiting to find out whether he’d given the right answer.

He heard his own voice come out level. “I want you to understand that Si-Yuan isn’t someone you can go on treating as though she has to earn the right to be respected.”

His mother looked at him. Then she laughed.

Not loudly. It was a short, incredulous sound, the laugh of someone who’d heard something so naïve she couldn’t help herself. “Pengcheng. You came all this way to tell me that?”

“I came to tell you it was wrong.”

She shook her head, still smiling. “Do you hear yourself? You’re a grown man. You’re counsel. You’ve spent years learning how the world works, and you’re standing in my study talking about respect like a boy in a television drama.”

“She was your guest.”

“She was your fiancée.”

“Yes.”

His mother laughed again, lower. “You’ve become very sentimental since she left. Do you imagine she’ll come back because you’ve decided to defend her now? Do you think she’s waiting for a declaration? She’s in Paris. She has her career. She has her sisters, and I’m sure they tell her every day how lucky she was not to marry into this family.”

“We weren’t married.”

“Fortunately,” said his mother, without a pause.

His face changed, and she saw it.

“Don’t look at me like that. You know perfectly well she was never suited to us.”

✦ ✦ ✦

There was the second sentence. He’d brought it with him all the way from his flat. He’d meant to tell her that she wouldn’t speak about Si-Yuan like that again. That if she couldn’t admit what she’d done, he’d stop pretending things between them were ordinary. That the family’s name didn’t give her the right to decide who was owed dignity. He’d meant to say that he’d spent his life mistaking her approval for the measure of his own decisions, and that he’d failed Si-Yuan because he was afraid of disappointing her, and that he wouldn’t make that choice again.

But she was already looking at him with the face he remembered from childhood: half amused, half disappointed, the face that made an argument childish before it had begun.

He was twelve, standing at this desk with a school essay in his hand, and she was laughing at one of his conclusions and telling him the world didn’t reward people for being idealistic, and he was going back upstairs to rewrite it. He was sixteen, and she was telling him that an excellent argument was worthless if it didn’t persuade the people who mattered. He was twenty-five, at breakfast, and she was telling him that girl was a logical match for no one.

He’d always found a way to make his choices fit inside what she expected. Even when it hurt someone else.

Now he was twenty-eight, in front of her desk, and the old instinct came back as if it had never been away. Explain. Clarify. Find the words she’d accept. Make her understand.

She pushed the folder across the desk to him. “Take this back. If your father wants to discuss chambers he can arrange a meeting of the partners.”

He’d come to say two things. He’d said one, and she’d laughed. He could say the second now. He knew what it was. He could force it out even if she laughed again. But the words seemed to have gone a long way off. He’d believed for so many years that the right sentence would change her mind. He was only beginning to see that she didn’t necessarily want to be persuaded. Perhaps she only wanted him to stay where he’d always been.

He picked up the folder. “All right.”

She looked satisfied. “Good. I hope you’ll think more carefully before you do things that affect the family. And think about your future while you’re at it. You can’t spend your life waiting for someone who’s already decided to go. Your father isn’t getting younger. Chambers needs stability.”
