There was no warmth in it. No sign she remembered what she’d done, or wondered about the woman who’d spent two years trying to make herself welcome in this house. Only impatience that her son’s life had become inconvenient.

“Goodbye, Mother,” he said, and went.

He passed the portrait on his way out and didn’t bow to that either. It was such a small thing that he nearly didn’t notice it. He’d come in without lowering his head to anyone and he was leaving the same way.

“Will you stay for dinner, Young Master?”

“No, thank you, Auntie.”

✦ ✦ ✦

It was only in the car that he realised his hands were shaking. He put the folder on the passenger seat and sat behind the wheel and didn’t start the engine. He could still hear her laugh. It was the same laugh he’d known all his life. It wasn’t angry, or even especially cruel, only dismissive, the laugh of someone for whom what he’d said was too small to answer.

There’d been a second sentence, and he hadn’t said it. That frightened him more than the laugh. He’d gone in believing he’d learned at last to speak, and when she laughed, he’d gone straight back into the silence he knew.

His father rang that evening while he was still in the car outside his own building.

“Did you see your mother?”

“Yes.”

“The papers?”

“Briefly.”

“And the other thing?”

He was quiet, and his father understood. “You didn’t say it.”

“She laughed. I told her what she’d done was wrong, and she laughed.”

“Your mother often laughs when she doesn’t want to answer.”

“I know.”

“Then why did you stop?”

He could have said he was tired, that he didn’t want another argument, that the conversation had stopped being useful. All of it would have been true. None of it was the reason. “I don’t know.”

His father breathed out. “You’ve spent your whole life learning how to talk to your mother. Perhaps you never learned how to disagree with her.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Upstairs he put his jacket over a chair and stood at the kitchen counter with a glass of water. The copy of his letter lay on the dining table. He’d kept it so he’d remember what he’d said. He wondered now whether he ought to keep a record of what he hadn’t.

He took out a notebook and wrote: I told her Si-Yuan deserved respect. She laughed. I left without saying what I’d come to say.

He thought of Si-Yuan at the banquet. She hadn’t left because she couldn’t speak. She’d left because she finally understood she couldn’t go on asking him to speak for her. He’d spent months trying to understand that moment, and today he’d had a small taste of it: standing in front of someone whose approval he’d spent his life seeking, knowing what had to be said, and finding he couldn’t say it.

The difference was that his mother wasn’t the one he’d promised to protect. Si-Yuan was. And she’d stood up alone. He closed the notebook.

✦ ✦ ✦

Two days later the senior clerk wrote to him. His mother had asked for the review to be postponed indefinitely. The email was polite and procedural, and it didn’t mention their conversation.

He forwarded it to his father with one line. We should go ahead as planned. He didn’t ring his mother. He didn’t ask whether she was upset. He didn’t withdraw it.

It was a small thing. It didn’t undo the afternoon in her study, or the two years Si-Yuan had spent reshaping herself for his family. It didn’t make him able, all at once, to say everything he should have said. But he didn’t retreat from it.

That night he opened her conversation. His last message was months old. He wanted to tell her he’d gone to the house, and said her name, and hadn’t bowed, and that his mother had laughed. He wanted to tell her he was trying.

He didn’t. She hadn’t asked for reports. He’d promised himself he wouldn’t make his efforts one more thing she had to carry.

In Paris she was learning lines for the next day. She didn’t know he’d been to the house, or said her name there, or left without finishing. None of it reached her yet, and he was beginning to understand that it couldn’t depend on her seeing it.

He was beginning to understand something harder too. Refusing to bow was one thing. Standing straight in front of the person who’d spent your whole life teaching you to lower your head was another.

chapters.title: Paris
chapters.desc: He flies to Paris without telling anyone. He waits outside the set in the rain. She walks past him. He waits again the next night.
chapters.content:
He didn’t tell anyone he was going. Not his father, not Ms. Lui, not the friend who’d once offered to arrange a meeting with her management. He booked the flight himself, and a hotel near the location for three nights, Monday to Wednesday, and packed one small case. He had no appointment, no invitation, and no reason to think she’d agree to see him. He went anyway.

He spent most of the flight reading documents he’d already read twice and looking out at the cloud. He’d imagined this journey a good many times. In some versions he met her in a café. In others he waited till she’d finished work and asked whether they could talk. Sometimes she was angry. Sometimes she was quiet. Once, in a weak moment, he’d imagined her smiling when she saw him, and he’d stopped allowing himself that one. He had no right to it.

Paris was grey when he landed. He left the case by the wardrobe, washed his face, changed his shirt and checked the address. The production had been announcing its schedule publicly: an old building on the east side of the city, exteriors all week. He hadn’t asked anyone to confirm she’d be there. He wanted to see her. That was all.

✦ ✦ ✦

The rain began a little after six. At first it was light enough that people walked through it without opening their umbrellas. Then the wind turned and it came down properly, hammering the pavement and the metal barriers outside the production entrance.

He stood under the narrow awning of a shut shop across the street, and his coat darkened at the shoulders. The crew had begun loading the vans: cables, folding chairs, plastic crates. He knew none of them.

Then a group came out of the entrance, and he saw her at once.

She had a dark coat on over her costume and her hair tied loosely back, and a girl from make-up was holding an umbrella over both of them and talking. Si-Yuan listened and nodded, and then laughed at something.

He stood still. He hadn’t heard that laugh in person for seven months. He remembered it from his kitchen, from the noodle stall, from the passenger seat when she’d made fun of the way he said some English word. It was exactly the same laugh. He didn’t know whether that made it better or worse.

She stepped away from the group with her bag on her shoulder and came towards the pavement. Towards him.

“Si-Yuan.”

She didn’t hear. A car went by between them and threw water over the kerb, and she turned to avoid it.

He said it again, and this time she heard. Her steps slowed. For a moment she didn’t turn. Then she looked across the wet street and found him.

He’d prepared for anger. He’d prepared for surprise, and for her asking why he’d come. He hadn’t prepared for her face, which showed neither. It was recognition, and a brief stillness, and her hand tightening on the strap of her bag. She looked at him for a few seconds. Then she lowered her eyes, turned up the collar of her coat, and walked on past him without a word.

He didn’t follow. He watched her go to the car waiting at the end of the street. The driver opened the door. She got in. The car pulled away into the rain, and he stood under the awning until the crew had gone.

✦ ✦ ✦

At the hotel he hung his wet coat over a chair and stood in the middle of the room. He’d imagined a great many first meetings. He hadn’t imagined her walking past. But she had, and he’d let her.

He thought about what she’d looked like. Not thinner, as he’d feared from the photographs. Steadier. She’d walked down that pavement in the rain as though it were hers, and in a way it was: she knew which kerb flooded and where the driver would be waiting and which of the crew would hold an umbrella over her without being asked. Seven months ago she’d needed him to tell her which fork to use at his mother’s table. She didn’t need anyone to tell her anything here. He’d wanted that for her in his letter. Seeing it was something else.

He typed I saw you today and deleted it. She knew he’d seen her. She knew he’d come. There was nothing useful in telling her what she already knew.

For the first time since landing he thought about changing his flight. It would be easy. He could tell himself he’d tried and she’d made herself clear and there was no point staying where he wasn’t wanted. But he knew that wasn’t why he’d come. He’d come to see her. He’d seen her. Now he had to accept that seeing her didn’t give him any right to speak to her.

He sat at the window until late, watching the rain on the roofs.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Tuesday he had nowhere to be, and it was the strangest feeling he’d had in years. At home every hour of his life had a purpose. Here there was nothing to do except wait for the chance of seeing someone who might not want to see him.

He answered the urgent emails in a café and shut the laptop. He walked along the river. He went into a bookshop and looked at a shelf of French novels whose titles he could half read. He passed a bakery with an old woman behind the counter and remembered an interview he’d translated in February, in which Si-Yuan had told a journalist about the woman in the bakery under her flat who always gave her the wrong change. The journalist had asked why she didn’t correct her. Si-Yuan had said the woman was old and probably tired, and the change was always in her favour anyway, and she’d come to think of it as a small daily present. He’d read it at two in the morning in his chambers with a dictionary, and smiled at it, and been unable to tell anyone why.

He hadn’t known, then, that she was building a whole life in a city where nobody knew him. He knew it now, walking through it.

✦ ✦ ✦

He went back to the location early. The rain had stopped and the pavement was dark and shining. A few people were smoking by the entrance, talking French. He hadn’t brought flowers. He’d thought about it and decided against: flowers would be one more gesture she’d have to answer, one more object with an expectation folded inside it. He had no gift and no speech. He waited.

The crew came out in twos and threes. Then she came out in a cream jumper under a long coat with her hair loose, talking to a man from the production with a script in her hand. She looked tired. He saw the small crease between her brows and the way she pressed her lips together when she listened and the movement of her fingers along the edge of the pages. He knew all of them. He’d once been the person she’d tell what was wrong. Now he was a man across the street with a familiar face.

Her eyes found him. This time she didn’t stop. She said something to the man beside her and kept walking, and he didn’t say her name. She passed the place where he stood with her eyes straight ahead, and got into the car, and was gone. At the corner his phone buzzed.

Father (Reads Everything): Are you still in Paris?

Pengcheng: Yes.

Father (Reads Everything): Work?

Pengcheng: No.

Father (Reads Everything): Then I hope you know what you’re doing.

He didn’t. There was no procedure for this, no sequence of steps that would guarantee a conversation, no amount of patience that would turn her decision into something else. He could wait. He could leave. He could send another apology. None of it would make her owe him anything.

✦ ✦ ✦

That night, in the back of the production van, Si-Yuan had her script open on her knee and wasn’t reading it.

Qiao-jie, who’d flown out for the last fortnight of the shoot, was answering emails beside her. “Straight home? You’ve an early call.”

“I know.”

“You’ve been very quiet.”

“I’m tired,” said Si-Yuan, and Qiao-jie looked at her for a second longer, and let it be.

Two evenings now. The first time she’d been so surprised that her body had stopped before her mind caught up. She’d known him at once, through the rain, by the way he stood. The second time she’d known he might be there, and she’d seen him before she reached the pavement, and she’d thought about stopping. Not because she was ready to speak. Because some part of her still answered the sight of him: the part that remembered waiting for his car, and knew the exact feel of his hand round hers, and had once been happy to see him at the end of a long day.

She hadn’t known what she’d say. Perhaps nothing. Perhaps she’d have asked why he’d come without telling her. Perhaps she’d have cried, which she wasn’t going to do in front of the crew.

The scene for tomorrow was one where Ning Yue walked away from a man who’d spent years asking her to stay. She’d underlined one line. You can’t keep asking me to come back to a place where I was never allowed to belong. She looked at it under the passing streetlights until it stopped meaning anything, and then shut the script.

✦ ✦ ✦

He packed on Tuesday night. He folded his shirts and put the papers in the side pocket and checked the wardrobe. His flight was in the morning. He hadn’t spoken to her. He hadn’t asked anyone to arrange anything. He’d waited outside the set two evenings, and she’d walked past him twice.

Ms. Lui wrote, late, to say the partners had confirmed Friday’s meeting. He told her to prepare the papers. Then he lay in the dark. He’d learned, in two days, that being close to someone didn’t mean he was allowed back into her life.

✦ ✦ ✦

At the airport in the morning he sat by the gate with his case beside his chair and opened her conversation one last time.

Pengcheng: I’m leaving Paris today. I won’t come to the set again unless you want me to. I’m sorry I came without telling you.

He nearly deleted it. He sent it. It showed as delivered, and he didn’t wait for an answer.

They called his row. People stood up round him and began to shuffle towards the desk with their passports and their bags. He stood up too, and picked up the case, and joined the end of the queue.

The man in front of him was on the phone telling someone he’d be home for dinner. A child was crying, not unhappily, two places further up. The queue moved. He was three people from the desk, and then two, and he looked down at the boarding pass in his hand and thought: I’ve done this before. I’ve done exactly this.

He’d sat at a table and waited for the difficult moment to pass. He’d sent a careful message afterwards and called it respect. He’d told himself that leaving was the decent thing, that not asking was a kind of courtesy, that she’d made her position clear and the gentlemanly thing was to accept it and go home. Every one of those things was true. Every one of them was also the easier thing. He’d never once in his life stayed in the place where it was hard, where the answer might be no and he’d have to stand there and hear it.

She hadn’t said no. She hadn’t said anything. She’d walked past him, and he’d let her, and he’d told himself that letting her was respect.

“Sir? Your boarding pass.”

He looked at the woman at the desk. He looked at the pass in his hand.

He heard himself say it quite calmly. “I’m sorry. I’m not travelling.”

She looked at him with the patience of someone who’d seen everything. “Your bag’s in the hold, sir?”

“No. I’ve only this.”

“Then you’re free to go,” she said, and he stepped out of the queue, and walked back up the jet bridge against the people coming down it.

✦ ✦ ✦

At the studio Si-Yuan read his message in a break between set-ups. Once, and again. She could ask whether he’d gone. She could tell him he shouldn’t have come without warning her, or that seeing him had made it hard to think for the rest of both evenings. She locked the screen and put the phone back in her bag.

The assistant director put his head round the door. “Si-Yuan, we’re ready.”

“Coming.”

She walked onto the set and did the scene, and walked away from a man who’d spent years asking her to stay, and did it again from three angles, and Moreau said it was the best she’d done it. She didn’t tell him why.

She didn’t know the plane had gone without him. She didn’t know that while she was doing the scene for the fourth time he was in a taxi going back into the city with his case on the seat beside him and the hotel on the phone, asking whether the room was still free for one more night.

It was. He took it. Then he sat on the bed, and for the first time since Monday he didn’t know what she would do, and he found he could bear not knowing. He’d stay. That evening he’d go back and stand across the street, and if she walked past him a third time he’d let her, and he’d still be there.

chapters.title: The Third Night
chapters.desc: On the third night she stops. On the bridge she kisses him to make him leave; he doesn’t. Her rented flat, nothing settled: explicit, angry, hungry, her on top, him finally saying her name.
chapters.epigraph: “I’m not doing it on this bridge.”
chapters.content:
He was across the street again on Wednesday, under the same awning, with no case this time and no coat over his arm, only his hands in his pockets and the evening coming down blue over the roofs.

She saw him before she reached the pavement. Two nights she’d walked past. She’d told herself she’d made her decision, that she didn’t need to know why he’d come, that seeing him didn’t oblige her to speak. She’d read his message at lunch and believed it. He was meant to be in the air. She stopped.

The crew went round her on both sides with their crates. Qiao-jie, a step behind, looked at her and then across the street, and said under her breath that she’d tell the driver to wait. Si-Yuan didn’t answer. She crossed the road.

He straightened when he saw her coming. “Si-Yuan.”

“You said you were leaving.”

“I was. I didn’t get on the plane.”

She let out a short breath that wasn’t a laugh. “You didn’t get on the plane.”

“I got to the desk, and I couldn’t.”

The crew were watching, and she didn’t want to do this under a shop awning in front of the people she worked with. “Walk with me. Not here.”

They walked without speaking to the river and onto the bridge she crossed most nights going home. The water went by underneath, breaking the lights into pieces. People passed behind them talking French. Halfway across she stopped and turned to him.

“You don’t get to do this. Come whenever you like and stand outside where I work until I notice you, and decide that means you’ve earned something.”

“I don’t think I’ve earned anything.”

“Then what are you doing?”

“I wanted to see you. I’ll go if you tell me to.”

“I’m telling you to.”

He nodded. He didn’t move. Neither did she.

She hated that he was still so composed. Even here he seemed to have folded every feeling into something small enough to carry without its showing. She wanted him angry. She wanted him to say something unreasonable, that he’d missed her so badly he couldn’t sleep, that he’d come because he couldn’t bear another month of not knowing whether she was tired or whether she still wore red. She wanted him to say something that would make it easier to hate him.

“You look well,” he said.

“Don’t. Don’t tell me I look well. Don’t tell me the film’s beautiful. You don’t get to stand on a bridge and talk to me like we’re still together.”

“All right.”

The wind lifted some of her hair and she pushed it behind her ear without thinking. He watched her hand. He’d done that for her once, when she was too busy talking to notice. He didn’t reach for her.

“I’m sorry,” he said.

She shut her eyes. “I know you’re sorry. I know you regret it. I know you love me. I know you lie awake thinking about what you should have done. And you keep coming to me with it as if being sorry changed what happened.”

“It doesn’t.”

“Then what do you want?”

“I know what I want. I don’t know what I’ve any right to ask for.”

She looked at him: the shadows under his eyes, the coat he’d plainly worn too many hours, his hair untidier than she’d ever seen it in daylight. He looked tired. She hated that she noticed. She hated that she still wanted to ask whether he’d slept.

She took hold of the front of his coat with both hands and kissed him.

There was nothing gentle in it: two nights of walking past him and seven months of swallowing it and everything she’d been afraid she’d feel if she ever stood this close to him again. She meant it to be the end of something. She meant him to feel it and go home.

For one second he didn’t move. Then his hand came up and stopped just short of her waist, and he kissed her back, and it was nothing like the careful man who’d once asked her whether she was sure. When she let go of his coat they were both breathing badly.

“Now go. That was so you’d go,” she said.

He looked at her. “I’m not going.”

“I kissed you so you’d leave.”

He didn’t raise his voice. “I know. I’m still not going. I’ve left every time it was hard. I’ve waited every time it was hard. I’m not doing it on this bridge.”

She looked at him. Then she turned towards the far end of the bridge.

“Come on, then.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Her flat was on the third floor of a narrow building with a staircase worn smooth in the middle of every step. She climbed with the keys already in her hand and didn’t look back, and he came up behind her. At the landing she opened the door and went in, and he stopped on the threshold.

“Are you coming in?”

“Are you sure?”

“Don’t make me say it twice.”

He came in. She shut the door and didn’t move away from it. It was a small flat: the narrow kitchen, the table by the window with her script spread over it, a cardigan on the back of a chair, two mugs in the sink. It was so plainly hers that he stood looking at it.

“Don’t look at the furniture.”

“I’m looking because you live here.”

That unsettled her more than she’d expected. “Do you know what I hate most? You’re so careful now. Asking whether you can come in. Whether I’m sure. Where was all this care when it mattered? You were careful with everyone except me. Careful not to embarrass your mother. Careful not to upset the family. Careful not to turn a birthday into a scene. And I was sitting next to you.”

“I know.”

“I waited for you to look at me.”

“I know.”

“You looked at your plate.”

He shut his eyes, and there was nothing he could say that would take the picture away. When he opened them he said the one thing she’d never heard from him.

“I was afraid. Of what would happen if I stood up to her in front of all those people. Of what it would do to the family and chambers and to me and her. And I let you pay for it. I kept telling myself I’d deal with it later, privately, that I could protect you without making it worse. I wasn’t protecting you. I was protecting myself from what it would cost to choose you.”

Si-Yuan went still. For a moment she didn’t seem able to breathe properly.

“Do you know how long I wanted to hear that? Two years. Two years of wondering whether I was asking too much. Thinking if I were a bit more patient, a bit more polite, a bit less noticeable, she’d look at me one day and think I’d do.”

“You always—”

She pressed her fingers to her forehead and lowered them. “Don’t. Don’t tell me now that I was always good enough. I don’t want to be good enough for your family any more. That’s what I learned when I left.”

She was standing right in front of him. She took hold of his shirt.

“Si-Yuan.”

“Stop saying my name like that.”

“Like what?”

“Like you missed me.”

“I did.”

“Then you should have missed me while I was sitting next to you,” she said, and pulled him down, and kissed him so hard his back met the door.

✦ ✦ ✦

This time there was no hesitation in him. His hand went to her face and the other to her back, and she rose on her toes and dragged him closer, and he met her with a hunger that had been held down for seven months. It wasn’t the easy, practised closeness of his flat. Nothing in it assumed they knew what came next. She kissed him as though she were furious with him for being there and more furious that she wanted him there, and he kissed her like a man who’d spent seven months trying not to remember the shape of her mouth.

She got his coat off his shoulders and let it fall. She pulled his shirt out of his trousers and got her hands under it, onto his skin, and felt him go rigid and then shudder. He said something against her mouth that might have been her name and might have been nothing.

“Tell me to stop and I’ll stop,” he said.

“I’ll tell you.”

She pushed him back against the door with her palm flat on his chest and opened his shirt button by button, not quickly, and kissed the base of his throat where his pulse was going hard. He let her. His hands were on her waist and they stayed there, and she understood that he was letting her decide every part of it, and that made her angrier, and wanting him made her angrier still. She bit his shoulder. He made a sound she’d never heard him make.

They didn’t get as far as the sofa. Her script came off the table when she caught it with her hip and fell open on the boards, and a cushion went, and she pulled him down to the floor and pushed him onto his back on the rug, and knelt over him and pulled her jumper over her head. He looked up at her. She put her hand over his eyes.

“Don’t look at me like that.”

“Like what?”

“Like you’re afraid I’ll disappear.”

He took her hand away, gently, and held it. “I am.”

“I’m here. So look at me properly.”

He looked at her properly. She undid his belt and he lifted his hips to help her, and she got out of the rest of her clothes without grace, and neither of them laughed. She took him in her hand and he shut his eyes and opened them again at once. Then she sank down onto him slowly, all the way, and stopped there with her hands spread on his chest and her hair falling round both their faces, and for a moment neither of them could move.

She moved first. She set the pace and kept it, slow and then not slow, and he let her, his hands on her hips not pulling or steering, only holding on. She watched his face. She’d never watched it like this, from above, in a lamp’s light, with nothing hidden in it. Everything he’d ever folded small was there: want and grief and something close to fear, and under it all the plain fact that he loved her, which she’d known and which had never once been enough.

“Si-Yuan,” he said.

There was no apology in it, no question, nothing he was afraid to ask for. Only her name, said out loud the way he’d never said it in bed in two years, and she put her hand over his mouth because she couldn’t bear it and then took it away because she couldn’t bear that either.

“Again.”

“Si-Yuan.”

She came with her hands braced on his chest and her head bowed and his name broken in her throat, and he held her through it, and then turned them both with his arm round her back so that she was under him on the rug, and looked at her, and waited.

“Yes. Don’t you dare stop.”

He didn’t. He moved in her with his forehead against hers and said her name every time she said his, and when he finished he did it with his face in her neck and her arms locked round him and her heels hard against the backs of his thighs, and lay on her afterwards breathing like a man who’d run a long way.

✦ ✦ ✦

Much later she was sitting on the floor with her back against the sofa in her own old T-shirt, and he was beside her with one knee up and his hand on the boards near hers. The room was a wreck. A glass had gone over and left a small lake by the table leg. The script lay open and bent. Her hair was in knots.

“You’ll have to help me clear this up,” she said.

“I will.”

She said it, and then heard herself, and her voice went tired. “You always say things like that. Sorry. That was unfair.”

“It was accurate.”

She leaned her head back. “It’s strange. I know your face. I know your voice and how you breathe asleep and how you take your coffee and how you fold your shirts. And I don’t know what to do with you any more.”

“I know.”

“No, you don’t.”

He accepted that.

She said it to the ceiling. “I used to imagine you coming to Paris. When I first got here. Not to take me home. Just to see where I lived. I was going to show you the bakery downstairs and the woman who always gets the change wrong, and the grocer’s where I keep buying the wrong yoghurt. I was going to walk you along the river and complain about the cold, and you’d tell me I should have brought a thicker coat. Then I stopped imagining it.”

She’d smiled faintly while she said it, and by the end the smile had gone.

“I knew about the bakery. You told a journalist. I read it in February with a dictionary.”

She turned her head and looked at him, and he couldn’t tell what she was thinking.

“I don’t know whether I can forgive you. I don’t know whether I want to. I don’t want to go back. Not to your mother’s house, or those dinners, or being your fiancée with everyone looking at me like something you’ve brought home to be approved.”

“You won’t have to.”

She moved her hand towards the rug. “Don’t promise things tonight. Don’t tell me it’ll all be different. And don’t think that because of that, anything’s mended.”

“I don’t.”

“Good. Because I still remember.”

He reached for her hand slowly enough that she could move it away. She let him take it. His thumb went once across her knuckles, and the familiarity of it closed her throat, and for a moment she leaned her head on his shoulder. He didn’t pull her closer. He stayed still and let her decide how much of herself she’d give him.

It was nearly two when she stood up. “I’ve an early call.”

“I should go.”

Neither of them moved. Then he got up and found his shirt where she’d thrown it, and she picked up the cushions, and he dressed by the door while she watched.

“Don’t come to the set tomorrow. Don’t wait outside. And don’t come here unless I ask you to.”

“I won’t.”

“Pengcheng.”

He looked up.

She didn’t know what she’d meant to say. “Goodnight.”

“Goodnight, Si-Yuan.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She shut the door behind him and stood with her forehead against it for a long time. Then she righted the glass and mopped the floor and picked up the script. It had fallen open at tomorrow’s scene, and caught between the pages was a small folded square of paper she’d forgotten she’d kept: an old note in his hand from some night years ago when he’d worked late and she’d waited up. Eat something before you sleep. I’ll ring when I’m done.

She sat on the edge of the sofa with it. She’d kissed him. She’d wanted him. She’d let him stay, and she’d been the one on top of him, and he’d said her name. None of that meant she was going back. None of it changed what he’d done.

Downstairs he walked out into the cool night and didn’t look up at her window. He didn’t message her from the hotel. He didn’t tell her he loved her. Not because he didn’t. Because he was beginning to understand that love wasn’t something he could keep putting into her hands and expecting her to carry.

For the first time in seven months they’d been close enough to touch. In the morning they’d still have to decide what to do with everything that was left between them.

chapters.title: Not Yet
chapters.desc: She doesn’t come home. He goes home anyway, and starts. He leaves her his schedule every day, for her to read or not.
chapters.epigraph: “I’m taking responsibility for my own life.”
chapters.content:
She didn’t come home. He’d understood that before he left Paris. He’d understood it when she told him not to come to the set, and not to wait outside, and not to come to her flat unless she asked. He understood it again on Thursday morning when he woke in the hotel and there was nothing from her: no breakfast, no question about his flight, no asking him to stay another day.

On the third night she’d let him in. She’d kissed him and held his face and been the one above him on the floor of her rented flat, and he’d said her name. Then she’d stood up and said she had an early call, and he’d dressed by the door. She hadn’t asked him to stay. He hadn’t asked her to come back. That was all they had. Nothing agreed. Nothing promised.

From the airport he sent her one message.

Pengcheng: I’m going home now. Thank you for letting me in. I won’t come to the set or the flat again unless you ask. I hope the rest of the shoot goes well.

He didn’t sleep on the flight. He didn’t think about the way she’d kissed him, or about the rug. He kept thinking about her sitting against the sofa afterwards saying that she knew his face and his voice and how he folded his shirts and didn’t know what to do with him any more. He had no answer to that. Perhaps he’d finally stopped trying to have one.

✦ ✦ ✦

His flat was as he’d left it. The curtains were shut. A thin film of dust lay on the table by the door. He put the case by the bedroom and stood in the living room without turning on a light. The second cup was in the cupboard. Her hair clip was in the drawer of his desk. The small cushion she always put behind her back was on the sofa, still flattened in the middle.

He’d thought of selling the place, on the worst nights, when every object in it seemed to be about a life he’d lost. He’d never meant it. Now he was home and it was still his, and he went to the window and opened the curtains and then the windows, and the warm air came in with the city in it, a horn, a voice shouting across from the building opposite, a drill somewhere a long way off.

He unpacked. He put his clothes away and washed the two shirts he’d worn in Paris. Then he cooked, for the first time in that kitchen in weeks, and ate at the dining table alone and washed the plate afterwards and put it away. He didn’t send her a photograph of it. He didn’t tell her he was home. She didn’t need to know. He had to learn to live here without expecting her to walk in.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Monday Ms. Lui looked up from her desk as he came in. “Your mother rang on Saturday. She asked whether you’d come to the family meeting on Thursday.”

“I won’t.”

Ms. Lui wrote it down. “She also asked whether the review could be put off again.”

“No.”

She looked up at that. He’d answered before she’d quite finished.

“Has my father confirmed it?”

“Yes. The partners have the revised agenda.”

“Then make sure the reviewers have everything they need. If my mother has something to say about the review, she can put it through the senior clerk.”

When Ms. Lui had gone he sat still. It wasn’t dramatic. Nobody would write about it. His mother would call it one more unnecessary complication. But he’d said no, and he hadn’t then spent ten minutes drafting an explanation to make it easier for her to bear.

He opened his diary. The day was full. He looked at it a while, and then he did something he couldn’t have explained to anyone, and copied it into a message.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her phone buzzed beside her script while she was in the make-up chair with her hair being pinned.

Pengcheng: Monday 4 August.

8.30 Chambers
9.00 Client conference
11.00 Chambers review
12.30 Lunch with the team
2.00 Call with Singapore
4.00 Junior’s draft
6.30 Home

There was no greeting, no question, no photograph, no explanation. She read it again. Then she put the phone away.

The make-up girl caught her face in the mirror. “Everything all right?”

“Yes. Ready.”

Qiao-jie came in later with tea and a new call sheet and asked whether she’d eaten, and Si-Yuan said she’d eat after this scene, and Qiao-jie said that was the third time she’d said so today, and Si-Yuan promised that this time she meant it.

That evening, at the little table by her window with a bowl of noodles and an interview playing on her laptop, the phone went again.

Pengcheng: Client conference ran long. Moved the draft to tomorrow. Leaving now.

She looked at the clock on the laptop and worked it out. He’d said half past six. He was twelve minutes late, and he’d told her. She nearly smiled. It was such a Pengcheng thing to report.

There was something strange about seeing his day laid out in front of her. For two years she’d known his schedule only where it touched hers: a dinner he couldn’t make, a meeting that ran late, a case that meant he’d sleep in chambers. She’d never known what his days looked like when she wasn’t waiting at the end of them. Now he was telling her. He wasn’t asking her to understand, or to wait. He was only telling her.

She finished her noodles. She didn’t answer.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next morning there was another, and the morning after that.

Pengcheng: Tuesday 5 August.

8.30 Chambers
9.00 Junior’s draft
10.30 Court
1.30 Client conference
3.00 Father, about the review
6.30 Home

She read it waiting for the car, in a loose blue shirt with her script in her bag, and typed You don’t have to send me this, and deleted it. She typed Why are you doing this? and deleted that too. She locked the phone and got in. She didn’t owe him an answer. He’d said so. She was beginning to suspect that was the point.

He sent it every morning. He never asked whether she’d read it, or whether she wanted him to go on. He didn’t send pictures of his lunch or the view from his window or long accounts of what he’d achieved. Only the day. When something changed that mattered, he said so. When it didn’t, he didn’t.

He began going home at a reasonable hour. Not every night: there were still hard cases and late calls. But he stopped treating every unfinished piece of work as a reason not to go back to his flat. He ate at his own table. He slept in his own bed. He rang his father on Sundays. He went to every meeting of the review and didn’t let his mother put them off because she disliked where they were going. The changes were small enough to be ordinary. That was exactly why he kept them up.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the Friday his father came to his room and found him marking a document in red.

“You look better.”

“I’ve been sleeping.”

“Your mother’s unhappy. She thinks you’re making things difficult for everyone.”

“Is the review going ahead?”

“Yes.”

“Then nothing’s being made difficult. A review’s being done.”

His father studied him, and sat down. “Usually when you disagree with your mother you spend twenty minutes explaining why. Today you answered the question. Have you seen Si-Yuan?”

“In Paris. She didn’t ask me to stay.”

“Did you ask her to come home?”

“No. She doesn’t want to.”

“Good. Don’t confuse respecting her decision with waiting for her to change it.”

“I don’t.”

His father looked at him until he looked away. “You spent a long time believing that if you waited quietly enough, things would settle. Your mother would accept her. Si-Yuan would understand. The family would find room for everything. Things did settle. Not the way you wanted. So don’t make her responsible for giving you a reason to change.”

He got up and went to the door, and turned there, and told his son to go home that night, since he had a perfectly good flat.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the Saturday she slept late after a shoot that had gone past midnight, and found the usual message, and under it something new.

Pengcheng: Saturday 9 August.

10.00 Case files
2.00 Father
6.00 Home

Pengcheng: I hope you have a quieter day.

It was the first time he’d added anything that wasn’t the day. She looked at it a long time. She typed You too. Her thumb hovered. She sent it.

He was in the middle of a case file when it came. Two words. His face didn’t change much. But his hand stayed round the phone a moment longer than it needed to.

Pengcheng: Thank you.

He put the phone down and went back to work. He didn’t send anything else. He didn’t ask whether she’d slept. He let the two words be exactly what they were.

✦ ✦ ✦

Si-Jie rang the next week, late in Paris. Si-Yuan was on the floor with her back to the sofa and a new script on her knees.

“How’s Pengcheng?”

Si-Yuan’s hand stopped on the page. “Why are you asking me?”

“Because he’s been sending you his diary. You told me on Sunday.”

She’d forgotten saying it. “He has.”

“Do you answer?”

“Twice.”

“Do you want him to keep sending it?”

Si-Yuan thought about it honestly. “I don’t know.”

Si-Jie didn’t push, which was so unlike her that Si-Yuan almost asked whether she was ill. “That’s fine. You don’t have to decide what he means just because he’s trying. And you don’t have to punish yourself for missing him.”

“I’m not.”

“Good,” said Si-Jie, and told her a long story about Arthur cooking soup, which had somehow ended up tasting like an interrogation, until Si-Yuan was laughing.

Afterwards she scrolled back through his messages. The fourth, the fifth, the sixth, every day. Meetings, lunches, court, the time he left. He’d sent every one, and she’d answered twice, and he’d never once complained.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the third Sunday there was something more after the day.

Pengcheng: I’ve been going home at night. I’m sleeping. The review at chambers is going ahead on time. You don’t need to reply. I only wanted you to know that I’m taking responsibility for my own life.

He looked at it after he’d sent it and wondered whether he’d said too much. Whether even that was another way of asking to be noticed. He’d have taken it back if he could.

She read it that night at her table with a bowl of fruit and tomorrow’s scene. I’m taking responsibility for my own life. It wasn’t a declaration. It wasn’t a promise to her. It wasn’t trying to persuade her of anything.

Si-Yuan: That’s good.

He was washing a plate when it came. He dried his hands before he picked up the phone. Then he finished the washing up.

✦ ✦ ✦

At the end of August the shoot grew heavier: nights, press, scenes that ran through the weekend. She left before it was light and came home after dark. Sometimes she read his messages at once. Sometimes she didn’t open them until the next morning. Sometimes she forgot to answer for days. He never asked.

One night after a hard day she came in and found the day waiting, and under it one line.

Pengcheng: The hearing went well. I hope your shoot did too.

She’d been crying on camera for nearly four hours. Her make-up had been taken off and put back so many times her face felt tight. She sat down on the sofa.

Si-Yuan: It was hard today.

She hadn’t meant to say it. She sent it anyway. He picked up the phone at once.

Pengcheng: I’m sorry. A difficult scene?

Si-Yuan: Yes. We did it again and again.

Pengcheng: Did you eat?

She looked at the screen and nearly laughed. Of course. Of everything he could have asked, he’d asked that.

Si-Yuan: Yes. You?

Pengcheng: Yes. I cooked. Rice and steamed fish and greens.

Si-Yuan: You still make too much rice.

For the first time that evening he smiled.

Pengcheng: I know.

He didn’t tell her he still cooked for two some nights. He didn’t tell her he’d nearly set out a second bowl. He put the phone down.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the last day of August she had a day off, and stood at her window in the morning with the sky clear over the roofs and his day in her hand.

Pengcheng: Sunday 31 August.

10.00 Chambers, alone
2.00 Father, at home
6.00 Home

She’d been in Paris more than six months. She’d worked and learned and made friends. She could order anything and ask any question and walk across the city without a map. She’d also missed someone. Both things were true.

She scrolled back to the first one, the morning after he’d gone home. She’d thought he’d send it once, perhaps twice, and then find some other way to ask for her attention. He hadn’t. He’d kept sending it, and somewhere in the month she’d stopped feeling she had to answer.

Si-Yuan: Have a good day.

Pengcheng: You too. Enjoy your day off.

She went out for coffee, and to a bookshop she’d passed a dozen times without going in, and found a novel she’d wanted for a year.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came home at six that evening, after his father, with something his father had said still in his head that he’d have to decide about by the morning. He cooked, and watered the plant on the balcony, and ate. He looked at the phone once. Nothing. He didn’t feel disappointed. Or he did, and he no longer let it become a reason to ask her for something.

He thought about the bridge, and her kissing him as though she wanted to punish him for missing her, and her head on his shoulder afterwards without a single promise in it. He missed her. That hadn’t changed. But missing her didn’t mean he had to reach for her every time it got hard to bear.

He typed Goodnight, and deleted it. Then the phone went in his hand.

Si-Yuan: I went to a bookshop and found a novel I’ve wanted for ages.

Pengcheng: Which?

She told him, and sent a picture of the cover, and he looked at it a long time.

Pengcheng: The cover’s beautiful.

Si-Yuan: It’s better inside.

Pengcheng: I believe you.

That was all. Nobody said they missed anyone. Nobody asked when they’d see each other. Nobody mentioned what came next.

Before she slept she looked at September in her calendar, and then at his messages, every day of August lined up one under another. She didn’t know what she wanted them to become. She didn’t know whether she’d ever wear the ring again, or whether the man who’d looked at his plate could become someone she trusted. But she’d stopped feeling she had to answer, and he’d stopped asking her to.

She was in Paris. He was at home. They weren’t engaged, and they weren’t anything else either. There were only two people who still knew each other’s habits: one learning to stand up without being asked, one learning that she could miss him without going back.

Every morning there’d be a small record of his day waiting for her. She could read it or not. He’d send it anyway.

chapters.title: His Firm
chapters.desc: He resigns from his family’s chambers and puts his own name on a door: Yang and Associates, alone. His mother cuts him off. He sends Si-Yuan a photograph of the new door.
chapters.content:
The first person he told was his father, on the last Sunday in August, in the small dining room of his parents’ house while his mother was at a friend’s. His father’s tea went cold beside his hand. Between them was a thin folder: a letter of resignation, a draft lease, and the registration papers for a practice that didn’t exist yet.

His father read the first page twice. “You’ve decided.”

“Yes.”

“You’ll lose your place in chambers. Your mother’s support. Some of your clients.”

“I’ve allowed for that. I won’t take anyone who belongs to chambers. Anyone who wants to stay stays. Anyone who comes to me of their own accord I’ll deal with by the rules.”

“You’ve thought about the professional side.”

“For months.”

“And the rest of it?”

He didn’t answer straight away.

His father looked at the folder rather than at him. “Your mother will take it personally. She’ll see it as a rejection of everything your grandfather built.”

“I know what my grandfather built.”

“Do you?”

He’d grown up in those chambers. His father had walked him round them as a boy: the library, the old case files in their glass cabinets, the portrait of the chief justice in the hall. He’d learned to read a pleading before he learned to drive. The name had opened doors for him long before he’d earned the right to walk through them, and he’d always known it. What he’d also believed, for years, was that loyalty meant staying where you’d been put.

“He built a practice to be respected. Not to make everyone in the family depend on it. And I don’t want to spend the rest of my career pretending that being Mother’s son is the same thing as being good at this,” said Pengcheng.

His father looked at him, and nodded. “All right.”

“You agree?”

His father pushed the folder back across the table. “I didn’t say that. I said all right. You’re old enough to make your own decisions. I won’t make this one for you. Just make sure the name on the door is one you can live up to.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He took the letter in on Monday the first of September.

The receptionist said good morning, Counsel Yang, as she’d said it every morning for six years. He went past the hall and the portrait and down the long corridor where he’d learned his work, and Ms. Lui was at her desk outside his room.

She looked at the envelope in his hand. “Is that—”

“My resignation.”

Her face changed. “Does Madam know?”

“Not yet. I’ll tell her myself.”

He put the envelope on his desk and began to clear it. Books he’d collected, his own notebooks, a photograph of his father at some dinner years ago. The chambers’ files he left. His own things went into two boxes.

Ms. Lui stood in the doorway. “May I ask whether you’re going because of the review?”

“No. I’m going because I want to build something of my own.”

“Will you be all right?”

“I think so.”

She smiled a little. “Then I wish you luck.”

“You’ve been very good to me,” he said, and meant it. He hadn’t always been easy. He’d been exacting, and often expected people to know what he wanted without his telling them. He hoped he’d learned something about that too.

✦ ✦ ✦

His mother had the letter twenty minutes later, and was waiting in the chambers conference room with it open on the table.

“Sit down.”

He stayed standing. “Mother.”

“Have you lost your mind? Resigning from these chambers without a word to me?”

“I’m telling you now.”

“You think that’s sufficient?”

“For the purposes of the rules, the letter’s sufficient.”

She pushed it towards him. “Don’t speak to me as though I were a client.”

He pulled out the chair after all and sat. “I’m setting up my own practice.”

“You’ve a senior place here. A name people respect. Clients who’ve trusted this family for forty years. Your grandfather spent his life building this. Your father has spent his keeping it. And you’ll throw it away because you don’t like being told what to do?”

“I don’t want my professional decisions to need the family’s approval.”

“Don’t lie to me. You think I don’t hear what people say? That you’ve been impossible since that actress left you?”

“Her name is Si-Yuan.”

“I’m not discussing her.”

“Then don’t bring her into this.”

The room went completely silent.

“You’ve changed,” his mother said.

“Yes.”

“Is this what she wanted?”

“She didn’t ask for any of it. This isn’t about her. It’s about the fact that I should have done it years ago. I should have been able to disagree with you without working out what it would cost me first.”

“You’ll lose half your clients.”

“Some will go.”

“You’ll lose the family’s name behind you.”

“I’ll still have my own.”

She smiled coldly. “Your name means nothing without this family.”

“Then I suppose I’ll find out.”

✦ ✦ ✦

It came faster than he’d expected. By Wednesday three clients had told chambers they’d stay. Two asked to see him privately about following him. One company whose work had come to the family for more than twenty years withdrew from him entirely. His mother hadn’t needed to ring anyone. The name had done it for her.

At the new premises, with plaster dust still on the windowsills, he went through the figures with an accountant and Ku Ka-ho, a young junior from another set who’d rung him the day the news got round and asked, rather breathlessly, whether he’d need anyone.

“That’s a big hole,” said Ku.

“Yes.”

“Are you worried?”

“Of course.”

Ku looked surprised to hear him say it.

Pengcheng went on before Ku could say anything kind. “We’ll cut the first year’s projections. We’ll be slow to hire, and I want the reserve protected. And we won’t take work we can’t do properly just to fill the gap.”

“Understood. Sir, do you regret it?”

He looked at the figures. “No. I regret how long it took me to see why I had to.”

✦ ✦ ✦

By the middle of September the office was ready: a modest floor of a modern building, with a reception desk, two meeting rooms, a small library with half its shelves still empty, and three rooms with doors. There were no judges’ portraits, no old wood handed down from anyone. The walls were pale and the furniture was plain, and he’d chosen all of it himself. He’d argued with the contractor about the lights in the meeting room. He’d sent back three designs for the reception desk. Ku told him nobody cared about the meeting-room lights. He said he did. He said a client who’d come to tell a stranger the worst thing that had happened to them ought at least to be able to see the stranger’s face, and Ku stopped arguing and went to find the contractor.

He’d hung nothing on the walls yet. Ku had suggested his practising certificate in a frame, and the photograph of his grandfather that every member of the old chambers kept somewhere in his room. He’d said no to both. He wanted the walls to stay pale for a while, until there was something on them that belonged to this place and not the other one.

On Monday the fifteenth the sign went up beside the glass doors. Plain dark letters on a pale panel: Yang and Associates. No crest. No second surname. Nothing to say where he’d come from. Only his name.

He stood in the corridor while the fitter came down the ladder.

“Is it straight, sir?”

He looked at it. “Yes.”

“Spacing all right?”

He looked again. “It’s fine.”

Ku came out with two coffees and handed him one. “Well?”

“It looks good.”

“Only good?”

“Very good.”

“That’s the most excited I’ve heard you all week,” said Ku, and went back inside laughing.

He’d thought the moment would feel like more. Relief, perhaps. Pride. What he felt instead was the weight of it settling into place. The sign was there and his name was on it, and there was nobody behind it now to stand between him and whatever came. That, he thought, was the point.

✦ ✦ ✦

His mother rang before lunch.

“You’ve opened the office. People have already sent me photographs.”

“Then you’ve seen it.”

“Do you find this amusing?”

“No.”

“I’ve spoken to the senior partners. Your access to chambers’ resources ends today. You’ll not represent chambers in any capacity. The family allocation stops. And I will not support this practice of yours in any way.”

“I didn’t ask you to.”

Her voice went colder. “You’re making a very serious mistake. Don’t come to me when you find out how hard it is to stand on your own.”

He looked through the glass wall at Ku, who was laughing at something the receptionist had said. “I won’t.”

She rang off. It had taken less than four minutes. He’d spent most of his life trying to make conversations with her end well: explaining, softening, adjusting his tone, hunting for the last sentence that would make her understand. This time there wasn’t a last sentence. She’d cut him off, as he’d known she would. Knowing hadn’t made it painless. He turned the phone off and went back to the draft in front of him.

✦ ✦ ✦

At lunchtime he sent Si-Yuan a photograph of the door with the sign beside it, and two words.

Pengcheng: Yang and Associates.

He thought about adding an explanation. That he’d resigned. That his mother had withdrawn everything. That clients had gone, and he was frightened about the first year, which he’d never have said to anyone in the office. He didn’t add anything.

She was between set-ups, in a folding chair by the monitor with tomorrow’s pages, when it came. She looked at the photograph for several seconds. The lettering was plain and dark. There was no family crest, nothing about his mother’s chambers. She made it bigger and saw a corner of a reception desk through the glass. She could picture him looking at it: checking the spacing, asking whether the letters were level, looking for longer than he needed to before saying it was fine. She smiled.

Si-Yuan: Your own firm?

Pengcheng: Yes. I resigned from chambers.

Si-Yuan: What happened?

He hadn’t expected her to ask. He answered honestly.

Pengcheng: My mother cut me off. Some clients have gone. We’ll be building it from nothing.

The dots appeared and went and came back.

Si-Yuan: Are you all right?

He couldn’t answer at first. It was such a small question. It was the first time in nine months she’d asked about something happening to him.

Pengcheng: I’m all right. It’s hard, but I expected it. I’m glad I did it.

She looked at the door again. She thought of a man so careful not to contradict his mother in front of three hundred people. She thought of him standing in her flat saying he’d been afraid. She thought of him going home and doing this without asking her to watch.

Si-Yuan: I’m glad you did it too. The door looks good.

He’d expected her to notice the door. He hadn’t expected what he felt when she said she was glad.

Ku knocked on the frame. “Mr. Yang? Your first client.”

“Thank you,” he said, and picked up the file, and went out to the man waiting in reception with his papers in a plastic folder, and shook his hand, and took him into the meeting room with the lights he’d argued about, and shut the door.

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening the day came to her as it always did.

Pengcheng: Monday 15 September.

8.30 New office
9.30 Sign goes up
11.00 First client
2.30 Practice papers
4.00 Accountant
6.00 Home

Pengcheng: It was a good first day.

She was on the sofa with her feet under her, and she looked at the door once more and studied his name a long time. She remembered the first morning she’d walked into his office to sign a contract: a big desk, a dark suit, a man looking at her as though he could already tell she’d be trouble. She’d asked him whether he was always that boring. Now he had a door of his own, with no family name over it and no mother deciding who came through it.

Si-Yuan: You should be proud.

He read it standing in front of the sign with his keys in his hand and the lights off behind him.

Pengcheng: I am.

✦ ✦ ✦

There was no dinner for him that night with family or old colleagues. There was no call from his mother. His father sent one line.

Father (Reads Everything): The door looks right. I hope the first day went well.

He ate alone and stood at his window afterwards. He’d lost chambers. He’d lost his mother’s support. He’d lost clients who’d trusted the name more than they trusted him. He hadn’t lost his work, or his own name. And he hadn’t sent her the photograph because he expected her to come back. He’d sent it because she’d once been the person he wanted to tell when something mattered. He still wanted to tell her. Perhaps that was all right, so long as he never turned the wanting into something she owed him.

In Paris she didn’t write anything more. She didn’t say she wished she could see it, or promise to visit. But before she went to bed she saved the photograph, not in the folder with the old pictures of them, but in a new one, which she named September, and put the door inside it on its own.

There was no ring on her finger and no agreement between them. She was still in Paris and he was still at home. But in the city he’d lived in all his life there was a new door, and this time his was the only name on it.

chapters.title: Her Premiere
chapters.desc: The Paris film premieres. He buys a ticket like anyone else: row thirty, seat eleven, the back. Her performance is reviewed as the best of her career. In the lobby she finds him.
chapters.content:
The announcement came to him in October in a trade newsletter Ku had forwarded with no comment at all, which was Ku’s way of commenting.

The Other Side of the River. A film by Étienne Moreau. With Yen Si-Yuan. Paris premiere, Friday 14 November.

He read it twice, and then he opened the cinema’s booking page. Most of the house had gone to the production and the distributors and the critics and the invited. A few hundred seats had been released to the public. He chose one, and paid for it, and the confirmation came back with the seat in bold: row thirty, seat eleven, rear stalls. Near the back. Close to the aisle. Not a good seat.

He could have rung the production company. He could have asked Qiao-jie. He could have found someone who knew someone and come away with an invitation by the end of the afternoon. He did none of it.

Ku came in with a revised contract and glanced at the screen before Pengcheng closed it. “You’re going?”

“Yes.”

“Have you got an invitation?”

“I bought a ticket.”

Ku looked at him, and then smiled. “Good seat?”

“Row thirty.”

“That’s practically the street.”

“I noticed,” said Pengcheng, and didn’t smile, but when the door had shut he looked at the confirmation again. He hadn’t told her. He didn’t know whether she’d want him there. If she didn’t, she could walk past him. He’d still have watched the film.

✦ ✦ ✦

He flew on the Thursday and slept badly in a hotel near the river, and on Friday evening he walked to the cinema in a charcoal suit with no tie and his dark overcoat, and got there forty minutes early, which she’d have laughed at.

The foyer was already full. Photographers by the doors, journalists with microphones, guests in knots round people from the production. A poster on an easel by the stairs showed her in profile against the dark blue of the Seine, looking just past the camera. It was the first time he’d seen her face so large. There was something lonely in it. He stood in front of it a moment, and moved on, and showed his ticket, and went in.

Row thirty was in the half-dark at the back. People were still edging along the rows murmuring apologies. He sat with his coat over his knees and found he could see the whole house from there. He could also see the empty seat on the aisle beside him. Years ago he’d have bought two without thinking. She always wanted the aisle. She hated asking people to move when she wanted to get out.

The lights went down.

✦ ✦ ✦

The film opened without music. A woman stood by a river holding a phone. The city behind her was grey. The wind took the loose ends of her scarf. He forgot to breathe for a moment.

She was different. Not in any way he could have described. The face was hers and the voice was hers, but she didn’t seem to be doing anything for the camera. She seemed to be living somewhere and letting it watch.

Ning Yue had come to Paris thinking she could start again. She worked in a bookshop and rented a room over a bakery and walked by the river at night. She wasn’t written as anyone remarkable. She was lonely and stubborn and often wrong. She said the wrong thing and was sorry later. She could be kind, but not always patient. She wanted to be understood without having to explain herself, and she was slowly learning that wanting a thing wasn’t the same as knowing how to ask for it.

In a café an older woman asked her whether she missed home.

“Sometimes.”

“Your family?”

“Sometimes.”

The woman waited. Ning Yue looked out of the window. “Sometimes I miss who I was before I knew I had to leave.”

He looked down at his hands. He remembered the evening she’d told him about Paris, her excitement, and the way she’d looked at him waiting to find out whether he wanted her to go. He’d told her to make the right decision. She’d made it. And he’d let her carry what it cost.

Halfway through, someone rang Ning Yue whom she hadn’t spoken to in months. You never heard the voice on the other end. Only her.

“I’m fine. No, I’m working. I don’t know.”

She listened, and smiled a little, and her eyes didn’t change at all.

“Don’t ask me to come back just because you’ve finally learned how to ask.”

His hand tightened on the programme. He knew it was fiction. He knew it was Moreau’s line and Ning Yue’s life and nothing to do with him. He also knew she’d lived close enough to it to understand every word, and that it was the line the whole house had gone quiet for.

The last scene was at dawn by the river. Ning Yue walked alone. A message came; you never saw the screen, only its light on her face. She read it. She didn’t answer. She put the phone in her pocket and walked on, and the camera stayed behind her, and the river was quiet, and it ended.

For a moment nobody moved. Then someone near the front began to clap, and it spread backwards row by row until it reached him, and he stood up with everyone else. When the lights came up she came out onto the stage with Moreau and the cast, in a dark red dress with her hair swept back and plain earrings, the colour of it vivid against the black curtain. He remembered a dress like it that she’d stopped wearing to his mother’s table, and a pair of red earrings he’d bought her once, and her telling him that red made her feel she could be seen.

She looked entirely at ease. He clapped until his palms hurt.

Moreau thanked the crew and the distributors and the weather, and then turned to her. “When Si-Yuan auditioned I knew she could play Ning Yue. I didn’t know whether she’d be brave enough to let her be unpleasant sometimes. Selfish and confused and angry, and still worth loving. She surprised me. She didn’t ask to be liked. She asked to understand.”

She thanked him in French, and the rest of them in English, steadily, and then looked out at the house.

“I think Ning Yue taught me something about leaving. At the start she thinks leaving is the same as being brave. Later she finds out it’s only part of it. You also have to decide what life you want once you’ve gone, and let yourself enjoy it. Thank you for watching her.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The first reviews were up before the foyer had emptied. He read the first one leaning against a pillar near the cloakroom, and then the full piece: Yen Si-Yuan gives the performance of her career. The critic praised Moreau’s restraint and the film’s patient eye and its refusal to make loneliness sentimental, and then gave his longest paragraph to her: controlled without coldness, open without self-pity, with a rare gift for letting a scene go on after the words had stopped. Another said she was the film’s heart. A third called the last scene one of the most affecting pieces of acting of the year.

He read them all. He’d seen her work before. He’d sat three rows behind her at her first award, pretending to be only her lawyer. He’d told her she’d done well after a hard night shoot when she’d come to a noodle stall still in costume and borrowed slippers. But this was different. The people writing these didn’t know she left food when she was tired, or talked to herself over scripts, or checked the weather every morning without ever changing what she wore because of it. They were seeing her only as an actress. They were right. She’d done something remarkable, and he was proud of her, and he wanted to tell her, and he didn’t know whether he should.

Across the foyer she’d finished with the photographers and was standing with Moreau and two people from the distributor, listening. Someone called her name and she turned and smiled and stood for a picture. He stayed where he was: close enough to see her, far enough that she could leave without having to know he’d come. He hadn’t come to interrupt her evening. He’d come to see the film. He’d seen it.

He took his coat off the back of a chair and turned towards the side doors. It would be easier. She wouldn’t have to decide whether to speak to him.

“Pengcheng?”

He stopped, and turned. She was a few metres away with a programme in her hand, and her smile had gone, and something quieter had taken its place.

“You came.”

“I bought a ticket.”

“Where?”

“Row thirty. Seat eleven.”

Her eyebrows went up. “That’s miles away.”

“I know.”

“Why didn’t you tell me?”

“I didn’t know whether you’d want me here. I thought if I sat at the back you could have your evening without worrying about me. I wanted to see the film. That’s all.”

She looked at him a long moment. “Did you like it?”

“I thought you were extraordinary. There were whole scenes where I forgot it was you.”

She looked down. “Thank you.”

“And the last scene—”

“Don’t. Don’t review it for me.”

He nearly smiled. “All right.”

She smiled too, briefly, and he saw it. Someone was calling her for another photograph. She turned and said she’d be a moment. He stepped aside to let her go.

She didn’t go. “Are you leaving?”

“I was going to.”

“Can you stay a little?”

“Of course.”

She told the photographer five minutes. Then she came to him across the foyer and stopped right in front of him, and for a second she looked unsure, and he didn’t reach for her and didn’t ask what she wanted. He waited.

She put her hand on his cheek and kissed him.

Not on a bridge in the rain, or in her flat after a fight, or out of anger or loneliness. In the middle of the foyer, in front of everyone, with the reviews already out and the photographers still there, because she’d decided to.

He went completely still. Then his hand found her waist and he kissed her back, gently, as though he still couldn’t believe she’d chosen it. For a few seconds there wasn’t any foyer.

When she drew back she stayed close. “You’re allowed to kiss me back properly.”

“I did.”

“You were being careful.”

“I was surprised.”

“Would you rather I hadn’t?”

“No,” he said, before she’d finished asking.

He pushed a loose strand of hair off her cheek.

“Congratulations. You worked so hard.”

“Do you know that?”

“I read the interviews. I saw the production photographs. I watched every minute.”

“Even the slow parts? There are a lot of slow parts.”

“I noticed,” he said, and she laughed.

✦ ✦ ✦

She still had people to see. Qiao-jie was looking for her and Moreau was talking to a journalist by the doors. He waited by a tall window and she came back a few minutes later with two glasses of water and gave him one.

“Your hair’s shorter.”

“Yes.”

“Your suit’s nice. Did you buy it for tonight?”

“No.”

“So you wore it for me.”

“I wore it because it seemed appropriate.”

There was something in her face he hadn’t seen for eleven months, something almost like teasing, and he felt it go into his chest and stay there. “Still boring. How’s the office?”

“Busy. We’ve lost some and gained a few.”

“Do you regret it?”

“No.”

“Even with your mother?”

“No. She rings sometimes. If there’s something professional, it goes through the proper people. Otherwise I leave it.”

She nodded. “That’s good. I looked at the photograph of your door a lot. I saved it.”

He couldn’t say anything at all for a moment.

“Don’t get emotional,” she said.

“I’m not.”

“You are.”

“Perhaps a little.”

A journalist came up to her before she could tease him further, and asked whether she felt the film was a turning point, and she said every film changed you a little and this one had taught her to be patient with a woman who didn’t know what she wanted. Then he asked whether she believed people could begin again with someone they’d left.

She didn’t look at Pengcheng. “I think people can change. But beginning again isn’t something one person can decide for two.”

When the journalist had gone, Moreau came and kissed her on both cheeks and told her to be proud, and then looked at Pengcheng. “Your friend?”

Si-Yuan paused. “Someone important to me.”

Pengcheng didn’t move.

Moreau held out his hand. “Étienne Moreau.”

“Yang Pengcheng. It’s a beautiful film.”

“She made it beautiful,” said Moreau, and told her to go and have some of the evening for herself.

✦ ✦ ✦

They went out by the side door into the cold. The street was quieter than the front, damp from an earlier shower, the streetlights lying in the wet. She pulled her coat round her and he began to take his off, and she caught his wrist.

“Don’t. I’ve got a coat. You don’t have to give me yours every time.”

He looked at her hand on his wrist. “All right.”

They walked. She told him about the scene that had taken longest, and the French she’d fought with, and the night Moreau had made her do something again because she’d been too careful. “He said I was trying to make her a good person. I said she wasn’t good all the time. He said that was exactly why I had to stop.”

“You’re doing it again,” she said a little later.

“Doing what?”

“Looking at me like you’re proud.”

“I am proud.”

“I know.”

“When are you leaving?” she said after a while.

“Sunday morning.”

“Will you come back?”

“If work brings me.”

“Would you tell me first? And not wait outside the set?”

“Yes. I promise.”

They went a few steps further, and she looked at a shop window she wasn’t interested in. “You can ask me to dinner. Not tonight. I’ve an early start. Another night.”

“Would you have dinner with me tomorrow?”

“Yes.”

He didn’t ask whether that meant they were trying again. She didn’t explain.

At the corner by her building she stopped, and took his hand, and her fingers went between his. It was a familiar thing, and it didn’t feel like the past. There was no ring and no promise, and no assumption she’d be beside him in the morning. He held her hand without tightening his.

“You can give me a proper review tomorrow. ‘Extraordinary’ isn’t a review.”

“Very well.”

“Goodnight, Pengcheng.”

“Goodnight, Si-Yuan.”

A few steps on she looked back. He was still there. She lifted her hand, and he lifted his, and she went in.

✦ ✦ ✦

Back in his room he hung his coat over the chair, and the phone went.

Si-Yuan: I forgot to say. I was happy you were there.

Pengcheng: I was happy to be there. You deserved every minute of that applause.

Si-Yuan: Goodnight. See you tomorrow.

He put the phone down and opened the programme at the cast page, and ran his thumb once over her name. He’d thought for years that loving her meant making room for her in his family. He’d been wrong. She’d made a place for herself without him, and tonight, for a while, she’d made room for him in it.

He put the programme beside the ticket. Row thirty, seat eleven. He’d sat at the back, where he could watch without being seen. She’d found him anyway, and kissed him first. It didn’t mean she was coming home, or that they were together. It meant that tonight she’d wanted him there. For now he’d let that be enough.

chapters.title: Home for Christmas
chapters.desc: She comes home for her sisters’ birthday, not for him. He waits until she asks. She asks: explicit, slow, eyes open, the first time he talks.
chapters.epigraph: “I’m going to tell you what I missed. Out loud.”
chapters.content:
She came home for her sisters. He knew that before her flight landed, and he reminded himself of it when Qiao-jie posted a photograph from the airport: three cases, a paper cup of coffee, and Si-Yuan’s hand making a small heart at the camera. Home for a few days.

He looked at it longer than he needed to, and closed it. He’d already sent the day that morning, as he did every morning. He hadn’t added that he knew what the date was. She didn’t need reminding that he remembered. He’d remembered every year.

✦ ✦ ✦

The birthday was at Si-Jie’s flat, because Si-Jie couldn’t go anywhere else. Arthur’s case had gone bad in the autumn, and for a fortnight now there’d been a police car parked across the street from her building, with two officers who changed at eight and eight and waved at her from the window when she put the bins out. She was allowed visitors. She was allowed to be twenty-two. She wasn’t allowed to walk to the shop on her own, and she’d taken it, Si-Wei said, the way a cat takes a bath.

Their mother had flown in from Taipei the day before with a suitcase full of things none of them had asked for and was now in Si-Jie’s kitchen reorganising it. The flat was full of flowers and food and the old noise of three sisters arguing about nothing.

“Why are there only two cake knives?” said Si-Jie.

“Because you’ve got two,” said Si-Wei.

“There are three cakes.”

“Then use a spoon.”

Si-Yuan, on the sofa with her feet tucked under her, laughed into her tea. It was the first birthday in two years that the three of them had been in one room.

Si-Jie had graduated in July and had hardly been able to celebrate it, with everything that had happened since. Arthur sat beside her with his hand near hers on the cushion. He wasn’t talkative round the family, but he’d learned she didn’t like being asked every few minutes whether she was all right. He watched her instead, and stepped in only when she began to wear herself out.

“You’re staring,” Si-Jie told him.

“I’m listening. You’re arguing about knives.”

“It’s serious.”

“Do you want me to find another one?”

She thought about it. “Yes.”

He got up at once and went to their mother in the kitchen, and Si-Wei watched him go. “That’s a useful skill. He knows when to lose.”

“I heard that,” said Arthur from the doorway, with a knife.

Beside Si-Wei, Geum Sung Jae laughed under his breath. He’d come with her that afternoon with a gift bag and a box of pastries and had spent most of the evening letting her steer him round the flat. When their mother asked whether he’d have more, he looked at Si-Wei first.

“He will,” said Si-Wei.

“I can talk,” said Sung Jae.

“I know. You’re just not much use when people ask you things.”

He looked at her, and took another dumpling without arguing.

Si-Yuan watched them all. Her sisters were different with the men they loved. Si-Jie got louder. Si-Wei got quieter, and her attention sharpened whenever Sung Jae was near her. And both men, in their different ways, had learned how to stay. She was happy for them. She was. There was a small ache under it that she’d got good at leaving alone.

✦ ✦ ✦

The three cakes stood on the table: strawberry cream for Si-Jie, dark chocolate for Si-Wei, vanilla with fresh fruit for Si-Yuan. Their mother made them stand together behind them for a photograph, and then another, and then one with Arthur and Sung Jae, and one where Si-Jie insisted everyone look serious, and one where Si-Wei refused to. It was ten minutes before the candles were lit.

“Make a wish,” said their mother.

Si-Yuan looked at the three cakes. Last year she’d spent this day in her own flat with her sisters on the floor, checking a phone that didn’t ring, with his car outside in the morning. This year she was here, and he’d sent her his day at eight o’clock with nothing extra in it, and she found she’d read it twice.

She shut her eyes and wished for nothing in particular. Perhaps that was enough. They blew them out together.

Si-Jie reached for the knife at once. “Mine first.”

“Why?” said Si-Wei.

“Because I’m in protective custody.”

“That isn’t a reason.”

Their mother took the knife away from both of them. “Then Si-Yuan’s, because she’s the eldest.”

“By four minutes,” said Si-Jie.

“Four minutes is not a personality,” said Si-Wei.

“It is when you’ve had them for twenty-two years,” said Si-Yuan, and took the knife out of Si-Jie’s hand, and Si-Jie shrieked, and their mother told all three of them to sit down, and for a little while there was no Paris and no distance and no history, only three sisters and three cakes and a police car outside.

✦ ✦ ✦

Late in the evening, while she was helping her mother pack the leftovers into boxes, she looked at her phone. Birthday messages from the crew, from friends, from Qiao-jie reminding her about the flight back. And under his morning schedule, one line he must have sent while she was blowing out candles.

Pengcheng: Happy birthday. I hope today was full of your sisters.

It wasn’t elaborate. He hadn’t written a paragraph about their first birthday, or last year’s, or the ones he’d imagined. He’d wished her a happy birthday.

Si-Yuan: Thank you.

She looked across the room. Arthur was packing strawberry cake. Sung Jae was holding a container while Si-Wei told him how to shut it. Her mother was humming. She was happy. And she wanted to see him. She wasn’t lonely, and she didn’t need him to finish the day for her; she wanted to see him, that was all.

Si-Yuan: Are you free tonight?

He was at his table with a contract and a cup of tea gone cold. He read it twice. He typed Yes, and stopped, because he didn’t want to assume what she meant.

Pengcheng: Yes. Would you like me to come to you?

Si-Yuan: Yes. My flat. Half an hour.

He put the contract away and changed his shirt and went.

✦ ✦ ✦
