She was waiting at the door of her building in a long coat over a cream jumper, with her hair loose. He saw her before she saw him, and stopped a little way off.

“Happy birthday.”

“You’ve said that.”

“I wanted to say it to your face.”

She came forward and put her arms round him. He held her carefully. She wasn’t going to break, he knew that; it was only that being allowed to hold her was nothing he could assume. She rested her cheek on his chest.

“It’s good to see you,” he said.

“It’s good to see you too. Come up.”

Her flat had more books than he remembered and a new plant by the window, and a suitcase already standing by the bedroom door. On the shelf, among the photographs of her sisters, was a small print of his office door.

He stood in front of it. “You kept it.”

She came back with the tea. “I wanted to. Don’t ask me to explain everything.”

They sat on the sofa and talked about ordinary things. Her work. His office. The new clients and the first year’s figures. Ku, who’d started bringing a dog in on Fridays without anybody’s permission.

“Does the dog have a position?”

“Morale.”

“Is it any good?”

“Better than some people,” he said, and she laughed, and he watched her push her hair behind her ear while she thought about something, and knew he’d missed this more than any memory of her. The ordinary fact of her in a room.

“Why did you keep sending me your day?” she said.

“Because you told me once I was hard to reach. After the anniversary. You said I always seemed to be somewhere else. I thought it might let you know where I was without having to ask.”

“Did you want me to answer?”

“Sometimes. I didn’t want you to feel you owed me one. If you’d never answered I’d have gone on sending it as long as you wanted it.”

Something in her throat tightened. The romance of it had nothing to do with it. He’d finally understood that she needed to be free to choose.

She put her cup down and reached for his hand, and he turned his palm up and let her fingers settle in it. Then she leaned over and kissed him, slowly, with her hand on his face.

He didn’t deepen it. He waited for her to come closer. She came closer.

“I want you to stay tonight,” she said against his mouth.

He waited until she’d drawn back far enough to see his face. “Then I’ll stay.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The lamp by her bed was the only light. She stood by the bed and watched him, and he stopped in front of her, and seemed to be deciding something.

“Let me,” he said.

He didn’t touch her clothes at first. He kissed her hair, and her cheek, and the corner of her mouth, and then took the hem of her jumper in both hands and stopped there.

His voice was low. “I’m going to tell you what I missed. Out loud. You can laugh.”

“I won’t laugh.”

He lifted the jumper slowly over her head, and looked at her, and folded it, because he was who he was, and put it on the chair.

He kissed her shoulder, and undid the button of her trousers, and didn’t hurry it. “Your voice in the morning, before you’ve decided to be awake. You talking to me while I was trying to read, and stopping when I put the book down, and starting again when I picked it up. Your books on my table. Your phone, which you lost every day in a flat with four rooms.”

She was laughing a little after all, and he looked up and smiled, and then didn’t.

He knelt and drew the trousers down, and she put her hand on his head to keep her balance, and he kissed the inside of her knee. “Your face when you came off a long shoot and saw my car. I didn’t know I was waiting for that every night until there wasn’t any car to wait in. I missed you angry with me. I knew I deserved it, and I missed it anyway, because it meant you were still there to be angry.”

“Pengcheng.”

He stood up again. She was in her underwear in the lamplight and he was still fully dressed, and he looked at her without hiding any of what it did to him.

He touched her face. “I missed being the person you wanted to tell things to. I missed holding you without wondering whether I had any right to. I know saying it now doesn’t change anything. I wanted you to hear it.”

She took his hands off her face and held them. “I missed you too.”

She opened his shirt. The last button stuck, and she wouldn’t let him help, and when it came free she looked so pleased with herself that he laughed and kissed her. Everything else went slowly. Every time he touched her he watched her face, and every time she drew him closer he came. They knew each other. They knew the places that made the other laugh, and the habits that had survived eleven months, and the small pauses that meant one of them wanted to say something.

But they weren’t going back to how it had been. He’d once been careful in ways that left her alone. Now he was careful in another way. He told her what he wanted to do before he did it. He asked her whether she liked it, and listened to the answer. When he put his mouth on her he said her name against her skin, and when she came, with her hand in his hair, he said it again.

When he moved over her she held his face. “Look at me. Don’t go off into your head.”

“I won’t.”

“Talk to me.”

He talked to her. He told her she was beautiful, which she’d heard from him before, and that he’d thought of this in Paris every night after the bridge, which she hadn’t. He came into her slowly with his eyes open on hers and stayed still until she moved, and neither of them closed their eyes, not once, and when he said her name it wasn’t a question or an apology. It was only her name, as if he wanted her to know exactly where he was.

“Again,” she said.

“Si-Yuan.”

She smiled, and pulled his head down, and for the first time in a long while there was no silence between them that had to be interpreted. Only the room, and their breathing, and the things they were finally prepared to say.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards she lay against him with her hair across his chest and her hand over his heart, and he traced a slow line up and down her arm.

“Are you comfortable?”

“Very.”

“Do you want water?”

“No.”

“Are you cold?”

She lifted her head. “I’m not going anywhere in the next five minutes. You can stop checking.”

He kissed her cheek and stopped.

After a while she asked him what he’d missed most. “One thing.”

He thought about it properly. “Your voice. I knew how it sounded when you were happy, and when you were pretending to be fine, and when you were trying not to laugh at me. I missed being able to tell the difference.”

She was quiet. “I missed your hands. You always held my hand while I was talking, even when you were reading something else.”

He took her hand and put it against his cheek. “I’m here.”

“Yes,” she said. Neither of them mistook it for a promise that anything was mended.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the morning he made eggs and toast while she sat on the counter in his shirt and told him he’d made too much.

“Two portions.”

“That’s too much.”

“You used to eat more.”

“I was younger.”

“You were twenty-one.”

“Exactly. Very young,” she said, and he laughed.

When they’d eaten she put her fork down. “We haven’t decided anything. I don’t want you to think that because I asked you to stay we’re back where we were. And I haven’t forgiven everything.”

“I know.”

“I wanted you here. I wanted last night. But I still need time.”

“Then you’ll have it.”

“Don’t say it like you’re waiting to be given something at the end.”

He understood at once. “I’m not. I’ve a life to build and so have you. I want to be in yours if you want me there. I won’t make you answerable for what I do with mine.”

She looked at him a long moment, and pressed his hand. “Good.”

At the door that afternoon he asked whether he could kiss her, and she told him he didn’t have to ask every time, and he said he knew and wanted to anyway, and she told him to get on with it, then. It was a quiet kiss, and a slow one.

“Send me your day tomorrow,” she said.

“I will.”

✦ ✦ ✦

It came the next morning, as it always did, and under it one more line.

Pengcheng: Thank you for asking me.

Si-Yuan: Thank you for coming.

She had three more days and then Paris again for the dubbing and the press. There was no ring on her hand and no new agreement between them. But she’d asked him to stay, and he’d stayed. She’d asked him to talk, and he’d talked. For once she hadn’t had to read his silence to know what he felt, and for once he hadn’t mistaken being let close for being entitled to remain.

Si-Jie wrote that evening from behind her police car.

Si-Jie (Questions): Did you have a good night?

Si-Yuan: Yes.

Si-Jie (Questions): Good. You don’t have to tell me anything.

Si-Jie (Questions): But you can.

Si-Yuan laughed, and didn’t, and cut herself a slice of the last of the vanilla cake and ate it standing at the counter. She didn’t know what they’d become. For the first time she wasn’t afraid of finding out slowly.

chapters.title: He Says No
chapters.desc: At a family dinner his mother insults her again. This time he speaks: “No. Not to her. Not ever again.” His mother walks out. Si-Yuan kisses him in front of everyone.
chapters.epigraph: “No. Not to her. Not ever again.”
chapters.content:
The invitation came on Thursday through the family group, addressed to his father, two uncles, an aunt and him. Dinner at the house, Sunday, seven. There was no mention of Si-Yuan. There seldom was.

“Are you going?” said Ku, putting a folder on his desk.

“Yes.”

“Will Miss Yen be going with you?”

“I haven’t asked her.”

“Will you?”

“No,” said Pengcheng, and Ku, who’d learned in four months what most of his answers meant, nodded and went out.

He’d spent years treating those dinners as something he couldn’t refuse without paying for it. He’d spent the last year learning that avoiding a fight was also a choice, and that it was usually somebody else who paid. He wasn’t going to take her into a room where she might be insulted again. But he was going himself. There were things he’d left unfinished at that table, and he wasn’t going to leave them unfinished again because his mother might dislike it.

✦ ✦ ✦

She was home until February: the film was opening there at the end of January, and Qiao-jie had filled the weeks before it with press. She saw the dinner in his day on Saturday morning, sitting cross-legged on her bed with a pile of clothes for a photo shoot.

Pengcheng: Sunday 18 January.

10.00 Office, alone
2.00 Father
6.30 Dinner at the house

Si-Yuan: Your mother’s?

Pengcheng: Yes. I wasn’t going to ask you.

She read that twice. There was consideration in it, and it made her unexpectedly sad. She knew why he hadn’t asked. He didn’t want to put her in a position where she’d have to choose between going and disappointing him. But she didn’t want to spend the rest of her life being kept out of rooms because someone in them might be unkind.

Si-Yuan: I’ll come if you want me there.

He didn’t answer until his meeting had ended.

Pengcheng: I’d like you there. Only if you want to come. You don’t have to prove anything to my family.

Si-Yuan: I’m not going to prove anything. I’m going because I want to go with you.

Pengcheng: Then I’ll come for you at six.

She sent him a heart. He looked at it a long time before he went back to work.

✦ ✦ ✦

At six she opened her door in a dark green dress and a black coat with small gold earrings, and he told her she looked beautiful, and gave her a paper bag with a pastry in it from the bakery she liked, the one by the studio gate. She looked at it and then at him. “You remembered.”

“I remember.”

She locked the door, and when she turned round he held out his hand, and she took it.

The house hadn’t changed. The plants by the door, the stone floor shining under the lights, the portrait in the reception room. Three years ago she’d come in here with a gift held in both hands and her greeting practised in the car, and bowed too low, and sat at the table trying to find the right moment to speak, and left telling herself that perhaps next time would be better. Tonight she didn’t rehearse anything.

His father met them in the hall. “Si-Yuan. It’s good to see you.”

“And you, Uncle.”

His mother was at the door of the dining room in a cream blouse and pearls. Her eyes went from her son to Si-Yuan and stayed there a moment. “You came.”

“Good evening, Madam Yang.”

His mother gave the smallest nod, and turned. “Dinner’s ready.”

✦ ✦ ✦

There were eight of them. The first half of the meal passed without anything happening. An uncle talked about a recent appeal. An aunt asked Si-Yuan about the film, more politely than curiously. Pengcheng mentioned a new client. His father listened. His mother said little.

Si-Yuan ate slowly and spoke when she had something to say. She no longer tried to fill every silence. She no longer wondered afterwards whether she’d talked too much.

“Will you live in Paris now?” said the aunt.

“No. I work here too.”

“It must be hard to keep acting when you’re travelling so much.”

“Sometimes.”

“Still, you’re young. There’s time to decide what you want.”

Si-Yuan smiled. “I’ve decided. I want to go on acting.”

His mother put down her chopsticks. “Decisions are easy at your age.”

The uncle went back to his appeal, and the table moved on.

It was over dessert that it changed. The uncle asked how the firm was doing without chambers behind it, and Pengcheng said it was different, not necessarily harder, and that they’d had a good few months.

His mother set down her cup. “Good months aren’t a secure future. You were given a position, a name and a practice built over three generations, and you walked away from all of it.”

“I made a professional decision.”

“You made an emotional one.”

“Let’s not make dinner about the firm,” said his father.

His mother didn’t look at him. She looked at Si-Yuan. “Do you understand what it means to be connected to this family?”

“Mother,” said Pengcheng.

She went on without looking at him. “You have your career. Your travelling. Your public appearances. You come and go as you like. You’ve no idea what it is to carry a name.”

Si-Yuan had heard a version of this speech before. She could almost have said the next sentence for her. “I understand it matters to you.”

“It should matter to you, if you mean to be part of it.”

“I’ve never said it didn’t.”

His mother laughed, and picked up her tea. “Then perhaps you should consider what you’d bring to it. An actress is admired one year and forgotten the next. There’s no security in that. A family like ours can’t be built round someone’s need to be looked at. And after everything that happened, I’d have thought you might have learned discretion. Instead you come back and expect us all to pretend nothing happened. Some women mistake being loved by a man for having a place in his family.”

The table went quiet. Si-Yuan’s face didn’t change. She didn’t look at Pengcheng. She didn’t need him to rescue her from a sentence. She needed him not to let it stand.

✦ ✦ ✦

He’d heard every word. He’d heard all the earlier ones too, the contempt dressed up as concern, and he’d watched her sit through them with her hands still on the cloth.

He remembered the ballroom. Three hundred people. His chopsticks in his hand and his eyes on his plate. He remembered the way she’d looked at him, waiting for him to look up, and the bow, and the doors closing. He remembered her voice on the phone afterwards: she’d wanted him to put down his chopsticks and look at her. He remembered the red dress she’d stopped wearing to this table, and the rules she’d learned for it, and the film she’d turned down so as not to make things difficult in this room. He remembered the letter she’d kept and not answered, and the bridge, and the premiere, and her saying in her kitchen that last night didn’t mean she’d forgiven everything.

He put his chopsticks down on the rest beside his bowl. Then he looked at his mother.

“No.”

It wasn’t loud. Everyone heard it.

His mother turned her head. “I beg your pardon?”

“No. Not to her. Not ever again.”

The silence was complete.

“You won’t speak to her like that. You won’t question her place at this table. You won’t suggest she has to earn the right to be treated decently. And you won’t use this family to make her small.”

“This is my house.”

“I know.”

“Then remember how you speak to me in it.”

“I’m speaking to you with respect.”

She laughed, once. “Respect? You bring her into my home and tell me what I may say?”

He didn’t look away. “I brought her because I love her. You’re free to disagree with anything I do. You’re not free to humiliate her. I let you do it before. I sat beside her and said nothing. I expected her to keep coming here and bear things I’d never have accepted for myself. I was wrong. I won’t ask her to bear it again. If she comes here, she’ll be treated with respect. If you can’t do that, we’ll go.”

“You’re giving me an ultimatum in my own house.”

“No. I’m telling you what I’ll do. I can’t decide how you behave. I can decide whether I stay.”

For several seconds nobody moved. Then his mother pushed back her chair, and the legs scraped hard on the floor.

“After everything this family has done for you.”

“I haven’t forgotten what it’s done for me. I haven’t forgotten what you did to her either.”

Something crossed her face that was anger, certainly, and under the anger something else: the shock of hearing her son say a thing plainly and not soften it afterwards.

“Then you’ve made your choice,” she said.

“Yes.”

She looked round the table at all of them, and walked out, and nobody followed her. The door closed behind her, and the sound of it seemed to stay in the room long after it had stopped.

✦ ✦ ✦

His hands were steady. His heart wasn’t. He could feel the old instinct rising: go after her, explain, repair it, make the room comfortable again. He knew exactly what she’d say if he did. That he’d shamed her. That he’d chosen an actress over his own blood. For most of his life those words would have been enough to make him take back every one of his. He didn’t move.

His father cleared his throat. “Pengcheng.”

“Father.”

His father looked at him a moment, and nodded once, and picked up his spoon. “Finish your dessert. Your mother has had more than enough people agreeing with her.”

The aunt looked at her plate. One uncle looked at the ceiling.

Si-Yuan sat still. She’d expected him to object, if he objected at all: to ask his mother to stop, to suggest they talk about something else. She hadn’t expected him to say it like that. Plainly, at the table, in front of everyone. Not ever again.

He turned to her. “Are you all right?”

She looked at him, and stood up, and came round the corner of the table to his chair. Six people watched her do it. She put one hand on his shoulder and the other on his face, and bent, and kissed him on the mouth in front of his father and his uncles and his aunt and the housekeeper standing frozen in the doorway with a teapot.

It wasn’t long. It didn’t need to be. When she straightened, his father was looking hard at his dessert, and one of the uncles had gone pink, and Pengcheng was looking up at her as if nobody else were there.

“Yes. I’m all right,” she said.

She went back to her chair and sat down and picked up her spoon. After a moment his father began, carefully, to talk about the weather.

✦ ✦ ✦

They left twenty minutes later. His father walked them to the door.

“Si-Yuan.”

“Uncle?”

“I’m sorry.”

She smiled at him gently. “Thank you.”

He looked at his son. “Look after her. Not with promises.”

“With what I do,” said Pengcheng.

His father gave a small nod and let them go.

In the car she sat looking out of the window, and he didn’t ask whether she was upset, or whether it had frightened her. He waited. At a red light she turned to him.

“You said it.”

“I should have said it years ago.”

“Why now?”

The light changed while he answered, and he drove on. “Because I heard her, and I knew exactly what would happen if I didn’t. You’d go home and wonder whether you’d said something wrong. You’d try to work out what she meant. You’d tell yourself she was only being difficult. You’d be alone with it again. I didn’t want you ever to have to wonder where I was.”

She looked at her hands. “I didn’t know whether you would.”

“I know. I’m sorry it took so long.”

“I’m not going to tell you everything’s mended.”

“I wouldn’t expect you to.”

“But I heard you.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Outside her building she didn’t get out. She sat a while with her seat belt still on.

“Do you know what I was thinking while she talked? How long I used to spend getting ready for those dinners. What to wear. What to say. Which relatives to greet first. I practised pouring tea. I wrote down what everyone liked to eat.”

“I didn’t know you did that.”

She turned and looked at him. “No. Tonight I didn’t get ready for anything. I wasn’t there to be accepted. I was there with you.”

“And I was there with you.”

“I’m proud of you,” she said.

For a moment he looked almost unable to take it. Then he said thank you, and she told him he didn’t have to thank her, and he said he wanted to.

His phone rang before he’d turned off the engine. His mother. Si-Yuan told him to answer, and he got out and stood by the car.

“You left without a word to me.”

“I thanked Father.”

“You humiliated me in front of my family.”

“I told you not to speak to Si-Yuan that way.”

“You chose her.”

He looked at the car, and at Si-Yuan through the windscreen, reading something on her phone. “I chose not to let you humiliate someone I love.”

“Do you think she’ll stay with you after all this?”

“That’s between her and me.”

“Don’t come to this house again until you understand what you’ve done.”

“I understand exactly what I did tonight. I don’t regret it,” he said, and rang off.

When he got back in she looked at him. “Your mother?”

“She doesn’t want me there until I understand what I’ve done.”

“Do you?”

“Yes.”

“Good,” she said, and leaned across and kissed him again, here, with nobody watching at all. She wasn’t rewarding him, or forgiving every year. She was choosing it now, and he understood the difference.

✦ ✦ ✦

Upstairs, before she slept, she opened his contact and looked at it, and changed it. It had said only his name since the night of the banquet. Now it said Pengcheng (Said No). Then she wrote to him.

Si-Yuan: I want you to remember something. Tonight, when you said no, I believed you. Not because you said you’d protect me. Because I watched you do it.

He was in his car still, outside his own building, when it came. He typed slowly.

Pengcheng: I’ll keep giving you reasons.

There was still a long way to go. His mother had walked out, and the family wouldn’t forget it, and Si-Yuan hadn’t forgotten the years she’d sat beside him waiting for him to speak. But in a room full of people who’d once watched her be humiliated, he’d finally made himself plain. He hadn’t asked her to bow, or to understand, or to wait. He’d said no. And this time she’d watched him mean it.

chapters.title: The Price
chapters.desc: His mother takes the family’s clients with her. Half his clients gone in a week. Si-Yuan doesn’t offer money; she offers lunch. He’s never lost before.
chapters.epigraph: “You’re allowed to be happy before everything’s finished, Pengcheng.”
chapters.content:
The first client went on the Monday. Ku forwarded the email with one line on top: Mr. Yang, I think you should see this now.

It was a family property group that had used the Yang chambers for nearly twenty years. Pengcheng had run their disputes before he left. They’d come to him of their own accord when he opened the door with his name on it, and he’d spent four months on their restructuring and an acquisition that was nearly done. The email was courteous. It thanked him for his work and his firm’s professionalism, and told him the board had decided to consolidate its legal representation elsewhere.

Elsewhere was his mother. He read it twice and sent it back to Ku. Prepare the closing papers and a final invoice. Make the handover clean.

He didn’t ring the client. He didn’t ask why. He knew.

Ku put his head round the door with a tablet. “Should I call them? We’ve a matter running.”

“No. They’ve decided. We’ll hand it over properly.”

“Is this to do with your family?”

“Yes.”

Ku looked as though he wanted to say he was sorry and knew he shouldn’t. “It’s business,” said Pengcheng, and went back to the draft in front of him, and didn’t notice that he’d been holding his pen without writing for most of a minute.

✦ ✦ ✦

The second went on Tuesday, and the third on Wednesday, and by Thursday they were coming in bunches. A private investment house. A construction group whose founder had played chess with his grandfather. A manufacturer whose files had sat in the same chambers archive for three generations. The reasons were nearly identical: a consolidation of legal services, a review of external counsel, a preference for continuity. The language was professional enough to make the meaning unmistakable.

His mother hadn’t rung anyone up and threatened them. She didn’t need to. She’d reminded them where they’d always belonged, and most of them were going home.

On Friday Ku put a printed list on his desk. “Six confirmed. Two more say they’re reviewing. If those two go the same way we’ll be at about half of what we had on the first of the month.”

The numbers weren’t a catastrophe. Not yet. There was a reserve. The clients who were left were steady. There were matters with good prospects and two new consultations booked for the following week. But the loss was concentrated. The ones who’d gone had brought the recurring work, the steady fees that made the months predictable and let him take people on without wondering about the next quarter.

“How much do we have to transfer?”

“Three big matters. The rest we can finish inside the existing terms.”

“Unpaid bills?”

“Two.”

“Send the reminders. Don’t hold them back because of the handover. And the new junior?”

Ku hesitated. “If the fees halve we may have to look at that.”

“Put it on hold. Nobody already here is to be touched until I’ve done the new figures.”

Ku went to the door and stopped. “Mr. Yang. Are you all right?”

It was an ordinary question, a reasonable one, and he could have answered it in a word. He looked at the list instead. “We’ve work to do.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He’d never lost before. Not like this. He’d lost cases now and then, but always knowing where he’d gone wrong: he could read the judgment and find the weak point in his argument and see what he should have done. He could accept a ruling when the law wasn’t on his side. This was nothing like that. There was no argument to improve, no evidence to put in, no negotiation that would persuade a client to stay when they’d decided for reasons that had nothing to do with his work.

He’d been careful. He’d refused to take anyone who belonged to chambers. He’d accepted that people wouldn’t follow him. He’d counted on losing his mother’s support. He hadn’t counted on her using the relationships he’d spent years looking after as a way to punish him.

He looked at the letterhead. Yang and Associates. His name. His responsibility. His loss. Then he rang the accountant.

✦ ✦ ✦

His father rang that evening while he was still at his desk.

“Have they all come in?”

“Most.”

“I spoke to your mother. She says clients are entitled to choose their representation.”

“They are.”

“She says they’re going back to a firm they trust.”

“They are.”

His father breathed out. “You don’t have to make it easy for her.”

“I’m not. I’m agreeing because it’s true.”

“How bad is it?”

“About half.”

“That’s a lot.”

“Yes. We’ll manage.”

His father didn’t sound reassured. “You know I can’t simply bring them back.”

“I haven’t asked you to.”

“Your mother has always believed the name is what holds chambers up. She thinks you’re proving her right by struggling without it.”

Pengcheng looked at the logo on his screen. “Then she misunderstands what I’m trying to build.”

“Which is?”

“A practice that can stand without anyone having to agree with my family.”

There was a pause. “Your grandfather would have understood that.”

He didn’t know whether it was true. He’d spent most of his career trying to become the kind of lawyer the old man would have been proud of. He’d been taught that a name carried weight because generations had given it meaning, and he still believed that. He was only beginning to understand that a name could also be a chain.

“Don’t make yourself ill proving a point,” said his father.

“I won’t.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Si-Yuan noticed on the Saturday, and not because he told her. She noticed because the day he sent that morning had nothing in it but the day.

Pengcheng (Said No): Saturday 7 February.

8.30 Office
11.00 Figures
2.00 Staff
7.00 Home

For six months his days had come with a small note when something hard was in them. This one had none, and she’d learned to read the absence. At lunchtime she wrote to him.

Si-Yuan: What did you have for lunch?

He answered nearly an hour later.

Pengcheng (Said No): Nothing yet. I’m looking at some figures.

Si-Yuan: Important figures?

Pengcheng (Said No): Yes.

Si-Yuan: Are you losing money?

He could have told her it was nothing. He could have said the firm was having a difficult month and some arrangements had changed. He wrote the truth.

Pengcheng (Said No): We’ve lost about half our clients this week.

She sat up. Because of your mother? He said yes. She put the phone down and looked at it. She remembered the dinner in January, his mother walking out, the word at the table. She remembered his mother on the phone telling him not to come back until he understood what he’d done. Now she could see what it was going to cost.

Si-Yuan: Are you at the office?

Pengcheng (Said No): Yes.

Si-Yuan: Have lunch with me.

Pengcheng (Said No): I’ve a meeting at two.

Si-Yuan: Then we’ve an hour.

Pengcheng (Said No): You don’t have to—

Si-Yuan: I’m asking you to lunch. I’m not offering to buy your firm.

He looked at that and, in spite of everything, smiled.

Pengcheng (Said No): All right.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was waiting outside a small place near the office when she came across the city in a long coat with her hair tied back. He’d chosen it because it was quiet and close enough to get back from without hurrying. He hadn’t expected her to come herself.

She looked at him. “You look tired.”

“Good afternoon to you too.”

“Very tired.”

“It’s been a busy week.”

“That isn’t the same thing,” she said, and took his hand, and he let her.

She ordered noodle soup and a dish to share. He ordered fish and rice. When the food came she pushed the shared plate towards him.

“Eat.”

“You sound like me.”

“Then listen to yourself for once.”

She watched him while they ate. He was trying to behave normally, and that was what worried her. He had a way of making hard things look manageable by putting them in tidy boxes: a problem became a document, a loss became a sum, a feeling became something to look at when the work was done. She knew the habit. She’d once mistaken it for strength. She understood now that sometimes it was only how he avoided admitting that something hurt.

“Tell me,” she said.

He told her. The first one on Monday and the rest behind it. Most of them back to his mother’s chambers. The handover notices, the revenue, the staffing plan. He said it all in an even, professional voice, and she listened to every word.

“Can you keep everyone?”

“For now. I’ll know when the new figures are done.”

“Will you let anyone go?”

“Not unless I have to. I’m putting off the new junior. There was a candidate. Good record, some commercial work. I’d hoped to bring her in by March.”

He said it without complaint, and that was how she knew it mattered.

“Have you ever lost this much before?”

He seemed to think about it properly. “No. I’ve lost cases. I’ve had clients unhappy with how things came out. I’ve made mistakes. I’ve never lost half my practice in a week.”

“What does it feel like?”

“I don’t know.”

“Try.”

He was quiet for a while. “Like someone taking a building down round me while I’m still working inside it. I know which rooms have gone. I know what has to be moved. I can work out what’s left. But I can’t stop thinking that I built it.”

His voice hadn’t changed. His eyes had. She reached across and put her hand over his.

“You did build it. People leaving doesn’t change that. You didn’t get worse at your work this week.”

“I know.”

“Do you? You look like somebody who’s decided he’s failed.”

“I don’t like losing.”

“I know.”

“I thought I’d prepared for this.”

“You prepared to lose your mother’s support. You didn’t prepare for her to take your clients. Those are different. You can be ready to lose something and still be hurt when it goes. You don’t have to turn everything into a lesson straight away.”

She smiled a little as she said the last of it.

He looked at their hands, and for a moment he let himself not say anything at all.

When the bill came he reached for his wallet, and she put her hand on it. “I asked you.”

“I can pay.”

“I know you can,” she said, and paid.

✦ ✦ ✦

Under the awning outside it was cold and clear.

“Thank you for coming.”

She looked at him. “I wanted to. I didn’t come because I think you need saving. And I’m not going to offer you money.”

“I wouldn’t take it.”

She took his hand. “I know that too. I came because I wanted to have lunch with you. Because you haven’t been eating. Because you told me something hard instead of pretending it was fine. And because I know what it’s like to have someone make you feel your place can be taken away from you. I don’t want to be one more person who treats your bad days as a problem you have to solve before I’ll spend time with you.”

He lifted her hand and kissed her knuckles.

“Go back to work. Eat dinner. Don’t work till two in the morning.”

“I can’t promise that.”

“Then I won’t believe you,” she said, and kissed his cheek, and walked away towards the street, and he watched her until she’d gone round the corner.

✦ ✦ ✦

The new figures took three days. He went through every matter, every recurring fee, every unpaid bill and every expense. He cancelled the extra floor. He put off the new junior. He took the lease for one more year instead of signing for somewhere bigger. Then he saw every member of staff on their own. He didn’t tell any of them it would all be fine. He told them what had happened, what the firm could afford, and what was being put off.

“So no redundancies,” said Ku, when it was his turn.

“Not now. If it gets worse we’ll look at it together.”

“Thank you for telling us straight.”

“You ought to know where you stand.”

Ku smiled a little. “That’s more than some places give you.”

Pengcheng didn’t answer. He was thinking of his mother. She’d built a practice where everyone knew exactly where they stood, so long as they understood the order of things. He wanted something else. Not a firm with nobody in charge. A firm where being in charge didn’t need anyone to keep quiet.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Wednesday one of the two who’d been reviewing their position wrote and asked to talk. A technology company, middle-sized, years with chambers before it moved its commercial work to him. He rang their general counsel and they talked for twenty minutes: the handover, his firm’s capacity now, whether they ought to go back. He answered everything. He didn’t mention his mother. He didn’t ask them to stay out of loyalty. He told them what his people had done and what they could go on doing.

The general counsel thanked him for his honesty and said they’d decide by Friday. On Friday they decided to stay.

He read it twice and didn’t smile at once. He forwarded it to Ku. Update the engagement records. We carry on. Ku wrote back within seconds that it was good news, and Pengcheng wrote that yes, it was, and put the phone down. The firm was still smaller than it had been a fortnight before. The figures were still hard. But one client had looked at the situation and chosen to stay. Not because of the name, and not because of his mother. Because they trusted his work. For the first time that week he let himself smile.

✦ ✦ ✦

She rang that evening.

“How was your day?”

“Better. One stayed.”

“That’s good. Did you celebrate?”

“Not yet. I haven’t finished.”

“You’re allowed to be happy before everything’s finished, Pengcheng.”

He looked at the papers on his desk and laughed. “I’ll try to remember.”

There was a sound of zips and drawers at her end. “Packing. I fly on Tuesday. A week in Paris for the French release, and then I’m back.”

He looked at the calendar. The seventeenth. “That’s soon.”

She heard him not say something. “Yes. Tell me.”

“I wish you weren’t going. I don’t mean change your plans. I only wanted to say it.”

She was quiet long enough for him to hear her breathe. “I know. I wish I could have lunch with you again.”

“When you’re back.”

Her voice went softer. “When I’m back. And you’ve done this well, you know.”

“By losing half my clients?” He tried to make it light.

“Because of how you lost them. You didn’t run back to your mother and ask her to make it stop. You didn’t make your people pay for something they didn’t do. You told them the truth and made a plan and kept working.”

“It isn’t enough yet.”

“It doesn’t have to be enough yet.”

“You sound like my father.”

“Your father sounds sensible. Listen to him.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He went home and cooked and ate at the table instead of the desk. Afterwards he went through the final figures one more time. They weren’t encouraging. They were survivable. He saved them.

There was a photograph on his phone: a pastry box from the bakery by the studio gate, sitting on top of her Paris script.

Si-Yuan: Found this while I was packing.

Pengcheng (Said No): You kept the box?

Si-Yuan: I kept the pastry.

Pengcheng (Said No): That was a month ago.

Si-Yuan: I ate it.

He stared at the screen, and laughed out loud in his empty kitchen.

Pengcheng (Said No): Please tell me you’re joking.

Si-Yuan: Goodnight, Pengcheng.

Pengcheng (Said No): Goodnight. Don’t eat anything questionable on the plane.

The flat was quiet. The firm was smaller. His mother’s clients had gone home to her and the future was a set of figures that might go either way. He’d never lost like this, and he didn’t yet know how to carry it without turning it into something to solve. But he hadn’t lost everything. He had the practice and the people in it and a handful of clients who still trusted him. And across the city a woman who’d spent two years trying to earn a place in his family had asked him to lunch. She hadn’t offered him money. She hadn’t told him she could make it go away. She’d sat across a table and watched him try to eat, and told him he was allowed to be hurt.

Tomorrow there’d be more calls, and more decisions, and something to rebuild. For the first time in his life he understood that working hard didn’t promise that he’d win. He turned off the light and went to bed anyway.

chapters.title: The First Case Alone
chapters.desc: His first case without the family name: a stuntwoman her studio cheated on an injury claim. He wins it for nothing. A kiss on the court steps, out loud.
chapters.epigraph: “She was the performer. She wasn’t the person responsible for making the set safe.”
chapters.content:
The case came to Yang and Associates in January, through a woman three other lawyers had told to count herself lucky she’d survived.

Her name was Luo Mei. She was thirty-four and had spent fourteen years doing stunts for film and television: doubling for actresses in fight scenes, coming off roofs, being dragged across concrete, learning how to make a fall look far worse than it was. She knew how to fall. She hadn’t known how to get up from the one that broke her back.

It had happened the year before on a period action drama. The production had planned a controlled fall from a raised platform onto a padded landing area. It was rehearsed twice. The safety coordinator signed off the rig. Then, shortly before they turned over, the director changed the camera angle. The landing area was moved. The platform went up. The stunt team asked for another rehearsal, and the production manager said no, because they were behind and the director wanted it before the light went.

She hit the edge of the landing platform before she hit the ground. Two vertebrae fractured. There was surgery, and months of rehabilitation, and a long stretch when she couldn’t stand without someone holding her.

The studio paid for the emergency treatment and then stopped. Its position was that she’d departed from the rehearsed movement and caused her own injury. Her contract called her an independent performer, and the studio said it owed her nothing for the rehabilitation, or the work she’d lost, or the work she’d never do again.

She had photographs of the landing area, and her medical records, and messages from the production coordinator. What she didn’t have was any money left to fight with.

She sat in his office with a stick propped against the chair. “I don’t want anyone feeling sorry for me.”

“That isn’t what we’re here for.”

“I want the studio to pay what it owes.”

“Then we’ll talk about what it owes.”

“Can you win?”

He’d learned not to promise an outcome before he’d seen the evidence. “I can tell you what we can prove, where it’s strong and where it isn’t, and what they’ll say. I think you have a case worth bringing.”

She nodded slowly, and asked what he’d known she’d ask. “How much will it cost?”

He closed the file. “Nothing. We’ll act for you without fees.”

“I can’t ask you to do that.”

“You haven’t asked.”

“Mr. Yang—”

“I don’t want you to agree because you feel you owe me something. I want you to understand we’ll take it seriously and prepare it properly and go after what you’re entitled to.”

“Why?”

He considered it. “Because a studio shouldn’t be able to get out of a safety failure by calling it your mistake.”

Her hand tightened on the head of her stick. For a moment she looked as though she might cry. She nodded instead. “All right.”

He opened the file again. “Then let’s start at the beginning.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The studio’s solicitors had acted for production companies for years and knew every contract and insurance arrangement and safety regulation that touched a set. They denied liability. They said the production manager had no authority to change the rig and that she’d been briefed and chosen to go ahead. They produced a signed risk acknowledgement, and a statement from the production supervisor saying the stunt performer herself had insisted the original landing area was enough.

Pengcheng read the statement twice and laid it beside the production schedule.

“They’re leaning on the acknowledgement. It’s signed,” said Ku.

“It shows she understood the risks of the stunt she rehearsed. It doesn’t show she agreed to the one they changed it into.”

“Can we prove the change came after she signed?”

“We have to.”

They asked for the production logs, the safety inspection records, the rehearsal footage, the internal emails and the footage from every camera round the rig. The studio objected to half of it. He applied for disclosure, and the court ordered it.

When the material came, Ku carried it into the meeting room in three folders. “There’s a problem. The production manager’s statement says the revised rig was approved by the safety coordinator. The safety coordinator’s log says it wasn’t.”

Pengcheng turned the page. Under the log was an email the production manager had sent in the late afternoon of the accident. We can’t lose another day. Go with the revised set-up. Performer has been briefed. There was no reply from the safety coordinator. There was no approval anywhere.

“Find the original metadata,” he said.

“Already asked. And the rehearsal footage has two angles. One shows the original rig. The other shows the change.”

“Good.”

“Is it enough?”

“It’s a start,” said Pengcheng.

✦ ✦ ✦

Si-Yuan found the hearing in his day the week before she flew to Paris.

Pengcheng (Said No): Monday 16 February.

8.00 Court
10.00 Luo Mei v. the studio

Si-Yuan: Is that the stuntwoman?

Pengcheng (Said No): Luo Mei.

Si-Yuan: Are you nervous?

He thought about saying no.

Pengcheng (Said No): Yes.

Si-Yuan: Good. It means you care. Eat breakfast tomorrow. And breathe.

Pengcheng (Said No): I’ll try.

On the morning it was cold. Luo Mei was waiting at the court entrance with her sister, standing carefully on her stick, and straightened when she saw him.

“Did you sleep?”

“Enough.”

She was looking at the doors. “I’m frightened. What if they make it sound like I did something stupid?”

He waited until she looked at him. “Then we’ll answer it with the evidence. You’ve only to tell the truth. Don’t guess. Don’t try to sound better than you are. If you don’t remember something, say so. Your job is to tell the court what happened. Mine is to make sure it has what it needs to understand it.”

Her shoulders came down a little. “All right.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Si-Yuan came in just before ten. She hadn’t told him. She’d seen the date, and checked the public list, and the hearing was open. She wore a dark coat and a plain jumper and a cap, with her hair behind her ears, and sat near the back of the gallery.

He was at the front, talking to Ku. He looked different in court. Not colder. More concentrated. He listened without interrupting and turned pages and leaned to Ku now and then to say something short.

She remembered him in his old chambers, where everyone already knew his surname, where his mother’s name opened doors before he’d knocked on them. This was different. There was no crest on his papers. No senior partner behind him. No family between him and the people across the court. Only his name and his work.

Counsel for the studio went first, calmly. Luo Mei had signed the acknowledgement. She was experienced. She knew the work. She’d been told the conditions. The studio had provided proper equipment and safety staff. The accident had happened because she hadn’t performed the stunt as rehearsed.

Pengcheng listened without looking up. When it was his turn he stood, and put two photographs up for the court: the original landing area, and the revised one. “My Lord, the defence depends on treating the stunt performed on the day as the same stunt Ms. Luo agreed to perform. It wasn’t. The acknowledgement refers to the first. There’s nothing signed to show she agreed to the greater height, the moved landing area, or the loss of the second rehearsal.”

“She was briefed,” said counsel for the studio.

“By whom?”

“The production supervisor.”

“Is there a record?”

“His statement confirms it.”

Pengcheng handed up the email. “His statement is contradicted by the safety coordinator’s log, written at the time, and by the production’s own emails. The production manager told the crew to go ahead with the revised rig without any safety approval at all.”

He didn’t raise his voice. He didn’t hurry. He took the court through the timeline and the photographs and the inspection records and the messages, one after another. The landing area had been moved after the rehearsal. The extra rehearsal had been refused. The safety coordinator had never approved the change. The studio had gone ahead anyway.

The judge looked up from the schedule. “Are you saying the defendant knew the rig had been changed and proceeded without the required approval?”

“Yes, my Lord.”

“Is there evidence of that?”

Pengcheng opened the last folder and handed up the email with the time-stamped logs beside it. The court went quiet.

Si-Yuan watched him. There was no flourish. No anger. No attempt to embarrass anyone. He only put the evidence where it needed to be.

✦ ✦ ✦

The worst was the cross-examination. The studio’s counsel asked Luo Mei whether she understood the risks of falling from height. Yes. Whether she’d signed the acknowledgement. Yes. Whether she’d done stunts like it before. Yes. Whether she’d known the landing area had been moved.

She hesitated. “I knew they were moving equipment.”

“So you knew the conditions had changed. And you went ahead.”

Pengcheng stood. “My Lord, the question assumes my client had authority over the rig.”

“Carefully, Mr. Yang.”

He turned to her. “Ms. Luo, who was responsible for approving changes to the stunt?”

“The safety coordinator.”

“Were you responsible for the height of the platform?”

“No.”

“For deciding whether the landing area was safe?”

“No.”

“Did you ask for another rehearsal?”

“Yes.”

“What happened?”

“The production manager said there wasn’t time.”

“Did the safety coordinator approve the change?”

“No.”

He paused. “Why did you go ahead?”

She looked down. “Because they told me it was ready.”

The studio’s counsel was on his feet. “My Lord, the witness is trying to avoid responsibility for her own professional decision.”

“She was responsible for performing the stunt. She wasn’t responsible for certifying the equipment, approving the platform, or deciding whether the landing area met the standard.”

“I understand your position, Mr. Yang,” said the judge, and Pengcheng sat. Luo Mei’s hands were shaking. He looked at her for a second and gave her the smallest nod, and she went on.

It took most of the day. He fought the studio’s claim that she’d made her own injury worse by ignoring medical advice, and put in the hospital records and the rehabilitation report that showed the studio had stopped paying before the treatment was finished. He fought their figures on her lost earnings with her old contracts and her bank records and an occupational report. He never called her helpless. He never asked anyone to feel sorry for her. He showed what she’d earned, and what she could no longer do, and what it had cost.

At the end he stood once more, and looked at the judge while he spoke. “This case isn’t about whether stunt work is dangerous. My client has never said it isn’t. She’s done this for fourteen years. She knows what a fall involves and what preparation it takes. She accepted the risks of the stunt that was rehearsed and approved. She didn’t accept a different stunt, on a different rig, without the approval the defendant’s own procedures required. The defendant changed the conditions, refused the rehearsal and went ahead over its own coordinator’s head. It now asks the court to treat that as her fault because she was the one who fell. She was the performer. She wasn’t the person responsible for making the set safe.”

He sat down. In the back row Si-Yuan’s fingers had closed round the edge of her coat, and for the first time that day she smiled.

✦ ✦ ✦

Judgment was reserved. In the corridor Luo Mei looked exhausted, with her sister holding her arm. “Did we win?”

“We don’t know yet. We’ve put the evidence in. The judge has to weigh it. Don’t decide the result before it comes.”

She nodded, and then said, “If they rule against me I still don’t regret bringing it. Somebody finally listened to the whole story.”

He was quiet a moment. “You shouldn’t have had to wait so long for that.”

When she’d gone he looked up the corridor, and Si-Yuan was standing by the window at the end of it with her cap in her hand.

“I didn’t see you,” he said, when he reached her.

She looked at him. “I sat at the back. Row thirty, more or less. You were very good.”

“I’m not sure yet.”

“I’m sure,” she said, and put her cap back on, because there were people in the corridor, and went to catch her flight in the morning.

✦ ✦ ✦

The judgment came eleven days later, on a Friday, while he was in a meeting. Ku brought the tablet in and said only, “Mr. Yang. It’s the decision.”

He read it in his office. The judge accepted that Ms. Luo had signed the acknowledgement but found that it didn’t cover the materially different rig used on the day. The production company had failed to follow its own safety procedures. The production manager had authorised the change without approval. The rehearsal had been refused at the performer’s request. The court rejected the argument that she’d caused her own injury by going ahead. The studio was liable. Damages for the injury, the medical costs, the rehabilitation, the lost earnings and the loss of future earning capacity. Costs.

He sat back.

“Mr. Yang?”

“We won.”

Ku stared at him, and then the relief went through his professional face all at once, and he laughed and put his hand over his mouth. “That’s our first big judgment.”

“Our first under this name.”

“Without the family’s.”

“Yes. Ring Luo Mei,” said Pengcheng.

She answered on the second ring, and he told her, and there was a long silence and then a small broken sound, and she asked whether that meant the treatment, and the money she couldn’t earn now, and he said it did, all of it. She cried, the way people cry who’ve been told for a long time that it was their own fault.

“You didn’t imagine what happened to you. The evidence said what you told us.”

“Thank you.”

“You don’t have to thank me for doing my job.”

“I know. I want to.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He sent Si-Yuan two words, and she was back in the city and wrote back within the minute that she was coming. She came into his office that afternoon in her coat and stopped in the doorway, and smiled, and told him congratulations.

“First case.”

“First judgment.”

“Without your family’s name.”

“Without it.”

She took his hand. “I saw you that day. I saw all of it.”

He’d wanted her to. He hadn’t said so to anyone. She read the judgment over his shoulder, the findings and then the part about the rig, and looked up. “You gave her back the truth.”

“She did most of that herself.”

“You gave her someone who’d listen. That’s a good thing to be.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They left together before six. She told him about a script she’d been sent that morning, a director who wanted to meet, a start date that might clash with something else, and he asked her what she wanted to do, and she said she wanted to read it all first, and he nodded. No advice. No deciding for her. A question about what she wanted.

Their way went past the court building. The steps were broad and pale in the last of the light, with a few people coming down them and a clerk talking at the top. He stopped at the foot of them.

She looked at him. He was looking at the doors.

“I thought I’d feel more nervous the first time I walked in there under my own name. I used to think the name was what made people listen. That if I lost it I’d spend my life proving I was allowed in the room. That day I stood up because someone trusted me to tell her story, and the court listened because we had the evidence. I didn’t need my mother’s name. I didn’t need my grandfather’s. I needed to do the work.”

“And you did.”

“And I did.”

She put her hand on his cheek. “I’ve never been so glad to watch anyone, Pengcheng.”

He looked at her, and said it clearly, at an ordinary volume, on the steps of a courthouse in the middle of an ordinary afternoon with people going past: “I love you.”

She went still. He’d said it before, but never like this, in daylight with nowhere private to go. He’d said it as a plain fact, with no apology or request in it, and nothing meant to make her stay.

“I love you too,” she said, and took his face in both hands and kissed him there on the steps in front of everyone, with no curtain and no shut door and no corner of anywhere to hide in. His hand settled at her waist and he kissed her back.

A clerk going past smiled. Ku, coming down the steps behind them with a folder under his arm, stopped dead, and looked at them, and smiled to himself, and went on round.

When she drew back he kept his forehead against hers. “Congratulations, Mr. Yang,” she said.

“Thank you, Miss Yen.”

“First case alone.”

“First case alone,” he said, and she kissed him once more, and they went home.

chapters.title: Out Loud
chapters.desc: He starts saying things out loud. It’s terrible at first. Explicit: he narrates; she laughs.
chapters.content:
The first time he did it he was in a client meeting. The second time he was on the phone to his father. The third time she was standing in his kitchen in one of his shirts eating a slice of cold pear. By the fourth she’d begun to suspect he was doing it on purpose.

✦ ✦ ✦

It started on a Tuesday. Her meeting with a director had been moved, so she’d come to his office with a script and was reading on the sofa in his room. He’d said he’d be an hour. It had been forty minutes, and she’d read the same paragraph three times, when the door opened.

“Would you come through for a moment? The client’s early and I need a file from the meeting room, and I’d rather not leave you sitting here like a parcel.”

“Like a parcel,” she said, and put the script down and followed him.

The client was a woman in her late forties from a cosmetics company, already at the table. She stood up when they came in. Pengcheng introduced Ku, and then Si-Yuan, and the woman smiled warmly and said she knew her work, that she’d seen the film at the cinema in January and her daughter adored her, and Si-Yuan said the easy gracious things she’d learned over years of being recognised in public.

Pengcheng found the file. Then he looked at Si-Yuan.

“You look beautiful today.”

The room went silent. Ku stopped turning a page. The client blinked.

Pengcheng went on, entirely serious. “The colour suits you. I noticed when you arrived. I didn’t say so then because we were talking about the meeting.”

Ku looked at the table. The client looked from one of them to the other. Si-Yuan’s lips parted.

“Thank you,” she said, in a controlled voice.

“You’re welcome,” said Pengcheng, and turned back to the client and began.

Si-Yuan stood by the door a moment longer trying hard not to laugh, and then excused herself, and got back to his room, and shut the door, and put both hands over her mouth. Her shoulders went.

He found her there fifteen minutes later, on the sofa with the script forgotten, laughing into the back of her hand.

He shut the door. “I don’t understand what’s funny.”

“You told me I looked beautiful in front of your client.”

“Yes.”

“You didn’t even wait till she’d gone.”

“I noticed it before she came.”

“That doesn’t make it better.”

He thought about that seriously. “Would you have preferred me to wait?”

She looked at him, and started again.

“You sounded like you were making a submission. You even gave the time you first noticed.”

“I thought you should know.”

“Why?”

He looked at her. The answer was obvious to him. Because he’d noticed. Because she was beautiful. Because he liked telling her. But he’d been keeping those thoughts to himself for so long that now he’d started saying them, they came out like evidence.

“I wanted to tell you,” he said.

Her face went soft, and then her mouth went again.

“Are you going to laugh every time?”

“Probably.”

“That’s encouraging.”

She got up and came over and straightened his tie. “You don’t have to explain every compliment.”

“I know. I’m trying.”

“I can tell.” She kissed him lightly. When she drew back he was plainly about to say something more, and she held up one finger.

“Don’t.”

“Don’t what?”

“Don’t explain the kiss.”

He shut his mouth, and she laughed into his shoulder.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Thursday his father rang while he was reading a contract. They talked about the firm and the clients who’d stayed and whether the judgment had brought anything in.

“Two. One’s already signed an engagement letter.”

“Good. You’re building a reputation.”

“Slowly.”

“Slowly’s better than carelessly. And Si-Yuan?”

He looked through the glass wall of his room. She was sitting outside with Ku, showing him something on her phone, and Ku was laughing.

“She’s well. She’s here. We’re seeing each other.”

His father made a small approving sound.

Pengcheng hesitated, and then before he could think better of it said, “I love her.”

There was a silence on the line. He looked down at the contract.

“I should hope so,” said his father.

“I meant—”

There was another pause before his father went on. “I know what you meant. You sound different saying it now. As though you want her to hear it.”

Pengcheng watched her tilt her head towards Ku’s phone, her face lighting up at something on it. “She does.”

“Then keep doing it,” said his father.

When the call ended he sat still. He’d said it without any occasion. Without an apology attached. Without needing anyone to say it back. He’d simply wanted his father to know, and perhaps, more than that, he’d wanted to hear himself say it.

✦ ✦ ✦

Over the next week she watched it happen. He began saying the things he’d only ever thought. He told her when he missed her. He told her when he was looking forward to seeing her. He told her when he was proud of her work, and when he liked her hair, and when he thought she was being unfair to herself. At first he was awkward. Very awkward.

One evening at his flat he came in with two cups of tea and said she’d been reading a long time.

“Have I?”

“Your shoulders are up by your ears. I think you should stop for a bit.”

“Are you telling me what to do?”

“No. I’m telling you what I think.”

“That’s better,” she said.

He sat down beside her and looked at her hands, and then reached for one of them. “You’re holding the pages very tightly. I think you’re worried about the audition. I think you’ll do well. And if you don’t get it, it won’t mean you aren’t good enough. You don’t have to prove you’re worth choosing every time you walk into a room. You’re allowed to want something without making yourself miserable over whether you deserve it.”

Her smile went. She looked at him a long moment, and then leaned over and kissed him, and he smiled against her mouth.

“I hadn’t finished,” he said, when she let him go.

“I know.”

“I had another thing.”

She touched his face. “Save it. Sometimes you can just kiss me.”

He considered that, and then he did.

✦ ✦ ✦

By the middle of March he’d developed a habit of announcing what he was about to do. It wasn’t quite deliberate. Once he’d started talking he found that stopping felt stranger than going on.

On the Saturday she’d stayed the night, and woke to find him standing by the bed in the pale morning looking for his watch. He found it on the bedside table and turned to her.

He picked up her empty glass. “I’m going to make breakfast. Eggs. You said you wanted something warm. I’ll bring you tea first. I’m taking this to the kitchen.”

She stared at him from under the covers.

He narrowed his eyes. “You’re laughing.”

“I’m not.”

“You are.”

She pulled the duvet up over her mouth.

He looked at her. “I’m going to kiss your forehead before I go.”

She burst out laughing. He shut his eyes, and then bent and pressed a kiss into her hair anyway.

“Now I’m going to the kitchen.”

From the bedroom she called after him to bring tea, and not to narrate the kettle, and he stopped in the doorway and, in spite of himself, laughed.

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening she had her legs across his lap on the sofa and his thumb was going absently round her ankle, and she asked him why he was doing it.

“Doing what?”

“Telling me everything.”

He thought about it properly, and turned the television down. “I used to think that if I did a thing you’d know what I meant by it. That remembering what you liked meant you’d know I cared. That turning up meant you’d know I wanted to be there. That being sorry meant you’d know I was. I didn’t think I needed to say it all. I know what I mean, but when I try to say it I sound like—”

“A lawyer.”

He gave her a look.

“Sorry. Go on.”

“Like I’m giving a statement. But I don’t want you to have to guess any more. I don’t want you to look at me and wonder whether I’m glad you’re here. Whether I missed you. Whether I thought you were wonderful. I want you to hear it.”

She looked at him a long time. “You don’t have to turn into someone who talks all the time. You can still be quiet. But when something matters, I want you to say it. And sometimes, when nothing matters at all, you can just tell me I look pretty.”

“I can do that.”

“Without the reasons.”

“I’ll try.”

✦ ✦ ✦

That night she found out that his narration fell apart when he was nervous.

She was sitting against the headboard in one of his shirts with a book when he came out of the bathroom in a dark T-shirt, and stopped by her side of the bed.

“I’m going to ask you something. Would you like me to come closer?”

“You’re standing next to the bed.”

“I know.”

“Then come closer,” she said, and he sat down beside her, and she put the book on the table.

He took her hand and kissed her fingers. “I’ve been thinking about you all day. I thought about kissing you in my office. I thought about your face when you were laughing at me. I thought about what you said on the court steps. May I kiss you?”

“Yes.”

The first one was gentle. The second lasted longer. “You can stop asking every time,” she said.

“I want to kiss you again.”

“Then do it.”

He did, slowly, with one hand at her waist, and when she leaned into him he stopped.

“I’m going to take this off you,” he said, touching the hem of the shirt. His shirt.

She looked down at it and then back at him, and her mouth twitched. “All right.”

He lifted it carefully. “Is this all right?”

“Yes.”

He got it over her head and folded it, and she watched him fold it, and pressed her lips together hard.

He kissed her shoulder first and told her afterwards. “I’m going to kiss your shoulder. Now I’m going to—”

She was already shaking. He lifted his head.

“Don’t stop. Please. Go on. Tell me,” she managed.

He gave her a long, injured look and went on, and it was the most ridiculous thing that had ever happened to her in bed. He told her he was going to kiss her neck, and then he kissed it. He told her he’d missed waking up next to her, and kissed her collarbone. He told her he’d missed her complaining that he made too much rice, and she laughed until she had to put her hand over her face, and he said, with great dignity, that he was going to move her hand, and moved it, and kissed her palm.

“I missed you stealing my shirts.”

“They’re comfortable.”

“I know. I missed seeing you in them. I’m going to take mine off now.”

“Oh my God,” she said into the pillow.

He took it off. He told her he was going to put his mouth on her breast, and she told him yes, all right, Counsel, and he did, and she stopped laughing for a little while. He told her he was going to touch her, and where, and she lifted her hips to let him, and he touched her there, slowly, the way she liked. “I’m going to—”

“Pengcheng.” Her voice wasn’t laughing at all.

He looked up at her and lost the end of the sentence.

That was how it went. He’d start to say something, and she’d laugh, and he’d go on, and the gaps between the words got longer. He told her he wanted her, plainly, and that was the last whole sentence he managed. After that there was her name, and then only her name, and then nothing at all, because she’d pulled him down by the back of his neck and wrapped her legs round him and he’d come into her with his forehead on hers, and whatever he’d been about to announce went out of his head entirely.

She stopped laughing too. She held his face and watched him lose every word he had, and found that she loved it more than any speech. He moved in her slowly and then not slowly, and she said into his ear, “Talk to me,” and he tried, and couldn’t, and she laughed once more, breathless, because that was exactly what she’d wanted, and then she couldn’t either.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards she lay against him with her fingers drawing a line down his chest.

“Are you tired?”

“A little.”

“I want to tell you something.”

“Another thing?”

He took a breath and brushed her hair back. “Yes. I love the way you laugh at me. It means you’re happy. I used to think I had to get everything right before I could say what I felt. Wait till I had the right words and the right moment. I don’t want to wait any more. I don’t want to wait until you’re leaving to tell you I don’t want you to go. I don’t want to wait until you’re hurt to tell you I should have stood up for you. I don’t want to wait until you aren’t here to tell you I want you here. I want to tell you while you are.”

She leaned her face into his palm. “Then tell me.”

“I want you here.”

“I’m here. And I love you.”

He looked almost overwhelmed by how simple it was. He kissed her temple. “I love you too.”

“You’re getting better,” she murmured, much later, when he’d thought she was asleep.

“At talking?”

Her voice was nearly asleep. “At telling me. Tomorrow you can say I’m beautiful again. Without the reasons. And not in front of a client.”

He laughed into her hair. “I’ll do my best.”

✦ ✦ ✦

In the morning she was at his mirror in a pale blue dress, brushing her hair for a meeting with Qiao-jie, and he looked at her in the glass while he put his watch on.

“You look beautiful.”

She paused, and smiled, and thanked him, and waited. He said nothing else. She turned round. “That’s all?”

He looked puzzled. “You said no reasons.”

She laughed and crossed the room and kissed him. “Very good, Mr. Yang.”

“Am I improving?”

“Considerably.”

When she picked up her bag he said, “I love you,” and she looked back, and her smile came at once.

✦ ✦ ✦

That afternoon she rang him at the office. Ku, at the desk outside his open door, went on typing, and then heard Pengcheng say, “I missed you.” Ku’s fingers stopped.

“Yes, I know you only left an hour ago. I still missed you,” said Pengcheng.

Ku looked hard at his screen.

When Pengcheng put the phone down, Ku looked up. “Sir? Could you perhaps close the door when you make personal calls?”

Pengcheng looked at him, and smiled slowly, and said of course. A few seconds later he said, “I did miss her, though.”

Ku shut his eyes. “Understood, sir.”

She came to the office that evening and found him at the window, and he put his papers down. “You look beautiful. I missed you.”

“I was gone five hours.”

“I know.”

“You really are going to keep doing this.”

“Yes.”

She looked at him, and her face softened. “Good.”

“I love you,” he said, and she kissed him before he could add the reason, and when she drew back he looked faintly surprised.

“I wanted to stop you before you explained,” she said.

He laughed, and kissed her again, and said it against her mouth, low and certain: “I love you, Si-Yuan.”

“I heard you.”

Outside the city was going towards evening. He was still learning that something didn’t have to be said perfectly to mean something. Sometimes it came out awkwardly. Sometimes he explained too much. Sometimes she laughed until he forgot what he’d meant to say. But he was saying it, and she was no longer being asked to guess.

chapters.title: Red
chapters.desc: She wears red to dinner with his mother. Si-Yuan bows exactly as much as is polite. He doesn’t look at his plate.
chapters.content:
She chose the dress on a Thursday afternoon. It was an old one, the dark red dress with the plain neckline and the sleeves that stopped just above the wrist, bought between two shoots three years ago because the colour made her feel brave, worn to his mother’s once and then not again until Paris. It had come home with her folded between two sheets of tissue. It didn’t sparkle. It didn’t ask to be looked at. It looked like her.

She was holding it against herself in front of the mirror when Si-Jie rang.

“Are you getting dressed? What are you wearing?”

“Red.”

There was a pause, and then a sound like a kettle that had been waiting years to boil. “RED? To that dinner?”

“Yes, Jie.”

“I could cry. I’ve waited years for this.”

“You’re being dramatic.”

Si-Jie’s voice came down. “You don’t have to go, you know. You don’t owe that woman another evening of your life.”

“I know.”

“Is he going to be next to you?”

“I think so.”

“Don’t think. Ask him. I’m not telling you to avoid his mother. I’m telling you not to walk into that room and start looking after everybody’s feelings again.”

“I won’t.”

“Promise?”

“I promise. I’ll send you a picture.”

His mother had sent the invitation herself, a week before, to his phone. Not through the family group or the secretary. Dinner on Friday. His father, and him, and Miss Yen. Nobody else. He’d shown it to Si-Yuan without saying anything, and she’d read it twice, and said she’d go.

She put the dress on and did up the small buttons at the cuffs, and smoothed it at the waist, and looked at herself. For a moment she remembered a younger woman at a wardrobe holding two dresses and wondering which would be least likely to offend. She remembered putting this one away. She remembered Pengcheng telling her he liked her in red, and her never telling him why she’d stopped. Tonight she didn’t want to remember any of it. She wanted to wear the dress because she liked it.

Pengcheng (Said No): Leaving the office now. With you in twenty minutes.

Si-Yuan: I’m wearing red.

Pengcheng (Said No): Good. I like you in red.

Si-Yuan: I know.

✦ ✦ ✦

When she opened the door he was halfway through putting his phone away, and he looked up and stopped. She stood in the doorway in the red dress with her hair loose and her make-up plain and small gold earrings in instead of the diamonds.

“You look beautiful.”

“Thank you.”

He came closer. “Are you comfortable?”

“Yes.”

“Are you sure?”

She studied him. “I chose it. I’m not wearing it to prove anything. I’m wearing it because I like it.”

His thumb moved over her knuckles, and he lifted her hand and kissed it. “Then that’s the only reason that matters. I want you to know something before we go. If my mother says anything about you tonight, I’ll answer her.”

“Even if there’s nobody else there to see?”

“Yes.”

“Even if it makes dinner uncomfortable?”

“Then dinner will be uncomfortable.”

She looked at him a moment, and nodded, and took her coat.

✦ ✦ ✦

The house hadn’t changed. The hall still smelled of polish and fresh flowers. The photographs were in their places with the same careful symmetry. The portrait looked down from the reception room. The only difference was the absence of people. There were no other cars on the drive. No relatives in the reception room, no cousins drifting between the dining room and the garden, no senior partners arriving with their wives. Since January the house had grown quiet.

The housekeeper opened the door. “Young Master. Miss Yen.”

His mother was waiting at the door of the sitting room in a dark silk blouse and pearls. Her eyes went first to her son, and then to Si-Yuan, and stopped for a moment on the dress.

“Si-Yuan.”

Si-Yuan stepped forward. “Good evening, Madam Yang.” And she bowed.

It wasn’t too low or too quick, and there was none of the anxious eagerness of a girl hoping to be let in: a proper greeting, composed and respectful, exactly as much as was polite and not a degree more.

His mother returned a small nod and a good evening, and then looked at her son. “You’re late.”

“It’s ten to seven. You said seven.”

“I expected you earlier.”

“I had a client.”

“You might have planned better.”

“I might,” he said. There was no apology in it, only acknowledgement.

His mother turned. “Your father’s waiting.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The table was laid for four at one end of a table that seated fourteen. The rest of it was polished and bare, and the arrangement looked less like a small dinner than one that had been reduced.

His father stood up when they came in. “Si-Yuan. You look well.”

“Thank you, Uncle.”

His eyes went to the dress. “Red suits you.”

She smiled. “Thank you.”

Pengcheng pulled out her chair and sat beside her. His mother sat opposite. The first course came.

For a while it was ordinary. His father asked about her work, and she told him about a film she was considering and the director she’d met. “The character has a hard relationship with her mother. But it isn’t written as a simple fight. They love each other. They just can’t talk without hurting each other.”

“That sounds interesting.”

“I’m still reading it.”

“She reads it every night,” said Pengcheng.

“Not every night.”

“Most nights.”

“Are you keeping count?”

“I notice,” he said, and his father laughed.

His mother went on eating. Then she said, “Acting schedules must still be very unpredictable.”

“They can be. It depends on the production.”

“It must be difficult to build a stable life round them.”

Pengcheng put down his chopsticks. “Mother. Si-Yuan’s work is part of her life. We don’t need to discuss whether it’s convenient.”

“I was making conversation.”

“I know.”

His mother looked at Si-Yuan. “I’m sure you’ve grown used to the arrangements.”

“I have. I enjoy my work.”

“Of course.”

The conversation moved to the firm. His father asked how the new office was, and Pengcheng said busy, and that they were being selective.

“Being selective is easier when there are enough clients,” said his mother.

“We have enough work.”

“For now. Some people begin with advantages. Others choose to throw them away. Some decisions are made for the sake of people who may not stay.”

The room went quiet. Si-Yuan didn’t move.

“Don’t make this about Si-Yuan,” said Pengcheng.

“I haven’t mentioned her.”

“You didn’t need to.”

His father put down his glass. “Let’s have dinner.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The second course came, and Si-Yuan thanked the housekeeper and moved her plate to make room. His mother watched her do it.

“You’ve become comfortable here.”

“I’ve been here before.”

“That isn’t what I meant. I imagine it’s easier now there are fewer family occasions to attend.”

“I don’t think comfort depends on the number of occasions.”

“Doesn’t it?”

“No.”

A faint silence followed. “You used to be very careful,” said his mother.

“I was. Now I know how to behave.”

It was perfectly polite. The meaning wasn’t hidden. His father looked down at his plate. His mother’s eyes sharpened.

Pengcheng’s fingers brushed Si-Yuan’s under the edge of the table. She didn’t need him to rescue her from a conversation. She wasn’t asking to be rescued. But he was there, beside her, looking at his mother.

“Some people mistake familiarity for belonging,” said his mother, picking up her chopsticks.

Pengcheng put his down. “No. Don’t talk about her like that.”

“I was speaking generally.”

“You weren’t.”

She held his eyes, and then turned to Si-Yuan. “You must be pleased. He’s become very protective.”

Si-Yuan took a sip of water. “I’m pleased he speaks honestly.”

Something warm went across his face.

“Honesty isn’t always the same as judgment,” said his mother.

“No. But neither is silence,” said Pengcheng.

His father looked at him. His mother didn’t answer.

It wasn’t a pleasant dinner. It wasn’t a disaster either. Nobody raised their voice and nobody left the table. The strain sat between the plates and in the pauses and in the careful way the housekeeper moved round them.

When the last dish came his mother turned to Si-Yuan once more. “That’s an interesting dress.”

Si-Yuan looked down at it, and then up again. “Thank you. I like it.”

“It’s rather noticeable.”

Pengcheng looked at his mother. Si-Yuan answered before he could. “I suppose it is.”

“Red has always drawn attention.”

She smiled politely. “Yes. I’ve always liked it.”

Pengcheng looked at her. She didn’t look at him. She didn’t need to. His mother picked up her teacup, and said, “I see,” and that was the end of it.

✦ ✦ ✦

After dinner his father went to take a call, and his mother stayed in the sitting room, and Pengcheng stood by the sofa while Si-Yuan waited near the door.

“You needn’t come here if you find it uncomfortable,” said his mother.

“I know.”

“Then why do you?”
