Si-Yuan thought about it, and spoke calmly. “Because Pengcheng asked me. And because I wanted to. I don’t expect you to like me, Madam Yang. I don’t expect you to approve of my work or what I choose. But I can be civil to you without pretending everything between us has been pleasant.”

His mother’s face went still. “I’ve never asked you to pretend.”

“Then we agree.”

For the first time that evening his mother seemed to have no answer ready. Pengcheng watched Si-Yuan with something close to admiration.

His mother turned to him. “You seem very pleased with yourself.”

“No. I’m glad she doesn’t feel she has to make herself smaller to be here.”

“You’ve changed.”

“Yes.”

“Not necessarily for the better.”

“I disagree,” he said.

She looked away. “Your father will want to say goodnight.”

At the door Si-Yuan bowed once more, exactly as much as was polite. His mother returned it. There was no warmth in it, and no acceptance. But there was no correction either.

✦ ✦ ✦

They were halfway down the steps when Si-Yuan stopped. “You didn’t look at your plate.”

He understood at once. For a moment he didn’t say anything. Then he smiled. “No.”

“Not once. You looked at her. And you answered.”

“You don’t need to thank me for that.”

She looked back at the lit windows. His mother was no longer in the sitting room. “I know. I didn’t need you to answer every sentence. I could answer some of them myself.”

“I know. I noticed when she looked at your dress. I noticed when she tried to make your work sound like a problem. I noticed every time she talked as though you were a guest who’d stayed too long. I wanted you to know I wasn’t going to sit there and let you deal with it alone.”

“I liked that you were there.”

He lifted her hand to his mouth. “I’ll keep being there.”

“Don’t say it like a promise you have to make tonight.”

“Then I’ll say it as something I mean to do tomorrow as well.”

“That sounds better,” she said.

He asked whether he could kiss her, on his mother’s front steps, and she told him he was ridiculous, and kissed him first. She held his face in both hands and kept him there longer than usual.

“Thank you for looking at me,” she said against his mouth.

“I should have done it years ago.”

“You’re doing it now.”

✦ ✦ ✦

In the car he asked whether she wanted to go home or eat something.

“Something warm.”

“There’s a place near the office.”

“The one where you order too much?”

“You always finish the extra.”

“Because you always order too much,” she said.

At a red light he took her hand. The city’s lights went across the glass and touched the red of her dress.

“Do you think she’ll ever change?”

“I don’t know.”

She thought about it. “I don’t think so either. That upsets me a bit. Not as much as it used to. I used to think if I behaved perfectly she’d one day look at me differently. I don’t think that any more.”

“I wish you hadn’t had to learn it.”

“So do I.”

He brought her hand to his lips. “I like you in red.”

“You’ve told me twice.”

“I wanted to say it again. You look beautiful in red.”

“Thank you,” she said, and he looked back at the road, and didn’t explain why.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later she sent the group the mirror photograph she’d taken before she left, the dress from shoulder to hem.

Si-Jie (Questions): RED!!!!!!!!

Si-Wei (Watching): Finally.

Si-Jie (Questions): DID SHE SAY ANYTHING?

Si-Yuan: A few things. I was polite.

Si-Wei (Watching): That isn’t what she asked.

Si-Yuan: Pengcheng spoke.

Si-Jie (Questions): Properly?

Si-Yuan: Yes.

Si-Wei (Watching): Did he look at his plate?

She glanced across the room. He was at his desk finishing an email, and looked up when he caught her smiling.

Si-Yuan: Not once.

Si-Jie sent a line of red hearts. Si-Wei sent one word.

Si-Wei (Watching): Good.

“What did you tell them?” he said, closing the laptop.

She took his hand when he came to her. “That dinner was fine. Not wonderful. Not terrible. Fine. I think I liked tonight. Not because of your mother. Because I could wear red, and bow once, and be polite, and leave without wondering whether I’d done enough.”

“You did enough.”

“I know.”

There was no new acceptance waiting at the end of the evening. No warmth from the woman who’d spent years making her feel like an outsider. His mother was still cold. But Si-Yuan hadn’t bent herself into someone else to get through the dinner, and he hadn’t looked away. For tonight that was enough.

chapters.title: His Mother Alone
chapters.desc: His mother falls ill and asks for him. Small in a hospital bed, she asks him to leave Si-Yuan. He says no, holding her hand. Two weeks later, on Sat 30 May, Si-Yuan is at Eliana Lin’s party for Yu Chen with two boxes of pastries; she doesn’t tell him she cried there.
chapters.epigraph: “I can love you without agreeing with you.”
chapters.content:
The call came early on a Wednesday in May. He was asleep, and reached for the phone without opening his eyes, expecting Ku or a client in another time zone. Then he saw the name and sat up.

His mother almost never rang him. When she wanted something it came through the housekeeper, or his father, or the family secretary, and since he’d left chambers there’d been little of even that.

“Mother?”

There was a pause, and then her voice, unfamiliar in how thin it was. “Pengcheng.”

He was wide awake. “What’s happened?”

“I’m at the hospital. Your father brought me. It’s nothing serious. I felt faint yesterday, and this morning it happened again.”

“What did the doctor say?”

“I don’t need you to cross-examine me.”

He shut his eyes. “I’m asking because I want to know whether you’re all right.”

Silence. Then: “Your father thought you should be told.”

“I’m coming.”

“There’s no need.”

“I’ll be there soon,” he said, and rang off gently, and was already reaching for his trousers.

Beside him Si-Yuan turned over, half asleep. “What’s wrong?”

“My mother’s in hospital.”

Her eyes opened properly. “Is she all right?”

“I don’t know yet.”

She sat up. “Go.”

“Will you come?”

She hesitated. It wasn’t that she didn’t care. Whatever had been between her and his mother, she’d never wished her harm. But his mother hadn’t asked for her. “You go first. She’s your mother. Ring me when you know something, and don’t worry about doing it straight away.”

He bent and kissed her hair, and stopped at the door, and thanked her, and she told him to go.

✦ ✦ ✦

The room was brighter than he’d expected. His father was at the window talking to a doctor. A nurse was adjusting a monitor. His mother lay under a white blanket with her hair loose round her face, and without her clothes and her jewellery and the way she held herself she looked smaller than he remembered. He’d seen her in courtrooms and conference rooms and at the head of her own table and in the study where she’d spent her life deciding things for other people. He’d hardly ever seen her lying down.

His father came over from the window. “Her blood pressure dropped. She was dizzy and nearly fainted. They’re keeping her to watch it.”

His mother turned her head. “You came.”

“Yes. How do you feel?”

“Fine.”

“She says that about everything,” said his father, without much humour.

“I can answer for myself.”

Pengcheng pulled a chair to the bed and looked at the untouched tray. “Have you had anything since yesterday?”

“Very little,” said his father.

“I’m here because I’m unwell, not because I’ve forgotten how to eat,” said his mother.

“I didn’t say you had.”

He sat and asked the practical things: what tests they’d done, when they thought she might go home, whether she’d been taking her tablets. She answered with varying degrees of irritation, and he listened. He’d learned to say things out loud. He hadn’t lost the habit of keeping quiet when someone was frightened and trying to hide it.

✦ ✦ ✦

When his father went out to find the doctor again the room went still.

His mother didn’t look at him. “Your father tells me you’ve been working too hard. He also says you’re still seeing that girl.”

“Si-Yuan.”

She looked away. “Must you correct me every time?”

“Yes. Her name is Si-Yuan.”

“You’ve made your point.”

“No, Mother. I’m telling you how I expect you to speak about her.”

Her mouth tightened. “You’re still putting her before everything.”

“I haven’t put her before everything.”

“Then what do you call leaving this family?”

“I call it leaving chambers.”

“You know very well what I mean.”

He did. He’d known for years. But he’d stopped answering questions made vague on purpose so that he’d have to guess what she wanted him to say. “I came because you’re ill. We don’t need to talk about the firm today.”

She studied him. “It isn’t the firm. It’s her. You’ve lost half your clients. You’ve lost your place here. You’ve a small office with your name on the door and no family behind it. You’ve made your life very much harder. And for what?”

“For the life I chose.”

She gave a faint, disbelieving laugh. “You talk as though this were some great act of independence.”

“It isn’t great. It’s only mine.”

“You could have had everything.”

“Not at that price.”

“What price?”

He looked at her. “Not being able to disagree with you.”

She didn’t answer. He hadn’t raised his voice. He hadn’t needed to.

✦ ✦ ✦

Near midday he went down to buy his father something to eat, and when he came back his mother was alone, propped higher on the pillows, looking at the television without watching it.

“Do you remember your grandfather’s funeral?” she said.

“Yes.”

“You were very young. You stood next to me the whole day. You never left my side. You were very quiet. You used to be a good son.”

He remembered: the black suit his father had bought him, the long line of relatives, the smell of the flowers, his mother not crying until the last guest had gone. He’d been a boy who believed she could bear anything.

“I’m still your son.”

“Then why are you doing this to me?”

The question was so familiar that for an instant he was back in the study, a boy trying to work out which answer would disappoint her least. He looked at his hands. Then he looked at her. “What am I doing to you?”

“You’ve made me lose you.”

“I haven’t stopped being your son because I left chambers.”

“You don’t visit.”

“You don’t ask me.”

“I shouldn’t have to ask.”

“I understand.”

Then she said what he’d been expecting, and had hoped she wouldn’t say here. “You don’t understand anything. Leave her. End it with Si-Yuan. You’ve lost enough. You can still come back. Your father can talk to the partners. We can put things back where they belong.”

“You want me to leave her so you can give me back my position.”

“I want you to stop ruining your life. You’ve made yourself vulnerable for a woman who has her own career and her own money and her own life. She doesn’t need you. She’s never understood what this family requires.”

“That isn’t the question.”

“Then what is?”

“Whether I love her.”

Her face hardened. “Love isn’t enough.”

“I know.”

“Then leave her.”

He was quiet. Then he moved his chair nearer the bed and reached for her hand. She didn’t take it at once. His fingers rested lightly against hers.

“Mother. I love Si-Yuan. I know you don’t want to hear it, and I know you don’t approve of her. I’m not going to leave her.”

“You’d choose her over your own mother?”

“I’m not choosing between you. I can love you without agreeing with you. I can be your son without giving you the right to decide who I marry. Those aren’t the same thing.”

Her fingers moved, slightly, under his. “You’ve become very good at saying things.”

“I’m trying to get better at meaning them.”

She turned her face to the window. For a while he thought she’d take her hand away. She didn’t.

✦ ✦ ✦

His father came back and stopped in the doorway. His son was sitting by the bed holding his mother’s hand, and she was looking out of the window, and neither of them was saying anything. His father came in and asked whether Pengcheng had eaten, and Pengcheng nodded at the paper bag on the table, and his father gave him a grateful look.

He stayed another hour. He spoke to the doctor, arranged for the housekeeper to bring her things, and made sure his father had every number. Before he left he drew the blanket up over his mother’s shoulder, and she opened her eyes.

“Are you going?”

“I’ll come back tomorrow.”

She hesitated. “You needn’t come every day.”

“I know. Rest, Mother,” he said.

In the corridor his father caught him up. “What did she ask you?”

“To leave Si-Yuan.”

“And?”

“I said no.”

His father looked at him, and nodded. “Good.”

“She was holding my hand.”

“She’s frightened. Don’t mistake that for an apology. And don’t mistake refusing her for a reason to stop caring for her.”

“I won’t do either.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Si-Yuan was at his flat when he got home that night. There was rice porridge on the stove and cut fruit on the table.

“How is she?”

“Steady. They’re keeping her in.”

“I made porridge.”

“You didn’t have to.”

She watched him take off his jacket. “I know. Was she frightened?”

He came to her. “I think so. She asked me to leave you.”

For a moment Si-Yuan didn’t know what to say. “What did you tell her?”

He took her hands. “No. I didn’t say it to hurt her or to win. I said it because it’s true. I can go to the hospital and see she’s looked after and be there while she’s ill. I won’t pretend that loving you is something I can bargain away when she asks.”

Her eyes went soft. She touched his face. “Did you hold her hand?”

He nodded. “She looked small.”

His voice had changed, and she moved closer. “She’s your mother. You can care about her. You don’t have to go cold because she’s been unkind to me.”

“I don’t want to.”

She put her arms round him and he held her hard, with his face in her hair, and they stood like that in the quiet flat.

“I don’t know how to be her son without letting her hurt you,” he said into her hair.

“Then perhaps you’re still learning. Come and eat.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She went home four days later. It wasn’t catastrophic, but it was serious enough for rest and tablets and regular check-ups. His father had the housekeeper stay longer each day and took on more of the house himself. Pengcheng went most days for a fortnight. He brought shopping and talked to the doctor and made sure the medication was written up clearly. He didn’t take Si-Yuan. Not to hide her. His mother hadn’t asked to see her, and he wouldn’t make Si-Yuan responsible for mending something she hadn’t broken.

His mother didn’t mention her again. Sometimes she talked about the firm, sometimes about his father. Once she asked whether he was eating properly, and said his face looked thinner.

“I’m fine.”

“You always say that.”

“I learned it from you.”

She didn’t smile. But she didn’t tell him to go, either.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Saturday the thirtieth of May, Eliana Lin threw a party for Yu Chen, who’d been offered emergency medicine at City Hospital, in the garden behind her house. She’d strung warm bulbs through the persimmon tree and along the back wall and propped little cards on the table that said Congratulations, Dr. Wang. Si-Jie brought wine, Si-Wei brought a printed timetable with no speech allowed over three minutes, and Si-Yuan brought two boxes of pastries she’d spent the morning choosing: fruit tarts with thin cream and fresh berries, and small almond cakes wrapped one by one so they’d be easy to share.

“You brought all this?” said Yu Chen, opening the boxes.

“Only a little.”

“This is not a little.”

“Then share it,” she said, laughing.

She was comfortable there. Nobody was measuring the depth of anything she did. Her phone buzzed in her pocket.

Pengcheng (Said No): How’s the party?

Si-Yuan: Good. Yu Chen says I brought too much.

Pengcheng (Said No): You probably did.

Si-Yuan: You’re meant to take my side.

Pengcheng (Said No): I am. You brought exactly the right amount.

It happened later, by the back wall under the lights. Someone was talking about visiting an elderly father in hospital, and someone else about how hard it was to see a strong person need others. Si-Yuan listened, and thought of his mother under a white blanket with her hair loose and her hand on the sheet. She thought of him saying she looked small. She thought of him beside the bed holding his mother’s hand and knowing he couldn’t give her what she wanted. And she thought of the years when she’d wanted him to hold her own hand in front of that woman, at the table, and not only in the car afterwards.

She’d spent so long wanting him to choose her that she’d almost forgotten he’d once been a little boy in a black suit standing beside his mother all day because he wanted her to be proud of him.

The thought hurt more than she’d expected. Her eyes began to sting, and she slipped away from the group through the back door into the quiet hall of the house, and stood there with the party muffled behind her and her fingers pressed under her eyes. She didn’t sob. She stood still and let it come.

“Si-Yuan?”

It was Eliana, with a stack of plates, and she stopped when she saw her face. “Are you all right?”

“Yes. It’s nothing.”

Eliana didn’t push. She put the plates down on the stairs and found a tissue in her cardigan pocket and held it out, and then stood beside her without asking anything at all until Si-Yuan had wiped her eyes.

“Sorry. I think I just got emotional.”

“That happens,” said Eliana, and squeezed her arm, and they went back out together.

✦ ✦ ✦

She ate a pastry and laughed at one of Ren Hao’s stories and stood in the photographs. When he messaged again she answered as though nothing had happened. She didn’t tell him she’d cried. She didn’t know how to explain that she’d cried for his mother, and for the boy he’d been, and for the woman she’d once been beside him. And she didn’t want him to think she regretted the line he’d finally learned to draw.

He rang that night as she was getting into bed.

“Did everyone like the pastries?”

“They went very fast.”

“Then bring fewer next time. You always say it’s only a little and bring enough for everyone.”

“Are you complaining?”

He paused before he answered. “No. My mother asked about you today. Whether you were still acting. I said you were. And I told her you’d taken pastries to a party. I don’t know why. I suppose I wanted to tell her something about you.”

“What did she say?”

“That you always bring too much food.”

Si-Yuan laughed. “She remembers.”

“She does.”

The silence after that was different from the old silences between them. It didn’t feel like something held back. It felt like two people thinking about what they could say without asking the other to carry too much.

“I’m glad you went to see her. And I’m glad you held her hand,” she said.

“I wanted to. I don’t think she understands what I was trying to tell her.”

“Maybe not yet. You don’t have to make her understand everything tonight.”

“So I keep being told,” he said, and she laughed, and said goodnight.

✦ ✦ ✦

Across the city his mother sat up in her bedroom with a glass of water and her tablets in a neat row. The house was quiet. On the table beside her was an old photograph from some family dinner: her son in a dark suit, his hand resting behind her chair, her smiling at the camera. He’d been younger. Before the firm. Before Si-Yuan. She picked it up and looked at it a long time, and put it back.

Her phone lit.

Pengcheng: The doctor says rest tomorrow. I’ll ring in the afternoon.

She could have told him there was no need. She could have reminded him she wasn’t helpless, or told him to spend his time on that firm of his.

Mother (Senior Counsel): Very well.

She looked at that, and added a line before she could change her mind.

Mother (Senior Counsel): Thank you for coming.

He read it in his kitchen, and answered that she was welcome, and to rest well. Then he went to bed, where Si-Yuan was already asleep, and lay down, and she turned towards him without waking. He didn’t know about the hall and the tissue. He only knew she’d been there when he came home, and had listened, and had never once asked him to stop loving his mother. He’d spent his life believing love meant keeping people from being disappointed. He was learning that he could hold his mother’s hand without letting go of hers.

chapters.title: The Ring Again
chapters.desc: He gives her back the ring she left. She doesn’t take it. “Ask me differently.” He asks differently.
chapters.content:
The ring had spent more than eighteen months in a drawer. He knew exactly where: the right-hand drawer of the desk in his flat, under a pile of old papers, beside a fountain pen he hardly used. He hadn’t moved it since the January afternoon she’d put it on his desk in chambers with a note under the box.

For a long time he couldn’t look at it. Then, slowly, he learned to open the drawer without feeling he was opening that day again. He’d taken it out twice. Once after the premiere, when he’d held it in his palm for several minutes wondering whether he could ever ask her to wear it again. Once after the court steps, when he’d almost put it in his pocket before meeting her, and stopped, because he hadn’t wanted to turn a day she was proud of him into a request she hadn’t asked for.

In August he took it out a third time. The diamond caught the afternoon light. He’d thought about replacing it with something bigger, something that might look like a beginning instead of a return to a broken promise. But he’d come to see that changing the ring wouldn’t change what it meant. It was the ring he’d given her when he asked her to marry him. It was also the ring she’d left on his desk when she couldn’t wait any longer for him to choose her.

He closed the box and put it in his jacket.

✦ ✦ ✦

She came over that evening after a day of meetings, kicked her shoes off at the door and went straight to the kitchen in a pale cotton dress and a cardigan, and stood at the counter eating slices of the cucumber he was cutting.

“You’re eating the ingredients again.”

“I’m checking them.”

“For what?”

“Whether they’re good.”

“You use that for everything.”

“Because it works.”

He smiled and turned back to the stove. “You could lay the table.”

“That isn’t helping.”

“It’s useful. Please.”

She smiled at the please. “All right, Mr. Yang.”

Dinner was simple: fish, greens, soup, rice. They talked about her filming schedule for the autumn and an interviewer she’d found unexpectedly funny, and a client who’d tried to negotiate a contract by sending him a voice message seventeen minutes long.

“Did you listen to all of it?”

“Seventeen minutes and forty-two seconds.”

“Poor you.”

“I was being paid to listen,” he said, and she laughed.

They washed up together. It was nearly ten when he came and sat beside her on the sofa, where she had her feet tucked under her and a cushion against her stomach and was scrolling through photographs on her phone. He watched her.

“I’ve something for you.”

She looked up, and he took the box out of his jacket and put it on the table between them, and her face changed at once.

“I kept it,” he said.

“I know.”

“I didn’t know when I’d give it back.”

She put her phone down. “Why now?”

He opened the box and picked it up, and the diamond sat in its old setting. “Because I think I’m ready to ask you again. I want to marry you. I still want the life we talked about. Waking up next to you, arguing about how much rice I make, going to your premieres, hearing about your work when you come home, being the person you ring when something happens. All of it. Not the version of you I thought would fit into my family. You. Your work, your decisions, your sisters, your red dresses, your habit of stealing my shirts. I know I can’t undo what happened. I know giving you this doesn’t prove I’ve changed. But I want to ask you again. Si-Yuan, will you marry me?”

She didn’t take it. For a moment he thought he’d misunderstood something.

She was looking at the ring. She remembered his kitchen on a Sunday evening two years ago, and the eleven days he’d kept it in his desk before he asked. She remembered his mother saying they should wait, and him not arguing. She remembered the September after, when a part had needed her unmarried and wardrobe had taken all her jewellery, and the ring had gone into a pouch in her bedside drawer, and stayed there long after the part was finished. She remembered the night of the banquet, setting it down beside the earrings and closing the drawer. Every one of those memories was true, and so was the man on the sofa beside her now. She didn’t know yet how to hold both.

She looked at him.

“No.”

It was quiet. His hand stayed where it was. “All right.”

He didn’t close the box. He didn’t ask her why. He waited.

“You’re asking me the same way,” she said.

“Am I?”

She folded her hands in her lap. “You’re asking me to marry you. You’re not asking me to choose you. I know you love me. I know you want to marry me. I know you’ve changed a great deal. But this is the same ring, and I’m not the same woman who said yes to it. I don’t want to be asked because you finally feel ready. I don’t want to be what you come back to once you’ve sorted out your life.”

“That isn’t what I mean.”

“I know. But I need you to see the difference. The first time, you told me you wanted to marry me and I believed you. I believed that if I stood next to you we’d face whatever came together. And when your mother made it hard, I was the one who adjusted. When she humiliated me, I was the one who left. When I gave the ring back, that’s when you finally understood what I’d been asking for. I don’t want to spend another engagement hoping that one day you’ll stand beside me.”

“You won’t have to.”

She reached for his hand. “Don’t answer too fast. I don’t want you to promise me a perfect marriage. I don’t need that. I want to know that when we decide things we’re deciding them together. That when something hard happens you won’t quietly work out what’s best for everyone and expect me to go along with it. And I want to choose you because I want to. Not because you’ve finally asked.”

She looked at him for a long time.

“Ask me differently.” It was barely a whisper.

✦ ✦ ✦

He went still. The words settled between them. He looked at the ring, and closed the box, and put it on the table. He didn’t look disappointed. He didn’t look angry. He looked like a man who’d finally understood there was a question he’d never asked.

He turned to her. “May I ask you something else?”

“Yes.”

He took her hand. “Do you want to build a life with me? Not because I asked you to marry me. Not because we were engaged before. Not because you think you owe me another chance. I want to know whether you want a future with me. One where you keep your work and your independence and your own decisions. One where my family is my responsibility and not yours. One where we disagree and I don’t leave you to deal with what comes of it alone. I want to be your partner, not one more person you have to make room for. And I only want to ask you to marry me if you want that future too.”

Her eyes had begun to shine. “That’s different.”

“I know.”

“You’re finally asking me what I want.”

“Yes.”

“What if I want to go away for six months?”

“Then we’ll work out how.”

“What if I get a part that means I can’t come home for our anniversary?”

“I’ll come to you if I can. If I can’t, we’ll have it when we’re together.”

“What if your mother never accepts me?”

He didn’t hesitate. “Then she doesn’t. I hope she comes to know you. I hope one day she can talk to you without making you feel unwelcome. But I won’t make our marriage depend on it.”

“And if I don’t want to live anywhere near that house?”

“We won’t.”

“If I want a home that’s ours?”

“Then we’ll find one.”

“You’ve answered all of that very fast.”

“Because I’ve thought about all of it. I used to think marrying someone meant bringing them into my life. I didn’t understand it meant making one together.”

“And if I change my mind about something?”

“Then you tell me.”

“And you?”

“I tell you.”

She laughed, a little wet. “That sounds suspiciously like communication.”

“I hear it’s important.”

“Very.” She leaned closer. He touched her face.

“There’s one more thing. I’m not asking because I’m afraid you’ll go again. I miss you when you’re away. I want you here. But I don’t want marriage to be a way of keeping you from going. I want you to come home because it’s home. Not because you promised.”

She stared at him. Then she whispered his name. “I’m frightened sometimes. Of believing you again. Not because I think you’re lying. I just remember how certain I was the first time.”

“You don’t have to pretend you’re not frightened.”

“And you won’t get impatient? You won’t tell me we’ve already been through this? You won’t say I ought to trust you because I’ve seen what you’ve done?”

He kissed her knuckles. “No. I’ll keep showing you.”

✦ ✦ ✦

For a while they sat without speaking, and the box sat on the table.

“Why did you keep it?” she said.

“I couldn’t throw it away.”

“Did you ever think of giving it to someone else?”

He turned his head. “No.”

“Not once?”

“No.”

“Good answer.”

“I wasn’t trying to give a good answer.”

She reached for the box and opened it, and lifted the ring out and held it between her fingers. “I know. I used to wear it every day.”

“I know.”

She looked at him. “Then I stopped. I didn’t stop loving you when I took it off. I was trying to stop waiting.”

“I understand that now.”

She put it back in the box and shut the lid. She didn’t put it on. Instead she moved closer and put her hand flat on his chest.

“I want to marry you.”

He went completely still.

“Not because you brought me the ring. Because I want to wake up next to you. Because I want to hear you talk too much when you’re nervous. Because I want to see your ridiculous office and complain about your cooking and be the person who comes home to you. And because I love you. But I want us to do it differently.”

“We will.”

“Not only tonight?”

“Not only tonight.”

She leaned in and kissed him, slowly, with nothing urgent in it and no attempt to wipe out the years in between. His hand came to her cheek and his arm went round her waist and held her close without pulling her into him. When they came apart he rested his forehead against hers and said thank you.

“For what?”

“For telling me what you wanted.”

“You should have asked sooner.”

“I know.”

“You’re still learning,” she said.

He kissed the corner of her mouth, and her cheek, and her forehead.

“Are you going to keep the ring in the box?” she said, with her eyes shut.

“Unless you want it.”

She looked at it. “Not yet. But don’t put it away too far.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Later she sat on his kitchen counter swinging one foot while he made tea, and took the cup he gave her.

“So. Are we engaged?”

He thought about it properly. “I don’t think we should pretend we are because we’ve agreed we want to marry.”

“That’s a very lawyer answer. Then what are we?”

“Two people who’ve decided they want to get married.”

“That’s an even more lawyer answer.”

“It’s accurate.”

She drank her tea and held out her hand, and he took it. “Fine. I like it. Then we’ll decide the rest together.”

“Together.”

She kissed him, and he told her he loved her, and she said she loved him too.

She didn’t stay. She had an early call and he had court. At the door she put her shoes on and picked up her bag, and turned back.

“Next time you ask me, I want a proper proposal.”

“A proper one?”

“Yes.”

“Flowers?”

“Maybe.”

“A restaurant?”

“Maybe.”

“Your sisters?”

“Not without warning them, or Si-Jie will faint.”

He nodded gravely. “Understood.”

“And don’t rehearse a speech for three weeks.”

“I wasn’t planning to.”

She raised an eyebrow.

“I may already have started,” he admitted.

She burst out laughing, and kissed him, and went down the corridor, and looked back once. He was still in the doorway.

“Put the ring somewhere safe,” she said.

“I won’t lose it again.”

She looked at him, and then she went.

He went back to the living room and picked up the box. For the first time in a long while it didn’t feel like a reminder of something he’d lost. It felt like something they hadn’t finished deciding. He took it to his desk, and this time he didn’t put it in the old drawer. He put it on the top shelf, where he’d see it every morning. Then he stood at the window for a while with the city going on below. He thought about the first time, in his kitchen, how sure he’d been that asking was the brave part. It hadn’t been. The brave part was everything after: the dinners, the table, his mother’s voice, the plate. He’d failed every one of those, and she’d paid for all of them. This time he wanted the asking to be the easy part.

There was no need to hide it. There was no need to hurry either. She hadn’t taken the ring. She’d taken his hand. For now, that was the answer he’d earned.

chapters.title: Differently
chapters.desc: He proposes in front of her sisters, his mother and the crew of her next film, with a speech, badly. Engaged, out loud. That night she leads: explicit.
chapters.epigraph: “I would like to formally request that you become my wife.”
chapters.content:
He’d rehearsed it seventeen times. He knew because Ku had counted.

Ku leaned in the doorway. “Seventeen. And that’s just since lunch.”

“Haven’t you got work?”

“Yes, sir. This is much more entertaining. One question. Have you considered that she might say no?”

“I have. Then I’ll accept it.”

Ku nodded, apparently satisfied. “Good. That’s a much better answer than you’d have given the first time.”

Pengcheng’s face went still, and Ku straightened at once and apologised.

“Get out.”

Ku went, laughing, and Pengcheng looked down at the paper. Three paragraphs. He’d crossed sentences out and rewritten others and taken out a whole section because it sounded like a closing submission. He’d tried to make it sound natural. It didn’t. The first line said: Si-Yuan, I have given considerable thought to the question I would like to ask you this evening. He crossed it out and said “Ridiculous” to the empty room.

Miss Yen (Page Seventeen): Are you busy tonight?

Pengcheng: A little. Why?

Miss Yen (Page Seventeen): I want to see you.

Pengcheng: I’ll come to you.

Miss Yen (Page Seventeen): Don’t be late.

He folded the paper. He had the ring in his pocket. He had a plan. He’d asked her sisters, and his father, and his mother, and the people from her next film. He’d arranged the stage with Qiao-jie and the director. He’d asked Si-Jie not to tell her. That had been the hardest part.

Yen Si-Jie (Sister, Talkative): I’m an excellent keeper of secrets.

Yen Si-Jie (Sister, Talkative): But if she says no I’m blaming you.

Si-Wei had sent one line, and he’d read it several times.

Yen Si-Wei: Don’t make her feel cornered.

He wouldn’t. The question would be asked in front of people who loved her, but the answer would belong to her alone. That was the difference.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was the first day of her new film, a contemporary drama with a director she’d worked with before, and the stage was still busy after the last set-up with a small gathering for the crew. Qiao-jie had told her the director wanted to thank everyone. She hadn’t questioned it. There was always a little party after the first day.

She came in a plain black dress with a long coat over her shoulders and her hair loose, and stopped at the door. Si-Jie was standing by the drinks table with Arthur. Si-Wei was beside Sung Jae. And by the monitors, in a grey suit, talking politely to the producer, was Pengcheng’s father.

“What’s going on?”

Si-Jie turned. “Surprise.”

“Whose?”

“Yours, apparently,” said Si-Wei.

“Jie. Why are you here?”

“To support your career.”

“On a Saturday night?”

“And you?” Si-Yuan said to Si-Wei.

“Same reason.”

Sung Jae nodded solemnly. “Very supportive.”

“You’re all terrible liars,” said Si-Yuan, and Si-Jie put an arm round her and pulled her in.

Then she saw him. He was near the middle of the stage, talking to Qiao-jie, in a dark suit with no tie, and his face had the particular composure he wore when he was nervous. He looked up and stopped talking. His eyes found hers at once, and she smiled, and he smiled back, and came to her.

“You look beautiful.”

“Thank you. Why are you here?”

“I wanted to see you.”

“You could have said so.”

He held out his hand. “I know. Will you come with me? Only over there.”

She looked past him. Beside the director’s chair there was a small arrangement of flowers. Nothing else. No candles, no arch, nothing that would make a crew feel they’d wandered into somebody’s wedding.

“What are you doing?”

“Come with me,” he said, and she took his hand.

✦ ✦ ✦

The stage went quieter as they walked into the middle of it. She saw Qiao-jie smiling. She saw Si-Jie with both hands over her mouth and Si-Wei with her face unusually soft. She saw his father a few steps away. And near the back, sitting alone on a folding chair in dark blue, she saw his mother. Her steps slowed. He felt it at once.

His voice was low. “She’s here because I asked her. You don’t have to speak to her tonight if you don’t want to.”

Si-Yuan looked across at his mother. His mother looked back. There was no smile and no visible warmth. But she didn’t look away.

“All right,” said Si-Yuan.

He pressed her hand once and turned to face the room. Someone turned the music off. The director stepped back.

In his office this had seemed straightforward. Now, with her beside him and some fifty people watching, he found that the speech had left him entirely.

He cleared his throat and looked down at her, and she smiled, and he took a breath. “Good evening. I’m not very good at this.”

A few people laughed. Si-Jie made a small sound, and he asked her please not to help, and the whole room laughed.

His eyes went to his father, and then to his mother, and came back to her. “I asked you all here because you matter to Si-Yuan. Her sisters. Her colleagues. The people who’ve supported her work. And my family. I’d prepared a speech.”

“I can see that,” she said.

“I wrote it down. I practised it. I was told it sounded like a legal submission, so I rewrote it. I had a much better opening than this and I can’t remember it. That’s partly your fault.”

“My fault?”

“You’re looking at me,” he said, and she laughed out loud, and something went out of his shoulders.

Then he was serious. “Si-Yuan. I asked you to marry me once. You said yes. I gave you this ring and thought that was enough to tell you what I wanted. It wasn’t. I loved you. I wanted a life with you. But I didn’t understand that wanting a life together meant standing beside you when it got hard. I let you carry things that should never have been yours to carry alone. I can’t give you back the days you waited for me to speak, or the times you had to wonder whether I’d choose you in front of other people. But I can tell you what I want now.”

The stage had gone completely quiet.

“I want to marry you. I want to be the one who celebrates your work and comes to your premieres and learns your schedule and waits up when you’re late. I want to argue with you about dinner and make too much rice and listen to you complain about it for the rest of our lives. I want to be there when your sisters need you, and when you need them. I want to know every version of you that you haven’t become yet. And I want you to know you’ll never have to make yourself smaller to fit into my life.”

“I don’t want to ask you to promise you’ll stay whatever happens. I want to promise I’ll keep choosing this with you. Not just today. Not only when it’s easy. Every time there’s something to decide. I want us to decide it together.”

Her eyes were shining. His hand was warm round hers. He took a breath, and said, with the gravity of a man delivering the most important statement of his career: “I would like to formally request that you become my wife.”

There was a beat of silence. Then she laughed. Not from embarrassment. Because he’d somehow managed to finish a beautiful speech by sounding like a man filing an application with a government department.

He shut his eyes. “I knew that sentence was wrong.”

The stage came apart with laughter. Even his father was smiling.

Si-Yuan had her hand at her mouth. “Pengcheng. Formally requesting?”

“I’d prefer a yes.”

She laughed again, and stepped closer. “You’ve forgotten something. You haven’t asked me.”

He went still. Then he understood, and his face changed, and he took the box from his jacket and didn’t open it. He looked at her.

“Yen Si-Yuan. Will you marry me?”

She looked at him, and then she smiled. “Yes.”

His breath went out of him. “Yes?”

“Yes, Pengcheng.”

He opened the box. The same diamond, the same setting. This time he didn’t try to put it on her at once. “May I?”

She held out her left hand. “Yes.”

He slid it onto her finger and it settled into place, and she looked down at it and then up at him, and he was smiling. Not the small held-in smile she remembered from the early years. A real one, all the way up.

“I’m going to marry you,” she said, with her hand on his face.

“Yes.”

“Again. Properly this time.”

“Properly this time,” he said, and she kissed him, and the stage went up.

✦ ✦ ✦

Somebody clapped and then everybody did. Si-Jie was crying openly. Si-Wei had her arm round Sung Jae and was smiling in a way Si-Yuan rarely saw. Arthur clapped with the reserved face he wore at formal things and eyes that weren’t reserved at all. His father looked like a man who’d been holding his breath for two years. And his mother stayed in her chair at the back and watched her son hold Si-Yuan’s hand, and watched the ring on her finger, and watched the people round them. She didn’t smile. She didn’t leave.

Si-Jie reached them first, grabbed Si-Yuan’s hand, stared at the ring, and then turned on Pengcheng. “It’s back. You sounded like you were filing a legal request, but you did it properly.”

She hugged him. It surprised him enough that he stood still for a second, and then he hugged her back, and she told him into his shoulder to look after her sister and not to make her come to his office again.

“I’ll try not to give you a reason.”

Si-Wei looked at the ring and then at him for a long moment without a word, and hugged her sister, and whispered something in her ear that made her laugh. He didn’t ask. He suspected it was better not to.

His father shook his hand, and then turned to Si-Yuan. “Congratulations, my dear. You can call me Father, if you’d like to.”

Her face went soft. She looked at Pengcheng, and back. “Thank you, Father.”

His father looked pleased, and kissed her cheek lightly, and stepped away to give them room.

His mother came last. The stage was loud again with the crew taking photographs and the director wanting a word and Si-Jie demanding a group picture, but when his mother stood up, he noticed. He turned a little towards Si-Yuan without letting go of her hand.

His mother stopped in front of them. “Congratulations.”

“Thank you, Madam Yang.”

His mother looked at the ring, and then at her son. “You seem very certain.”

“I am.”

“You’ve thought about it?”

“For a long time.”

She looked at Si-Yuan. “I hope you both understand what marriage asks of you.”

“We do,” said Si-Yuan.

His mother’s eyes rested on her for a moment. Then she turned to her son. “Take care of yourself.” It wasn’t an apology. It wasn’t acceptance. It wasn’t even especially warm. But it was the first time in a long while she’d spoken to him without making it a demand. She gave a small nod and went back to her chair.

“Are you all right?” he said.

“Yes,” said Si-Yuan, and he kissed her temple, and the director called them over for photographs, and the photographs took half an hour. In the one Si-Jie arranged he wasn’t looking at the camera. He was looking at her.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was nearly eleven when they left. She kept looking at the ring.

“That’s twenty times,” he said.

She turned her hand under a streetlamp. “It’s been a long while. Do you remember the first time?”

“You were in one of my shirts with a pencil behind your ear. You hit my arm before you said yes.”

“And now?”

He stopped walking. “Now I want to marry you because I love you, and because I know what it means to choose you. And because I want to keep choosing you.”

She kissed him in the middle of the pavement.

✦ ✦ ✦

That night she led. Not because he was unsure, and not because he needed leading. Because she wanted to decide how it went.

In his flat she took his jacket off him and hung it up herself, and lifted her left hand between them so the ring caught the light. “Look.”

“It suits you.”

“You’re supposed to say something more romantic.”

He thought about it. “It belongs on your hand.”

He kissed the ring and then the inside of her wrist. “Better. Tonight I want you to let me do everything,” she said.

“All right.”

She undid his collar and then the buttons of his shirt one at a time with her fingers on his throat, and he stood still and let her. When she kissed him she did it slowly and then with more certainty, her hands on his shoulders, and when she drew back he didn’t follow. He waited. She liked that. She liked that he could want her without assuming what she wanted back.

At the bedroom door she stopped. “I want tonight to be ours. Not a celebration for everyone else. Not a reward for getting engaged. Not proof that everything’s mended. And I want to keep the ring on. Only the ring.”

“Then it’s ours,” he said.

She sat him on the edge of the bed and stood between his knees and took her time. She took his shirt off him and kissed his shoulders. When he reached for her she caught his hands and put them on the bed either side of him. “Let me.” She undressed in front of him, slowly, everything, until there was nothing on her but the ring, and he watched her with a look that made her smile.

“You’re staring.”

“I know.”

“Do you like what you see?”

“Yes.”

“Then tell me.”

“You’re beautiful.”

“Again.”

“You’re beautiful, Si-Yuan.”

She pushed him back onto the pillows and climbed over him, and the ring brushed his chest, and he looked at it and then at her.

“Still looking?”

“It’s hard not to.”

“Then look,” she said, and he lifted her hand and kissed it.

She decided all of it. When to stop and when to go on, when to bring him closer and when to let the room go quiet. She took him into her hand and then into her body, slowly, and sat back on him with her palms flat on his chest, and held there, and watched his face. He followed where she went. He watched every change in her and asked when he wasn’t sure, and listened when she answered. There was no audience now and no applause and no family waiting to congratulate anyone. Only the two of them and the room they knew and the ring on her finger catching the lamp each time she moved.

She kept her left hand on his cheek at the end, and he turned his head and kissed her palm, and when she said his name he answered it out loud, not because he’d rehearsed it but because he wanted her to hear him. Then he said hers, and she came apart over him with the ring pressed to his face, and he followed her with his hands on her hips and her name in his mouth.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards she lay against him and held her hand up between them, turning it.

“Do you regret saying yes?”

“No.”

“Are you sure?”

“Pengcheng.”

“Sorry. I think I may ask that a lot.”

She put her head on his chest. “Then I’ll keep answering. Your speech was terrible. You formally requested that I become your wife.”

“Please don’t repeat it.”

“I can’t believe you said it.”

“I was nervous. There were fifty people.”

“That’s your defence?”

“No.”

She laughed into his chest. Then she lifted her head. “I liked it, though. All of it. Even the end. You weren’t trying to sound perfect. You were trying to tell me the truth. You used to think that if you couldn’t say a thing properly you should wait till you could. I’m glad you didn’t wait.”

“I’m glad you said yes.”

Her phone was going on the bedside table. The group had thirty-seven messages.

Si-Jie (Questions): I’M STILL CRYING.

Si-Wei (Watching): You were crying before he’d started.

Si-Jie (Questions): BECAUSE I KNEW.

Si-Yuan: I’m engaged.

Si-Jie (Questions): WE KNOW.

Si-Wei (Watching): Congratulations, eldest.

✦ ✦ ✦

Across the city his mother was awake, with his father asleep and the house quiet and an old photograph of him as a boy on the table beside her. Her phone lit.

Pengcheng: She said yes. We’re engaged.

A photograph followed, taken by someone on the crew: Si-Yuan’s hand over his, the ring showing, both of them smiling. She looked at it a long time. She could have written something formal.

Mother (Senior Counsel): I see.

She read it, and it looked cold, and she added a line.

Mother (Senior Counsel): Congratulations to you both.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the morning he woke and found her sitting up beside him looking at her hand.

“Still there,” he said.

“Of course it is.”

He took her hand and kissed the ring. “Good morning.”

“Good morning. What’s for breakfast?”

“Something warm. I’ll make the right amount.”

“You always say that.”

“I’ll keep trying,” he said, and she leaned against him, and the ring caught the morning light, and there was no question left waiting to be answered and no silence he needed to explain and nobody else he needed permission from. Everyone who mattered had heard him ask.

chapters.title: His Mother’s Answer
chapters.desc: On the triplets’ birthday his mother sends a gift with a card for the first time. One line: “Wear red.” Si-Yuan cries for the first time in a year.
chapters.content:
The parcel came up early on the thirteenth of December, carried by the man from the desk downstairs, who said a driver had left it. A small box in cream paper with a dark red ribbon, and a cream envelope tucked under the bow.

“Who from?”

He looked at the card. “Madam Yang.”

Si-Yuan went still. She was in the kitchen in her slippers with her hair tied up anyhow and the kettle going behind her. On the table three small cakes waited under their glass covers. She thanked him, and he went, and for several seconds she didn’t touch it.

Then she picked up the envelope. Her name was on the front. Not Miss Yen, or Pengcheng’s fiancée. Si-Yuan, in a precise, slightly slanting hand that could only have been his mother’s.

Inside was a small card with one line on it.

Wear red.

She read it once, and again, and stood still. Then she untied the ribbon. Folded in tissue was a silk shawl, a deep warm red like the skin of a pomegranate, with a faint woven pattern that showed only when the light caught it. There was no jewellery. No other message. No explanation. Only the shawl and the card.

She sat down and touched the silk. She remembered a dark red dress at a Sunday lunch, and a woman looking at it before she looked at anything else and asking whether there was an occasion. She remembered a blouse in August and It draws attention. She remembered putting red away and buying navy and grey and beige instead, colours that wouldn’t be remarked on, colours that would let her sit at that table and leave without anyone remembering what she’d worn. She remembered a pair of red earrings he’d bought her, and his telling her red suited her, and her never once explaining why she’d stopped. Then Paris, and the dress coming out of the wardrobe, and her sisters in capital letters. She’d thought red had become hers again.

And now, on her twenty-third birthday, his mother had sent her a red shawl. Wear red. No I’m sorry, no I was wrong, not even happy birthday. One line. But it was the first thing his mother had ever sent her herself. The first time she’d written her name. The first time she’d given her anything that wasn’t a test.

Her eyes blurred. The tears came before she understood she was crying, and she put her hand over her mouth. She hadn’t cried like this in more than a year. There’d been hard days. There’d been a few quiet tears in a stranger’s hall in May that she’d wiped away with a borrowed tissue. She’d learned to let things pass, to breathe through them, that sadness didn’t always have to turn into tears. This was the other kind. She was crying over a shawl. A piece of red silk, and two words that didn’t undo anything at all. She pressed the card to her chest.

✦ ✦ ✦

He found her twenty minutes later. He’d come out of the shower in a white shirt with his sleeves rolled, expecting to find her making breakfast or on the phone to her sisters, and found her on the sofa with the box beside her and her eyes red, and crossed the room at once.

“Si-Yuan? Are you hurt? Has someone rung?”

She shook her head. He looked at the box, and then at the card in her hand, and his face changed. “My mother sent this?”

She nodded.

He read it. For a moment he didn’t say anything. “Do you want me to ring her?”

“No.”

He put the card down. She wiped her cheek with the heel of her hand. “I don’t know why I’m crying. It’s only a shawl. She didn’t even write happy birthday.”

He looked at the card again. “No. It’s the first thing she’s ever sent you herself. And she wrote your name. I think she remembered.”

She shut her eyes. She’d wanted his mother to remember her. For years she’d wanted to be remembered as more than the actress who’d come into the family and failed to become what it expected. She’d wanted his mother to notice what she loved, the work she did, how she cared for her son, the person she was when nobody was looking. She’d wanted one small sign that she wasn’t invisible. Now there was one. Nothing was wiped out by it. But it was enough to hurt.

He pulled her gently against him and she put her face in his shoulder.

“I’m not forgiving her because of this,” she whispered.

“I know.”

“And I don’t want you to think everything’s all right now.”

“I won’t.”

She cried again, and he didn’t tell her to stop, and he didn’t try to make the shawl mean more than it did. He held her while she cried over a card.

✦ ✦ ✦

Si-Jie came first with a bag of breakfast and Arthur behind her with flowers, calling out happy birthday to all three of them from the door, and then she saw Si-Yuan’s face and put the bag down. “Why have you been crying?”

Si-Wei came a few minutes later with Sung Jae, took one look at both her sisters and went quiet. “What is it?”

Pengcheng nodded at the table. Si-Yuan picked up the card. “Madam Yang sent me something.”

Si-Jie read it and her face changed. “Wear red.”

Si-Wei took it from her and read it more slowly, and looked at Si-Yuan, and said only, “Oh.”

“I know,” said Si-Yuan, with a weak laugh.

Si-Jie sat down and put both arms round her. “Oh, Yuan.”

“I don’t know what to do with it.”

“You don’t have to do anything with it.”

“It’s a beautiful shawl.”

“Then wear it.”

“Do you think she meant it?”

Si-Jie didn’t answer straight away. She knew better than to offer certainty where there wasn’t any. “I think she meant something. I don’t know exactly what.”

Si-Wei put the card down carefully. “Neither do I. But it isn’t nothing. She remembered red. Perhaps she remembered what she said. Perhaps she saw you in it again and understood something. Perhaps she only wanted to give you a present. We don’t have to decide which today.”

“You can be happy about it without pretending the past didn’t happen,” said Si-Jie.

“And you can still be angry,” said Si-Wei.

Si-Yuan laughed through it. “You two always agree when I’m crying.”

“We’re very united,” said Si-Jie.

Arthur cleared his throat. “Should the breakfast go somewhere?”

“Not now.”

“Of course.”

Sung Jae put the flowers on the table and wished Si-Yuan happy birthday, and then all three of them, and glanced at the box. “It’s beautiful.”

“It is,” said Si-Yuan.

✦ ✦ ✦

The birthday started late. There were three cakes, as there always were, because the three of them had spent their lives insisting that sharing a birthday didn’t mean sharing a cake. Si-Jie’s had small white flowers on it. Si-Wei’s was dark chocolate. Si-Yuan’s was strawberry, with red fruit round the edge.

Their mother rang from Taipei in the middle of it, on Si-Jie’s phone, propped against the fruit bowl so she could see all three of them at once, and sang to them in a voice that cracked on the high note as it had every year of their lives, and asked Si-Yuan why her eyes were pink, and Si-Yuan said onions, and their mother said there were no onions in a birthday cake, and let it go.

She wore the shawl, and not because she felt she had to, or to prove anything to anyone. She liked the colour. It sat on her shoulders, soft against her skin, and when she came out of the bedroom Si-Jie looked up and made a small sound and came to straighten the edge of it.

“It looks beautiful.”

“It suits you,” said Si-Wei from across the room.

Pengcheng, who’d been putting candles in three cakes with great care, looked up and smiled. “It does.”

“Your mother has good taste,” Si-Yuan said.

He laughed a little. “She does.”

She looked at him, and he understood what she meant, and for once neither of them needed to say anything else.

After the candles, and the photographs, and Si-Jie insisting they sing it twice because Arthur had come in half a beat early, the room went quieter. The sisters sat together on the sofa. The three men were in the kitchen washing plates, and Sung Jae was being shown by Arthur, with great patience, how Si-Jie liked them stacked.

“Will you wear it to his mother’s?” said Si-Jie.

“Maybe.”

“You don’t have to.”

Si-Yuan touched the edge of the silk. “I know. I used to think that if I wore red she’d think I was trying to draw attention. Now I think I just don’t want to make myself invisible any more.”

Si-Jie kissed her temple. “Good.”

Si-Yuan looked through the kitchen door. Pengcheng was laughing at something Arthur had said, with his sleeves rolled up, drying a plate. He looked happy. She looked down at the ring on her hand. The ring and the shawl. Two things she’d once stopped wearing. One had come back through a promise. The other through a single line on a card.

✦ ✦ ✦

While she was seeing her sisters to the lift he rang his father from the kitchen.

“She sent Si-Yuan a present. A shawl. Red. With a card in her own hand,” he said.

There was a pause on the line. “I know. I didn’t know she’d send it today. I knew she’d bought it.”

“When?”

“In October, after the stage. She went to the silk shop on the old street herself, in the rain. She hasn’t bought a present with her own hands in fifteen years. She’s always sent the secretary.”

His father was quiet, and when he spoke again his voice had gone softer. “She asked me, the week before, what colour Si-Yuan had worn in the photographs from the Paris premiere. I told her red. She didn’t say anything. She only nodded, and went back to her book.”

Pengcheng stood at the counter with a tea towel in his hand. “She wrote two words.”

“Your mother has never in her life written more words than she meant. You know that better than anyone. Don’t ask her for more than two. And don’t tell her I told you about the rain.”

“I won’t.”

“Is Si-Yuan all right?”

He looked through the door, at Si-Yuan coming back down the corridor with the shawl round her shoulders and her eyes still a little pink, laughing at something Si-Jie had shouted from the lift. “She cried. She’s all right.”

“Good. Tell her happy birthday from me. And from your mother, if she’ll take it secondhand,” said his father.

✦ ✦ ✦

When the others had gone he found her by the window with the shawl still round her, and stood behind her with his hands on her shoulders.

“Cold?”

She reached up for his hand. “No. I’m wearing it because I like it. Did you know she’d send something?”

“No. I’m as surprised as you.”

“Do you think she’s trying?”

He took his time. “I think she made a gesture.”

“That isn’t the same thing.”

“No.”

She leaned back against him. “I don’t want to mistake one gesture for a change. But I don’t want to throw it away either.”

“You don’t have to.”

They watched the lights of the city. “I cried,” she said.

“I noticed.”

“Not because I want her approval. I think I only wanted her to see me.”

“She sees you.”

“Maybe.”

He touched the shawl at her shoulder. “And she knows you like red.”

She looked down, and laughed. “That’s a start.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Late that night a message came to his phone.

Mother (Senior Counsel): I hope the shawl fits.

He read it, and looked at her. “It’s from my mother.”

She held out her hand and he gave her the phone. She looked at the screen, and then typed into it herself.

Pengcheng: This is Si-Yuan. It fits beautifully. Thank you, Madam Yang. I like the colour very much.

She sent it and gave the phone back and didn’t wait. She went into the bedroom and took her earrings off at the dressing table, with the shawl still round her shoulders, and he came and stood behind her and met her eyes in the mirror.

“You look beautiful in red.”

“You’ve told me that before.”

“I’ll keep telling you.”

She turned round. “Even when I’m old?”

“When you’re old and when you’re tired and when you’ve just come off a night shoot and don’t want to be told anything,” he said, and she laughed and put her arms round him.

Half an hour later the phone lit once more.

Mother (Senior Counsel): Good.

She read it, and looked at him. He was watching her, but he didn’t ask what she felt. She put the phone down.

“Good,” she said, and he smiled, and she rested her forehead against his chest.

For the first time she let herself imagine that one day she might sit at a table with his mother in red and not think about whether it was too much. Not because she’d finally learned the right way to behave. Because nobody would ask her to make herself smaller. She didn’t know whether that day would come. She didn’t need to know tonight.

Tonight she was twenty-three. Her sisters had been there. He’d been there. And somewhere in the house of the woman who’d once made her feel she didn’t belong, there was an empty box where a red silk shawl had been. It was a small thing. It was the first thing his mother had given her without asking her to become someone else.

chapters.title: Two Careers
chapters.desc: She takes a film in Seoul. He comes for a week and works from the hotel, and learns to wait without being silent. In October they go home for Eliana Lin’s wedding.
chapters.epigraph: “Now I think it means letting you have your life and making sure you know I’m here.”
chapters.content:
The first thing he learned about a film in Seoul was that a call sheet could ruin breakfast. The second was that she could read one while eating toast, answering Qiao-jie and correcting a line in her script, and lose track of none of them. The third was that he was much worse than he’d thought at pretending he wasn’t waiting for her.

“Your coffee’s going cold,” she said.

He looked up from his laptop. She was across the little table in their hotel suite, dressed already, with her hair pinned back and the script open by her plate and her phone propped against a glass of water.

“It’s fine.”

“You’ve been looking at the same paragraph for ten minutes.”

“It’s an important paragraph.”

She looked at his screen. “It’s an email.”

“It’s an important email.”

She smiled. He shut the laptop halfway. “What time are you called?”

“Quarter to seven.”

“It’s ten past six. You should eat. That isn’t much.”

“Pengcheng.”

He stopped himself. Then, differently: “Would you like me to order something else?”

Her face went soft. “No. This is enough. You’re getting better at that.”

“At what?”

“Not turning every worry into an instruction.”

“I’m trying.”

She reached over and touched his hand. “Eat your breakfast, lawyer.”

“Yes, actress.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He’d meant to come for three days and stayed for seven. A meeting had moved, a hearing had been adjourned, and a contract dispute had turned into something that needed him personally. He could have gone home and run it from the office. Instead he’d brought it with him, and Ku had objected to a hotel room being used as chambers, and he’d ignored Ku.

The suite had a small sitting room, a desk and a window over the city. His laptop and files and two notebooks took one end of the table. Her scripts and call sheets and make-up bag took the other. Their lives shared a table.

In the mornings she left with Qiao-jie and the production driver. He stayed. He ate lunch between calls. In the afternoons he read documents and rang Ku and sat in meetings on a screen. Sometimes she came back for ten minutes to change. Sometimes she sent him a photograph of whatever the production had ordered for lunch. Sometimes she didn’t send anything at all, and he was learning that that didn’t mean anything was wrong.

On the second day he made the mistake of asking Qiao-jie whether the afternoon had changed.

Ou Qiao: Mr. Yang, she’s on set. I’ll tell her you asked.

He looked at it for a while, and wrote back that there was no need. A few minutes later his phone went again.

Miss Yen (Page Seventeen): Did you ask Qiao-jie where I am?

Pengcheng: I wanted to know if your day had changed. I was thinking about dinner.

Miss Yen (Page Seventeen): You can ask me.

He read that twice.

Pengcheng: You’re right. I’m sorry.

Miss Yen (Page Seventeen): I finish about eight. If you’re free, let’s eat together. And don’t interrogate my manager.

Pengcheng: Understood.

Miss Yen (Page Seventeen): That’s a very lawyer answer.

Pengcheng: I’ll work on it.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first night she came back late he was still awake at the desk. She came in nearly at one with her shoes in her hand, and stopped when she saw the lamp.

“You’re still working?”

“Finishing something.”

“That’s what you said two hours ago.”

“Did Qiao-jie tell you?”

“No. I can read a clock.”

She kissed his cheek and went to wash, and came back in a loose shirt with her hair down, and stood by him a moment, and asked whether he was coming to bed soon.

“In a little while. Don’t wait for me.”

“I’m reading,” she said, and got into bed with her script.

When he finally shut the laptop she was asleep with the pages on her chest. He took them away carefully. She stirred.

“Finished?”

“Yes.”

He got in beside her and she moved towards him without opening her eyes, and he put his arm round her.

“You don’t have to stay up till I come back,” she said into his shoulder.

“I know.”

“Then why do you?”

He thought about it. “Because I like knowing when you’re home.”

She opened one eye. “You could ask me to message you.”

“I could.”

“Then do that.”

“I’ll ask,” he said, and she shut her eye again.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the Thursday she had a hard scene: an argument in a hospital corridor and then a breakdown alone in an empty stairwell, which the director wanted restrained to the point of being uncomfortable to watch. She’d spent the morning on it, and at lunch she came back to the hotel and found him on a call in English, taking a client through a clause in a measured voice, asking exact questions. He looked up and lifted one finger, and she nodded and sat on the sofa and watched him.

She liked watching him work. Not because she needed him to impress her. She’d seen him in court and in his office and at his mother’s table and in the quiet hours after bad conversations. But she liked this part of him too: the man who could disappear entirely into a problem, who wouldn’t pretend to understand something he hadn’t looked at yet, who asked questions until the answer made sense.

When he’d finished he closed the laptop. “How was it?”

She waited after she’d said it. “Difficult. You’re supposed to ask what happened.”

He smiled. “What happened?”

“He thinks I’m making it too emotional. He wants less crying. More holding back.”

“Do you agree?”

“Maybe.”

“What do you think is missing?”

He didn’t offer an opinion. He waited. She began to explain: the character and her brother, the argument, the way the woman had spent years trying not to be a burden to anyone. He listened, and asked two questions, and then said slowly, “Perhaps she isn’t trying not to cry. Perhaps she’s trying not to let him see that she wants him to stay.”

Si-Yuan went quiet and looked at him.

He frowned a little. “Does that make sense?”

She smiled slowly. “Yes. That’s what I couldn’t find. You’re useful sometimes.”

“Sometimes?”

“Don’t get proud,” she said, and kissed him, and went back to set, and from the door said that she was glad he was there. For the rest of the afternoon he didn’t look at the clock once.

✦ ✦ ✦

Ku wrote that evening.

Ku Ka-ho: How is Seoul?

Pengcheng: Fine.

Ku Ka-ho: I assume you’re being very supportive.

Pengcheng: What does that mean?

Ku Ka-ho: Nothing, sir. Just don’t forget you also have a job. The client’s sent the revised draft.

He opened it and worked until midnight, and when she came in he was already in bed, and she slid in beside him and found his hand.

“Finished?”

“Yes.”

She kissed his shoulder. “Good. The food on set tonight was terrible.”

“Tomorrow I’ll find somewhere better.”

She shook her head on the pillow. “You don’t have to plan everything. Sometimes you can just wait for me to come home.”

He touched her cheek. “I can do that.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On the sixth day his father rang about a client referral, and at the end of it asked how long he was staying.

“Till tomorrow.”

“And Si-Yuan?”

“Another week of filming.”

“You’re coming home without her?”

“Yes.”

“You sound disappointed.”

He looked at the table, where her call sheet for the next day was spread out, starting before it was light. “I’ll miss her.”

His father laughed. “You’re allowed. Does she know?”

He thought about that, and when the call was over he wrote to her.

Pengcheng: I’m leaving tomorrow afternoon. I wish I could stay longer. I’ll miss you.

She answered between set-ups.

Miss Yen (Page Seventeen): I’ll miss you too. But I want you to go home and sleep in your own bed.

Pengcheng: Are you dismissing me?

Miss Yen (Page Seventeen): Yes. Stop being a lawyer.

Pengcheng: I’ll try.

The last morning they ate breakfast without saying much. She turned the pages of her script. He finished one last thing on the laptop because he’d promised he’d finish it before he left. Nobody asked the other to fill the silence. But when she reached across the table his hand was there, and when he had to go, he told her.

“I should go.”

“I’ll come down with you.”

At the entrance the car was waiting. He put his bag in and turned to her. “Message me when you’ve finished tonight. And eat properly.”

She raised an eyebrow.

He smiled at himself. “Sorry. Would you please eat properly?”

“Better,” she said, laughing.

He kissed her, and touched her face. “I’ll ring tonight.”

“You don’t have to.”

“I want to.”

“Then ring,” she said, and stood under the hotel awning until the car pulled away, and raised her hand, and he raised his, and the car turned the corner.

✦ ✦ ✦

They were both home by October, she straight from the last day in Seoul, he two days before her. Eliana Lin and Wang Yu Chen were getting married on the Saturday.

It was three and a half years since the morning on the university steps when Eliana had come up the hill holding his hand, and Si-Jie had made a noise like a kettle and Si-Yuan had taken her sunglasses off to see. Now she stood at her wardrobe on the Friday night deciding between two dresses, one pale champagne and one deep red, while he sat on the bed with the invitation.

“Which one?”

“The red.”

“You didn’t even look properly.”

“I looked. It’s red.”

“That’s your entire argument?”

“It suits you.”

She held it up against herself. “Your mother might even be pleased.”

“Wear it because you like it.”

She sat beside him. “I do. Will you come with me to my sisters’ first in the morning? Even if Si-Jie spends the whole time asking when we’re getting married?”

He looked at the ring on her hand. “We’re engaged.”

“That isn’t what she’ll ask.”

He laughed. “I know.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The wedding was in two back gardens that had become one: Eliana’s and the house next door, with a new gate cut through the old wall between them and the chairs set out in a curve under the persimmon tree. The guests came in from four. The October air was mild and the light came through the leaves in soft warm bands.

The three of them found each other at the gate. Si-Jie with Arthur, Si-Wei with Sung Jae, Si-Yuan in red with Pengcheng beside her. They looked at one another for a second, and then Si-Jie lifted her hand and shouted “Yuan!” and Si-Yuan laughed and went to her.

“You look beautiful.”

“So do you.”

Si-Wei kissed her cheek. “Was the flight all right?”

“Long.”

Pengcheng shook Arthur’s hand, and Sung Jae’s, and Sung Jae glanced at the ring and congratulated him again, and Si-Jie looked Si-Yuan up and down.

“Red again. I’m starting to think you don’t own anything else.”

“I do. At home.”

“Convenient.”

“You’re all standing in the gateway,” said Si-Wei, and they went through together and sat down in a row in the curve of chairs: Si-Jie bright and already looking for the bride, Si-Wei composed with her hand in Sung Jae’s, Si-Yuan in red with her ring catching the late light. Somebody behind them said under her breath that they looked like three exclamation marks, and Si-Jie heard, and was delighted.

At half past five the guests were seated. The bride came down from the house a little after, and her father was waiting at the new gate in the wall. When she came through it on his arm Si-Jie began to cry almost at once, and Si-Wei passed her a tissue without taking her eyes off the ceremony.

“Your sister’s crying,” murmured Pengcheng.

“She cries at everything.”

“Not everything.”

“She cried when I cut my hair.”

“That was a significant change,” he said, and she had to bite her lip.

When the vows began she felt his thumb move over her knuckles. They were talking about the life they meant to make and the ordinary days after the wedding, and choosing each other when the excitement had gone. She looked at him. He was watching the couple under the tree. Then he turned his head and found her already looking, and smiled, and she smiled back, and nobody needed to say anything.

✦ ✦ ✦

At the reception Eliana came over with Yu Chen and hugged the sisters, and Si-Jie demanded a photograph at once, and Yu Chen said gravely that Eliana had no choice, and there was one, and another, and then one with all the partners, with Pengcheng’s hand at Si-Yuan’s waist.

“Do you remember the hill?” she said to him while they waited for the photographer.

“Yes.”

“I never thought we’d all be here.”

“Neither did I.”

Later, when the music got loud, she slipped out to the far end of the garden for some air, and he asked whether she wanted him to come, and she told him to come if he wanted to. They stood under the trees away from the lights.

“Seoul was nice. I liked having you there,” she said.

“I liked being there.”

“You didn’t get bored? Waiting for me?”

He looked at her. “I wasn’t waiting all the time. You had work and I had work. Sometimes we ate together and sometimes we didn’t. Sometimes I missed you. And I told you. I used to think waiting meant keeping quiet until the other person came back. Now I think it means letting you have your life and making sure you know I’m here.”

She was quiet, and then she looked up. “That’s better.”

“I’m glad.”

She kissed him, small and warm, and touched his cheek. “I’m glad we have two careers.”

“Three, if you count managing your sisters.”

“That’s a full-time job.”

“An exhausting one.”

“Don’t let Si-Jie hear you,” she said, and when they went back Si-Jie was already looking for them with a photographer, saying they’d taken fifty and needed fifty-one, and Si-Wei lifted her glass and said just take it. The three of them stood together again, and the partners stood beside them, and Eliana and Yu Chen came and stood with them too, and the camera went.

Afterwards she looked at the picture. Her sisters first. Then Eliana and Yu Chen. Then him beside her, holding her hand. She thought about the woman she’d been the first time she went into his mother’s house, rehearsing how low to bow. She’d spent years believing that a life together meant learning to fit into somebody else’s. She understood it differently now. A life together meant there was room for both of you. His work and hers. His family and her sisters. Seoul and home. The days you were together and the days you had to wait.

She looked up and found him already looking at her. When the music began again he held out his hand, and she took it, and they went back in together.

chapters.title: The Wedding
chapters.desc: A small wedding. She doesn’t bow to anyone. His mother in the second row. He kisses her first, before the celebrant.
chapters.content:
There were thirty-six guests. Si-Yuan had counted them twice: once by the chairs while the planner walked her round the garden, and once by the names on the final list at midnight, when Pengcheng was already asleep beside her. Thirty-six. Not three hundred. No ballroom full of people whose opinions mattered more than the two who were getting married. No receiving line, no seating plan arranged to show who stood where in which family. Their sisters, their closest friends, the people who’d seen them before and after they found their way back. A small garden, and flowers, and a celebrant. And him.

“Are you counting again?”

He was in the bedroom doorway in his suit trousers and white shirt with his tie hanging loose. She was at the dressing table in a silk robe with the list in her hand.

“No. I’m checking whether everyone’s coming.”

“Everyone’s said yes.”

She looked at him in the mirror. “I know. I’m checking whether thirty-six is enough.”

He came and put his hands on her shoulders and kissed her cheek. “If we had six it would be enough.”

“And two?”

“I’d still marry you.”

“None?”

“I’d still marry you.”

She put the list down and told him it was a good answer, and he held out his tie. “Will you?”

She stood up and did it for him, pulling the silk through the knot carefully, and he watched her face the whole time.

“You’re staring.”

“I like looking at you.”

“That’s my line.”

“I learned it from you.” She tightened the knot, and loosened it a fraction, and smoothed his collar, and left her hands flat on his chest.

“Today,” she said.

“Yes.”

“I’m marrying you.”

He covered her hands with his. “Yes.”

“It’s strange.”

“Good strange?”

“Very,” she said, and he pressed a kiss into her hair.

✦ ✦ ✦

The ceremony was at four. The garden was small and walled with trees, with four short rows of chairs and a narrow aisle between them. There was no stage and no arch. There was only a low arrangement of flowers where the celebrant would stand, and a small table under the trees for the signing afterwards. She’d chosen the flowers herself: white ranunculus, pale roses, a few branches of green. She’d sent back the first arrangement because it was too formal, and the second because it was too big, and the third because the florist had called it grand. She wanted it to look as though it had grown there. He’d watched her decide all of it and hadn’t interfered once. He’d only asked whether she liked it. She did.

He stood at the gate to greet people. His father came first, with a small gift, and shook his hand and then held him by both shoulders. “You look well. Nervous?”

“A little.”

His father looked towards the house. “Good. It means you know what today is. Tell her she needn’t worry about anything.”

“I think she knows.”

Si-Jie came with Arthur in a soft ivory dress with a little posy in her hands, insufferably happy, as she had been since the eighth of April, when she’d married him. She marched straight up to Pengcheng.

“Is she nervous?”

“A little.”

“Are you?”

“Yes.”

She looked at him more carefully. “Good. You look different. Less like you’re going to a legal conference.”
