“She means you look happy,” said Arthur.

“I am,” said Pengcheng, and Si-Jie’s face went soft, and she reached up and straightened his tie and told him not to mess this up, and Arthur took her hand gently and told her to let the man breathe.

Si-Wei came a few minutes later with Sung Jae, in dark green, with the expression of someone who’d already noticed three things that needed correcting. She looked at his tie. “It’s crooked.”

“I’ve just fixed it,” said Si-Jie.

“You fixed it crooked,” said Si-Wei, and did it herself, and Arthur said this wasn’t his area, and Sung Jae said it wasn’t his either.

Then she looked at Pengcheng, and something in her face eased. “Ready?”

“Yes.”

“Good.” It was one word, and he understood all of it. Six years ago she’d sent him four words on the night he first met them. He hadn’t always kept to them. He couldn’t take that back. But he could keep choosing better.

“I’ll look after her,” he said.

“She can look after herself.”

“I know.”

Si-Wei said good again, and hugged him, briefly and sincerely, and said into his shoulder, “Look after each other.”

✦ ✦ ✦

His mother came shortly before four, in red. Not bright red. A deep, quiet shade, with a plain neckline and long sleeves. He saw her before anyone else did and went to her. She looked at his suit, and at the garden.

“Your father’s already here?”

“Yes.” He offered her his arm. She looked at it a moment before she took it.

Her seat was in the second row, between his aunt and an old friend of the family. Not the front. She looked at it, and at him. “You’ve put me here?”

“Father’s in the front. Si-Jie and Si-Wei will be standing with Si-Yuan, and her mother’s flown in from Taipei for the front row.”

His mother looked at the front, and at the two names on the card as witnesses, and adjusted her bag. “I see. It’s fine.”

“You’re my son,” she said, when he thanked her for coming, and told him to go and get ready, and he went, and on the way he looked back once at her dress.

“Red suits you.”

She looked down at it, and up at him. “It does.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Si-Yuan was ready a few minutes before four. Her dress was plain and clean, light fabric falling as it liked, a soft neckline, light sleeves, the back modestly open. She’d chosen it because she wanted to feel like herself in it. Not like an actress at a premiere, or someone playing a part. Her engagement ring was on her hand. A thin bracelet was on her other wrist, gold, with one small red stone: he’d given it to her the morning after he’d proposed for the second time, and said he’d bought it two years before for a birthday he’d never managed to give it to her on. Her sisters had chosen the earrings. There was no long veil and no heavy jewellery.

Si-Jie was behind her with the last pin, telling her not to move. Si-Wei was at the window with her eye on the time.

“Don’t rush her,” said Si-Jie.

“I’m not. The ceremony starts in three minutes.”

Si-Yuan laughed, and they both looked at her.

Si-Wei came and straightened the edge of a sleeve. “You look beautiful.”

Si-Jie came round to the front of her and was already crying.

“Don’t,” said Si-Yuan.

“I haven’t said anything.”

“You’re married. You ought to be used to this.”

“It’s different when it’s you,” said Si-Jie, and Si-Wei handed her a tissue and said she’d ruin her make-up, and Si-Yuan laughed again, and then didn’t.

“Thank you. For being here.”

“Oh, Yuan,” said Si-Jie, and hugged her carefully round the dress, and Si-Wei put her arms round both of them, and for a moment the three of them stood together and nobody said anything at all.

Then Si-Wei stepped back. “Ready?”

“Yes.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He’d been told to wait at the front and not turn round until the music started. He did as he was told. At the first notes he turned.

She was at the end of the aisle with a sister on each side holding her hands. She looked at him and smiled, and he forgot to breathe. For a moment there wasn’t any garden. There were no guests and no flowers and no celebrant. There was only her coming towards him.

He’d first seen her across a desk in a production office, a girl of eighteen who’d read clause fourteen aloud under protest and asked whether he had a girlfriend, and left her black fountain pen on his desk. He remembered her in costume and borrowed slippers at a noodle stall at four in the morning. He remembered the first time she’d bowed to his mother, and the last time she’d walked away from his table. He remembered Paris, and the bridge, and the ring she’d refused, and the night she’d said yes. And now she was walking towards him again. Nobody had asked her to, and nobody had decided she belonged there; she’d come because she wanted to.

Si-Jie kissed her cheek and let go. Si-Wei squeezed her hand and stepped aside. She walked the last few steps alone, and he met her halfway and held out his hand, and she took it.

“Welcome, everyone. Thank you for being here to witness this,” said the celebrant.

He was still looking at her.

“You’re staring. Everyone can see,” she whispered.

“I know.”

The celebrant went on about two people who’d chosen to build a life together. He’d written his vows by hand and rewritten them after she’d told him the first draft sounded like a skeleton argument. He’d practised them. He’d even asked his father whether they sounded natural. Now, standing in front of her, he found he was thinking about something else entirely.

He wanted to kiss her. Not after the vows or the rings. Now.

She saw his face change. “What are you—”

He lifted her hand, and stepped in, and kissed her. Before the celebrant. Before the vows. Before anyone could tell them it was time. It wasn’t hurried and it wasn’t for show. He held her face, and she smiled against his mouth and kissed him back.

A small laugh went through the chairs. Si-Jie put her hand over her mouth. Arthur smiled. Si-Wei shook her head. The celebrant paused, and then said, warmly, “I see we’re starting a little early,” and everyone laughed.

He drew back just far enough to look at her. “I wanted to kiss my bride.”

“I’m not your bride yet.”

“Not for long.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He went first. He unfolded the paper and she looked at it.

“Of course you wrote them down.”

He smiled, and looked at her instead of the paper, and the chairs laughed once in the middle when he got to the rice. “I used to think that loving someone meant being sure you wanted them. I was wrong. Love isn’t only what I feel when we’re alone. It’s what I do when other people are watching. It’s the choices I make when they’re hard. It’s whether I speak when it would be easier not to. I can’t promise I’ll never make mistakes. I will. But I promise I won’t make you carry them alone. I’ll listen when you tell me I’ve hurt you. I’ll tell you what I’m thinking instead of leaving you to guess. I’ll respect the life you’ve built and the work you love and the person you keep becoming. I’ll be proud of you on a stage, and on a set, and at home in my shirt complaining that I’ve made too much rice. And I promise that when I’ve something important to say, I’ll say it where you can hear me. I choose you. Not because I’m afraid of losing you. I choose you because I want to build this with you, and because I want you free to keep choosing it too. I love you.”

Her eyes had filled. She took a breath before she unfolded hers, and her voice shook once in the middle, and steadied.

“I used to think that if I loved someone enough I could learn to fit into their life. I learned how to bow. I learned when to speak and when to keep quiet, what to wear and what to say, and how to make myself easier to accept. I don’t want to do that any more. I don’t want to become someone else to be loved. I want to be myself, even when I’m difficult, even when I’m tired, even when I don’t know what to say. And I want you to be yourself. Not the perfect man. Not the lawyer who always knows what to do. Just you. I promise to tell you when I’m hurt instead of pretending I’m fine. I promise to let you help me when I need it, and to give you room when you need it. I promise to keep choosing you, and not to lose myself doing it. I loved you at eighteen when I didn’t know what I was doing. I loved you at twenty-one when I walked away. I love you now, knowing much more about what it asks of us. And I want to spend my life finding out what else we can become.”

His eyes were wet. She held his hand. “I’m ready.”

The rings went on. He put the band on her finger beside the ring she’d worn for nineteen months, and she did the same for him.

The celebrant smiled at them both. “By the promises you’ve made here, I’m delighted to pronounce you married. You may kiss your bride.”

Pengcheng laughed. “I already have.”

“Come here,” said Si-Yuan, and he did, and this time it was followed by applause. Si-Jie was crying. Si-Wei was smiling. Their mother was dabbing at her eyes in the front row. His father was on his feet. And in the second row, in red, his mother watched her son kiss his wife.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards, in the photographs, the three sisters stood in a row like three exclamation marks, as somebody had once said at another wedding under a persimmon tree, with Arthur and Sung Jae and Pengcheng beside them. Si-Jie told the photographer to make sure he got the ring, and the camera went.

His mother came to them when the photographs were done. He saw her first and turned a little towards Si-Yuan.

“Congratulations,” said his mother.

“Thank you, Madam Yang.”

His mother looked at the band on her hand, and at the dress, and at the flowers. “You chose a small wedding.”

“Yes.”

She paused over something before she went on. “It suits you. The dress is beautiful.”

Si-Yuan’s face went soft. “Thank you.”

His mother looked at him. “You look happy.”

“I am.”

“Take care of each other,” his mother said, and Si-Yuan said they would, and his mother gave a small nod and went.

“Are you all right?” he said.

“Yes,” said Si-Yuan, and he waited, and she smiled, and he believed her.

✦ ✦ ✦

The reception had no long programme and no speech from every relative. They ate and talked and laughed. Si-Jie gave a speech that started with Si-Yuan stealing her dessert when they were six and ended with her crying so hard that Arthur had to bring her water. Si-Wei’s was shorter. She said Si-Yuan had always been the most stubborn of the three of them, and she was glad she’d found someone stubborn enough to keep choosing her. Then she looked at Pengcheng. “Don’t take that as permission to argue with her.”

“I won’t,” he said.

“You will,” said Si-Yuan.

“Probably,” he said, and everyone laughed.

Near the end he found his mother alone at the edge of the garden, and stood beside her for a while without speaking.

“Your grandfather would have wanted a larger wedding,” she said.

“He’d have wanted a great many things.”

She looked across at Si-Yuan, laughing with her sisters with a glass in her hand, and then down at her own hands. “I chose this dress because of her. I remembered what I said to her about red. I thought about it when I saw her wearing it again.”

There was a long pause, and he didn’t fill it.

“I was wrong to tell her not to,” said his mother.

He looked at his mother carefully. “Yes.”

“I know.”

It wasn’t a whole apology. Not yet. But it was the first time she’d named something she’d done without defending it. He didn’t rush to comfort her. He didn’t tell her it was all right. “I’m glad you told me.”

“Go back to your wife,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

They danced slowly, late, when there were only a few people left on the floor. She rested her cheek on his chest.

“Hello, husband.”

“Hello, wife.”

“Say it again.”

“My wife.”

She looked at the rings. “It’s real.”

“Yes.”

“You’re very calm.”

“I’m trying not to cry.”

“You can,” she said, and touched his cheek, and he kissed her in the middle of the garden with the flowers moving a little in the evening air.

In the car home she rested her head against the window, and at a red light she looked at their rings, and turned to him.

“Today I didn’t bow to anyone.”

“No.”

“Not once. I used to think I’d spend my whole life learning to do it properly.”

He lifted her hand and kissed her knuckles. “You never had to.”

“I know that now.”

At home he helped her out of the dress, and she sat on the end of the bed while he put things away, and then he knelt and took her shoes off and rubbed her ankles, and she told him he didn’t have to, and he said he wanted to. She put her hands on his face.

“I’m happy because I married you. Not because everything’s perfect. Not because your mother’s changed. Not because there won’t be hard days. I’m happy because I know we can talk to each other when they come. I’m happy because I chose you.”

He rested his forehead on hers. “And I chose you.”

There was no audience now, no family table, nothing to live up to. There was only the life they’d chosen. And for the first time she hadn’t had to bow to come into it.

chapters.title: Out Loud, Always
chapters.desc: Ten years after the contract, he still reads every clause aloud to her, and she initials page seventeen with her own pen.
chapters.content:
Ten years after the contract he still had the pen. A black fountain pen with a silver clip, heavier than the cheap ones the assistants carried, with three initials engraved along its side. Y.S.Y. He remembered the production office and the winter light across the desk and the girl opposite him who’d plainly decided within a minute that he was the most boring man she’d ever met. He remembered asking her to read clause fourteen aloud. He remembered her looking at him over the top of the page. He remembered putting the pen in his jacket when she’d gone, and her coming back to the door. Mr. Yang? My pen. And him telling her it was safekeeping.

“Are you listening?”

His wife was in the bedroom doorway with a document in her hand. He closed the book on his lap. “I’m listening.”

“You’re remembering something. You’ve got that face. The one where you’re thinking about something and pretending you aren’t.”

“Sit down.”

She handed him the document. It wasn’t a production contract this time, or not the kind he used to draft. It was the agreement for a new film, a lead, and Qiao-jie’s office had sent the draft over that afternoon.

“You want me to look at it?”

“I want you to read it to me. All of it.”

“The dull parts too?”

“Those most of all.”

He smiled. “Come and sit.”

She climbed onto the bed beside him with her legs under the blanket and her tea in both hands, and leaned on the pillows. “Go on, Counsel.”

“That’s my title, not my personality.”

“It’s both,” she said, and he laughed, and began.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first clauses were ordinary. The production’s obligations. Payment. Dates. Publicity. He read each section aloud and stopped now and then to explain a phrase or ask whether something matched what Qiao-jie had told her. She listened. Sometimes she interrupted. Sometimes she asked him to read a sentence again. Sometimes she disagreed. He never once assumed that because he understood the language, he understood what she wanted.

By the middle of it she’d finished her tea and moved closer. “Next.”

He turned the page. “Clause fourteen.”

She smiled.

He looked at her over his glasses. “Public conduct, morality and reputational obligations.”

She laughed out loud.

“Are you remembering the first time?” he said.

“You made me read it aloud.”

“You needed to understand it.”

“You were so serious.”

“I was production counsel.”

“You were twenty-five.”

“That isn’t especially young for a lawyer.”

“It is when you’re sitting across from an eighteen-year-old and behaving as if the future of the profession depends on whether she understands a morality clause.”

“You were very young.”

“And you were very boring.”

“I’ve improved.”

“Debatable,” she said, and he shook his head and went on.

“’Any conduct by the talent which, in the reasonable opinion of the producer, may bring the production, its distributors or associated commercial partners into public disrepute—‘”

“Stop. Do you still think that’s reasonable?”

“No. It’s drafted far too broadly. It gives the producer much too much say over private life. It ought to require material harm instead of resting on someone’s opinion of reputation.”

“Look at you.”

“I always knew that.”

“Then why did you make me read it?”

He looked at her. “Because you were signing it. And now I want you to understand every word before you sign anything.”

She put her head on his shoulder. “That’s why I still make you read them.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They’d changed in ten years, though not in any way a stranger would have noticed. He still wore dark suits to work and still read every document twice and still disliked meetings without a purpose. She still worked long hours, still read scripts with a pencil, still disliked being told what kind of actress she ought to become, and still left her earrings in places where earrings didn’t belong.

But other things had changed. Yang and Associates had a whole floor now, and a name of its own that owed nothing to the one he’d left. Ku had his own room with a window and a dog on Fridays. His mother had grown older and quieter and less sure that every disagreement had to be won. It had never become easy between them, but it had become possible. She and Si-Yuan could sit at one table without either of them having to pretend the past hadn’t happened. They still had hard conversations. They still disagreed. But his mother had stopped expecting Si-Yuan to bow her way into the family, and Si-Yuan had stopped trying. Once, the summer before the wedding, his mother had cooked for her.

He still didn’t know what had started it. It had been an ordinary Sunday at the house, with his father reading and the housekeeper away visiting her sister, and his mother had stood up in the middle of the afternoon and gone into the kitchen, where she hadn’t cooked anything in his memory, and been there forty minutes. Si-Yuan had looked at him. He’d looked back and shaken his head. When his mother came out she was carrying one bowl: braised fish in a dark sauce with ginger and spring onion, the dish her own mother used to make, she said, when anyone in the house was tired. She set it down in front of Si-Yuan without another word and went back to her chair and picked up her book.

Si-Yuan had eaten all of it. Then she’d taken the bowl into the kitchen and washed it, and come back and thanked his mother, and his mother had said, without looking up, that she’d put too much ginger in it, and Si-Yuan had said she liked ginger, and his mother had said, after a long moment, “I know.” That was all. He’d thought about it for weeks. He still thought about it.

Her own work had grown too. Films and awards and productions abroad, hard parts, long stretches when they’d lived in different cities. Seoul. Paris again. Other places. Weeks when they’d shared a hotel room and barely seen each other awake. Missed anniversaries, late flights, arguments about schedules, all the ordinary bargaining of two people who both had work they loved. They’d learned to say when they missed each other. They’d learned to ask instead of assuming. And he’d learned that the most loving thing he could say was often Tell me more, and only afterwards I understand.

“Are you finished?” she said.

“Almost. There are two more provisions.”

She groaned. “I regret asking.”

“You’d regret it more if you signed without understanding.”

She leaned over and kissed his cheek. “That’s why I married you.”

“Because I read contracts?”

“Among other things. You make a good breakfast. You know my call times. You don’t mind me stealing your shirts.”

“I’ve accepted I’m never getting them back.”

“And you tell me when you’re thinking something.”

He went quiet, and she touched his cheek, and told him that one mattered most.

He turned his head and kissed her palm. “I know.”

When he’d finished he closed it and put it on the bedside table. “I’ll send my notes to Qiao-jie in the morning.”

“Thank you.”

She settled closer. “Do you remember what happened after you made me read it?”

“You asked whether I was always that boring.”

“That was before.”

“You asked whether I had a girlfriend. I told you it wasn’t relevant to the contract.”

“You were so annoying.”

“I was trying to maintain professional boundaries.”

“You were hopeless at it. You kept my pen.”

“Safekeeping.”

“And six weeks later you bought me noodles at the stall by the studio gate, and drove me back at four in the morning, and I was in costume and borrowed slippers, and I kissed you in your car,” she said.

He laughed. “You did.”

“You looked so surprised.”

“I hadn’t expected it.”

“You could have kissed me first.”

“I could have.”

“But you didn’t.”

“No.”

“Good thing I did,” she said, and he leaned over and kissed her, and said against her mouth that it was a good thing.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later, with the lamp off and the contract forgotten on the table, she lay facing him in one of his old shirts with her wedding ring catching a little light from the window.

“Do you know what today is?”

He put his phone down. “The third of January.”

“Ten years.”

He touched her face. “Ten years since the contract.”

“Since you made me read clause fourteen.”

“Since you nearly refused to.”

“I was right.”

“You were eighteen.”

“And right.”

“All right,” he said.

“Have you still got the pen?”

He reached across to the bedside drawer and took out a small black case, and gave it to her. She opened it. The pen lay inside, a little worn now, the initials still clear.

“You kept it ten years.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

He thought about the question honestly. “Because it was yours. It was the first thing you ever left with me.”

She looked at the pen, and then at him.

“I kept it because I remembered that morning. You looked at me as though I were the dullest man alive.”

“You were.”

“And I remember thinking I wanted to see you again. I didn’t know what would happen. I didn’t know whether you’d like me, or whether I’d make you happy. But I wanted to try.”

She closed the case and put it carefully on the table. “I’m glad you did.”

He smiled against her mouth. “So am I. I like being married to you.”

“That’s lucky.”

“Very.”

She touched his cheek. “Read it again.”

“What?”

“Clause fourteen.”

“Now? It’s nearly midnight.”

“It’s our anniversary. Ten years since the first one.”

“You want me to read a morality clause in bed on our tenth anniversary.”

“It’s romantic.”

“Your idea of romance is unusual.”

“You married me.”

“I did.”

“And you love me.”

He said very much, and reached for the contract, and found the page, and read it in the dark in a quiet voice. “’Clause fourteen. Public conduct, morality and reputational obligations. Any conduct by the talent which, in the reasonable opinion of the producer—‘”

She lifted her head. “Stop. Do you think loving someone should count as a risk to your reputation?”

He put the paper down. “No.”

“Even if people talk?”

“No.”

“Even if they don’t approve?”

“No.”

“Even if it makes things harder?”

“Then most of all,” he said.

She smiled, and kissed him, and he put the contract aside and drew her in, and she held his face with her ring against his skin.

“Ten years. And you’re still reading me contracts,” she whispered.

“I mean to keep doing it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Just after midnight her phone went on the table.

Si-Jie (Questions): Happy ten years since contract day.

Si-Yuan: How do you remember that?

Si-Jie (Questions): Because you rang us that night and complained for an hour that he’d made you read a morality clause.

Si-Wei (Watching): And for three days after.

Si-Yuan: I didn’t.

Si-Jie (Questions): You absolutely did.

Si-Wei (Watching): Happy anniversary, Yuan.

She sent them a heart and told them he said hello, and turned the phone off.

“Happy anniversary,” he said.

She smiled against his mouth. “Happy anniversary, Pengcheng. Do you remember what you said when I asked about a girlfriend?”

“That it wasn’t relevant.”

“And now?”

He pushed her hair back from her face. “Now it’s still not relevant. I have a wife.”

“Very clever,” she said, and he kissed her again and held her.

✦ ✦ ✦

Ten years before, he’d made her read a contract aloud because he wanted to be sure she knew what she was signing. Ten years later he still read every clause aloud to her, though she’d long since stopped needing anyone to understand a contract for her. She deserved to hear it in full, and he’d learned, at last, that the things that mattered most in a marriage should never be left for the other person to guess.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the morning she was up before him, which never happened, sitting at the kitchen table in his shirt with the contract open beside her coffee and the pen in her hand. She’d unscrewed the cap and was turning it over, the silver catching the window.

“Does it still write?”

“It wrote forty things once.”

“In ten years? Once?”

“It isn’t mine.”

She ran her thumb along the three letters on the barrel. “Qiao-jie wants to send them notes on the promotional clause today. Fourteen days’ notice, a fixed number of appearances, the usual.”

“Then you don’t need my notes.”

She turned the pen so the nib caught the light. “I haven’t needed your notes since Seoul. I’d still like them. You always find the sentence nobody else reads, and then you read it to me as if it had personally offended you.”

“Most of them have.”

She tipped her head. “I know. It’s my favourite part of the morning. Write them before your first meeting. And then ring me after the hearing, not just a text. I want to hear how it went.”

He said he would, and meant it, and she knew he meant it, because he’d already taken out his phone to put it in his diary, and she reached across and took the phone out of his hand and put it face up on the table and kissed him instead. Then she pulled the draft towards her, turned to the page with clause fourteen on it, and in the bottom corner, where you initial a page you’ve read, she wrote three letters in black ink with her own pen. Y.S.Y. She blew on them, and capped the pen, and held it out to him.

“Safekeeping,” she said.

He took it and put it in the pocket of his shirt, the one she wasn’t wearing, and she laughed at him, and he let her.

He told her when he loved her. He told her when he missed her. He told her when he was afraid, and when he was proud, and when he disagreed, and when he was wrong. And when she asked him to read clause fourteen again, he did. Out loud. Always.

chapters.title: Clause Fourteen
chapters.desc: The morality clause, its whole life: read aloud at eighteen, answered in thirteen pages, construed alone in chambers after the ballroom, marked by her own hand in Seoul, and narrowed at last for an eighteen-year-old co-star, who reads it aloud.
chapters.content:
The clause was older than either of them. It had been in the studio’s standard agreement since before Si-Yuan was born, a paragraph of eleven lines on page seventeen that nobody read and everybody signed, and by the time Yang Pengcheng was lent to the production he’d defended it twice in negotiations with other people’s agents without once thinking about who it was for.

Public conduct, morality and reputational obligations. Any conduct by the talent which, in the reasonable opinion of the producer, might bring the production into public disrepute. It was badly drafted. He knew it was badly drafted. On the third of January 2022 he made an eighteen-year-old girl read it aloud to him anyway, because she was about to sign it and he’d decided she was going to understand every word, and she read it in a flat voice with her chin on her hand and then asked him whether he was always this boring.

He thought about that morning more often than he admitted. He thought she’d been right, mostly. And he thought that if he’d been a better lawyer, or a braver one, he’d have crossed the clause out there and then and made the studio argue for it.

He didn’t. He made her read it. It took him years to understand the difference.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first time it mattered was March 2023, and it mattered for a day and a half.

A newspaper photographed them under the studio’s side entrance in the rain. Mr. Tam reached for clause fourteen before the day was out, and Pengcheng answered him in thirteen pages, and the notice was withdrawn in writing at 9.05 the following day. Pengcheng forwarded the withdrawal to her without a word of his own, because there was nothing to add to it.

She read it on set between takes, in costume, with a girl from make-up holding a mirror. Then she wrote to him and asked for the thirteen pages.

He sent them that night. He didn’t ask why.

She read them in the back of the car on the way home, and again in bed, slowly, with a pencil, the way she read scripts. Most of it was dry. Some of it she didn’t understand until she’d read it three times. But on page nine there was a sentence she underlined so hard the pencil went through: The producer’s legitimate interest in the reputation of its production doesn’t extend to the lawful private life of the artist, and no reading of this clause can be made to say that it does.

She kept the pages in the drawer with her passport. She didn’t tell him for a long time. When she finally did, years later, he went quiet, and then asked which page, and she told him nine without having to look.

✦ ✦ ✦

The second time, there was no notice. On the Monday after his mother’s sixtieth birthday, Pengcheng sat in his room at the family chambers with the door shut and Si-Yuan’s file open on the desk. He hadn’t meant to take it out. He’d gone to the cabinet for something else and his hand had found it, and now her original agreement was in front of him, open at page seventeen.

He read the clause. He read his own thirteen pages. He read the sentence on page nine. He’d written it after midnight in a fury so controlled that Ms. Lui, typing it up, had asked whether he wanted it softened, and he’d said no. He’d stood in a conference room and told a legal director that a company couldn’t make a young woman’s dignity conditional on its opinion of her. He’d believed every word. He’d won.

On Saturday night his mother had said, loud enough, that some girls married up by the hour, and he’d looked at his plate.

He sat with that. Nobody had sent a letter. There was no clause to construe, no breach to deny, no harm to put a figure on. There’d only been a table and three hundred people, and the woman he meant to marry standing up on her own and bowing once and walking out of the room while he stayed in his chair.

He’d always thought the law was the hard part. He’d thought that if he could find the right words, in the right order, he could keep her safe. He could. He’d done it once, in thirteen pages. What he hadn’t understood was that most of the things that could hurt her would never be written down, and the right words for them were short, and had to be said out loud, at the time, in front of the person who’d done it.

He shut the file and put it back in the cabinet. He didn’t ring her. He didn’t know yet what he’d say that she’d want to hear.

✦ ✦ ✦

The third time, he didn’t wait.

In January 2026 his mother began, over a dish of greens and in a perfectly pleasant voice, to say what she thought about actresses who travelled and worked late and spent their days among men who weren’t their husbands. Si-Yuan heard where it was going a sentence before it arrived. She’d heard it go there before. She put her chopsticks down and waited for the plate.

Pengcheng said no. Then he said it again, more slowly, so that nobody at the table could pretend not to have heard: not to her, not ever again.

Later she’d tell him that for one second, while his mother’s chair scraped back, she’d thought of the sentence on page nine. That was the voice, she said. The one from the thirteen pages. She’d read it so many times she knew it, and she’d never once heard him use it on anyone he loved.

She kissed him at the table, in front of his father and the cooling dishes, and when they got home she went to the drawer and took out the thirteen pages and showed him the line she’d underlined. He looked at it a long time.

“You kept these.”

“You wrote them for me.”

“I wrote them for Mr. Tam.”

“You wrote them for me,” she said, and he didn’t argue.

✦ ✦ ✦

By the autumn of 2027 she was reading her own contracts.

She was in Seoul, three weeks into the shoot, with the draft for her next film spread over the hotel desk and a pencil behind her ear, when he rang from home.

“Have you got to fourteen yet?”

“I’m on it.”

“And?”

“There’s a promotional obligation that runs six months past the end of filming. No limit on the number of appearances. No notice period. And they’ve put the morality wording back in, the old version, the one that says in the opinion of the producer.”

There was a short silence on the line. “Do you want me to look at it?”

“I’ve marked it. Too broad. Defined number of appearances, fourteen days’ notice, and harm has to be material, not a matter of opinion. I’ve sent it to Qiao-jie.”

“That’s what I’d have written.”

“I know. I learned it from someone.”

“Is he handsome?”

“Extremely boring, apparently.”

She heard him laugh, low, the way he did when he was alone in his office and didn’t think anyone was listening. She looked down at the Seoul street, all wet lights and umbrellas.

“When I met you, I thought you were the kind of man who believed you could fix anything if you found the right paragraph,” she said.

“And now?”

“Now I think you know some things have to be said before anyone gets a chance to write them down.”

He didn’t answer straight away. Then he said he was glad, and that he missed her, and that he’d be there on Friday, in that order, and she smiled at the window for a while after he’d gone.

✦ ✦ ✦

Their own agreement, the spring they married, ran to four pages. There was nothing in it about conduct. There was property, and careers, and what would happen to the flat, and a schedule nobody would ever need to read again.

She read it twice and put it down on his kitchen table. “Something’s missing.”

“What?”

“You haven’t made me read anything aloud.”

He looked at her over the papers. “Would you like to?”

She thought about it. “No.”

“Then don’t.”

“That’s all?”

“That’s all,” said Pengcheng, and she signed it, and so did he, and she picked the pages up and squared the edges on the table with a degree of precision she’d learned from him, and he pretended not to notice.

✦ ✦ ✦

In March 2030 her agency sent her the draft agreement for a film she’d already said yes to, and attached, because Si-Yuan had asked for it, the draft for the girl who’d play her daughter.

The girl was eighteen. It was her first lead. Her name was on the front page in the studio’s typeface, and on page seventeen, word for word, was the paragraph Si-Yuan had read aloud in a production office with a ticking strip light eight years before.

She rang the producer herself. She was polite. She said she was happy with her own terms. She said she’d be happier if clause fourteen in the young lead’s agreement read the same as it did in hers, which was to say narrowly, with a notice period and a requirement of material harm and nothing at all about anybody’s opinion. The producer said it was standard wording. Si-Yuan said she knew; she’d signed it once. The producer said he’d see what could be done. She said she’d be delighted to sign her own agreement as soon as he had.

It took a week. On the morning the girl came in to sign, Si-Yuan was in the building for a fitting, and she knocked on the door of the office and asked if she could sit in, and the girl, who’d watched her films, went pink and said yes.

The lawyer across the desk was young and pleasant and in a hurry. He turned to the signature page.

“Page seventeen first,” said Si-Yuan.

The girl looked at her.

“Read it aloud. All of it. Then tell me what it means.”

The girl read it. She stumbled once, on material, and Si-Yuan explained it, and the girl read the sentence again. At the end she looked up. “That’s quite fair, isn’t it?”

“It is now,” said Si-Yuan.

✦ ✦ ✦

She told him that night in the kitchen, with her shoes off and her elbows on the counter, while he cut fruit she hadn’t asked for.

“You made her read it aloud.”

“Every word. She tried to skim. I didn’t let her.”

“Did she ask whether you were always this boring?”

“She asked if I’d sign her script.”

He put a piece of pear in front of her. He didn’t say anything. Then he came round the counter and stood beside her and looked at nothing in particular.

“I should have crossed it out. That first morning. I knew it was wrong,” he said.

“You were twenty-five.”

“That isn’t an excuse.”

“No. But you wrote page nine,” she said.

He looked at her. She took the pear and ate it, and then took his hand, and held it on the counter between them, and didn’t let go for a while.

The clause had followed them for eight years: through a photograph and a ballroom and a family dinner, and through every contract since, into hotel rooms and across her desk and onto his. It had never once been the thing that nearly ended them. That had been quieter, and harder to put in writing. It had been a man who knew the right words and didn’t say them.

He said them now. He said them in kitchens and in courtrooms and at his mother’s table, and once, in the dark, he said he thought he’d learned more from page seventeen than from anything he’d read at law school. She told him that was the most boring thing anyone had ever said to her in bed. He said he knew.

He said he loved her too. He didn’t leave that to be understood either.

chapters.title: The Triplets Vote
chapters.desc: Si-Jie, Si-Wei and Si-Yuan vote on him three times, by the rules Si-Wei wrote at nine: two to one at the restaurant window, one to two on their twenty-first, three to nothing in her kitchen. He hears about the third.
chapters.epigraph: “It’s my vote. I’m allowed to spend it on whatever I want.”
chapters.content:
The Yen triplets had settled things by vote since they were nine years old. Who got the bed by the window. Which film on a Friday. Whether their grandmother in Taipei needed to know about the vase. The rules had been drawn up by Si-Wei, on a sheet of exercise paper that their mother still kept in a drawer, and there were only three of them. Everybody votes. Nobody can vote twice. And anybody who won’t say yes, said Si-Wei at nine with great seriousness, has said no.

They voted on Yang Pengcheng three times. He found out about the third.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first was in May 2022, on a Saturday, in a restaurant with steamed-up windows two streets from Si-Yuan’s flat.

He’d answered everything. Si-Jie had asked him eleven questions before the soup and he’d answered all of them without once looking at his watch, and he’d told them, plainly, that he’d never ask their sister to stop acting even if his family disagreed. When Si-Jie asked why her, of all people, he’d thought about it before answering, and then said that she noticed things other people missed and that she was stubborn, and that he liked both. Si-Wei had put her cup down at that.

When he went to pay, Si-Jie leaned across the table. “Well?”

“Don’t,” said Si-Yuan.

“I’m yes. Obviously. He’s handsome, he answered everything, he didn’t try to be charming, and he wants you to keep working. I’m yes.”

Si-Wei turned her cup a quarter turn on the saucer. “Yes. For now.”

“For now isn’t a vote.”

Si-Wei looked at their sister. “It’s my vote. Yuan?”

“I’m not voting. I’m going out with him.”

“Everybody votes.”

Si-Yuan looked at the counter, where he was standing straight with his card, listening to the owner explain something about the till as though it were a matter of law. Her mouth went soft at one corner. Then she looked back at them and lifted her chin. “I’m still considering.”

Si-Jie groaned. Si-Wei only nodded, and wrote nothing down, and didn’t need to.

He came back. They said goodbye on the pavement. Si-Jie hugged him, which he hadn’t expected, and Si-Wei shook his hand, which he had. The two of them went back into the restaurant to finish the tea and stood at the window to watch their sister walk him to the car park, because they’d never once in their lives pretended not to be nosy about each other.

Si-Yuan stopped by his car. He said something. She looked at his mouth, and then she put both hands flat on his chest and kissed him, properly, under the street light, for a long time.

Si-Jie grabbed her sister’s arm. “Look. They’re kissing again.”

“I have eyes.”

“He’s actually very handsome.”

Si-Wei watched the car park a second longer. “You said that ten minutes ago. Two votes to one.”

“Two to one? She’s kissing him.”

“She said she’s still considering. That’s not a yes. Rule three.”

“You made rule three up when you were nine.”

“And it’s never once been wrong. He’s passed. For now,” said Si-Wei. She took out her phone and typed with one thumb, and Si-Jie got hers out too and typed something entirely in capitals, and across the street their sister read both messages at the open car door and put her arms round him.

What neither of them said, that night or for a long time after, was that rule three had been written for exactly this. For the times one of them wanted something so much she was afraid to say yes out loud. Si-Wei had been the one who wrote it. Si-Wei had always known.

✦ ✦ ✦

The second vote was on their twenty-first birthday, the Friday after the banquet, on the floor of Si-Yuan’s flat.

There’d been a cake with three candles and too much cream. They’d sung to each other in three keys. Si-Jie had shown her a photograph from the year before, with Pengcheng in the background by a doorway, not looking at the camera, looking at her, and asked if she wanted it deleted, and Si-Yuan had said to keep it. The phone on the sofa had stayed dark all afternoon.

Si-Wei was cutting fruit at the counter. She put the knife down and came back and sat cross-legged on the rug facing them both. “We should vote.”

Si-Yuan didn’t look up. “On what?”

“You know on what.”

“It’s my birthday.”

“It’s all our birthdays,” said Si-Jie, and took her hand.

Nobody spoke for a while. Somewhere in the building a door shut. Si-Jie was the one who started, because she always was.

She said it to the rug. “I’m changing mine. I liked him. I liked him from the first dinner. I thought he was serious and careful and that he’d look after you. And he would, if anyone outside the family ever came for you. He’d write them thirteen pages. But it’s never anyone outside the family, is it. And he sat there. So I’m no.” She looked up.

Si-Yuan’s eyes filled, and she didn’t say anything. “No. I said for now. I meant it. I wanted to see what he’d do when it cost him something to stand next to you. Now I’ve seen,” said Si-Wei. There wasn’t any satisfaction in it. She sounded tired, and older than twenty-one.

They both looked at their sister. Si-Yuan could have said no. It would have been three to nothing and they’d have held her and nobody would have said another word about it. She looked at the dark phone on the sofa. She thought about his kitchen, and the eleven days he’d kept the ring before he asked, and how he’d looked at his plate.

“Yes. I’m yes,” she said.

“Yuan.”

Her voice wobbled and held. “I know. I know what he did. I was there. I’m not saying he deserves it. I’m saying I still love him. It’s my vote. I’m allowed to spend it on whatever I want.”

Si-Wei looked at her, and then nodded once. “One to two.”

“One to two,” said Si-Jie, and leaned her head on her sister’s shoulder, and Si-Yuan cried for a little while into Si-Jie’s hair, and nobody tried to make her stop.

Towards evening Si-Jie’s phone went, and she took it into the corridor and came back pink, and said Arthur was taking her away for the weekend and wouldn’t tell her where, and Si-Wei told her to pack for rain. When the door had shut behind her and they were clearing up, Si-Wei dried her hands and came and stood next to her sister at the sink.

“Do you think he’ll change?” said Si-Yuan.

“I think he can.”

“Do you think he will?”

Si-Wei took a long time to answer. “That’s not our vote any more. It never really was.”

Pengcheng never knew about the second vote. He only knew that, after that December, Si-Jie stopped hugging him at doors and Si-Wei stopped asking about his cases, and that neither of them was ever once rude to him, which was so much worse.

✦ ✦ ✦

The third was in March 2026, on the Sunday after the judgment, in Si-Yuan’s kitchen.

He’d won Luo Mei’s case on the Friday, in his own name, for a fee he’d waived, and she’d been in the gallery for all of it. On the court steps she’d kissed him in front of the cameras. On Sunday her sisters came for lunch, and he was there too, in his shirtsleeves, putting bowls out on the counter while a pot of soup that had been on since eleven did whatever soup did.

“That’s too much rice,” said Si-Yuan.

“It’s not much.”

“You always say that.”

“You always say I make too much.”

“Because you do.”

Si-Jie laughed at the table. “Some things never change.”

He looked at her. Then he picked up a clean bowl. “Would you like some?”

Si-Jie looked at the rice, and at him. “Yes. Please.”

He filled it, and put it in front of her, and she thanked him, and he said she was welcome. Si-Wei asked for the soup without looking up from her phone. He passed it and told her to mind, it was hot, and she glanced at him and said thanks.

Si-Yuan almost didn’t notice. It was so ordinary. Her sisters weren’t watching him any more to see whether he’d make a mistake. They were just having lunch with him.

After they’d eaten his phone went. It was Ku, about the costs, and he took it out onto the balcony and slid the door shut behind him. Si-Jie watched him through the glass for a moment. Then she put her chopsticks down and turned to the others with the face she’d had at nine years old whenever there was a vote.

“Again?” said Si-Yuan.

“Rule one,” said Si-Wei, and put her phone face up on the table.

Si-Yuan looked out at the balcony. He was standing with one hand in his pocket, listening, his head bent. He looked tired. He’d lost half his clients in a month. He’d lost his chambers and his mother and the easy way doors opened for his name. He’d built something out of little, and it was his. And somewhere in the last year he’d learned to say things out loud: to his mother, to a judge, to her. He wasn’t perfect. He still asked whether she’d eaten before he asked about her day. He still tried to solve things too fast. But he asked now. And when she answered, he listened all the way to the end.

“Yes,” she said.

“Yes,” said Si-Jie.

Si-Wei looked at the balcony a moment longer. “Yes.”

Si-Jie stared at her. “Really? You?”

“Did you expect me to say no?”

“You were the hardest.”

Si-Wei turned her cup on the saucer, a quarter turn. “I was right to be the hardest. He didn’t change because she begged him, or because he wanted us to like him. He changed because he finally understood what he’d been doing. And then he kept on understanding it when nobody was watching.”

“Three to nothing,” said Si-Jie, and held up three fingers.

“Three to zero.”

“Same thing.”

“Not mathematically.”

“Si-Wei.”

The balcony door slid open and he came back in, putting his phone away, and stopped. All three of them were looking at him.

“Has something happened?”

“You’re very suspicious,” said Si-Jie.

“You’re all smiling at me.”

Si-Yuan got up and took his hand and brought him to the table. “Tell him,” she said.

“Absolutely not,” said Si-Wei, and picked up her phone again.

He looked down at Si-Yuan. “Tell me what?”

“We voted on you.”

He took that in. “Voted.”

“Three times.”

He looked from one sister to the other, and then back. “Should I be worried?”

“You should have been worried the first time,” said Si-Jie.

“And much more the second,” said Si-Wei, without looking up.

“The first was two to one. Si-Jie said yes. Si-Wei said for now. I said I was still considering, and in this family that counts as no,” said Si-Yuan.

He nodded slowly. “That seems fair.”

“The second was one to two.”

His face changed. He didn’t ask when. He knew. She held his hand a little tighter.

“The one was me.”

He looked at her, and she let him look, and didn’t explain, and he didn’t ask her to.

“And today?” he said at last.

Si-Jie sat back with her arms folded. “Three to zero.”

He turned to Si-Wei. “You too?”

She raised her cup an inch. “Don’t make me reconsider.”

He laughed, properly, and said he understood. Si-Jie got up and gathered the bowls and informed him on her way past that it wasn’t a permanent approval. Si-Wei added that it remained subject to continued performance. He said of course. Si-Yuan told him he was taking it seriously, and he said he’d read the terms.

✦ ✦ ✦

When they’d gone she found him at the counter putting the rest of the soup into a box. She came up behind him and put her arms round his waist and her cheek against his back.

“Are you pleased?”

“Three to zero is a respectable result.”

“It isn’t a judgment, Counsel.”

“No?”

She held on. “No. The first one wasn’t a promise that you’d never hurt me. And today isn’t a promise that you won’t. It isn’t a certificate. You can’t bring it out at New Year and tell everybody you’ve been approved.”

“I wouldn’t dare.”

“They didn’t vote against you because they stopped loving me. They voted because they love me.”

He put the lid on the box and turned round inside her arms. “I know. I think they were right. All three times. I wanted them to like me because I loved you. I thought that would be enough. It never occurred to me that they’d watched you get hurt, and had every reason to be careful with me.”

She put her hand on his cheek. “That’s why they like you now.”

“Because I understand?”

“Because you’re still trying to.”

He kissed her. She stayed with her face against his shirt for a while, listening to his heart, which was steadier than it used to be.

Her phone went on the counter behind him. The sisters’ chat had been called Three Exclamation Marks since Si-Jie named it at fourteen, and neither of the others had ever managed to get it changed.

Si-Jie (Questions): Official record: third vote, three to zero.

Si-Wei (Watching): Subject to continued conduct.

Si-Yuan: You two are ridiculous.

Si-Jie (Questions): The first time I liked him because he made you happy. The second time I hated that he let you be unhappy on your own.

Si-Wei (Watching): The third time I said yes because he finally understood that loving you means standing next to you when it costs him something.

She read it twice. Her eyes went warm. She typed slowly.

Si-Yuan: Thank you for loving me enough to vote against him.

Si-Jie sent three hearts. Si-Wei sent one. And from the bedroom doorway, where he’d gone to find her a jumper because she’d said she was cold, he asked whether she was all right, and she said she was happy, and he said good, and held out the jumper, and she went to him.

chapters.title: Night Shoot Noodles
chapters.desc: A week after the first kiss: a night shoot, a difficult moon, forty-three minutes across the city, and oranges from beside the till. The owner asks if he’s her boyfriend; she says he’s her lawyer. The stall becomes theirs.
chapters.content:
A week after she kissed him in his car, Yen Si-Yuan was standing under a fake street lamp on a fake street at the back of the studio lot, beginning to hate the moon.

It hadn’t done anything to her personally. It was a lamp on a crane, forty feet up, with a blue gel over it. But the director had spent the best part of an hour saying the moonlight was wrong, and every time they reset, a man climbed the crane and did something to the gel, and she went back to her mark in a thin cream blouse and a long skirt and a period coat that was mostly decorative, and waited.

“Again,” the director called.

Her character was waiting for a man who’d promised to come back. She’d waited through the evening and the night and was still waiting when the street emptied. Si-Yuan looked down the road at the place where somebody should have been, and didn’t cry, and didn’t move.

“Better. But I need her to look as though she hasn’t slept in three days.”

“I haven’t,” said Si-Yuan.

The director blinked at her over the monitor. The cinematographer laughed out loud. “Good. Use it.”

She used it. They got it on the next take. Somebody called for the close-up and a make-up girl came at her with a powder puff, and Qiao-jie appeared at her elbow with a coat and a bottle of warm water and the news that the close-up would be another forty minutes at least, because the crane had to come down.

She sat on an apple box behind the lights with her coat round her shoulders and her feet, in the embroidered costume shoes that wardrobe swore were authentic to the period, slowly dying. She took her phone out. She hadn’t meant to. She’d been not-meaning-to all week.

Mr. Yang (Boring): Are you still filming?

It had come in an hour ago. She looked at it for a while. Since Friday he’d written to her four times, each one shorter than the last, and she’d answered every one within a minute and then lain awake feeling foolish about it.

Si-Yuan: Yes. Waiting for the moon to cooperate.

Mr. Yang (Boring): Has it?

Si-Yuan: No. Very difficult colleague.

Mr. Yang (Boring): When did you last eat?

She looked across at the catering table. Two untouched boxes of rice, gone hard at the edges, and a tray of something green that had been there since dusk.

Si-Yuan: Technically at dinner.

Mr. Yang (Boring): Technically.

Si-Yuan: I’m hungry. Is that what you want me to say?

Mr. Yang (Boring): What would you like?

She looked towards the gate, though she couldn’t see it from there. She could picture it: the faded red awning, the four plastic tables, the television muttering to itself behind the counter.

Si-Yuan: Noodles. Beef. A little spicy.

Mr. Yang (Boring): Forty minutes.

Si-Yuan: Where are you?

Mr. Yang (Boring): Nearby.

She looked at that word. Then she put the phone in her coat pocket and found that she was smiling at the back of a flat, and made herself stop before the make-up girl saw.

✦ ✦ ✦

The close-up took fifty minutes, not forty. When she came out through the gate, still in costume with her trainers in one hand, he was already at the far table under the awning with two bowls in front of him, and he stood up when he saw her.

He was in his work clothes with the tie gone and the sleeves turned back, and his hair wasn’t quite as neat as it was in the daytime. He looked at the costume, and then at her feet, which were in the borrowed slippers again because she’d made a deal with wardrobe.

“Don’t,” she said.

“I haven’t said anything.”

She sat down. “Your face has. You said nearby.”

“It’s not far.”

“Your office is on the other side of the city.”

“It’s forty-three minutes at this time of night.”

She stared at him. “You timed it?”

“I know the route,” said Pengcheng, and pushed the bowl an inch towards her, and she started laughing and couldn’t stop for a moment.

The owner came out from behind the counter, wiping his hands on a cloth. He was a short broad man with grey hair cut close, and he looked at her costume and then at Pengcheng and then back at her. “Back again.”

“Back again,” said Si-Yuan.

He put a glass of hot water by her hand. “He came last week and asked what you liked. Nobody asks me what anybody likes. Your boyfriend?”

Pengcheng opened his mouth. Si-Yuan got there first. “My lawyer.”

The owner considered this. He looked at the two bowls, ordered in advance, and at the man who’d driven forty-three minutes in the middle of the night to sit at a plastic table and wait for her. “Lawyer,” he said, without any expression at all, and went back behind his counter.

She didn’t dare look at Pengcheng. She picked up her chopsticks and ate, and the first mouthful was so hot and so good that she shut her eyes.

“Better?”

“Don’t talk to me. I’m busy.”

He didn’t. He ate slowly, the way he did everything, and watched her eat with grave attention, and every so often moved the little dish of pickled greens nearer to her side of the table without comment. A taxi driver at the next table finished and paid and left. The television behind the counter was showing a cooking programme with the sound almost off. A truck backed up somewhere inside the lot with its warning beep going.

When she’d slowed down she propped her chin on her hand. “The director wanted me to look more tired.”

“And did you?”

“I told him I was. He said use it.”

“Efficient.”

She stirred her broth. “He’s a very good director. He’s just not a very kind one. We got it in the end.”

“Are you happy with it?”

She looked at him. “You always ask that.”

“Would you rather I asked whether the lighting was technically adequate?”

She smiled into the bowl. “No. Nobody else asks that. They ask if it went well, or whether the director was pleased. You ask whether I am.”

He didn’t seem to know what to say to that. He took a sip of water instead. She decided she liked it, the way he went quiet when something touched him, and seemed to put it somewhere safe before he went on.

“You’re not very good at talking about films,” she said.

“I know.”

“You haven’t seen half the ones I’ve told you about.”

“I saw the last one.”

“After I told you three times.”

“I was busy.”

She pointed a chopstick at him. “Excuses. Why do you keep asking, then?”

He thought about it. He always thought about things before he answered them, even small things, even at a noodle stall at the end of the night, and she was beginning to wait for the pause with a kind of private pleasure.

“Because you’re different when you talk about something you love. You talk faster. You forget to be careful. You make very specific complaints about things nobody else would notice,” he said.

She stopped stirring.

He seemed to feel this needed explaining. “I’m a lawyer.”

“That doesn’t explain everything.”

“No. It doesn’t,” said Pengcheng.

✦ ✦ ✦

When she’d finished the last piece of beef she sat back with both hands on her stomach and looked at his bowl, which still had noodles in it.

“Eat faster.”

“Why?”

“Because I want something sweet, and I can’t have it until you’ve finished.”

“There isn’t anything sweet.”

She nodded at the counter. Beside the till was a saucer of orange segments, for the owner, probably, or his regulars. “There.”

“Those aren’t for customers.”

“We’re customers.”

“You’re very difficult.”

“Please,” said Si-Yuan, and leaned across the table, and looked at him, and he held out for about three seconds and then turned in his chair and asked the owner, politely, whether they might possibly have a few slices of orange. The owner looked at him, and then at her, and then brought the whole saucer and put it down between them and said nothing whatsoever, which was somehow louder than anything he could have said.

She held a piece out to him. He took it. She took one for herself, and looked past him at the gate and the lit windows of the soundstage and the road beyond the awning, empty right to the end.

“Do you think we’ll still be coming here in ten years?”

He looked up. “Here?”

“Here. This table.”

“Why wouldn’t we?”

“I don’t know. Maybe I’ll be too famous for plastic stools.”

“Would you prefer a private room?”

“No.”

“Then we’ll come.”

“Even if you’re busy?”

“I’ll make time.”

“Even if I’ve got a night shoot?”

“Then I’ll bring the noodles to you.”

“Even if it’s raining?”

“There’s an awning.”

“Even if he closes?”

He considered that one properly. “Then I’ll find out where he’s gone.”

She laughed. She leaned her shoulder against his across the corner of the table, just for a moment, and felt him go still and then not move away. Under the table, carefully, not quite sure he was allowed to, he found her hand.

“I like it here,” she said.

“Because of the noodles?”

“Because you came.”

✦ ✦ ✦

It was nearly four in the morning when he drove her back round to the production entrance. She’d talked most of the way and then stopped, the way she had the week before, with one leg folded under her and the skirt of the costume gathered round her knees. He pulled up under the security lights and left the engine running.

“Go to sleep when you get in. Don’t read your scenes till it’s light.”

“How do you know I do that?”

“You told me.”

“You remember everything I tell you.”

“Yes,” said Pengcheng, simply, and she turned her head on the seat and looked at him.

She’d kissed him first last week. She’d lain awake every night since wondering whether he’d minded, whether he’d been too polite to say, whether a man who read every page twice could possibly want a girl who skimmed. He’d written to her four times. He’d driven across the city. He’d timed it.

She leaned over and kissed him again. It was a small kiss this time, warm, tasting of broth and orange, and when she drew back he was looking at her with an expression she’d never seen on him in the office, and she was fairly sure nobody else had either.

“What was that for?”

“Dinner.”

“That’s a generous thank-you.”

“Would you prefer a letter?”

“I’d keep it.”

She laughed and got out of the car, and leaned back in through the open door with her trainers in one hand. “Goodnight, Mr. Yang.”

“Goodnight, Miss Yen.”

She was halfway across the car park in the borrowed slippers when her phone buzzed in her pocket.

Mr. Yang (Boring): You forgot to ask for your pen.

She stopped under a light and laughed out loud, by herself, at nothing, and a security guard in his booth looked up. She typed with her thumb.

Si-Yuan: I’ll ask next time.

She didn’t. She came back for it three more times that winter and never once asked, and he never once offered, and by spring they’d both stopped pretending that was what she was coming back for.

✦ ✦ ✦

The stall became theirs that year without either of them deciding it should.

He met her there after night shoots. She met him there after his long days in court. In April it rained for a week and the owner rigged a sheet of plastic off the awning and they ate with water drumming on it. In June it was so hot that the broth was unbearable and the owner made them cold noodles, which weren’t on the menu, and charged them for hot ones. In August Si-Yuan brought her sisters, and Si-Jie talked to the owner for half an hour about his grandchildren, and Si-Wei looked at the plastic stools and then at her eldest sister and then at the lawyer and said nothing at all, and ate everything.

He never once called her his girlfriend there. After March he didn’t need to. The owner had started putting extra greens in her bowl and a second glass of water by his, and setting the saucer of oranges down between them without being asked, and on the Tuesday of her nineteenth birthday, in December, when she came through the gate in costume at the end of a long night, he put a single candle in her noodles and lit it with the lighter from behind the till, and stood back with his arms folded while she blew it out.

She asked Pengcheng afterwards whether he’d told him.

“No.”

“Then how did he know?”

He paused. “I don’t know. Perhaps he asked someone what you liked. Nobody asks him what anybody likes.”

She looked at him across the table, under the faded awning, with the television muttering and the steam going up between them, and thought about a man forty-three minutes away who’d timed the drive. Then she held out a piece of orange, and he took it.

chapters.title: His Note
chapters.desc: The note she left under the ring box, and the eleven months it spent in his jacket: chambers, Paris, the jet bridge, the premiere. The morning after her sisters’ birthday she finds it, and puts it away.
chapters.content:
The note was small enough to fit under the ring box. That was the first thing he noticed about it, afterwards: that she must have folded it to that size on purpose, so that it would sit exactly underneath and nowhere else, and he’d have to lift the box to find it.

It was a Friday in January, in his room at the family chambers, with the door still a little open where she’d gone out through it. The chair opposite his desk was pushed back. The box sat between two stacks of files. She’d already told him everything in person: that she’d accepted the film in Paris, that she was going, that she didn’t know any more whether she wanted to marry him. She hadn’t raised her voice once. She’d put the ring down gently, as though it might break.

The note was a square of paper from the pad she kept in her bag for scripts, folded once, in her round quick hand.

You never once said no to her.

He read it three times. Seven words. No accusation beyond them, no explanation, nothing asking him to understand. She’d done all the explaining she was going to do. This was what was left over, when she’d run out.

He’d disagreed with his mother before. He’d argued with her in private, often. He’d defended Si-Yuan in law, against a studio and a legal director and thirteen pages of other people’s assumptions. He’d told his mother more than once that she didn’t decide his life.

He’d never said no when it mattered. He’d said nothing at New Year, when Si-Yuan bowed lower than she’d ever bowed and his mother spoke only to him, and nothing at the Sunday lunches, and nothing when she was offered Paris the first time and his mother said no actress of hers would live abroad. He’d said nothing in the ballroom. There’d always been a reason why this wasn’t the moment. Her birthday. The guests. The chambers. The risk of making it worse. He’d treated every chance to stand beside her as something that could be adjourned, and she’d stopped waiting for the next hearing.

He folded the note along its crease and put it in the inside pocket of his jacket, over his heart, where he’d once put her pen. He didn’t decide to. His hand did it.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first time he took it out again was three days later, reaching for a pen in the middle of a conference with a client. His fingers found the paper and for half a second he didn’t know what it was. Then he did. He finished the conference without hearing much of it.

That night he hung the jacket on the back of a chair and looked at it, and didn’t take the note out.

In the morning he put the same jacket on.

By February it had become part of how he left the house. Wallet, phone, keys, and then, without looking, two fingers against the inside pocket. He wore that jacket on days that were too warm for it. He wore it when he slept in his chambers, which was most nights, on the sofa under the window with the lamp on and a dictionary open beside him and one of her interviews from a Paris paper, translated a sentence at a time.

His father noticed, the way his father noticed everything.

“You’ve worn that one all week.”

“It’s comfortable.”

“You have other jackets.”

“I know.”

His father looked at him over his reading glasses for a moment longer than was polite, and didn’t ask.

✦ ✦ ✦

In March Ms. Lui offered to send the jacket out to be pressed. She said it kindly. It had begun to look like a jacket that was slept in, which it was.

“Leave it on the stand. It’ll be back this afternoon,” she said.

He took it off and held it out to her, and then took it back before she’d closed her hand on it, and turned away and slid two fingers into the inside pocket and took out a folded square of paper and put it in his shirt pocket instead. When he turned round again she was looking at the floor with great tact. She took the jacket away and didn’t say a word, then or ever, and the next morning he found a small clear envelope on his blotter, the kind they used for exhibits, with nothing written on it. He didn’t use it. But he kept it in the drawer, and he thought of her kindly for the rest of the year.

The paper was going soft at the folds. He was careful with it. He never left it on the desk. He never put it in a file or let it get caught between the pages of anything. Nobody else was meant to see it, and it proved nothing to anyone but him. It was hers, and he was afraid that if he put it somewhere safe he’d learn, little by little, to live without looking at it.

✦ ✦ ✦

In April he found out from an entertainment page, not from her, that she’d be home for two weeks between shooting blocks.

He wrote to her by hand. Two pages. He apologised for the ballroom, and for the years before it. For Paris the first time. For the contract he’d renegotiated without asking her. For the anniversary he’d forgotten until the middle of the night. For letting her carry his family’s disapproval by herself and calling it patience. He didn’t ask her to come back. He didn’t ask her to forgive him. He didn’t promise anything would be different, because he’d made promises before.

He carried the letter in his jacket for a day before he sent it, beside the note. Two pieces of paper, one in his hand and one in hers. He didn’t know that she’d read his twice and put it inside her script, or that she’d kept it. He didn’t know she’d never thrown away the pad the note had come from. They were both carrying pieces of the same mistake, and neither of them knew where the other had put theirs.

✦ ✦ ✦

In May Si-Jie came to chambers without an appointment, sat down opposite him, and told him that saying nothing was taking her side.

He’d never heard it put that way. He sat still while she said the rest of it. When she’d gone he took the note out and read it, and understood for the first time that the seven words and Si-Jie’s six were the same sentence, said by two people who loved the same woman, and that he’d needed to hear it twice.

In June he went to his mother’s house to say three things. He said one sentence. Her name is Si-Yuan. His mother laughed at him, not unkindly, the way she’d laughed when he was nine and said he’d be a judge, and he left without the second sentence. He sat in the car outside her gate with both hands on the wheel and then took the note out and held it against the wheel and read it in the evening light.

You never once said no to her.

He’d gone there to prove he could speak, and he’d stopped halfway. He put it back. He drove home. He didn’t sleep much.

✦ ✦ ✦

It went to Paris with him in July, though he’d told nobody he was going. It stood with him under the awning of a shut shop across from her set in the rain, two evenings running, while she walked past him. It was in his pocket on the Wednesday morning at the airport, in the queue for the desk, when he looked down at his boarding pass and thought: I’ve done this before. I’ve done exactly this. And it was in his pocket when he stepped out of the queue and walked back up the jet bridge against the people coming down it.

He didn’t take it out that night, in her flat. He didn’t think of it at all, for once. But in the hotel afterwards, in the small hours, he hung the jacket over the chair and stood in the middle of the room and touched the pocket, and it was still there.

✦ ✦ ✦

In August he began sending her his day, every morning, as a list. In September he resigned from his family’s chambers and put his own name on a door. YANG AND ASSOCIATES, no crest, nothing else. He took a photograph of the door and sent it to her, and she wrote back later that the door looked good. He didn’t tell her about the note. He didn’t want her to feel she was responsible for the man he was trying to become. She hadn’t asked him to leave the chambers. He’d finally understood the decision was his.

In November he sat in row thirty, seat eleven, at the back of a cinema in Paris, and watched her be extraordinary for two hours, and she found him in the foyer afterwards and kissed him in front of everyone. In the hotel that night he took the note out and unfolded it on the desk. The paper had gone as soft as cloth. The ink was perfectly clear.

She’d kissed him. She hadn’t said she was coming home. He wasn’t going to turn one kiss into a promise she’d never made. He folded it up and put it back.

✦ ✦ ✦

In December the lining of the jacket gave way at the corner of the inside pocket. He found it one morning, a small gap along the seam, just wide enough for a folded square of paper to slip through and be lost.

He stood at the wardrobe with the old jacket in one hand and a new one in the other for longer than he’d have admitted to anyone. Then he took the note out of the old one, frayed now at the edges and grey along the folds, and put it into the inside pocket of the new one, and pressed the pocket flat with his palm.

His phone went on the bed.

Miss Yen (Page Seventeen): Are you busy?

Pengcheng: Not now.

Miss Yen (Page Seventeen): What are you doing?

He looked at the jacket.

Pengcheng: Moving something.

Miss Yen (Page Seventeen): Important?

Pengcheng: Yes.

Miss Yen (Page Seventeen): What is it?

He could have told her. The answer seemed too small for the year it stood for.

Pengcheng: Something I want to keep safe.

She sent nothing back for a moment. Then a heart, the first since January. He looked at it until the screen went dark.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the Saturday she came home for her sisters’ birthday, and that night, at her flat, for the first time since Paris, she asked him to stay.

She woke before him in the morning. She lay for a while watching him sleep, his face turned into her pillow, his hand still open on the sheet where hers had been. Then she got up and put on his shirt from the floor, because it was nearer than her robe, and picked up his jacket from where it had landed over the arm of the chair, to hang it up.

Something stiff in the inside pocket. She knew the feel of folded paper; she’d spent her life with scripts. She took it out without thinking, meaning to put it on the chair.

It was her own handwriting. It took her a moment, because the paper was so worn, grey and soft and furred at the edges, the folds nearly through. She unfolded it standing by the window in the cold early light.

You never once said no to her.

She sat down on the chair with it in her lap.

When he woke she was still sitting there, in his shirt, with her bare feet tucked under her, holding it. He looked at her hands and then at her face and sat up slowly.

“You kept it,” she said.

“Yes.”

“Where?”

“In my jacket.”

“Every day?”

“Every day. Since January.”

She looked down at it. “You took this to Paris.”

“Yes.”

“To the premiere?”

“Yes.”

“Did you take it into court?”

“Every time,” said Pengcheng.

She shook her head slowly. Her eyes had filled and she didn’t wipe them. “Why?”

He took a while. “Because I needed to remember what I’d done. And how easy it was. I didn’t want to get comfortable again, just because things were better. I didn’t want to become him again by accident.”

“It’s the worst thing I ever said to you.”

“It’s the truest thing anyone’s ever said to me.”

She got up and came and sat on the bed beside him with the note in her hand, and turned it over once, and looked at her own seven words, which seemed harsher now than she remembered writing them. Or perhaps she’d only forgotten how tired she’d been, that Friday, at his desk.

“You can stop carrying it now,” she said.

“I’m afraid I’ll forget.”

She put her hand flat on his chest. “Then remember me instead. Not the day I left. Not this. Remember what I was asking for. I never needed you to be perfect, Pengcheng. I needed you to stand next to me.”

“I know.”

“And you do now.”

He looked at her. Then he said, that he did.

She folded the note along its old crease, carefully, so it wouldn’t tear. She leaned across him and opened the drawer of the bedside table and laid it inside, on top of a hairbrush and a box of earrings and an old script with a two-page letter folded into the back of it. She left the drawer a little open. It wasn’t hidden and it wasn’t thrown away. It just didn’t need to go everywhere with him any more.

That afternoon, putting his jacket on to go, he reached for the inside pocket out of habit and found it empty. He stood still in her hall with his hand against his chest.

She was in the kitchen doorway with a cup of tea, watching him.

“I put it away,” she said.

He nodded. He didn’t say anything for a while. Then he came back down the hall and kissed her, in the doorway, with the tea held carefully out to one side, and she let him, and when he finally went she stood at the window and watched him cross the road without his hand going once to his pocket.

chapters.title: Paris in the Rain
chapters.desc: The three nights outside the set, from her side: what she saw from the make-up trailer window, the message on Wednesday morning, and the moment she saw he hadn’t gone.
chapters.epigraph: “I won’t come to the set again unless you want me to.”
chapters.content:
The make-up trailer had one window, a small square of scratched plastic above the mirror, and if Si-Yuan sat in the second chair with her head tipped back for the girl doing her hair, it looked straight across the street at a shop that had been shut since she’d arrived in February. Dusty glass. A green awning. A sign in the door that she’d translated, her first week, as Closed for family reasons, and had liked, and had never found out the reasons for.

On the Monday it started raining a little after six. She’d done the long scene by the river twice and they were relighting for the third, and she was in the second chair with her eyes half shut and a girl called Inès pinning the wet ends of her hair, when she opened them and looked at the window and saw a man under the green awning.

Black coat. No umbrella, though he was holding one, furled and apparently forgotten. He was standing quite still, not on his phone, not smoking, not waiting for anyone she could see. Just facing the set.

Her body stopped before her mind caught up. She knew him through the plastic and the rain and forty feet of wet street, before she could see his face, by the way he stood: straight but not stiff, his weight a little on one leg, the way he’d stood at the side of every room she’d ever walked into with him.

“Ça va? You moved,” said Inès.

“Sorry.”

She kept still. Inès finished the pins. Si-Yuan looked at the window the whole time, in the mirror, so that nobody could see her doing it.

She’d imagined him in Paris. That was the embarrassing part. Not in any way she’d have admitted to: she’d never rehearsed a conversation, never chosen a dress for it. She’d only wondered, sometimes, crossing the bridge late, whether if he ever turned up she’d be angry enough not to feel anything else. She’d thought Paris might make him look smaller. A man from a life she’d left.

He didn’t look smaller. He looked tired and careful and exactly like himself, standing in the rain outside her work without having told her he was coming, and she hated that her first thought was that his shoulders were getting wet.

They called her for the third take. She went. She did it well. Afterwards, coming out with the others under Inès’s umbrella, laughing at something the boom operator said, she heard him say her name across the street and didn’t turn, because a car went by and she had a second to decide, and then he said it again and she couldn’t not.

She looked at him. She let him see that she’d seen him. Then she turned up the collar of her coat and walked to the car.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the back of the production van that night Qiao-jie asked whether she was all right.

“I’m tired.”

“You’ve been very quiet.”

“I’m tired,” said Si-Yuan again, and Qiao-jie, who’d known her since her first screen test and had flown out for the last fortnight of the shoot precisely because she knew her, looked at her a second longer and let it be.
