At the flat she didn’t turn the light on. She stood at the window in the dark for a while and looked at the street, in case. He wasn’t there. She went to bed and didn’t sleep.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Tuesday she told herself she wasn’t going to look.

She looked from the moment she got into the chair. Inès was doing a more complicated thing with her hair for the evening scene and it took most of an hour, and Si-Yuan sat through it with her script open on her knee, not reading it, watching the green awning in the corner of the mirror.

He came while the light was going. The rain had stopped. He didn’t have the umbrella this time. He stood under the awning with his hands in his coat pockets and looked across at the production entrance, and once, when the trailer door banged in the wind, at the trailer, and she went hot all over and was sure he couldn’t see in.

He didn’t do anything. That was what undid her. He didn’t call. He didn’t send flowers to the set; a man from props would have told her. He didn’t try to talk his way past the barrier, which he could have done, she knew, in three sentences and a business card. He just stood there and waited for the chance of seeing her, with no idea whether she’d want to be seen.

She wondered whether he’d eaten. She wondered where he was staying. She wondered how many evenings he’d decided on before he’d booked the flight, and whether he’d let himself book a return at all. Then she wondered why she was wondering, and shut the script hard enough that Inès jumped.

The scene for the next day was the one where Ning Yue walks away from a man who’d spent years asking her to stay. She’d underlined one line. You can’t keep asking me to come back to a place where I was never allowed to belong. She’d underlined it in February, in pencil, without thinking of anyone in particular. She looked at it in the trailer now with him across the street, and couldn’t stop thinking of someone in particular.

When they wrapped she came out talking to the second assistant director about the morning’s call. She knew where he was before she reached the pavement. She thought, for one step, about stopping. Not to talk. Just to stop. Some part of her still answered the sight of him the way it always had: the part that remembered waiting for his car at the gate, and the feel of his hand closing round hers, and being glad, simply glad, to see him at the end of a long day.

She kept walking. He didn’t say her name. She passed the green awning with her eyes on the car at the end of the street and got in, and as the car pulled away she looked back once through the rear window, which she’d promised herself she wouldn’t do, and he was still standing exactly where she’d left him.

✦ ✦ ✦

The message came on Wednesday morning while she was in the chair having her face done for the first set-up.

Pengcheng: I’m leaving Paris today. I won’t come to the set again unless you want me to. I’m sorry I came without telling you.

She read it with Inès’s brush going across her cheekbone. She read it again. She turned the phone over on her knee and sat still, and Inès said “Ferme les yeux,” and she closed them, and was grateful.

So that was that. Two evenings. He’d come and stood in the rain and she’d walked past him twice and now he was going home, the way he always went home, the way he’d always done the reasonable thing and waited for her to understand it. She told herself she was relieved. She told herself it was what she wanted. She went out to the river in the grey morning light and shot the scene where Ning Yue walks away.

She did it in four takes. On the fourth she said the line, you can’t keep asking me to come back, to an actor who’d been perfectly kind to her all summer, and saw something cross his face that wasn’t in the script, and walked out of shot and kept walking until someone called cut and ran after her with an umbrella because it had begun to rain again. Moreau came over himself. He didn’t say anything about the take. He looked at her and then he put his hand on her shoulder, briefly, and went back to the monitor.

All day she didn’t look at the window. Between set-ups she sat in the trailer with her back to it. When the light went and they moved to the street for the evening scenes she sat in the second chair facing the mirror and kept her eyes on her own face, and talked to Inès about Inès’s boyfriend, and laughed in the right places.

It was nearly the end of the night, while Inès was taking the pins out, that she lifted her eyes to the mirror without meaning to, and looked past her own shoulder at the little square of scratched plastic, and the green awning, and the man underneath it. He hadn’t gone.

He was standing in the same place, in the same coat, wet through at the shoulders, with no umbrella and no case and no idea, she was quite sure, whether she’d even come out of this door tonight or another one. He’d told her he was leaving. He’d meant it; she knew what he sounded like when he meant things. And then something had happened between his message and the airport, and he hadn’t.

She sat with her hands in her lap and let Inès finish. She didn’t feel relieved. She didn’t feel angry, or not only. She felt as if the floor of the trailer had tilted a little and she was waiting to see which way it would settle.

He’d always gone home. Every time it was hard. He’d done the reasonable thing and adjourned and waited, and she’d been the one left standing in the room. He hadn’t gone home.

“C’est fini,” said Inès, and touched her shoulder, and Si-Yuan stood up and took her coat off the hook and went out.

✦ ✦ ✦

The crew were loading the vans. They went round her on both sides with their crates and their cables, and she stood still on the wet pavement under the light from the trailer door and looked across the street. Qiao-jie, a step behind her, looked at her and then at the green awning, and said, low, that she’d tell the driver to wait. Si-Yuan didn’t answer. She crossed the road.

✦ ✦ ✦

Much later, in the small hours, she stood at the window of her flat in the dark with her hair down and his warmth still on her, and watched him come out of her building into the street.

Nothing was settled. She’d told him so. He’d agreed. On the bridge she’d kissed him to make him go, and he hadn’t gone, and she’d brought him up the stairs and shut the door and not moved away from it, and they’d been angry with each other and hungry for each other, and it had been nothing like before. Now he walked out under the street light with his hands in his coat pockets and turned towards the river.

He didn’t look up at her window. She waited for him to. She found she wanted him to so badly that her fingers had closed on the curtain. He didn’t. He walked to the corner and round it and was gone, and she understood that he hadn’t looked up because he was leaving it to her, all of it, every next step, and that he’d go on leaving it to her for as long as it took.

She stood there a long time. Then she went to bed, and slept, for the first time in three nights.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the morning she went down to the bakery under the flat for bread, the way she did every day. The old woman behind the counter, who was tired and kind and had never once given her the right change, counted coins into her palm with her lips moving, and got it wrong again, in Si-Yuan’s favour, as she always did.

Si-Yuan stood looking at the coins. She’d told a journalist about this woman in February. She’d said it had become a small present every morning, and that she’d never correct her. Last night, in the dark, Pengcheng had said that he knew about the bakery. That he’d read the interview in his chambers in the middle of the night, a sentence at a time, with a dictionary. He’d said it plainly, the way he said everything.

“Merci, madame,” she said, and put the coins in her pocket, and went out into the street with the bread under her arm. It was raining again, lightly. She didn’t put her hood up. She walked to the corner where he’d turned and stood there, looking down towards the river.

Then she took her phone out. She didn’t write anything. She only opened his name and looked at it, the plain one, with nothing after it, the way she’d left it on the night of the banquet. She didn’t change it. Not yet.

But she didn’t delete the message from Wednesday morning either. She kept that.

chapters.title: Red Dresses
chapters.desc: Six months married, she brings home the eleventh red dress and counts them all for him: the ones she stopped wearing, the one she never bought, and the ones she started again.
chapters.content:
She came home on a Tuesday in November with a shop bag over her arm and didn’t say anything about it, which was how he knew it mattered.

They’d been married six months. He was at the dining table with a brief he’d promised himself he’d finish before she got in, and he didn’t finish it. He watched her go through to the bedroom with the bag. He heard the wardrobe doors open, and hangers sliding, and then a long pause in which nothing happened at all.

When he went to look she was standing in front of the open wardrobe with a dress on a hanger in her hand. It was red, a deep wine-red, with a soft drape across the shoulders and a narrow waist. She’d pushed everything else along the rail to make room for it at the very front, right in the middle, where she’d see it every time she opened the doors.

“That’s new.”

“Yes.”

“It’s beautiful.”

“I know. It’s the eleventh,” said Si-Yuan, and hung it up, and stood back to look at it.

“The eleventh what?”

She turned round. She had the look she got sometimes before she told him something she’d decided, months ago, to tell him one day: a little stubborn, a little shy, her chin up. “Red dress. Since I met you. Counting one I never bought, and a blouse, because Si-Wei ruled that a blouse counts.”

He sat down on the end of the bed. “Tell me.”

She looked at him, and then sat down next to him, and began.

✦ ✦ ✦

Si-Yuan smiled. “The first one was cherry red. Cotton, with little buttons down the front and a collar. Si-Jie made me buy it, the autumn after we met. She said I dressed as if I were going to an awards dinner every day of my life and I needed something that was just for being eighteen. I wore it to the noodle stall, and to your flat the next Saturday, and you looked up from the sofa and said I looked nice.”

“I remember.”

“You don’t.”

“You had your hair up with a pencil through it. You’d been reading a script on the bus. You put the script on my table and it had a ring from a coffee cup on the front page.”

She stared at him. Then she looked away, and he saw her mouth go soft at the corner, and she went on.

“I wore it all that winter. I didn’t think about it once. That’s the point of the first one. I didn’t think about it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She looked at her hands. “The second was the dark red. The plain one. Plain neck, sleeves just above the wrist. I bought it between two shoots in the spring because the colour made me feel brave, and I wore it to your mother’s in May, to the Sunday lunch, and I was so happy about it. You looked up from your phone and said I was beautiful in red.”

“I did.”

“And your mother came in ten minutes later and looked at the dress before she looked at anything else, and asked whether there was an occasion.”

He didn’t say anything. He remembered the question. He remembered thinking it was an odd thing to say and then forgetting it before the soup.

“In the cloakroom afterwards I looked at myself in the mirror, and it didn’t look brave any more. It looked like I’d tried too hard. I hung it at the back of the wardrobe that night,” said Si-Yuan.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Three was the silk blouse. August. I’d come straight from work and we were going straight to your parents’ and I hadn’t even thought about the colour until I was in your office. And at dinner she reached for her tea and said, You’re wearing red again. It draws attention. I put that one at the bottom of a drawer. I didn’t throw it away. I just didn’t want to see it,” She said it lightly, in a voice that was almost his mother’s, and the lightness was worse than if she’d said it angrily.

“Si-Wei counted it.”

“Si-Wei counts everything. She said a blouse is a dress from the waist up, and if it hurt like a dress it counts like one.”

He let out a breath that wasn’t quite a laugh.

“That was the year I learned your mother’s rules. There were eleven. I never told you. Rule three was that one dresses appropriately. Not too young. Not too fashionable. And never as though one wanted to be looked at. After August, red was in rule three,” she said, and turned her ring round on her finger.

✦ ✦ ✦

She looked at the new dress on the rail. “Four is the one I never bought. We went shopping one Saturday that autumn. A shirt for you and a present for Si-Jie. There was a dress in the department store near the entrance, deep wine-red, with a drape across the shoulders and a narrow waist, and I slowed down in front of it, and you said I should try it on.”

He was quiet. He remembered the store. He didn’t remember the dress.

“I said I didn’t need it. You tugged my hand and said come on, your sister’s present, and I went. And neither of us looked back. I thought about that dress for about a year.”

He looked at the new one at the front of the wardrobe, the drape, the waist, and understood. She saw him understand, and didn’t say anything, and went on.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Five was Si-Jie’s birthday present. Our twenty-first. She came over with two shopping bags and a cake, and one of the bags had a red jersey dress in it, and she said I’m not asking you to wear it, I’m asking you to own it. That was the week after the banquet. I hung it up with the tags on. It stayed like that for more than three years.”

He looked at the floor between his feet. That week, he’d sat outside her building all night on the Sunday and not rung the bell.

Her voice changed; he heard it lift. “Six was in Paris. I found the dark red at the bottom of my case, the one from May, and I wore it to a production dinner, and nobody said anything except that it suited me. Si-Jie wrote FINALLY in capitals. So the next week I bought another one. Red linen, from a stall in a market on the boulevard, for about the price of lunch. It had a stain on the hem by July. I wore it every Sunday. I wore it to buy bread. The woman in the bakery told me I looked like a poppy.”

“You sent your sisters a picture.”

“How do you know that?”

“Si-Jie sent it to me. In June. With no message. I think she wanted me to see what you looked like happy,” said Pengcheng.

Si-Yuan was quiet. “She never told me.”

“I never told you either.”

✦ ✦ ✦

“Seven was the premiere.”

“I know that one.”

“You were at the back.”

He looked at her. “Row thirty. You came out on stage at the end with your hair back and that dress, against the black curtain, and I thought of the earrings I bought you once and the dinner in May, and I clapped until my hands hurt. I didn’t know about two to five. I thought you’d just stopped liking red. I didn’t know anyone had stopped you.”

She took his hand. “Nobody stopped me. That’s what I want you to understand. Your mother asked one question and made one remark. I did all the rest myself. And you didn’t notice. Those are two different things. I’ve stopped being angry about the second one.”

✦ ✦ ✦

“Eight was in Seoul. The press evening. You’d been there two days and you were on the phone in the suite when I came out of the bathroom, and you told the person you’d ring them back and put the phone down without saying goodbye,” she said, more gently.

“That was opposing counsel.”

She smiled. “I know. You said I looked beautiful, and I asked whether you were going to tell me to change, because it was red, and you looked so confused. You said you didn’t think about your mother’s opinions when you looked at me. Nine was the wedding in the garden, Eliana’s, the October after. I couldn’t choose between red and champagne and I asked you, and you said the red, and I said you haven’t even looked, and you said I looked. It’s red.”

“It was red.”

“Si-Jie said she was beginning to think I didn’t own anything else.”

“Ten?”

She laughed. “Ten was Si-Jie’s own wedding, in April. I was her witness. She told me if I turned up in anything but red she’d have me removed. I wore her jersey dress. Number five. I cut the tags off that morning, in her bathroom, with her nail scissors, and she cried and ruined her make-up and we had to start again.”

He’d been there. He remembered the dress. He remembered Arthur, unexpectedly, saying it was a good colour on her, and Pengcheng agreeing with him, which neither of them had enjoyed.

✦ ✦ ✦

“And eleven,” she said.

They both looked at it.

She took a breath. “I saw it in a window on the way home today. Not for anything. Not for a dinner, or a wedding, or your mother, or you. I didn’t stop to think whether it was too much. I didn’t think about rule three. I just liked it. And then I was standing there holding it and I realised it was nearly the same dress. The one by the entrance, five years ago. The one I said I didn’t need.”

He didn’t trust himself to speak straight away.

She lifted her chin. “I paid for it myself. In case you were going to ask.”

“I wasn’t going to ask.”

“You were reaching for your wallet in your head. I could see it.”

He shook his head, and then, because she was right, he laughed. She leaned against his shoulder.

“Do you wish you’d noticed sooner?” she said.

He thought about it properly, the way he thought about everything she asked him, and she waited, because she’d learned years ago that the pause was where the true answer lived.

“Yes. Every time you stopped doing something you loved because you thought it would make things easier for me. Every time you made yourself a little smaller and I thought you were settling in. I can’t give you those years back. I can only keep noticing now. And I’ll tell you when I do. Out loud,” he said.

“That’s a very serious answer.”

“It’s a very serious wardrobe.”

She laughed into his shirt. Then she sat up and looked at the rail, at the new dress at the front, and the dark red one from that first May hanging just behind it, and the jersey one with its tags gone, and the linen one from the market with its stain on the hem that she’d never had cleaned.

“I used to think I had to be careful about everything. What I wore. How loudly I laughed. How long I stayed at the table. I don’t any more. But sometimes I still remember,” she said.

“Then tell me when you do.”

“It’ll be eleven dresses’ worth of complaints.”

“I’ve got time.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On Saturday they went to his parents’ for lunch. She wore the eleventh.

His mother looked at it when she came in. She looked at it, the way she’d once looked at a dark red dress at a Sunday lunch before she’d looked at anything else. Then she looked up at Si-Yuan’s face.

“That’s a good colour,” said his mother.

“Thank you. I chose it myself,” said Si-Yuan.

His mother nodded, as if that were the only possible answer, and turned to ask his father where the good teapot had gone. Pengcheng held his wife’s hand under the table. She held his back, once, and let go, and reached for her cup, and stayed at the table exactly as long as she wanted to, which was quite a long time.

chapters.title: His Mother’s Kitchen
chapters.desc: The summer before the wedding, the housekeeper is away and Si-Yuan falls asleep in an armchair. His mother goes into a kitchen she hasn’t cooked in for thirty-nine years. One bowl, a truce.
chapters.content:
Madam Yang hadn’t cooked anything since the year she was called to the bar. She’d been twenty-four. Her mother had still been alive then, and had said, watching her daughter put on a black gown for the first time, that she hoped the law fed her better than the kitchen had, because she’d never once got the rice right. Madam Yang had taken it as permission. For thirty-nine years there had been other people to cook: her mother, then a woman from her mother’s village, then the housekeeper, who had been with them since before her son could walk and who called him Young Master still, at thirty, to his evident discomfort.

On the last Sunday in August the housekeeper had gone to visit her sister on the other side of the harbour. She’d left a fish on a plate in the refrigerator under a cloth, and a note in her slow careful hand saying what to do with it at six. Madam Yang had read the note at breakfast and put it back exactly where it had been.

Her son and the girl came after lunch. Madam Yang still called her the girl, in her head. She had stopped calling her that out loud.

✦ ✦ ✦

It had been a quiet afternoon. Her husband read in his chair by the window, as he had read in that chair every Sunday of their marriage. Pengcheng talked to his father for a while about a case of his, a commercial matter that his firm had taken from under the nose of two of the big partnerships, and his father asked three questions and then said good in the particular way he did, which Madam Yang had heard perhaps a dozen times in thirty-five years. She watched her son take it. He didn’t look pleased. He looked like a man putting something carefully in a pocket.

Si-Yuan didn’t say much. She’d come straight from a fitting, Pengcheng said, for the film in Seoul, the third that week. She was flying on Thursday. She sat in the armchair across from the sofa with a script on her knee, and when Madam Yang asked about the part she answered politely and well and didn’t go on too long, and then she went back to the script, and Madam Yang went back to her book and didn’t read it.

She watched the girl instead. She’d been watching her for five years. She’d watched her bow lower than anyone needed to bow at New Year, and sit through Sunday lunches answering every question correctly and never once interrupting, and stand up at a banquet in front of three hundred people and bow once, perfectly, and walk out. She’d watched her come back through that door in red, and bow exactly as much as was polite and not a degree further. Madam Yang had spent her whole working life watching people across a courtroom, what they did with their hands, where their eyes went when a question frightened them, what they left on their plates at the lunch break. She had never once been able to stop.

At some point in the middle of the afternoon she looked up and the girl was asleep.

She hadn’t meant to be. It was plain from the way she’d gone, sitting up, with the script still open under one hand and her head tipped against the wing of the chair and her mouth a little open. Her face, asleep, looked younger. It looked, for a moment, like the face of an eighteen-year-old who had sat in this room for the first time on a cold New Year’s afternoon with her knees together, waiting to be spoken to, and hadn’t been.

Madam Yang looked at her son. He’d seen too. He’d put his finger to his lips, at his own mother, in her own house, and was sitting still on the sofa so as not to wake her, his whole body turned a little towards the chair.

She thought of her own mother. She thought of a narrow kitchen behind a shop, and the smell of ginger and soy, and her mother saying, whenever anybody in the house was ill or sad or simply worn out, that there was only one thing for it, and going to the stove.

She put her book down and stood up. The small sound of it woke the girl, who sat up with a start and went scarlet, and Madam Yang didn’t look at her. She went into the kitchen.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t know where anything was. That was the first difficulty. The housekeeper’s kitchen was immaculate and entirely foreign, and she stood in the middle of it for a full minute opening drawers before she found a knife she trusted. The fish was where the note had said. The ginger was in a basket by the window with the garlic. The spring onions took longer.

She hadn’t done this in thirty-nine years and her hands did it anyway. They remembered: the fish patted dry and scored, three cuts each side; the ginger in thin coins and then in matchsticks, far too much of it, the way her mother had always done, because her mother had said ginger was what did the good; the oil in the pan until it shivered. They remembered the sound when the fish went in. They remembered how long to leave it, and the dark sauce, soy and a little sugar and wine and water, and the lid on, and the low heat, and the waiting.

She stood at the stove with her arms folded, waiting, and found that her eyes had gone hot, and was annoyed with herself, and put it down to the onions.

In the sitting room her husband turned a page. She heard her son murmur something. She heard nothing at all from the armchair.

It took forty minutes. She’d forgotten it took forty minutes. When it was done she lifted the fish out whole, carefully, with two spatulas, the way she’d seen it done a thousand times and never done herself, and laid it in a bowl, and poured the sauce over, and put the spring onions on top in a neat green line, and stood and looked at it.

It looked like her mother’s. It wasn’t. Her mother’s had never been so tidy.

✦ ✦ ✦

Si-Yuan had woken to the sound of a book being put down.

For a moment she didn’t know where she was. Then she did, all at once, and sat up so fast the script slid off her knee onto the floor. She’d fallen asleep. At his mother’s. In the middle of the afternoon, in front of his mother, who was now walking out of the room without a word. Her face went hot to the roots of her hair.

She looked at Pengcheng. He looked back at her and slightly shook his head. He didn’t know either. She could see it on him: he was as lost as she was, sitting on the edge of the sofa with his hands between his knees, looking at the kitchen door.

Then there were sounds from the kitchen that nobody in that house had heard in thirty-nine years. A drawer, and another drawer. A knife on a board, quick and steady. Oil. His father lowered his paper an inch and looked at the doorway over the top of it with an expression Si-Yuan couldn’t read at all, and then raised it again and didn’t turn a page. She picked up the script and held it and didn’t read it either. Nobody spoke. It went on for forty minutes, and she sat through every one of them with her back straight, the way she’d sat in that chair the first time.

When his mother came out she was carrying one bowl. A whole fish in a dark glossy sauce, with ginger cut so fine it was almost thread, and a line of spring onion along its back, and the steam coming off it.

“It’s braised fish. My mother made it when anyone in the house was tired,” she said.

She set it down on the low table in front of Si-Yuan, with a pair of chopsticks across the rim, and went back to her chair by the other window, and picked up her book, and turned a page, and didn’t look up. She picked up the chopsticks.

It was good. The fish came apart at a touch. The sauce was dark and salty and a little sweet and full of ginger, almost too much, so that it warmed the back of her throat, and she’d always loved ginger, and she ate all of it. She ate it slowly, and properly, the way she’d been taught to eat in that house, and she didn’t look up once in case she cried, and when she’d finished she put the chopsticks together across the empty bowl and sat for a moment with her hands in her lap.

Then she picked the bowl up and took it into the kitchen.

It was the first time she’d been in it. She’d walked past the door for five years. It was clean and quiet, except that the stove had a pan on it with a little dark sauce still in the bottom, and there were ginger peelings in a neat heap on a board by the sink, more of them than anyone could possibly have needed, and a knife washed and laid on a cloth to dry. On the windowsill was a note in an old woman’s careful handwriting about what to do with the fish. It had been turned over.

She washed the bowl and the chopsticks and the spoon. She dried them and found where they went. She stood at the sink longer than she needed to with her hands on the edge of it and looked at the heap of ginger peelings.

Then she went back in and stood in front of his mother’s chair.

“Thank you. It was the best thing I’ve eaten in a long time,” she said.

His mother didn’t look up from her book. “I put too much ginger in it.”

“I like ginger.”

There was a long pause. His mother turned a page she hadn’t read.

“I know,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the car he drove for ten minutes without saying anything, and then pulled over in a side street under a tree and turned the engine off and sat with both hands on the wheel.

“I’ve never seen her cook. Not once. Not in my whole life,” he said.

“I know.”

“I don’t know what started it.”

Si-Yuan looked out of the window at the leaves. She thought about waking up. She thought about the heap of peelings, and the note turned over on the sill, and an old woman’s voice saying I know to the pages of a book, and about five years of Sunday lunches in that house, every one of them, at which she’d eaten the slivers of ginger out of every dish because she liked them, while everybody else left theirs at the side of the plate. She hadn’t thought anyone had noticed. Nobody had ever said a word.

Somebody had been watching. Somebody had been watching the whole time.

“I fell asleep,” she said.

“My father falls asleep in that room every Sunday.”

She put her hand over her eyes. “I fell asleep in your mother’s sitting room. In front of your mother. I’m never going to be able to go back.”

“You’re going back on Sunday week. She’ll want to hear about Seoul.”

“She won’t.”

“She will, and she’ll pretend she doesn’t,” said Pengcheng, and Si-Yuan took her hand away from her face and looked at him, and he was smiling, not very steadily.

She reached over and put her hand on his on the wheel.

“Don’t make it bigger than it is. It’s one bowl. It doesn’t mean everything’s all right,” she said.

“I know.”

“It doesn’t undo anything.”

“I know.”

“But it was a good fish,” said Si-Yuan, and he laughed, and leaned his head back against the seat and shut his eyes, and she kept her hand where it was until he started the car again.

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening Madam Yang stood in the kitchen with the light off. The pan had been washed and put away. The peelings had gone. She’d turned the housekeeper’s note the right way up again and left it on the sill where it had been, so that tomorrow nobody would have to explain anything.

Her husband came and stood in the doorway. He didn’t turn the light on either. He’d been married to her for thirty-five years and he’d learned when not to.

“What made you?” he said.

She looked at the stove for a while.

“She was tired,” said Madam Yang.

He waited, the way he waited when he was reading something difficult and knew the next line would explain the last. It didn’t come. After a moment he nodded, as though it had, and went back to his chair. She heard him pick up his paper.

She never told her son. He wondered about it for weeks. He went on wondering about it for years, in fact, and once, long afterwards, lying awake beside his wife, he told her that he still didn’t know what had started it, and Si-Yuan, half asleep, said she did, and he asked what, and she said she’d tell him one day, and went to sleep.

She didn’t, in the end. It wasn’t hers to tell. She’d only been the one asleep in the chair.

chapters.title: The Premiere Ticket
chapters.desc: Row thirty, seat eleven, from the stage: she sees him before Moreau finishes his first sentence. A year later she finds the stub in his wallet, where he keeps ordinary things.
chapters.content:
When the lights came up and they walked her out onto the stage, Si-Yuan looked at the back of the house first.

She always did. She’d done it at every screening and every award and every first night since she was eighteen, and she’d only understood why a year or two ago. It was because of him. Because at her first award he’d sat three rows behind her, pretending to be only her lawyer, and she’d learned to look for him past the people who’d come to be seen. He always sat where he could see the whole room. He always sat near an aisle. He always sat further back than he needed to.

She looked at the back of the house in the cinema in Paris, past the critics in the good seats and the distributors and the people from the production, over five hundred people on their feet, and she didn’t expect to see anything. He was on the other side of the world. He’d sent her his day that morning, as he’d sent it every morning since August. Meetings, a hearing, lunch with Ku. He hadn’t said anything about Paris.

There was a man standing in the second row from the back, close to the aisle, in a charcoal suit with no tie, clapping.

She couldn’t see his face. It was too far and the light was wrong. She knew him anyway, the way she’d known him through the rain in July: by the way he stood, straight, not quite part of the crowd around him. He was clapping, and showed no sign of stopping.

Moreau was talking. Moreau was thanking the crew, and the distributors, and the weather, and then turning to her and saying generous things she’d thought about for months afterwards. She heard about half of them. She was standing in a dark red dress in front of a black curtain with her heart going so hard she was afraid the front rows could see it, and when Moreau handed her the microphone she held it in both hands for a moment, the way she did when she was frightened, and then let one hand drop to her side, the way she did when she’d decided not to be.

She’d written down what she was going to say. She said it. She said that Ning Yue had taught her something about leaving: that at the start Ning Yue thought leaving was the same as being brave, and found out later it was only part of it. You also had to decide what life you wanted once you’d gone, she said, and let yourself enjoy it. She said thank you for watching her.

She didn’t look at the back of the house while she said it. She’d have lost her place.

✦ ✦ ✦

The foyer afterwards was like every foyer. Photographers by the doors. Microphones. People from the distributor steering her from one cluster to the next with a hand at her elbow. Somebody pressed a glass of champagne into her hand and somebody else took it away again before she’d drunk any. Qiao-jie appeared at her shoulder every few minutes, like a lighthouse, with the next name.

She smiled. She answered questions. She stood for pictures with Moreau and with the actor who’d played the man Ning Yue walked away from and with a woman from the ministry of culture. Between every one of them she looked for a charcoal suit.

She found him on the third look. He was leaning against a pillar near the cloakroom, alone, with his coat over his arm and his phone in his hand, and he was reading. She knew that face. It was the face he wore for a contract, completely still, absorbed. She realised after a moment that he must be reading the reviews. The first ones had gone up before the credits had finished; Qiao-jie had been showing her lines from them on her own phone in the wings.

He didn’t look up. He didn’t try to come over. He stood exactly far enough away that she could go home without ever having to know he’d been there.

“Who are you looking at?” said Qiao-jie, under her breath.

“Nobody.”

Qiao-jie followed her eyes to the pillar and back, and pressed her lips together, and said nothing at all, which from Qiao-jie was a speech.

She didn’t go to him. Not for a long time. She did another interview, and another photograph, and listened to a man from the distributor talk about festivals, and all the while she was arguing with herself.

If she went over, it would mean something. Everybody would see. There’d be photographs. And she didn’t know what she wanted it to mean. In July she’d let him in, on the third night, and told him nothing was settled, and he’d gone home and done exactly what she’d asked: nothing. He’d sent her his day. He’d resigned from his family. He’d put his own name on a door and sent her a picture of it. He’d never once asked whether she was coming back.

And now he’d bought a ticket. Not an invitation. She knew him well enough to be sure of it. He could have rung Qiao-jie, or the production, or anyone, and been in the third row by lunchtime. He’d sat at the back instead, in a seat anyone could have had, so that she could have her night without him in it if that was what she wanted.

She looked across at the pillar again. He’d put his phone away. He’d picked up his coat. He was turning towards the side doors.

It was so like him that she almost laughed. He’d watched the film. He’d read the reviews. He’d seen what he came for, and now he was going, before she could be troubled with him. The reasonable thing.

She put down the programme she didn’t remember picking up and then picked it up again and walked away from the man from the distributor in the middle of his sentence.

“Pengcheng?”

✦ ✦ ✦

He turned round.

Afterwards she remembered almost everything he said and nothing that she did. He said he’d bought a ticket. He said row thirty, seat eleven, and she said that was miles away, and he said he knew. He said he hadn’t known whether she’d want him there, and that he’d thought if he sat at the back she could have her evening without worrying about him. He said he’d only wanted to see the film. He said she’d been extraordinary, and that there’d been whole scenes when he forgot it was her.

He started to say something about the last scene, and she stopped him, because she couldn’t have borne it, not then. He nearly smiled. He said all right.

Someone called her for another photograph. She turned and said she’d be a moment. He stepped aside to let her go, of course he did, and she found she couldn’t.

“Are you leaving?”

“I was going to.”

“Can you stay a little?”

“Of course,” said Pengcheng, simply.

She told the photographer five minutes. Then she went back to him across the middle of the foyer, with everyone there, and stopped in front of him, and for a second she didn’t know what she was going to do. He didn’t reach for her. He didn’t ask. He stood still and let her decide, the way he’d stood under the green awning in July and let her walk past him twice.

She put her hand on his cheek and kissed him.

She’d decided. That was what she remembered most clearly, later. Not the cameras, which went off all round them, or Qiao-jie’s face, or the man from the distributor with his mouth open. She remembered deciding. She’d kissed him on a bridge in July to make him go away. She’d kissed him in her flat because she was angry and lonely and had missed him for seven months. This was the first time since the banquet that she’d kissed him because she wanted to, in a room full of people, with nothing to prove and nobody to punish.

He went completely still. Then his hand found her waist and he kissed her back, gently, as if he still couldn’t believe she’d chosen it.

When she drew back she stayed close. “You’re allowed to kiss me back properly.”

“I did.”

She went to have her photograph taken. A few steps on she looked back. He was still there, coat over his arm, exactly where she’d left him. She lifted her hand. He lifted his.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the car back to the flat she held her phone in her lap for ten minutes before she wrote anything.

Si-Yuan: I forgot to say. I was happy you were there.

Pengcheng: I was happy to be there. You deserved every minute of that applause.

She read it three times. Then she wrote Stay tomorrow and deleted it, and wrote Come for breakfast and deleted that too, because it was too much, too soon, and she didn’t trust herself.

Si-Yuan: Goodnight. See you tomorrow.

She hadn’t asked him whether he’d be there tomorrow. She hadn’t needed to.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t think about the ticket again for a year.

It was November again, a month after he’d stood on the stage of her new film with a microphone and his heart in his mouth and formally requested, in front of her sisters and his mother and the whole crew, that she become his wife. They were at his flat on a Sunday afternoon, she on the sofa with a script, he at the table with a brief, and she needed the card for the gym in the basement, which lived in his wallet because she always lost hers.

“In the side,” he said, without looking up.

She opened the wallet. She found the card. Behind it, folded once along a crease that had gone soft and furry with handling, was a small rectangle of paper that she didn’t recognise until she’d opened it out on her knee.

Rang 30, place 11. Orchestre arrière.

The print had faded. The edges were worn round. There was a thumbprint on one corner that had gone grey.

“Pengcheng.”

He looked up and saw what she was holding, and something went across his face that she’d never once seen when he was looking at a brief: a kind of guilt, a little embarrassed, tender.

“You kept this.”

“Yes.”

“In your wallet. For a year.”

He put his pen down. “It’s been in my wallet since the night itself. Behind my identity card. The programme’s in the drawer. I put them side by side in the hotel that night. Then I took the ticket back out. The programme seemed like something you keep. This seemed like something you carry.”

She turned it over. “Why? Of everything from that night?”

He took a while, the way he always took a while, and she waited, the way she’d learned to.

“Because nobody gave me that seat. I paid for it like anybody else. I sat at the back because I didn’t know whether you’d want me there, and I didn’t want you to have to decide. And it was the first time I ever watched you work without being there as anything. Not your lawyer. Not your fiancé. Just someone in the audience. I liked being someone in the audience. I’d never let myself be one before.” He looked at the paper in her hand.

She looked down at it. “I looked for you at the back. The minute the lights came up. Before I even got to the middle of the stage,” she said.

He went still.

She smiled, not quite steadily. “I always look at the back first. I have since my first award. Because that’s where you always sit. Where you can see the whole room. I saw you before Moreau had finished his first sentence. You were standing in the second row from the back clapping like an idiot.”

“You never told me.”

“You never told me about this.”

He got up and came and sat beside her on the sofa, and took the ticket gently out of her fingers, and looked at it.

“I thought you’d found me by chance. In the foyer. That you happened to look over,” he said slowly.

“I looked over about forty times.”

“Forty.”

“Qiao-jie counted.”

He laughed then, with his head down, and she leaned against his shoulder and watched him fold the ticket back along its crease.

“Keep it,” she said.

“I was going to.”

“I mean keep it there. In the wallet. Not in a drawer. Not in a frame. Where you keep ordinary things.”

He looked at her. Then he opened the wallet and slid it back behind his identity card, exactly where it had been, and closed the wallet and gave it to her, and she found the gym card where she’d dropped it on the cushion and put it back in too.

She didn’t go to the gym. She sat on the sofa with her head on his shoulder for the rest of the afternoon, and he didn’t go back to the brief, and at some point she fell asleep there and woke to find he’d put his jacket over her and was reading her script, carefully, from the beginning.

chapters.title: Out Loud, a List
chapters.desc: Engaged a month, she asks him for forty things he’s learned to say. He writes them by hand, at night, with her pen.
chapters.epigraph: “I like that you still ask me to say things.”
chapters.content:
The list began because he said something unnecessary, which, according to Si-Yuan, was becoming a habit.

“You’ve got a little line here,” he said.

It was nearly midnight, in his kitchen, a month after he’d proposed to her on a stage in front of a film crew. She’d come straight from a late press evening and was standing barefoot at the counter with her earrings still in, and he’d kept soup warm for her, and was taking the lid off the pot when he reached over with his free hand and touched the space between her eyebrows.

“What line?”

“Here. When you’re reading something you don’t like. You’ve had it since the car park.”

She stared at him. “That isn’t a line. That’s my face.”

“I know.”

“Then why are you reporting it to me?”

“Because I noticed,” said Pengcheng, and ladled soup into a bowl.

She narrowed her eyes, but the corners of her mouth were already giving her away. “You’ve become very talkative.”

He thought about that. He put the ladle down. “I used to notice things and assume you knew.”

Her face changed. “I know.”

“I don’t want to do that any more.”

She took the bowl from him and drank some of the soup and hummed, and looked at him over the rim. “Then make a list.”

“Of what?”

“Things you want to tell me. Things you’ve learned to say. All the things you used to keep in your head and assume I’d guessed.”

“I tell you things.”

“You tell me about your clients, and Ku, and whether the printer’s behaving.”

“The printer’s been very unreliable.”

“Pengcheng.”

He smiled.

She put the bowl down and leaned her hip against the counter. “I’m serious. Forty things.”

“Forty.”

“You’re a lawyer. You like lists.”

“I like evidence.”

“Then it’s evidence. And don’t make them all about how beautiful I am,” said Si-Yuan.

“I wasn’t going to.”

“Good.”

He considered her. “But you are.”

She turned round to the sink so he wouldn’t see her face and laughed into the tap until her shoulders shook.

✦ ✦ ✦

He wrote it three nights later.

He didn’t write it at the office, where he could have drafted it in ten minutes between calls, or on his laptop, where he’d have revised every sentence until it read like a submission. He sat at the dining table after she’d gone to bed with a sheet of plain paper, and took a pen out of the inside pocket of his jacket. A black fountain pen with a silver clip, engraved along its side with three initials that weren’t his.

He’d been keeping it safe for nearly five years.

He wrote the heading first. Then he sat for a long time with the page empty underneath it. He’d thought the hard part would be remembering. It wasn’t. The hard part was admitting how many things he’d once thought it unnecessary to say.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the morning there was a folded sheet of paper propped against her coffee cup.

She was barely awake. Her hair was in a knot at the back of her head and she had one of his jumpers on over her pyjamas and she picked the paper up with the hand that wasn’t holding the cup.

“What’s this?”

“Your list.”

She looked up. “You’ve done it?”

“Read it.”

She unfolded it. His handwriting, neat, even, in a dark blue-black ink she knew at once, because she’d chosen it herself at eighteen to go in a pen her sisters had given her. She looked at the ink before she looked at the words.

“You wrote it with my pen.”

“It seemed right.”

She read.

FORTY THINGS I SHOULD HAVE SAID OUT LOUD
1. I like hearing you come home. I know your footsteps from the lift.
2. I miss you before you’ve left.
3. You don’t have to be cheerful when you see me. I want to see you on the bad days too.
4. I tell Ku about your work. Not only when you win something.
5. I like the way you talk about acting, especially when you forget to explain the technical parts.
6. I notice when you’re tired. I should ask, not assume.
7. I like your red dresses. I’d like to see more of them.
8. You were never difficult to bring into my family. I was difficult to stand beside.
9. I should have stood up at the banquet before you had to.
10. You weren’t asking me to fight my mother. You were asking me not to leave you on your own.
11. Your career isn’t smaller than mine.
12. I don’t want you to cancel a trip because I miss you. I want you to come back because you want to.
13. I like your voice when you’re half asleep.
14. You steal the blanket and then deny it. I’ve stopped minding.
15. You eat the vegetables first and save the best part. I’ve watched you do it for five years.

She stopped. “You watch me eat?”

“Sometimes.”

“That’s strange.”

“I’m marrying you.”

“Not yet.”

“That’s an argument for another day,” said Pengcheng, and she shook her head and went on.

16. I don’t need you to make my life easier by making yours smaller.
17. I want to know when you’re unhappy with me, even if I don’t like hearing it.
18. You can disagree with me. You can change your mind. You can say no.
19. I mistook your patience for permission. I won’t again.
20. I want to be the person you ring when something good happens, and when something bad does.

She read the twentieth twice. The kitchen was quiet except for the fridge.

“Twenty,” she said.

“Halfway.”

“You’re very ambitious.”

“I had a deadline.”

“Who gave you a deadline?”

“You did,” he said, and she smiled down at the page.

21. I like watching you work.
22. I like watching you do nothing.
23. My silences won’t be used to punish you. If I’m quiet, it’s because I’m thinking, and I’ll tell you what about.
24. If I’m upset, I’ll say so. I won’t make you guess.
25. Bring me things you haven’t decided yet. You don’t have to bring me finished plans.
26. You’re allowed a life I’m not part of. I want to hear about it anyway.
27. I miss Paris. Not the city. The woman who was learning to live without waiting for me.

She looked up. “You miss that me?”

“I miss knowing you were happy.”

“You didn’t know it then.”

“No. I saw it afterwards. In your interviews. In the photographs Si-Jie sent me.”

“I was lonely too.”

“I know.”

“But I was happy in Paris.”

“I know that as well,” he said, and she looked at him and then went back to the page.

28. I want to travel with you. I don’t want you to travel less.
29. I’m glad you have friends who make you laugh when I’m not there.
30. I’m glad your sisters are protective of you, even when they vote on me.
31. I want to grow old with you. Not because we’ve spent so long together already, but because I still want to know who you’ll be.
32. I want to be there for the next award, and the one after, and the one you pretend doesn’t matter.
33. I like your face when you’re trying not to laugh.
34. I like it better when you stop trying.
35. I like waking up next to you. I like that you’re unreasonable before breakfast.

“Unreasonable?”

“You asked for honesty.”

“I’m perfectly reasonable.”

“You once told me the coffee tasted different because I’d used the wrong spoon.”

“It did taste different.”

“Of course,” he said gravely, and she tried to hold on to the outraged face and couldn’t.

The last five were written a little closer together, as though he’d wanted to fit them on without turning the page.

36. I’m not afraid of hard conversations with you any more. I’m afraid of becoming the man who avoided them.
37. I won’t ask you to trust me because I’ve changed. I’ll keep giving you reasons to.
38. I love you when you’re next to me, and when you’re somewhere I can’t reach.
39. I choose you. Not after everyone agrees. Not when it’s convenient. Not only when the room is quiet.
40. I love you. I should have said it more. I mean to say it for the rest of my life.

She got to the end and turned the paper over to see whether there was any more.

“That’s all?”

“Forty.”

“You could have written more.”

“I could have.”

“Why didn’t you?”

“You asked for forty.”

“You really are a lawyer,” said Si-Yuan, and put the list down on the table and kept her hand flat on it.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Which one was hardest?” she said, after a while.

He didn’t answer straight away. He looked at his own handwriting upside down on the table: lines he’d been able to write much more easily than he could ever have said them, once.

“Eight.”

She knew without looking. You were never difficult to bring into my family. I was difficult to stand beside.

“Why?”

He pulled out the chair beside hers and sat. “Because I used to tell myself I was being reasonable. That I was managing things carefully. That I was protecting our future by not making it worse. And all the while I was asking you to put up with things I’d never have put up with myself.”

“I don’t want you to keep apologising for the same things.”

“I don’t want to.”

“Then don’t.”

“I won’t.”

She looked at him, searching his face for the old instinct to soften a hard thing until it was easier to hold. It wasn’t there. He reached for her hand instead.

“I can’t change what I didn’t say then. But I can make sure you never have to wonder now,” he said.

Her eyes had gone warm. “You’ve been doing that.”

“I know.”

“And you’re getting better at it.”

“Mm.”

“You’re very confident this morning.”

“I’m trying not to be modest about loving my wife.”

“Fiancée.”

“Future wife.”

“That’s better,” said Si-Yuan.

✦ ✦ ✦

She asked if she could keep it. He said he’d written it for her. She said she knew, but she wanted to keep it, and he said then keep it, and she folded it along its crease and put it in the drawer of the dining table, the one where they kept spare keys and receipts and the things neither of them could bring themselves to throw away. The programme from a premiere in Paris was in there already.

Then she came back and stood in front of him.

“There’s something missing.”

“From the list?”

“Forty things. Surely there are more.”

“There are.”

“Then tell me one. Now. Out loud.”

He thought about it. Then he reached up and tucked a loose piece of hair behind her ear.

“I’m happy you’re here.”

She smiled. “Forty-one.”

“No. That’s one I should say every morning,” he said.

“Then you have to.”

“I will.”

“When I’m away filming?”

“I’ll ring.”

“When you’re in court?”

“I’ll find a moment.”

“When we’re arguing?”

“Then most of all.”

She leaned down and kissed him. A small kiss, warm and ordinary, the kind that belonged to a Tuesday morning and not to an occasion. When she drew back he was smiling.

“What?”

“I like kissing you.”

She rolled her eyes. “Forty-two.”

He caught her hand before she could go. “I like that you still ask me to say things.”

The teasing went out of her face. She bent and rested her cheek against the top of his head and stayed there.

“I don’t need forty things every day. I just need the important ones. And I need to know they’ll still be true tomorrow,” she said into his hair.

“Then I’ll tell you tomorrow.”

Outside, the morning went on without any ceremony at all. A delivery van stopped in the road below. A neighbour’s door opened and shut. The coffee on the table was going cold.

He told her he loved her. Then, later, when she was looking for her keys, he told her again. By the time she reached the door he’d said it three times, and she turned round in the doorway with her bag on her shoulder, laughing at him.

“You’re going to run out.”

He was standing in the hall with one hand in his pocket and the pen in his other, absently, the silver clip catching the light, looking at her with all the time in the world.

“I don’t think so,” said Pengcheng.

He was right. There’d been forty things on the list. The life they were making would give him thousands more, and he said a great many of them, out loud, at the time, to her face; and the pen went back into his inside pocket, where it lived, for safekeeping.

chapters.title: Anniversary on Set
chapters.desc: Their first anniversary, in his old production office on the lot, now a store room. She takes his chair and makes him read clause fourteen first; then the door is locked. Explicit. Noodles at the gate afterwards.
chapters.content:
On the morning of their first wedding anniversary Si-Yuan told him to wear a suit and not to ask where they were going, and he did both, which she said afterwards was the most romantic thing he’d done all year.

She drove. That was unusual enough that he watched the road with interest for the first ten minutes and then, when he understood which road it was, stopped watching it and looked at her instead. She kept her eyes in front and her mouth straight, and gave herself away at the second set of lights by humming.

It was a Sunday in May, warm and grey. The studio lot was nearly empty. Her new film had been shooting on stage four since March, and she’d been coming through these gates every morning for ten weeks, past the security booth and the long blank walls of the soundstages, and he’d known that, and had somehow never connected it with anything. She waved at the guard, who waved back and looked at Pengcheng with frank curiosity, and she parked by the production buildings in the space marked for the lead, and turned the engine off.

“You’ve brought me to work,” he said.

“I’ve brought you to your work.”

“I haven’t worked here for years.”

“I know,” said Si-Yuan, and got out.

✦ ✦ ✦

Fong was waiting outside a long low prefab at the end of the row with a key on a cardboard tag in one hand and a coffee in the other. She’d been an assistant director with a headset and three phones when Si-Yuan was eighteen. She was the studio’s head of production now, with an office in the main building and one phone, and she looked exactly as tired as she always had.

She looked at the two of them for a moment. Then she held out the key.

“It’s been a store room for four years. Don’t touch the boxes. I told her once you were thorough. That she’d be glad of it,” said Fong, looking at Pengcheng over her coffee.

“She told me.”

“Was I right?”

“I hope so.”

“She married you, so I’ll take that as a yes,” said Fong, and she went off across the car park without looking back, and Si-Yuan laughed and unlocked the door.

It was smaller than either of them remembered. Somebody had stacked archive boxes three deep along one wall, labelled in marker pen with the names of productions that had wrapped years ago. But the desk was still there, the same cheap grey desk, pushed back under the window. The same two chairs. The same window onto the car park, with the same view of a row of bins and a strip of sky. And the strip light overhead, when she flicked the switch, came on with the same faint stuttering tick.

He stood in the doorway and didn’t come in.

“It still ticks,” he said.

“It’s been ticking for seven years. Nobody ever fixed it.”

“It ticked the whole time you were reading.”

She put her bag on the desk. “I know. I counted. I got to four hundred and something and you said page seventeen again. Sit down.”

He went to the chair behind the desk, by habit.

“Not that one.”

He stopped. She came round the desk and sat down in his chair, the lawyer’s chair, with the window behind her, and folded her hands on the grey top, and looked at him across it with no expression on her face whatsoever. It was a good imitation. He recognised it at once and had to look away.

He sat down in the other chair. Her chair. It was low and hard and not quite steady on its legs, and it put him slightly below her eye line, and he understood for the first time in seven years that it always had.

She took a folded document out of her bag and opened it on the desk between them and turned it round to face him. The paper had gone soft and yellowish at the edges. It had been in a drawer with her passport and thirteen other pages for a long time.

“Page seventeen,” said Si-Yuan.

He looked at her. She looked back. Not a muscle moved.

“Aloud, Mr. Yang.”

He picked it up. He found the page. He read clause fourteen to her in the voice he’d used for it once, in this room, to a girl with her chin on her hand, every word of it, every badly drafted line, in the reasonable opinion of the producer, public disrepute, associated commercial partners, all of it, while the strip light ticked overhead.

When he’d finished she let a moment go by.

“Do you understand it?”

“Yes.”

“Explain it to me.”

He put it down. “It’s far too broad. It gives the producer an unlimited discretion over the talent’s private life and dresses it up as a reputational interest. It ought to require material harm. It ought to give notice and a right of reply. It ought never to have been put in front of an eighteen-year-old without someone crossing half of it out.”

“Would you sign it?”

“No.”

“Would you let me sign it?”

He opened his mouth, and closed it, and started again. “I’d advise you strongly against it in its present form. The decision would be yours.”

She tilted her head, considering him. “Better.”

“Are you going to grade me?”

“Eight out of ten.”

“Why eight?”

“You forgot to say it’s written in a way that makes nobody want to read it.”

“That isn’t a legal defect.”

“It’s a human one,” said Si-Yuan, and then she couldn’t hold the face any longer, and it broke all at once into a grin, and he laughed out loud in the little prefab with the archive boxes and the bins outside, and she came round the desk.

✦ ✦ ✦

“I’ve got another question.”

“Go on.”

She leaned against the front of the desk, between his knees, so that he had to tip his head back to look at her. “Do you have a girlfriend, Mr. Yang?”

“That isn’t relevant to the contract.”

“Answer the question.”

“No. I have a wife,” he said.

She looked down at him. Then she put her hand on his tie, lightly, the way she had once in his office at chambers after thirteen pages, and drew him up out of the low chair by it, and kissed him.

He’d thought of this room more often than he’d ever have admitted. Not like this. Never once like this; not when she was eighteen, not for months after, not until a noodle stall and a borrowed pair of slippers and a girl leaning over to kiss him first in his car. He’d been careful. He’d been so careful that she’d teased him for it for a year. But he’d thought about the girl across this desk, and the way she’d looked at him over the top of page seventeen, and he’d put her pen in his pocket and told her it was safekeeping, and he’d known even then, somewhere he didn’t look, that it was a lie.

She drew back. “Lock the door.”

He went and locked it. The key was stiff. The click was loud in the little room. When he turned round she was sitting on the desk with her shoes off and the contract pushed to one side, unfastening her earrings, and she put them down one at a time on clause fourteen.

“Somebody might come,” he said.

Si-Yuan held out her hand. “Fong’s guarding it. She told me she would. She said it was the least she could do, after the noodles. Stop being production counsel.”

“I stopped about four minutes ago.”

“Then come and prove it.”

He came. She kissed him as he reached her, sitting on the edge of the grey desk with her knees either side of him, and pulled his tie loose and dropped it on the floor among the archive boxes, and began on his shirt. He let her. He’d learned to let her; it was one of the things he’d had to learn. When she got to the last button she spread her hands flat on his chest and looked at him.

“Say something.”

“I’ve wanted to kiss you in this room for seven years.”

“Since when exactly?”

“Since you asked whether I was always this boring.”

“That was in the first ten minutes.”

“I’m aware,” said Pengcheng, and she laughed into his mouth.

He undid the zip at the back of her dress slowly, and told her he was doing it, because she liked that now, though it had made her laugh until she cried the first time. He kissed her shoulder where the strap came down, and the side of her neck, and the place below her ear that made her breath catch. He told her she was beautiful, without reasons, the way she’d once asked him to. She pushed his shirt off his shoulders and it went the way of the tie.

When he laid her back on the desk the old contract slid off the far end and onto the floor, and neither of them went after it.

He took his time. He’d always taken his time with her, but there’d been years when he’d done it in silence, and now he didn’t. He told her what he loved as he found it: the shape of her ribs under his hands, the sound she made when he put his mouth to her breast, the way her hand went into his hair and held on. He told her he’d missed her all week, though they’d slept beside each other every night of it, because she’d been on set before dawn and back after dark and he’d only seen her asleep. She said I know, I know and pulled at his belt with her bare foot until he laughed and helped.

She wanted him then, plainly, and said so, and he went into her standing at the edge of the grey desk with her legs locked round him and her arms round his neck and the strip light ticking over both of them. She said his name. Then she said it again, differently. He held her hips and moved slowly, and watched her face, which was the thing he’d never once let himself do in this room, and she watched his, and neither of them looked away.

It went on a long time. The desk creaked under them, steadily, and once a stack of archive boxes shifted against the wall and they both froze and then both laughed, helplessly, with their heads together, and went on. He told her he loved her. She told him to say it again. He did, and again, and the last time he couldn’t finish it, because she’d tightened round him and arched up off the desk with her mouth open and his name in it, and that took the end of the sentence and everything after it out of his head.

Afterwards they stayed there, tangled on the grey desk, breathing, with her face in his neck. The strip light ticked. Somewhere outside a car door slammed and an engine started and went away across the lot.

“Four hundred and twelve,” said Si-Yuan, into his skin.

“What?”

“Ticks. The first time. I just remembered the number.”

He started laughing and couldn’t stop, and she lay against his chest and let him, and after a while she started too.

✦ ✦ ✦

They dressed slowly. She did up his shirt for him, because he was doing the buttons wrong, one off all the way down, and told him he was a disgrace to his profession. He found her earrings on clause fourteen and put them in her palm. She fastened them by the dark reflection in the window. His tie had gone behind a box marked with the name of a film she’d made at nineteen, and he went and got it, and looked at the box, and didn’t say anything.

She picked the contract up off the floor and smoothed it on the desk.

“Have you got my pen?”

He put his hand to his inside pocket out of habit, and then stopped, and looked at her.

“You knew I would.”

“You always have it. You think I don’t notice.”

He took it out. A black fountain pen with a silver clip, a little worn now along the barrel, three initials engraved on its side. He held it out to her across the desk. For a moment she looked at it, and he thought she’d take it, and found that he’d braced himself, slightly, the way he had at the door of this room once when a girl came back and said Mr. Yang? My pen.

She closed his fingers back round it with her own.

“Keep it. You’re doing all right with it,” she said.

“Safekeeping.”

“Safekeeping,” said Si-Yuan, and he put it back where it lived.

✦ ✦ ✦

She left the contract on the desk. He asked if she wanted it, and she said it had lived in a drawer for seven years and could spend one night where it had started. Then she turned off the light, which stopped ticking, and they went out, and locked the door, and she put the key under the mat for Fong.

The noodle stall was still there by the gate, under a new awning that was already fading. The owner was greyer and slower and had a grandson behind the counter with him now, and he looked up when they came through the gate together in their good clothes, she with her hair coming down and he with his tie in his pocket, and he looked at them.

“Back again,” he said.

“Back again,” said Si-Yuan.

He brought two bowls of beef noodles without being asked, a little spicy, with extra greens in hers. He brought a second glass of water for Pengcheng. And after they’d eaten, he came out from behind the counter and put a saucer of orange slices down between them and stood there with his arms folded.

“One year?” he said.

Si-Yuan stared at him. “How did you know?”

The old man shrugged. “Somebody asked me what you liked,” he said, and nodded at the lawyer across the table, and went back behind his counter, and turned up the television.

She looked at Pengcheng. Pengcheng looked hard at the oranges.

“You came here. This week. Without me,” she said slowly.

“On Thursday. To ask whether he’d still be here on Sunday.”

“And you didn’t say anything.”

He picked up a slice of orange and held it out to her. “You’d told me not to ask where we were going. I assumed it might be here eventually. You always end up here. I wanted him to know.”

She took the orange. She sat and looked at him across the plastic table under the faded awning, in the grey warm evening, with the studio lights coming on behind the gate, and couldn’t think of a single thing to say, which almost never happened to her.

So she leaned across the table and kissed him instead, in front of the owner and his grandson and a taxi driver at the next table who’d seen everything there was to see at that stall in thirty years, and the taxi driver went on eating, and the owner turned the television up again, and nobody said anything about it at all.
